questions.prompt: Meeting at a New Hampshire resort hotel in July 1944, 44 Allied nations pegged global currencies to a gold-backed U.S. dollar and founded both the IMF and the World Bank.
clues: John Maynard Keynes championed an international 'bancor' unit, but U.S. negotiator Harry Dexter White's dollar model won.
Its fixed exchange system governed global trade until Richard Nixon ended gold convertibility in 1971.
questions.whyExplanation: The 1944 Bretton Woods system stabilized postwar international finance and created the institutional architecture of the modern global economy.

questions.prompt: Signed inside a former French-designed railway car in a forest clearing in March 1918—forcing Bolshevik Russia to surrender a third of its European population—this pact pulled Russia out of World War I.
clues: Leon Trotsky briefly stalled talks with his paradoxical formula 'neither war nor peace' before German armies resumed advancing.
Germany's collapse eight months later annulled its massive eastern territorial gains.
questions.whyExplanation: Lenin accepted the punishing Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in March 1918 to preserve the fragile Bolshevik regime during Russia's civil war.

questions.prompt: Triggered when British officers ordered sepoys to bite paper rifle cartridges rumored to be greased with beef and pork fat, this 1857 uprising ended East India Company rule.
clues: Rebels rallied around aging Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah II in Delhi and Queen Lakshmibai of Jhansi.
In its aftermath, Parliament transferred governance directly to Queen Victoria's British Raj.
questions.whyExplanation: The 1857 uprising across northern India abolished both the Mughal court and the East India Company, inaugurating direct British Crown rule.

questions.prompt: Transforming Japan from feudal samurai domains into a railway-building industrial power within a single generation after 1868, this political upheaval restored imperial rule in name.
clues: Its Five Charter Oath pledged to seek knowledge throughout the world while abolishing hereditary stipends.
Its era name translates as 'Enlightened Rule' under young Emperor Mutsuhito.
questions.whyExplanation: Starting in 1868, the Meiji Restoration dismantled the Tokugawa shogunate, drafted a modern constitution, and made Japan Asia's first industrialized power.

questions.prompt: Nailing—or circulating—95 Latin theses challenging papal indulgences at Wittenberg in October 1517, Augustinian monk Martin Luther unintentionally ignited this continent-splitting movement.
clues: Johannes Gutenberg's movable-type presses spread Luther's German pamphlets across Europe in weeks.
Within decades, Calvinist, Anglican, and Anabaptist churches reshaped Western Christianity.
questions.whyExplanation: Luther's 1517 challenge to indulgence sales shattered Western Christendom's unity and reshaped European literacy, politics, and law.

questions.prompt: On July 14, 1789, Parisian crowds stormed a medieval royal fortress hunting for gunpowder—freeing just seven stunned prisoners inside while shattering absolute monarchy's mystique.
clues: Marquis de Lafayette later mailed the fortress's iron front key to George Washington at Mount Vernon.
France still celebrates the anniversary each July as its premier national holiday.
questions.whyExplanation: Although the Bastille held only seven inmates, its fall on July 14, 1789 symbolized the collapse of royal tyranny and launched the French Revolution.

questions.prompt: Beginning at a Gdansk shipyard when electrician Lech Walesa scaled the wall to lead striking dockworkers in August 1980, this independent Polish union became the first cracks in the Soviet bloc.
clues: Banned under General Jaruzelski's 1981 martial law, it survived underground with moral support from Pope John Paul II.
Its sweeping 1989 parliamentary victory paved the way for peaceful democratic transitions across Eastern Europe.
questions.whyExplanation: Solidarnosc grew to ten million Polish members in 1980-1981 and ultimately toppled communist rule in Poland through the 1989 Roundtable talks.

questions.prompt: Jangling keys in Prague's Wenceslas Square to signal 'time is up,' Czech and Slovak demonstrators toppled four decades of communist rule in six bloodless weeks in late 1989.
clues: Dissident playwright Vaclav Havel went straight from prison earlier that year to president in December 1989.
Its smooth textile nickname celebrated the total absence of gunfire or casualties.
questions.whyExplanation: Mass civic strikes and student marches in November-December 1989 peacefully ended one-party rule in Czechoslovakia.

questions.prompt: Triggered by a garbled live press-conference answer from official Gunter Schabowski on November 9, 1989, ecstatic crowds climbed atop concrete slabs dividing a city for 28 years.
clues: Asked when new East German travel visas took effect, Schabowski shuffled his notes and mumbled 'immediately, without delay.'
Cellist Mstislav Rostropovich soon flew in to play Bach suites beside Checkpoint Charlie.
questions.whyExplanation: Schabowski's unscripted remark sent tens of thousands of East Berliners to border crossings on November 9, 1989, opening the Berlin Wall overnight.

questions.prompt: In 1893, after Kate Sheppard presented a glued-together petition over 270 meters long bearing nearly 32,000 signatures, this Pacific nation became the first self-governing country to grant women the vote.
clues: Governor Lord Glasgow signed the Electoral Act on September 19, 1893, ten weeks before that year's general election.
Kate Sheppard's portrait now graces the country's ten-dollar banknote.
questions.whyExplanation: Led by Kate Sheppard's Women's Christian Temperance Union campaign, New Zealand granted all adult women—including Maori women—the vote in 1893.

questions.prompt: Starting in Paris in February 1848 and sweeping Vienna, Berlin, Budapest, and Milan within weeks, this continent-wide wave of liberal revolts earned a floral seasonal nickname.
clues: Although royal armies crushed nearly every barricade by 1849, serfdom vanished permanently across Habsburg lands.
Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published The Communist Manifesto in London just days before barricades rose.
questions.whyExplanation: The Revolutions of 1848—the Springtime of Nations—formed Europe's most widespread revolutionary wave, accelerating constitutionalism and national unification.

questions.prompt: On April 25, 1974, Portuguese soldiers slipped red flowers gifted by a Lisbon waitress into their rifle barrels, toppling Europe's longest-running right-wing dictatorship almost without bloodshed.
clues: Radio stations broadcast Portugal's Eurovision ballad and the banned folk song 'Grandola, Vila Morena' as secret go-signals.
Ending the Estado Novo regime also led swiftly to independence for Angola, Mozambique, and Guinea-Bissau.
questions.whyExplanation: Portugal's Armed Forces Movement overthrew Marcello Caetano on April 25, 1974, beginning Europe's 'third wave' of democratization.

questions.prompt: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz shocked planetary theorists in 1995—and later shared a 2019 Nobel—by spotting this Jupiter-sized world hugging its sun-like star in a blistering 4.2-day orbit.
clues: Its impossible proximity to its host star birthed the "hot Jupiter" class and earned the IAU name Dimidium.
Named for the winged-horse constellation Pegasus, it was the first exoplanet confirmed around a Sun-like star.
questions.whyExplanation: 51 Pegasi b (Dimidium) was discovered via radial velocity in 1995, upending formation models that assumed gas giants could only orbit far from their stars.

questions.prompt: Belgian astronomers tipped their hats to monastic brews when naming the telescope—and this ultracool dwarf 40 light-years away in Aquarius—that hosts seven tightly packed Earth-sized worlds.
clues: All seven of its rocky planets fit comfortably inside the distance between Mercury and our Sun.
Announced in February 2017, three of its seven worlds—e, f, and g—lie squarely inside its habitable zone.
questions.whyExplanation: TRAPPIST-1 takes its name from Belgium's TRAnsiting Planets and PlanetesImals Small Telescope (a playful nod to Trappist beer) and holds seven terrestrial planets.

questions.prompt: Even at the speed of light, a postcard from this rocky world announced in August 2016 would take 4.24 years to reach Earth, making it the closest known planet beyond our solar system.
clues: It orbits a flare-prone red dwarf every 11.2 days and sits inside the star's temperate zone.
Its host is the dimmest member of the triple star system nearest our Sun.
questions.whyExplanation: Proxima Centauri b orbits the red dwarf Proxima Centauri 4.24 light-years away, making it the nearest confirmed exoplanet to Earth.

questions.prompt: NASA hailed it as "Earth's cousin" in April 2014 when this Cygnus red-dwarf orbiter became the first validated Earth-sized planet found inside another star's habitable zone.
clues: Orbiting as the outermost of five known planets in its system, it receives about one-third the sunlight Earth gets.
Named after NASA's famed planet-hunting telescope, its catalog number falls between 180 and 190.
questions.whyExplanation: Validated in 2014, Kepler-186f proved that Earth-sized rocky worlds exist in the temperate habitable zones of other stars.

questions.prompt: Three years before any planet was found around a Sun-like star, Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail detected the first confirmed exoplanets in 1992 circling this dead millisecond pulsar.
clues: The IAU later nicknamed this Virgo neutron star Lich and its three eerie planets Draugr, Poltergeist, and Phobetor.
Detected via tiny glitches in radio pulse timing at Arecibo, its catalog name starts with PSR B12.
questions.whyExplanation: In 1992, radio timing anomalies around millisecond pulsar PSR B1257+12 yielded the first confirmed exoplanets ever discovered.

questions.prompt: Unofficially dubbed Osiris as its boiling hydrogen tail streamed into space, this Pegasus gas giant became the first exoplanet caught transiting its star in 1999 and the first with a measured atmosphere.
clues: Hubble detected sodium in its skies in 2001, opening the field of exoplanet atmospheric spectroscopy.
Its Henry Draper catalog number is 209458, followed by the standard first-planet letter.
questions.whyExplanation: HD 209458 b was the first transiting exoplanet observed (1999) and the first whose atmosphere was spectroscopically detected (2001).

questions.prompt: Racing around its host star in just 18 hours, this scorching super-Earth nicknamed Janssen sparked a 2012 media frenzy when researchers proposed its carbon-rich interior might be packed with diamond.
clues: It sits in the Crab constellation and was later probed by JWST for signs of a volatile-rich magma-ocean atmosphere.
Its designation pairs the number 55 with the Latin genitive of Cancer, plus the letter e.
questions.whyExplanation: 55 Cancri e (Janssen) is an ultra-short-period super-Earth (~18-hour orbit) famously hypothesized in 2012 to possess a carbon- and diamond-rich mantle.

questions.prompt: Tidal gravity is literally stretching this Auriga ultra-hot Jupiter into an egg while stripping its mass, yet it traps 94 percent of incoming starlight—making it blacker than fresh asphalt.
clues: Completing an orbit in barely 26 hours, it is spiraling slowly toward total destruction by its host star.
Discovered in 2008 by the Wide Angle Search for Planets, its designation pairs WASP with the number 12.
questions.whyExplanation: WASP-12b orbits so close to its star that tidal forces deform it into an egg shape while its superheated atmosphere absorbs almost all visible light.

questions.prompt: Double sunsets stepped out of Star Wars and into astrophysics in 2011 when astronomers confirmed this Saturn-sized world as the first unambiguous circumbinary planet orbiting two stars.
clues: Reporters promptly nicknamed it Tatooine, though at roughly minus 100 degrees Celsius it is far chillier than Luke Skywalker's home.
It carries a two-digit number in the teens from NASA's primary transit-hunting space telescope.
questions.whyExplanation: Kepler-16b was the first confirmed circumbinary planet seen transiting a pair of eclipsing stars, earning the inevitable nickname Tatooine.

questions.prompt: Do not let its serene cobalt-blue tint fool you: Hubble's 2013 color measurement of this Vulpecula gas giant hinted at 5,400 mph winds whipping razor-sharp silicate glass sideways like rain.
clues: Located just 64.5 light-years away, it is one of the closest transiting hot Jupiters to Earth.
Its Henry Draper catalog number begins with 1897 and ends with 33 b.
questions.whyExplanation: HD 189733 b became the first exoplanet with a measured visible-light color (deep azure blue), likely caused by high-altitude silicate particles.

questions.prompt: Using Keck and Gemini adaptive optics in 2008, Christian Marois's team bypassed indirect wobbles to capture the first direct multi-planet portrait around this young star in Pegasus.
clues: A fourth giant planet joined its three siblings in 2010, and time-lapse footage now shows all four orbiting live.
Its Bright Star Catalog designation starts with HR followed by a four-digit number ending in 99.
questions.whyExplanation: HR 8799 hosts four massive young planets (b, c, d, and e) that yielded the landmark first direct imaging of a multi-planet extrasolar system in 2008.

questions.prompt: In January 2020, NASA's TESS planet hunter scored a milestone by unveiling this Dorado red-dwarf orbiter—its very first Earth-sized discovery sitting inside a star's habitable zone.
clues: Spitzer confirmed it 101 light-years away after high-school-aged citizen scientists helped refine its star's temperature.
Its name stands for TESS Object of Interest followed by 700 and the fourth lowercase letter.
questions.whyExplanation: TOI-700 d was confirmed in January 2020 as the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite's first Earth-sized habitable-zone exoplanet.

questions.prompt: Stargazers braced for a daytime supernova during the 2019–2020 "Great Dimming" of Orion's crimson shoulder, only for astronomers to blame a colossal dust cloud belched by this red supergiant.
clues: Placed at the center of our solar system, its bloated photosphere would engulf Earth and approach Jupiter's orbit.
Its Arabic-derived name is famously echoed in a 1988 Tim Burton ghost comedy.
questions.whyExplanation: Betelgeuse (Alpha Orionis) dimmed by over 60 percent in late 2019–early 2020 because a massive surface ejection condensed into light-blocking dust.

questions.prompt: Before Alvan Graham Clark ever spotted its dense white-dwarf "Pup" in 1862, Friedrich Bessel deduced that Earth's brightest night-sky star was wobbling from an unseen partner.
clues: Its heliacal rising before dawn heralded the annual flooding of the Nile and gave us the "dog days" of summer.
It is the blazing Alpha star of the constellation Canis Major.
questions.whyExplanation: Sirius (the Dog Star) is a binary system whose white-dwarf companion, Sirius B, was inferred gravitationally by Bessel in 1844 and seen in 1862.

questions.prompt: By spotting Cepheid variable stars inside this fuzzy patch in 1924, Edwin Hubble settled the Great Debate and proved the Milky Way was not the entire universe.
clues: Cataloged as Messier 31, it is the farthest object easily visible to the unaided human eye at 2.5 million light-years.
Named for a chained princess of Greek myth, it is on a 4.5-billion-year collision course with our Milky Way.
questions.whyExplanation: Hubble's Cepheid distance measurement to M31, the Andromeda Galaxy, demonstrated that spiral nebulae were independent island universes far beyond our galaxy.

questions.prompt: Charles Messier kicked off his famous catalog of comet false alarms in 1758 with this Taurus cloud—the expanding wreckage of a 1054 CE "guest star" logged by Song dynasty skywatchers.
clues: At its heart spins a city-sized pulsar rotating 30 times every second.
Designated M1, it takes its crustacean name from an 1844 sketch by Lord Rosse.
questions.whyExplanation: The Crab Nebula (M1) is the supernova remnant of SN 1054, documented by Chinese astronomers and later listed first in Charles Messier's catalog.

questions.prompt: Earth's 26,000-year axial wobble means it only holds its navigational title temporarily—and what looks like a single steady beacon at Ursa Minor's tail tip is actually a pulsing triple star.
clues: Its primary component is the closest Cepheid variable star to Earth.
Sitting less than one degree from the north celestial pole, it is better known as the North Star.
questions.whyExplanation: Polaris (Alpha Ursae Minoris) is a triple star system dominated by a Cepheid variable that serves as our current North Star due to axial precession.

questions.prompt: Jeff Hester and Paul Scowen used Hubble in 1995 to immortalize these towering trunks of star-birthing gas inside the Eagle Nebula—even though a nearby supernova shockwave may have already toppled them.
clues: The tallest of these three interstellar columns stretches roughly four to five light-years from base to tip.
Both Hubble (in 2014) and JWST (in 2022) revisited this iconic M16 landmark.
questions.whyExplanation: Photographed by Hubble in 1995 inside Messier 16 (the Eagle Nebula), the Pillars of Creation remain one of astronomy's most famous images.

questions.prompt: Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez won the 2020 Physics Nobel for tracking stars whipped around this 4-million-solar-mass gravitational anchor—before the Event Horizon Telescope snapped its glowing ring in 2022.
clues: Its radio-source label ends in an asterisk chosen by co-discoverer Robert Brown to signify an "exciting" find.
Located 26,000 light-years away, it is the supermassive black hole at the heart of the Milky Way.
questions.whyExplanation: Sagittarius A* is the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole, confirmed via stellar orbits and directly imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope in May 2022.

questions.prompt: Johann Bayer gave Orion's foot only the Beta designation in 1603—likely ranking the Hunter north to south—even though this blazing blue-white supergiant usually outshines Alpha Orionis.
clues: Its Arabic name literally translates to "foot," marking the bottom-right corner of Orion's hourglass.
Roughly 860 light-years away, it pours out tens of thousands of times more energy than the Sun.
questions.whyExplanation: Rigel (Beta Orionis) is a luminous blue supergiant that is generally brighter than Betelgeuse despite carrying the second Greek letter in Bayer's catalog.

questions.prompt: Before serving as the zero-point benchmark for stellar brightness, this rapid spinner in Lyra became the first star beyond our Sun ever photographed—on an 1850 Harvard daguerreotype.
clues: Spinning so fast it bulges at the equator, it forms the brightest vertex of the Summer Triangle.
Earth's wobbling axis will return this star to the role of North Star around the year 13727.
questions.whyExplanation: Vega (Alpha Lyrae) was photographed by William Bond and John Whipple in 1850, anchored the magnitude-zero brightness scale, and will be a future pole star.

questions.prompt: In April 2019, a planet-sized array of radio dishes turned this giant Virgo elliptical galaxy into front-page news by revealing the fiery donut shadow of its 6.5-billion-solar-mass black hole.
clues: Also known as Virgo A, it fires a relativistic jet of plasma stretching roughly 5,000 light-years into space.
Its catalog number sits in the high eighties of Charles Messier's classic deep-sky list.
questions.whyExplanation: Messier 87 hosts M87*, whose event-horizon shadow became the first black hole ever directly imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope in April 2019.

questions.prompt: During its 1840s "Great Eruption," this unstable southern binary briefly outshone every night-sky star except Sirius and wrapped itself in the twin-lobed Homunculus Nebula.
clues: Hiding 7,500 light-years away in the Keel constellation, its larger star packs around 100 solar masses.
Its Bayer designation combines the seventh Greek letter with the Latin genitive of Carina.
questions.whyExplanation: Eta Carinae survived a massive 1843 outburst that expelled the bipolar Homunculus Nebula and made it temporarily the second-brightest star in the sky.

questions.prompt: Despite spanning just 68 square degrees—making it the tiniest of all 88 official constellations—this southern asterism earns prime billing on the national flags of Australia, Brazil, and New Zealand.
clues: Its kite-shaped quartet of bright stars points mariners toward the south celestial pole.
Known in English as the Southern Cross, its four-letter Latin name also means "cross."
questions.whyExplanation: Crux (the Southern Cross) is the smallest of the 88 IAU constellations by angular area yet serves as an iconic southern hemisphere emblem.

questions.prompt: Christiaan Huygens discovered it in 1655, and 350 years later his namesake lander parachuted through its thick orange nitrogen smog onto pebbles of water ice washed by liquid methane.
clues: It is the only moon in the solar system known to possess a dense atmosphere and stable surface lakes.
Larger than the planet Mercury, it is Saturn's biggest natural satellite.
questions.whyExplanation: Saturn's largest moon, Titan, was found by Huygens in 1655 and explored in 2005 by ESA's Huygens lander, revealing a methane-driven weather cycle.

questions.prompt: Crisscrossed by reddish cracks instead of ancient craters, this smooth Galilean world hides a global salty ocean beneath its ice shell—twice the liquid water of all Earth's seas combined.
clues: NASA launched the Clipper spacecraft in October 2024 specifically to make nearly 50 close flybys of its icy crust.
Named for a Phoenician princess carried off by Zeus, it is the smallest of Jupiter's four Galilean moons.
questions.whyExplanation: Jupiter's icy moon Europa conceals a tidally warmed subsurface saltwater ocean, making it a top astrobiology target for NASA's Europa Clipper mission.

questions.prompt: Stitched into the Bayeux Tapestry as an omen over King Harold in 1066, this icy wanderer earned its modern name after an English astronomer used Newton's laws in 1705 to forecast its 1758 return.
clues: Mark Twain famously arrived with it in 1835 and predicted he would "go out with it" in 1910—and did.
Returning roughly every 75 to 76 years, it is next due at perihelion in 2061.
questions.whyExplanation: Edmond Halley realized sightings from 1531, 1607, and 1682 were one periodic comet; its 1066 apparition also appears on the Bayeux Tapestry.

questions.prompt: In March 1979, navigation engineer Linda Morabito enhanced a routine Voyager 1 frame to spot faint background stars—and accidentally caught a 300-kilometer volcanic plume erupting off this moon.
clues: A gravitational tug-of-war with Jupiter and sibling moons flexes its interior into over 400 active volcanoes.
Dotted with yellow-orange sulfur flows like a pizza, it is the innermost Galilean moon with a two-letter name.
questions.whyExplanation: Tidal heating from its orbital resonance makes Io—Jupiter's innermost Galilean moon—the most volcanically active body in the solar system.

questions.prompt: Giuseppe Piazzi rang in the 19th century on January 1, 1801 by spotting this body—first hailed as a missing planet, then demoted to an asteroid, and since 2006 the inner solar system's lone dwarf planet.
clues: NASA's Dawn spacecraft revealed bright sodium-carbonate salt spots gleaming inside its Occator Crater in 2015.
Accounting for roughly a third of the main asteroid belt's mass, it is named for the Roman goddess of agriculture.
questions.whyExplanation: Discovered in 1801 by Piazzi, Ceres has been classified as a planet, an asteroid, and finally a dwarf planet—the only one inside Neptune's orbit.

questions.prompt: Barely 500 kilometers wide, this gleaming white moon of Saturn vents towering geysers of salty water and organic molecules from south-polar "tiger stripes"—literally building Saturn's E ring.
clues: Reflecting nearly 100 percent of sunlight, it is the most reflective body in our solar system.
Cassini flew directly through its icy plumes in 2008 and later detected molecular hydrogen, hinting at hydrothermal vents.
questions.whyExplanation: Saturn's small icy moon Enceladus shoots cryovolcanic plumes from fractures at its south pole, feeding the E ring and signaling a habitable subsurface sea.

questions.prompt: Spotted by William Lassell just 17 days after Neptune itself in 1846, this nitrogen-geyser world is the only large moon in the solar system orbiting backward—a smoking gun of Kuiper Belt capture.
clues: Voyager 2 photographed its wrinkled "cantaloupe terrain" in 1989 and measured surface temperatures near minus 235 Celsius.
Named for Poseidon's sea-god son, its retrograde orbit means tidal drag will eventually shred it into rings.
questions.whyExplanation: Neptune's largest moon, Triton, moves in a retrograde orbit opposite Neptune's rotation, strongly implying it was captured from the Kuiper Belt.

questions.prompt: Shredded by Jupiter's Roche limit into a luminous "string of pearls" of 21 fragments, this doomed wanderer bruised the gas giant with Earth-sized dark scars over six dramatic days in July 1994.
clues: It provided astronomers with their first direct ringside view of an extraterrestrial planetary collision.
Named for a married planetary-geology duo and a Canadian amateur astronomer, it was their ninth periodic find together.
questions.whyExplanation: Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 broke apart around Jupiter and slammed into its southern hemisphere in July 1994, leaving dark impact scars visible from Earth.

questions.prompt: Wider than the planet Mercury, this Jovian giant baffled planetary scientists in 1996 when NASA's Galileo probe revealed it is the only moon known to generate its own intrinsic magnetic field.
clues: Because of its liquid iron-rich core, Hubble has observed shimmering oxygen auroras dancing around its poles.
Named for Zeus's mythological cupbearer, it is the largest moon anywhere in the solar system.
questions.whyExplanation: Ganymede is the solar system's largest moon (5,268 km across) and the sole satellite known to produce an internal magnetosphere.

questions.prompt: Spotted by Hawaii's Pan-STARRS1 telescope in October 2017 after whipping past the Sun, this tumbling, reddish visitor—whose Hawaiian name means "scout"—became our first confirmed interstellar object.
clues: Showing no visible comet tail yet accelerating slightly away from the Sun, it triggered lively debates over nitrogen icebergs and light sails.
Cataloged officially as 1I/2017 U1, its musical nine-letter name begins and ends with a vowel.
questions.whyExplanation: 1I/2017 U1, named Oumuamua ("messenger from afar arriving first"), was the first interstellar object ever detected traversing our solar system.

questions.prompt: When NASA's OSIRIS-REx touched down on this spinning-top near-Earth asteroid in October 2020, its surface behaved so much like a plastic ball pit that the spacecraft nearly sank before snatching 121 grams.
clues: Its pristine carbonaceous dust landed in the Utah desert in September 2023, revealing organic building blocks of life.
Named by a nine-year-old boy after an Egyptian heron deity, this diamond-shaped rubble pile has a five-letter name.
questions.whyExplanation: OSIRIS-REx sampled asteroid 101955 Bennu in 2020 and returned 121.6 grams of carbon-rich material to Earth in 2023—revealing a loosely bound rubble pile.

questions.prompt: Named for an Egyptian serpent of chaos—with a wink to the TV series Stargate SG-1—this 340-meter asteroid will skim closer than geosynchronous satellites on Friday, April 13, 2029.
clues: Early 2004 calculations briefly gave it a scary 2.7 percent impact chance before radar ruled out any collision for at least a century.
Cataloged as asteroid 99942, it will be greeted during its 2029 Earth flyby by the repurposed OSIRIS-APEX spacecraft.
questions.whyExplanation: Asteroid 99942 Apophis will safely pass about 32,000 kilometers from Earth on April 13, 2029, bright enough to see with the naked eye from the Eastern Hemisphere.

questions.prompt: Despite launching 16 days after its twin in 1977, its faster trajectory let it turn around in 1990 at Carl Sagan's urging for the "Pale Blue Dot" portrait—and enter interstellar space in 2012.
clues: It carries a gold-plated copper phonograph record greeting aliens with Bach, Chuck Berry, and whale songs.
Now over 24 billion kilometers away, it is the farthest human-made object from Earth.
questions.whyExplanation: Voyager 1 took the iconic Pale Blue Dot photo from 6 billion km away in 1990 and crossed the heliopause into interstellar space in August 2012.

questions.prompt: With 1202 computer overload alarms blaring and barely 25 seconds of hover fuel remaining, lunar module Eagle skipped over a boulder field in July 1969 to seal this historic touchdown.
clues: Michael Collins kept command module Columbia orbiting solo overhead while his two crewmates walked the Sea of Tranquility.
Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin spent just over 21 hours on the lunar surface during this mission.
questions.whyExplanation: Apollo 11 achieved the first crewed lunar landing on July 20, 1969, after Margaret Hamilton's priority-scheduling software gracefully handled 1202 overload alarms.

questions.prompt: Barely the size of a beach ball and carrying no cameras or scientific instruments, this polished 83.6-kilogram sphere stunned the world on October 4, 1957 simply by beeping from orbit.
clues: Its four trailing whip antennas broadcast radio pulses for 21 days until its silver-zinc batteries ran dry.
Launched atop a Soviet R-7 rocket, its Russian name translates to "fellow traveler."
questions.whyExplanation: The Soviet Union's Sputnik 1 became Earth's first artificial satellite in October 1957, sparking the Space Race with its unmistakable shortwave radio beeps.

questions.prompt: Carrying an ounce of Clyde Tombaugh's ashes at 58,000 kilometers per hour, this piano-sized probe zipped past Pluto in July 2015 to reveal a vast nitrogen-ice glacier shaped like a heart.
clues: After flying past Pluto and Charon, it sailed on to visit the snowman-shaped Kuiper Belt object Arrokoth on New Year's Day 2019.
Launched in January 2006—seven months before Pluto's reclassification—its two-word name promises fresh vistas.
questions.whyExplanation: NASA's New Horizons made the first reconnaissance of Pluto in 2015, discovering the heart-shaped Tombaugh Regio before flying past Arrokoth in 2019.

questions.prompt: To guarantee its plutonium-powered hull would never crash-contaminate Enceladus or Titan, mission controllers steered this 20-year Saturn explorer into a fiery 2017 "Grand Finale" plunge.
clues: Its joint NASA-ESA-ASI name pairs a 17th-century Italian-French observer of Saturn's ring gap with a Dutch discoverer of Titan.
Before vaporizing in Saturn's skies, it threaded the razor-thin gap between the planet and its innermost rings 22 times.
questions.whyExplanation: Cassini-Huygens orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017, deploying the Huygens Titan lander and ending with a deliberate atmospheric burn-up for planetary protection.

questions.prompt: Folded like origami inside an Ariane 5 fairing on Christmas Day 2021, this observatory unfolded a tennis-court-sized five-layer sunshield and 18 gold-plated beryllium mirror hexagons at Sun-Earth L2.
clues: Designed primarily for infrared light, it keeps its detectors chilled to near minus 233 degrees Celsius.
Named for NASA's Apollo-era administrator, it delivered its first deep-field galaxy image in July 2022.
questions.whyExplanation: Launched December 25, 2021, the James Webb Space Telescope uses a 6.5-meter gold-coated beryllium mirror at L2 to peer into the infrared early universe.

questions.prompt: After enduring "seven minutes of terror" in August 2012, this car-sized nuclear rover was winched softly onto Gale Crater by a hovering rocket "sky crane"—and later sang itself "Happy Birthday."
clues: Officially the Mars Science Laboratory, it has spent over a decade climbing the layered flanks of Mount Sharp.
Its name was chosen in a 2009 student essay contest won by Kansas sixth-grader Clara Ma.
questions.whyExplanation: NASA's Curiosity rover pioneered the sky-crane landing in Gale Crater in 2012 and proved ancient Mars once held habitable freshwater lakes.

questions.prompt: Crushed to silence after 23 minutes of faint telemetry from 475-degree-Celsius hell in December 1970, this heavily armored Soviet capsule became the first probe ever to soft-land on another planet.
clues: Its parachute tore during descent, causing it to roll onto its side on Venus—yet its weak signal was later rescued from audio tapes.
Built to withstand 180 atmospheres of pressure, it was the seventh numbered craft in the USSR's Venus program.
questions.whyExplanation: On December 15, 1970, the Soviet lander Venera 7 touched down on Venus and transmitted temperature data, marking humanity's first soft landing on another planet.

questions.prompt: A mirror ground flat by just two micrometers—one-fiftieth the width of a human hair—turned this 1990 orbital icon into a punchline until STS-61 spacewalkers fitted it with corrective optics in 1993.
clues: Astronauts serviced it five times aboard Space Shuttles, installing instruments like COSTAR and Wide Field Camera 3.
Named for the astronomer who revealed cosmic expansion, its 2.4-meter mirror still orbits Earth.
questions.whyExplanation: Launched in 1990 with spherical aberration in its primary mirror, the Hubble Space Telescope was restored to crisp vision by the 1993 STS-61 repair mission.

questions.prompt: Earth finally fought back for the dinosaurs on September 26, 2022 when this vending-machine-sized NASA kinetic impactor smashed into asteroid moonlet Dimorphos, trimming its orbit by 33 minutes.
clues: Its Italian CubeSat companion LICIACube trailed behind to photograph the bright plume of rock blasted off the Didymos system.
Its sharp four-letter acronym stands for Double Asteroid Redirection Test.
questions.whyExplanation: NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) deliberately collided with Dimorphos at 6.1 km/s in 2022, proving kinetic impact can deflect an asteroid.

questions.prompt: Becoming the first NASA mission named after a living scientist, this carbon-shielded speed demon launched in 2018 and dipped inside the Sun's scorching corona three years later.
clues: Repeated Venus gravity assists have accelerated it past 635,000 kilometers per hour—the fastest human-made object ever built.
Its 91-year-old namesake watched the launch in Florida, sixty years after predicting the solar wind.
questions.whyExplanation: Named for astrophysicist Eugene Parker, NASA's Parker Solar Probe launched in 2018 and became the first spacecraft to fly through the solar corona in 2021.

questions.prompt: Not content with scooping surface dust off asteroid Ryugu, this JAXA explorer fired a copper cannonball to blast an artificial crater in 2019 before dropping 5.4 grams of pristine rock into Australia.
clues: It also deployed tiny hopping MINERVA-II rovers and the German-French MASCOT lander onto the diamond-shaped asteroid.
Its Japanese name translates to "Peregrine Falcon" followed by the numeral 2, succeeding a 2003 ancestor.
questions.whyExplanation: Japan's Hayabusa2 mission blasted an artificial crater on Ryugu to collect subsurface material, returning its sample capsule to Woomera in December 2020.

questions.prompt: Astronomers caught a mysterious yellow spectral line in the Sun's chromosphere during an 1868 eclipse—27 years before William Ramsay ever isolated this featherweight noble gas on Earth.
clues: It is the only element on the periodic table first discovered beyond Earth, taking its name from the Greek sun god.
Number 2 on the periodic table, it stays liquid even near absolute zero at normal pressure.
questions.whyExplanation: Helium (named for Helios) was spotted spectroscopically in sunlight in 1868 by Janssen and Lockyer before Ramsay extracted it from cleveite ore in 1895.

questions.prompt: Medieval tin smelters cursed this dense mineral as "wolf's foam" because it devoured their yields—explaining the odd symbol W on the pure metal with the highest melting point on Earth.
clues: Refusing to melt until 3,422 degrees Celsius, it powered a century of incandescent lightbulb filaments.
Its English name means "heavy stone" in Swedish, while its symbol derives from the German mineral wolframite.
questions.whyExplanation: Tungsten (atomic number 74, symbol W from German Wolfram) melts at 3,422 °C—the highest melting point of any pure metal.

questions.prompt: Dmitri Mendeleev boldly predicted its exact density as "eka-aluminum" in 1871, and four years later Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran isolated this silvery metal that melts right in your palm.
clues: Prankster chemists cast spoons from it because its 29.76-degree-Celsius melting point makes them vanish in hot tea.
Element 31 takes its Latinate name from France—and slyly puns on its discoverer's surname, meaning "rooster."
questions.whyExplanation: Discovered in 1875 by Lecoq de Boisbaudran, gallium (Ga, Z=31) matched Mendeleev's predicted eka-aluminum and melts at 29.76 °C, just above room temperature.

questions.prompt: Roasted out of crimson cinnabar ore since antiquity, this heavy liquid metal carries a chemical symbol borrowed from Greek for "liquid silver"—and once drove felt hatmakers slowly mad.
clues: With symbol Hg and atomic number 80, it is the sole metallic element liquid at standard room temperature.
Sharing its English name with the Roman messenger god, it once filled classic glass barometers and thermometers.
questions.whyExplanation: Mercury (Hg, from hydrargyrum, "liquid silver") is the only metal liquid at standard temperature and caused neurological poisoning in 19th-century hatters.

questions.prompt: Emilio Segrè and Carlo Perrier filled a stubborn gap in 1937 using cyclotron-blasted molybdenum foil, naming element 43 from Greek for "artificial" as the lightest purely radioactive element.
clues: Despite having zero stable isotopes, its metastable 99m form is the workhorse tracer of hospital nuclear-medicine scans.
Sitting between molybdenum and ruthenium with symbol Tc, it was the first element created artificially.
questions.whyExplanation: Synthesized in 1937 by Perrier and Segrè, technetium (Z=43) was the first human-made element and remains the lightest element with no stable isotopes.

questions.prompt: When Smithson Tennant dissolved platinum residue in aqua regia in 1803, a sharp, pungent stench inspired the Greek name of this bluish metal—the densest naturally occurring element on Earth.
clues: Tipping the scales at 22.59 grams per cubic centimeter, a softball-sized sphere of it would weigh nearly 15 kilograms.
Bearing symbol Os and atomic number 76, its name derives from the Greek word osme, meaning "smell."
questions.whyExplanation: Osmium (Z=76) has the highest natural density of any element (22.59 g/cm³) and was named by Tennant in 1803 for the acrid odor of its volatile tetroxide.

questions.prompt: Antoine-Jérôme Balard distilled this fuming dark-red liquid from Montpellier salt marshes in 1826, borrowing a Greek word for "stench" to name the only nonmetal liquid at room temperature.
clues: Tucked between chlorine and iodine in the halogen column, its dense reddish vapor turns toxic quickly.
Its symbol is Br and its atomic number is 35.
questions.whyExplanation: Isolated in 1826 by Balard, bromine (Br, Z=35, from Greek bromos, "stench") is the sole nonmetallic element that is liquid at standard room temperature.

questions.prompt: Saxony silver miners blamed mischievous goblin sprites for this stubborn, arsenic-laced ore—yet its vivid blue salts later colored Ming porcelain, stained glass, and Van Gogh's Starry Night.
clues: Today it is prized inside lithium-ion EV battery cathodes and jet-engine superalloys.
Atomic number 27, its name derives from the German goblin word Kobold.
questions.whyExplanation: Cobalt (Co, Z=27) takes its name from German Kobold sprites cursed by medieval miners; its oxide yields the brilliant blue glass and ceramic pigment.

questions.prompt: So fleeting that less than a single ounce exists in Earth's entire crust at any instant, this radioactive halogen—Greek for "unstable"—was first forged at Berkeley in 1940 by bombarding bismuth.
clues: Its longest-lived isotope decays with a half-life of barely 8.1 hours, preventing anyone from seeing a bulk chunk.
Occupying atomic number 85 beneath iodine, it carries the two-letter symbol At.
questions.whyExplanation: Astatine (At, Z=85, from Greek astatos, "unstable") is the rarest naturally occurring element in Earth's crust, first synthesized at UC Berkeley in 1940.

questions.prompt: Named for the Greek rainbow goddess after its brilliantly colored salts, this platinum-group metal became paleontology's smoking gun when Luis and Walter Alvarez found a global spike at the dinosaur boundary.
clues: Rare in Earth's crust yet abundant in asteroids, its 66-million-year-old clay layer signaled the Chicxulub impact.
Atomic number 77, it bears the symbol Ir and ranks as the second-densest natural element.
questions.whyExplanation: Iridium (Ir, Z=77, named after Iris) is enriched in meteorites; its worldwide enrichment in K-Pg boundary clay proved an asteroid ended the non-avian dinosaurs.

questions.prompt: Humphry Davy stunned London in 1807 by zapping moist caustic potash with a giant battery to free silvery globules of this alkali metal—whose odd symbol K traces back to Arabic for plant ashes.
clues: Tossed into water, it skitters across the surface and bursts into a lilac flame.
Essential for nerve impulses and famous in bananas, it is element 19—with symbol K from Neo-Latin kalium.
questions.whyExplanation: Isolated via electrolysis by Humphry Davy in 1807, potassium (Z=19) takes its symbol K from kalium, derived from Arabic al-qalyah (calcined plant ashes).

questions.prompt: Officially christened in November 2016 as only the second element ever named after a living scientist, this fleeting superheavy noble-gas-column giant caps the seventh row at atomic number 118.
clues: Relativistic electron effects are predicted to make it a reactive solid rather than an inert gas if bulk atoms could last.
Bearing symbol Og, it honors Russian-Armenian nuclear physicist Yuri Oganessian of Dubna.
questions.whyExplanation: Element 118, oganesson (Og), was synthesized in Dubna and named in 2016 for Yuri Oganessian—joining seaborgium as an element named for a living person.

questions.prompt: Chemist August Kekulé famously credited an 1865 fireside daydream of a snake biting its own tail for unlocking the cyclic six-carbon ring of this sweet-smelling aromatic hydrocarbon.
clues: With formula C6H6 and molar mass 78.11 g/mol, its six delocalized pi electrons make all carbon-carbon bonds identical.
Michael Faraday first isolated this carcinogenic solvent from illuminating gas in 1825.
questions.whyExplanation: Benzene (C6H6) is the parent aromatic ring; Kekulé's 1865 cyclic model—inspired by an Ouroboros reverie—revolutionized organic structural chemistry.

questions.prompt: Borrowing its name from an ancient Egyptian desert temple of Ammon where camel-dung salts were scraped, this pungent nitrogen-hydrogen gas now sustains roughly half of humanity through synthetic fertilizer.
clues: Its trigonal pyramidal molecule carries formula NH3 and a light molar mass of 17.03 g/mol.
The high-pressure Haber-Bosch process manufactures over 150 million metric tons of it every year.
questions.whyExplanation: Ammonia (NH3) derives its name from sal ammoniac near Libya's Temple of Ammon; industrial Haber-Bosch synthesis made modern global agriculture possible.

questions.prompt: Roman soldiers' pay allowances gave English the word "salary"—a linguistic monument to this cubic ionic crystal with molar mass 58.44 g/mol that geologists mine under the name halite.
clues: In solid form, alternating positive and negative ions lock into a face-centered cubic lattice melting at 801 degrees Celsius.
Formula NaCl, it is better known on every dining table on Earth as common salt.
questions.whyExplanation: Sodium chloride (NaCl, mineral halite) forms cubic ionic crystals and shaped ancient trade routes and Roman pay etymology.

questions.prompt: Laser-vaporizing graphite in 1985 yielded a mysteriously stable 60-carbon cluster shaped like a soccer ball of 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons, named for a visionary American geodesic-dome architect.
clues: Its discovery won Harold Kroto, Robert Curl, and Richard Smalley the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
With formula C60 and molar mass 720.66 g/mol, chemists affectionately shorten its mouthful of a name to "buckyball."
questions.whyExplanation: Buckminsterfullerene (C60) is a truncated icosahedron of 60 carbon atoms discovered in 1985 and named after geodesic-dome pioneer R. Buckminster Fuller.

questions.prompt: Young Humphry Davy hosted giddy 1799 parlor parties inhaling this sweet gas—and even noted its toothache-numbing power decades before American dentists adopted it as surgical anesthesia.
clues: Carrying formula N2O (44.01 g/mol), it also serves as a whipped-cream propellant and rocket oxidizer.
Its euphoric effect earned it the classic nickname "laughing gas."
questions.whyExplanation: Nitrous oxide (N2O) was studied by Davy in 1799–1800 and pioneered clinically in dentistry by Horace Wells in 1844 as "laughing gas."

questions.prompt: Seeking a gentler derivative of bitter willow-bark salicylic acid for his arthritic father, Bayer chemist Felix Hoffmann synthesized this ester in August 1897—launching the world's most iconic pill.
clues: With formula C9H8O4 (180.16 g/mol), it irreversibly blocks COX enzymes to calm pain, fever, and blood clotting.
Bayer trademarked it in 1899 under the household brand name Aspirin.
questions.whyExplanation: Synthesized in pure stable form by Felix Hoffmann at Bayer in 1897, acetylsalicylic acid became Aspirin—one of medicine's most widely used drugs.

questions.prompt: Medieval alchemists called it "oil of vitriol," Venus drapes its clouds in it, and modern industry manufactures more tonnage of this dense diprotic liquid (98.08 g/mol) than any other chemical.
clues: Its dehydrating greed turns ordinary white table sugar into a steaming black tower of pure carbon.
Formula H2SO4, it is the corrosive electrolyte sloshing inside conventional lead-acid car batteries.
questions.whyExplanation: Sulfuric acid (H2SO4, historically oil of vitriol) is Earth's highest-volume industrial chemical and forms the thick reflective cloud deck of Venus.

questions.prompt: Evolution armed chili peppers with this oily alkaloid to hijack mammalian TRPV1 heat nerves—yet birds lack the matching pain response, happily eating the fruit and scattering intact seeds far and wide.
clues: Because it is hydrophobic (C18H27NO3), water barely helps after a fiery bite, whereas milk casein washes it away.
Wilbur Scoville devised a famous heat-unit scale in 1912 to measure its concentration.
questions.whyExplanation: Capsaicin binds mammalian TRPV1 pain receptors to trigger a burning sensation, deterring seed-chewing mammals while leaving seed-dispersing birds unaffected.

questions.prompt: Only people carrying the right olfactory gene detect its faint scent of bitter almonds—a fateful quirk of this 65.12 g/mol salt that suffocates cells by jamming mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase.
clues: Even though blood stays rich in oxygen, this fast-acting toxin stops cells from actually using it.
Carrying formula KCN, its lethal anion consists of a carbon atom triple-bonded to nitrogen.
questions.whyExplanation: Potassium cyanide (KCN) halts cellular respiration by binding iron in cytochrome c oxidase; the ability to smell its bitter-almond odor is genetically variable.

questions.prompt: Louis Jacques Thénard dubbed it "oxygenated water" in 1818; in nature, bombardier beetles mix this unstable 34.01 g/mol oxidizer with hydroquinones to fire boiling defensive jets at predators.
clues: Stored in brown opaque bottles to stop sunlight from breaking its weak oxygen-oxygen single bond, it fizzes vigorously on cuts.
Its formula H2O2 packs just one extra oxygen atom compared to ordinary water.
questions.whyExplanation: Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) decomposes exothermically into water and oxygen—powering everything from wound fizzing and rocket monopropellants to bombardier beetles.

questions.prompt: When DuPont's Roy Plunkett sawed open a supposedly empty Freon-research cylinder in 1938, he scraped out a slippery white powder—accidentally creating this unreactive fluoropolymer known as Teflon.
clues: Strong carbon-fluorine bonds cloak its backbone so thoroughly that almost nothing—even gecko feet—can stick to it.
Abbreviated PTFE, its name stacks "poly," "tetra," "fluoro," and "ethylene" into one 23-letter mouthful.
questions.whyExplanation: Roy Plunkett accidentally polymerized tetrafluoroethylene gas in 1938 into PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene), commercialized by DuPont as nonstick Teflon.

questions.prompt: Christian Friedrich Schönbein named this pale-blue gas in 1840 after the Greek verb "to smell"—a sharp, triatomic paradox that poisons lungs at street level yet shields all life from UV rays aloft.
clues: Often smelled as a crisp tang after lightning storms or near copy machines, its bent molecule has molar mass 48.00 g/mol.
Its formula is O3, and the 1987 Montreal Protocol curbed CFCs to heal its Antarctic depletion.
questions.whyExplanation: Ozone (O3, from Greek ozein, "to smell") is a ground-level smog irritant yet forms the vital stratospheric shield absorbing solar ultraviolet radiation.

questions.prompt: Refining tons of Austrian pitchblende in a leaky Paris shed, she remains the only human ever to claim Nobel Prizes in two distinct sciences—naming one of her new elements after her conquered homeland.
clues: After sharing the 1903 Physics Nobel with her husband Pierre and Henri Becquerel, she won the 1911 Chemistry prize solo.
She isolated radium and polonium—the latter named for Poland—and her laboratory notebooks remain radioactive today.
questions.whyExplanation: Marie Curie won the 1903 Physics Nobel and 1911 Chemistry Nobel, isolating polonium and radium and pioneering the science of radioactivity.

questions.prompt: Though he infamously proposed a flawed triple-helix model of DNA, this Oregon-born titan of the chemical bond remains the only individual in history to win two completely unshared Nobel Prizes.
clues: His 1954 Chemistry Nobel honored orbital hybridization and protein alpha helices; his 1962 Peace Prize saluted his nuclear test-ban crusade.
Late in life he sparked decades of medical debate by championing megadoses of vitamin C.
questions.whyExplanation: Linus Pauling won unshared Nobel Prizes in Chemistry (1954) and Peace (1962), transforming chemical bonding theory and structural molecular biology.

questions.prompt: Despite severe rheumatoid arthritis, this Oxford crystallographer mapped the 3D structures of penicillin, vitamin B12, and insulin—winning the 1964 Chemistry Nobel after mentoring a young Margaret Thatcher.
clues: A British tabloid hilariously headlined her 1964 solo Nobel victory "Oxford Housewife Wins Nobel."
Born Dorothy Crowfoot, she spent 35 years refining her X-ray diffraction map of insulin.
questions.whyExplanation: Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin won the 1964 Chemistry Nobel for solving complex biomolecules via X-ray crystallography, and supervised Margaret Roberts (Thatcher) at Oxford.

questions.prompt: Perhaps science's starkest moral paradox, this German chemist won the 1918 Nobel for turning thin air into life-giving fertilizer—just years after overseeing the First World War's deadly chlorine gas attacks.
clues: His wife, fellow chemist Clara Immerwahr, died by suicide in 1915 after protesting his chemical-warfare leadership at Ypres.
Though his catalytic process saved billions from famine, he fled Nazi Germany in 1933 because of his Jewish heritage.
questions.whyExplanation: Fritz Haber received the 1918 Chemistry Nobel for synthesizing ammonia from atmospheric nitrogen, even while drawing condemnation for leading WWI gas warfare.

questions.prompt: A self-described "chap who just messed about in a lab," this British biochemist won two Chemistry Nobels 22 years apart—sequencing insulin, then inventing chain-termination DNA reading.
clues: His 1977 dideoxy DNA sequencing method laid the foundation for the entire Human Genome Project.
Winning in 1958 and 1980, he was the first person ever to claim the Chemistry Nobel twice.
questions.whyExplanation: Frederick Sanger won Chemistry Nobels in 1958 (insulin structure) and 1980 (DNA sequencing), giving genomics its foundational sequencing chemistry.

questions.prompt: Teaming up with Emmanuelle Charpentier after a 2011 Puerto Rico conference chat, this UC Berkeley biochemist shared the 2020 Chemistry Nobel for reprogramming bacterial CRISPR-Cas9 into genetic scissors.
clues: Their 2020 win marked the first time in history a science Nobel Prize went exclusively to women.
She chronicled the race and ethics of gene editing in her book A Crack in Creation.
questions.whyExplanation: Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier won the 2020 Chemistry Nobel for developing CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, the first all-female science Nobel.

questions.prompt: Denied a Nobel Prize largely due to rival Svante Arrhenius's committee opposition, this Siberian-born icon arranged known elements like solitaire cards in 1869 and left daring blanks for undiscovered metals.
clues: When gallium, scandium, and germanium turned up matching his predicted weights and properties, skepticism vanished.
Radioactive element 101 was named in his honor in 1955 to salute his periodic table.
questions.whyExplanation: Dmitri Mendeleev published the periodic table in 1869 and predicted missing elements' properties with uncanny precision, despite never receiving a Nobel Prize.

questions.prompt: After he named oxygen, dismantled phlogiston, and proved matter is conserved, France's Reign of Terror guillotined him in 1794—prompting Lagrange to sigh that a century would not produce another head like it.
clues: His downfall stemmed not from chemistry, but from his day job collecting taxes for the despised Ferme Générale.
Working alongside his illustrator wife Marie-Anne, this Frenchman is hailed as the Father of Modern Chemistry.
questions.whyExplanation: Antoine-Laurent de Lavoisier established conservation of mass and modern chemical nomenclature before being executed in 1794 during the French Revolution.

questions.prompt: By firing laser flashes lasting a quadrillionth of a second—like a slow-motion camera for colliding atoms—this Egyptian-American Caltech scientist founded femtochemistry and won the solo 1999 Chemistry Nobel.
clues: He became the first Arab scientist ever awarded a Nobel Prize in a scientific field.
One femtosecond compares to a single second roughly the way one second compares to 32 million years.
questions.whyExplanation: Ahmed Zewail won the 1999 Chemistry Nobel for pioneering femtochemistry, using ultrafast laser pulses to observe chemical transition states in real time.

questions.prompt: Cruising down moonlit California Highway 128 in 1983, this surfing biochemist hatched the cycling-heat trick behind PCR—winning the 1993 Chemistry Nobel for letting labs multiply one DNA strand into billions.
clues: He worked at Cetus Corporation when he devised polymerase chain reaction, transforming forensics and viral diagnostics.
Known for his eccentric memoir Dancing Naked in the Mind Field, he shared the 1993 prize with Michael Smith.
questions.whyExplanation: Kary Mullis invented the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in 1983, earning a share of the 1993 Chemistry Nobel for revolutionizing molecular biology and testing.

questions.prompt: Chain-smoking in his trademark blue suit and tie, this Harvard virtuoso of total organic synthesis built quinine, chlorophyll, and vitamin B12 from scratch before winning the 1965 Chemistry Nobel.
clues: He also co-formulated the orbital-symmetry conservation rules that earned his younger collaborator Roald Hoffmann a 1981 Nobel.
His legendary three-hour blackboard lectures started at the upper left with multicolored chalk and finished cleanly at bottom right.
questions.whyExplanation: Robert Burns Woodward won the 1965 Chemistry Nobel for total syntheses of complex natural products and co-authored the landmark Woodward-Hoffmann rules.

questions.prompt: Wanting to tag sugars on living cancer cells without poisoning them with copper catalysts, this Stanford chemist coined "bioorthogonal chemistry" and shared the 2022 Chemistry Nobel for click reactions.
clues: Before leading modern glycoscience, she played keyboards in a college rock band called Bored of Education alongside Rage Against the Machine's Tom Morello.
Her strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition clicks molecules together safely inside live organisms.
questions.whyExplanation: Carolyn Bertozzi shared the 2022 Chemistry Nobel (with Sharpless and Meldal) for bringing click chemistry inside living cells via bioorthogonal reactions.

questions.prompt: Famous for cracking Los Alamos safes and playing bongos, this 1965 QED Nobel laureate delivered an unforgettable 1986 TV lesson by clamping a Space Shuttle Challenger O-ring into a glass of ice water.
clues: His squiggly pictorial diagrams turned fiendish quantum electrodynamics integrals into intuitive sketches of subatomic collisions.
His bestselling anecdotes bear the cheeky title Surely You're Joking, Mr. ...
questions.whyExplanation: Richard Feynman shared the 1965 Physics Nobel for QED, popularized physics through his Lectures, and demonstrated the cold-brittle O-ring flaw on the Rogers Commission.

questions.prompt: Barred initially from a paid Göttingen professorship because of her gender, this algebraist stunned Einstein with a 1918 theorem proving every continuous symmetry of nature dictates a conservation law.
clues: Under her mathematical cornerstone, time-translation symmetry guarantees conservation of energy and rotational symmetry guarantees angular momentum.
David Hilbert famously rebuked opponents of her faculty appointment by declaring a university was not a bathhouse.
questions.whyExplanation: Emmy Noether's 1918 theorem revealed the deep equivalence between symmetries and conservation laws, becoming a bedrock pillar of modern theoretical physics.

questions.prompt: Aiming a handmade 20-power spyglass at Jupiter in January 1610, this Pisan polymath spotted four tiny moons circling another planet—shattering geocentric dogma before ending his days under house arrest.
clues: He published his telescopic bombshells in Sidereus Nuncius and slyly named Jupiter's four moons the "Medicean Stars" to flatter Florence's rulers.
Legend also links him to dropping uneven spheres from Pisa's Leaning Tower and muttering "And yet it moves."
questions.whyExplanation: Galileo Galilei's 1610 observations of Jupiter's moons and Venus's phases provided decisive evidence against Ptolemaic geocentrism.

questions.prompt: At age 19 on an 18-day steamship voyage from India to Cambridge in 1930, he calculated the 1.4-solar-mass limit beyond which white dwarfs collapse—only for Arthur Eddington to publicly mock the math.
clues: Vindicated decades later by neutron stars and black holes, he won the 1983 Physics Nobel and inspired NASA's flagship X-ray observatory.
He was the nephew of fellow Indian Physics Nobel laureate C. V. Raman.
questions.whyExplanation: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar derived the 1.4-solar-mass white-dwarf limit in 1930; initially dismissed by Eddington, it earned him the 1983 Physics Nobel.

questions.prompt: Measuring the outer edges of spiral galaxies with Kent Ford in the 1970s, this astronomer caught stars orbiting far too fast to stay bound—providing the breakthrough observational proof of dark matter.
clues: As a graduate student she was initially barred from Palomar Observatory because it lacked a women's restroom—until she taped a skirt silhouette onto the door.
Chile's massive 8.4-meter survey observatory on Cerro Pachón now carries her name.
questions.whyExplanation: Vera Rubin's flat galaxy rotation curves demonstrated that invisible dark matter halos contain far more mass than luminous stars.

questions.prompt: Between writing the four equations that proved light is an electromagnetic wave and inventing a thermodynamics-defying "demon," this Scotsman helped produce the first durable color photograph—a tartan ribbon.
clues: In 1859 he also proved mathematically that Saturn's rings could not be solid or liquid, but swarms of tiny particles.
Einstein hung his portrait alongside Newton and Faraday on his study wall.
questions.whyExplanation: James Clerk Maxwell unified electricity, magnetism, and optics in the 1860s, formulated kinetic gas theory, and demonstrated three-color photography in 1861.

questions.prompt: Spotting a rhythmic 1.33-second radio "scruff" on miles of Cambridge chart paper in 1967, this graduate student nicknamed it "Little Green Men"—discovering pulsars while her supervisor collected the 1974 Nobel.
clues: When awarded the $3 million Special Breakthrough Prize in 2018, she donated every penny to fund underrepresented physics grad students.
Born in Northern Ireland, she built the four-acre dipole array largely by hand with stakes and miles of copper wire.
questions.whyExplanation: Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered the first radio pulsar (PSR B1919+21) in 1967 as a PhD student; her advisor Antony Hewish received the 1974 Physics Nobel.

questions.prompt: During a December 1938 walk in the Swedish snow with her nephew Otto Frisch, this exiled Austrian sketched the math of splitting uranium—explaining nuclear fission before the Nobel committee overlooked her.
clues: While longtime Berlin partner Otto Hahn took the 1944 Chemistry Nobel alone, she was nominated for a Nobel an astonishing 49 times.
In 1997, synthetic superheavy element 109 was officially named in her honor.
questions.whyExplanation: Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch provided the theoretical explanation of nuclear fission in 1938–1939; though passed over by the Nobel committee, element 109 honors her.

questions.prompt: Cooling radioactive cobalt-60 near absolute zero in late 1956, this "First Lady of Physics" proved electrons shot out preferentially in one direction—shattering the cherished law of parity conservation.
clues: Her precision Columbia and NBS experiment confirmed Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang's hunch, winning the two theorists the 1957 Physics Nobel.
Earlier during the Manhattan Project, she diagnosed why the Hanford plutonium reactor kept shutting down from xenon-135 poisoning.
questions.whyExplanation: Chien-Shiung Wu's 1956–1957 beta-decay experiment proved the weak nuclear force violates parity symmetry, earning Lee and Yang the 1957 Physics Nobel.

questions.prompt: Nailing a horseshoe above his cottage door—joking it works even if you doubt it—this 1922 Nobel laureate quantized hydrogen's orbits and told Einstein to stop telling God what to do.
clues: After escaping Nazi-occupied Denmark to Sweden in 1943, he helped found CERN and championed peaceful international atomic control.
His Copenhagen institute gave its name to the classic probabilistic interpretation of quantum mechanics.
questions.whyExplanation: Niels Bohr won the 1922 Physics Nobel for his quantized atomic model, led the Copenhagen interpretation, and famously sparred with Einstein over quantum indeterminacy.

questions.prompt: Interrupting his celestial calculations to defend his own mother against witchcraft charges, this German mathematician wrestled Tycho Brahe's Mars logs into proving planets trace ellipses, not perfect circles.
clues: His three laws of planetary motion later gave Isaac Newton the mathematical target needed to verify universal gravitation.
NASA named its prolific 2009–2018 transit-hunting exoplanet space telescope after him.
questions.whyExplanation: Johannes Kepler derived the three laws of elliptical planetary motion from Tycho Brahe's observations while spending six years successfully defending his mother from witchcraft charges.

questions.prompt: So notoriously terse that Cambridge peers joked a "one-word-per-hour" unit bore his name, this Briton's 1928 relativistic electron equation forced physics to predict antimatter before it was seen.
clues: Carl Anderson spotted his predicted positively charged electron—the positron—in cosmic-ray cloud chambers in 1932.
He shared the 1933 Physics Nobel with Erwin Schrödinger and has his sleek equation engraved on Westminster Abbey's floor.
questions.whyExplanation: Paul Dirac's 1928 relativistic quantum equation unified special relativity with quantum mechanics and predicted the positron, launching antimatter physics.

questions.prompt: Contrary to popular myth, Albert Einstein won his 1921 Physics Nobel not for relativity, but for unlocking quantum light packets to explain this phenomenon in which photons kick electrons out of metal.
clues: Classical wave physics could not explain why dim violet light easily frees electrons while blazing red light frees none below a threshold frequency.
Its modern applications power rooftop solar panels and digital camera sensors.
questions.whyExplanation: Einstein's 1905 quantum explanation of the photoelectric effect proved light travels in discrete energy quanta (photons) and earned him the 1921 Physics Nobel.

questions.prompt: To test this 1842 Austrian frequency-shift prediction in 1845, Christoph Buys Ballot put horn players on a speeding Dutch railcar—and astronomers later used its optical redshift to gauge cosmic expansion.
clues: It explains why an ambulance siren plunges in pitch the instant it shrieks past you.
In astrophysics, receding galaxies stretch starlight toward red wavelengths through this shift.
questions.whyExplanation: Proposed by Christian Doppler in 1842 and confirmed acoustically by train-mounted musicians in 1845, the Doppler effect governs siren pitch shifts and cosmological redshift.

questions.prompt: Nobel laureate John William Strutt solved why noon skies glow azure and sunsets burn crimson by showing air molecules deflect light inversely to the fourth power of wavelength—a process bearing his noble title.
clues: Because short blue wavelengths scatter roughly ten times more strongly than long red ones, sunlight loses blue light over long twilight paths.
Strutt—who also co-discovered argon to win the 1904 Physics Nobel—is far better known as the 3rd Baron of this name.
questions.whyExplanation: Rayleigh scattering (named for Lord Rayleigh, John William Strutt) preferentially scatters short-wavelength blue sunlight off atmospheric gases.

questions.prompt: Nothing outruns light in a vacuum, yet charged particles zipping faster than light's reduced speed in water create an eerie blue optical sonic boom inside nuclear reactors—winning a 1958 Physics Nobel.
clues: Giant underground water tanks like Japan's Super-Kamiokande catch its cone-shaped blue flashes to detect ghostly neutrinos.
It is named for the Soviet physicist who spotted the faint bluish glow in 1934 and shared the 1958 Nobel with Frank and Tamm.
questions.whyExplanation: Cherenkov radiation occurs when a charged particle exceeds light's phase velocity inside a dielectric medium like water, emitting a cone of blue light.

questions.prompt: By stretching a laser pulse in time, boosting its energy, and squashing it back down without melting the optics, Donna Strickland and Gérard Mourou won the 2018 Physics Nobel for this technique behind LASIK.
clues: Strickland's 1985 doctoral breakthrough made her only the third woman in history to win the Nobel Prize in Physics.
Abbreviated CPA, its bird-call first word refers to sweeping a pulse's frequency over time before recompression.
questions.whyExplanation: Chirped pulse amplification (CPA) enabled petawatt ultrashort lasers for precision eye surgery and physics, earning Strickland and Mourou half of the 2018 Physics Nobel.

questions.prompt: Arthur Eddington's 1919 eclipse photos of displaced Hyades stars made Einstein famous by confirming this cosmic distortion that turns massive galaxies into natural telescopes.
clues: When a background galaxy aligns cleanly behind a foreground cluster, this effect warps it into glowing halos called Einstein rings.
Predicted by general relativity, it happens because massive objects bend spacetime—and with it, passing beams of light.
questions.whyExplanation: Gravitational lensing bends light rays around massive objects, verified during the 1919 eclipse and now used to map dark matter and magnify distant galaxies.

questions.prompt: Chilling solid mercury to 4.2 kelvin in 1911, Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes watched electrical resistance abruptly plunge to zero—winning the 1913 Physics Nobel for discovering this frictionless state.
clues: Materials in this quantum state also expel internal magnetic fields via the Meissner effect, letting magnets levitate midair.
Today it powers hospital MRI electromagnets, CERN's LHC dipoles, and Japanese maglev test trains.
questions.whyExplanation: Discovered in 1911 by Kamerlingh Onnes in liquid-helium-cooled mercury, superconductivity enables lossless electric currents and magnetic levitation.

questions.prompt: Red and green versions had glowed for decades, yet white solid-state lighting stayed out of reach until Akasaki, Amano, and Nakamura tamed gallium nitride crystals in the 1990s—winning the 2014 Physics Nobel.
clues: Shuji Nakamura built his breakthrough device at a tiny Japanese chemical firm called Nichia, defying managers who ordered him to quit.
Completing the RGB primary trio of light-emitting diodes, it revolutionized smartphones, giant billboards, and energy-saving bulbs.
questions.whyExplanation: Akasaki, Amano, and Nakamura won the 2014 Physics Nobel for inventing efficient gallium-nitride blue LEDs, unlocking bright white solid-state lighting.

questions.prompt: Hungarian-British engineer Dennis Gabor invented this interference-based 3D imaging art in 1947 to sharpen electron microscopes—13 years before lasers existed to make it shine, winning the 1971 Physics Nobel.
clues: Unlike flat photographs that capture only brightness, it records both the amplitude and phase of light waves on a plate.
Its name derives from Greek for "whole writing" and today guards credit cards against counterfeiting.
questions.whyExplanation: Dennis Gabor invented holography in 1947 (winning the 1971 Physics Nobel), recording optical wavefront interference patterns that reconstruct true 3D images under coherent laser light.

questions.prompt: Captivated by the Mediterranean's deep blue on a 1921 voyage, an Indian physicist proved molecules shift scattered photons' wavelengths—winning Asia's first science Nobel in 1930.
clues: Because each chemical bond shifts incoming laser light by a unique vibrational fingerprint, NASA's Perseverance rover carries a spectrometer using it on Mars.
India celebrates National Science Day every February 28 to mark Chandrasekhara Venkata's 1928 discovery of this inelastic light shift.
questions.whyExplanation: Discovered in 1928 by C. V. Raman (earning the 1930 Physics Nobel), Raman scattering reveals molecular vibrational fingerprints via inelastic photon frequency shifts.

questions.prompt: Strike the boundary between glass and air past Snell's critical angle, and light refuses to escape—bouncing losslessly through undersea fiber-optic cables pioneered by 2009 Physics Nobel laureate Charles Kao.
clues: This same optical trapping gives finely cut diamonds their dazzling brilliance and lets doctors peer through flexible endoscopes.
Its three-word name describes 100 percent of a ray mirroring back inside a denser optical medium.
questions.whyExplanation: Total internal reflection traps light inside optical fibers whenever the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle, enabling modern high-speed telecommunications.

questions.prompt: A 19th-century French engineer derived this apparent deflecting force for spinning waterwheels—not weather—yet it twists Northern hurricanes counterclockwise and turns Foucault's pendulum.
clues: Despite a stubborn urban legend, it is far too weak to determine which way water spirals down a household bathtub drain.
Arising purely from Earth's rotating reference frame, it curves free-moving air masses right in the North and left in the South.
questions.whyExplanation: Described by Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis in 1835 for rotating machinery, the Coriolis effect deflects planetary winds, ocean gyres, and long-range trajectories.

questions.prompt: Returning from a September 1928 Scottish vacation to a cluttered London lab, this bacteriologist spotted stray blue-green mold dissolving bacteria on an unwashed Petri dish—launching antibiotics.
clues: He originally dubbed the mold's antibacterial brew "mold juice" before naming it penicillin and sharing the 1945 Medicine Nobel.
Six years earlier, an accidental nasal drip onto a culture plate had already led him to discover the enzyme lysozyme.
questions.whyExplanation: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 at St. Mary's Hospital in London; Florey and Chain later purified it for mass wartime use, sharing the 1945 Nobel.

questions.prompt: Noticing English dairymaids stayed unscarred by smallpox, this Gloucestershire country doctor scratched cowpox pustule fluid into eight-year-old James Phipps in May 1796—giving "vaccination" its Latin cow root.
clues: Weeks after the mild cowpox infection cleared, he deliberately exposed young Phipps to deadly smallpox and proved the boy was completely immune.
His method ultimately culminated in the 1980 global eradication of smallpox.
questions.whyExplanation: Edward Jenner's 1796 cowpox inoculation of James Phipps founded immunology and gave vaccination its name from Latin vacca (cow).

questions.prompt: Demoted and denied tenure at the University of Pennsylvania while doggedly chasing synthetic mRNA, this Hungarian biochemist shared the 2023 Medicine Nobel after her nucleoside tweak unlocked COVID-19 vaccines.
clues: Partnering with immunologist Drew Weissman after a photocopier-line chat, she swapped uridine for pseudouridine to silence lethal immune inflammation.
She smuggled 900 British pounds sewn inside her daughter's teddy bear when immigrating from communist Hungary in 1985.
questions.whyExplanation: Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman discovered that modifying mRNA nucleosides avoids destructive inflammation, enabling the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna vaccines.

questions.prompt: Working on secret Project 523 without a PhD or MD, she drew on a 1,600-year-old Chinese herbal text to cold-extract antimalarial artemisinin from sweet wormwood—winning the 2015 Medicine Nobel.
clues: Realizing boiling water destroyed the plant's active compound, she followed 4th-century healer Ge Hong's cold-juice clue using low-boiling ether.
Before clinical trials, she volunteered herself as the first human test subject to prove her extract's safety.
questions.whyExplanation: Tu Youyou became China's first Medicine Nobel laureate in 2015 for isolating artemisinin from sweet wormwood, a therapy that has saved millions from malaria.

questions.prompt: Slashing Vienna maternity-ward deaths from over 10 percent to under 2 percent in 1847 by ordering doctors to wash in chlorinated lime, this tragic physician was mocked by peers and died in an asylum.
clues: He noticed mothers delivered by midwives fared far better than those attended by physicians coming straight from cadaver autopsies.
His name now labels the psychological "reflex" of rejecting valid new evidence that clashes with entrenched beliefs.
questions.whyExplanation: Hungarian physician Ignaz Semmelweis pioneered antiseptic handwashing in 1847 to stop childbed fever, only to face fierce medical rejection before germ theory vindicated him.

questions.prompt: Asked by Edward R. Murrow on television in April 1955 who owned the patent to his newly triumphant polio vaccine, this Pittsburgh virologist famously replied, "Could you patent the sun?"
clues: Unlike rival Albert Sabin's later oral sugar-cube drops, his injectable formula used formaldehyde-killed poliovirus.
Before launching the 1954 trial on 1.8 million "Polio Pioneers," he tested the shot on himself, his wife, and his three young sons.
questions.whyExplanation: Jonas Salk developed the first safe, effective inactivated polio vaccine in 1955 and chose not to patent it, prioritizing rapid worldwide immunization.

questions.prompt: Her razor-sharp May 1952 X-ray diffraction image "Photo 51" exposed the unmistakable X-pattern of DNA's double helix—yet ovarian cancer claimed her at age 37, four years before her rivals shared the Nobel.
clues: Shown her King's College London photograph without her consent, James Watson and Francis Crick swiftly assembled their famous 1953 model.
Before her death in 1958, she also revolutionized structural virology by mapping tobacco mosaic virus and polio virus.
questions.whyExplanation: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray crystallography data—especially Photo 51—was decisive in proving DNA's double-helical structure, though she died before the 1962 Nobel.

questions.prompt: After swan-neck flasks disproved spontaneous generation and saved French vineyards, this non-physician risked his fame in 1885 by giving nine-year-old Joseph Meister the first human rabies shots.
clues: Severely mauled by a rabid dog, young Meister survived and spent his adult life guarding the Paris institute bearing his savior's name.
His heat-treatment technique for killing milk and wine spoilage bacteria made his surname an everyday supermarket verb.
questions.whyExplanation: French chemist-microbiologist Louis Pasteur established germ theory, developed pasteurization, and created the anthrax and human rabies vaccines.

questions.prompt: Exasperated that doctors blamed stomach ulcers on stress instead of bacteria, this Australian gulped a flask of live Helicobacter pylori in 1984 to give himself gastritis—and won a 2005 Nobel.
clues: After biopsying his own inflamed stomach to fulfill Koch's postulates, he cured himself with a quick course of antibiotics.
Sharing the 2005 Medicine Nobel with pathologist Robin Warren, he turned chronic peptic ulcers from lifelong surgery into a two-week pill cure.
questions.whyExplanation: Barry Marshall famously drank Helicobacter pylori in 1984 to prove bacteria cause peptic ulcers, sharing the 2005 Medicine Nobel with Robin Warren.

questions.prompt: Dismantling 1,400 years of Galenic doctrine in his 1628 treatise De Motu Cordis, King Charles I's physician calculated blood output to prove the heart pumps a closed, one-way loop guided by venous valves.
clues: Because microscopes were still too crude to reveal capillaries, he deduced invisible tiny connectors linking arteries to veins.
Critics dubbed him "the Circulator"—a Latin pun on traveling quacks—before anatomy proved him completely right.
questions.whyExplanation: English physician William Harvey published De Motu Cordis in 1628, demonstrating the continuous systemic circulation of blood pumped by the heart.

questions.prompt: Shut out of Depression-era chemistry labs and lacking a PhD, this pharmacologist pioneered rational drug design—yielding leukemia, gout, transplant, and herpes cures to share the 1988 Nobel.
