clues: Inspired by her grandfather's agonizing cancer death, she worked alongside George Hitchings at Burroughs Wellcome to craft antimetabolites.
Her antiviral drug acyclovir proved for the first time that medicines could selectively halt viruses without wrecking human cells.
questions.whyExplanation: Without a doctorate, Gertrude Elion revolutionized pharmacology via rational drug design (including 6-MP, azathioprine, and acyclovir), sharing the 1988 Medicine Nobel.

questions.prompt: Jotting a 25-word midnight hunch in October 1920 and borrowing a stifling Toronto attic lab with student Charles Best, this Canadian surgeon isolated insulin and won the 1923 Medicine Nobel at age 32.
clues: Furious that the Nobel committee rewarded lab chief Macleod instead of his assistant Best, he promptly split his own prize money with Best.
Selling the insulin patent to the University of Toronto for just one dollar, he remains the youngest Medicine Nobel laureate ever.
questions.whyExplanation: Frederick Banting led the 1921–1922 Toronto discovery of insulin for diabetes, winning the 1923 Medicine Nobel at 32—the youngest winner in that category.

questions.prompt: Hired chiefly as a gentleman dinner companion for moody Captain Robert FitzRoy on HMS Beagle, this seasick naturalist delayed publishing for 20 years until a rival's 1858 letter forced his hand.
clues: Galápagos mockingbirds, finches, and giant tortoises nudged him to question whether species were fixed forever.
His 1859 masterwork On the Origin of Species sold out its entire initial print run on opening day.
questions.whyExplanation: Charles Darwin sailed on HMS Beagle (1831–1836) and spent over 20 years amassing evidence before Alfred Russel Wallace's letter prompted publication of Origin of Species in 1859.

questions.prompt: Hand-pollinating nearly 28,000 garden pea plants behind a Brno monastery between 1856 and 1863, this Augustinian friar cracked dominant and recessive heredity—only for his paper to gather dust for 34 years.
clues: He twice flunked his Austrian high-school teaching exams—including biology—before becoming abbot of St. Thomas's Abbey.
Three European botanists independently rediscovered his 3-to-1 trait ratios in 1900, crowning him Father of Modern Genetics.
questions.whyExplanation: Gregor Mendel's painstaking Pisum sativum breeding experiments uncovered the laws of segregation and independent assortment, forming the bedrock of classical genetics.

questions.prompt: Boasting "God created, I arranged," this 18th-century Swedish botanist standardized two-word Latin species names in Systema Naturae—and cheekily named a foul-smelling weed after a rival critic.
clues: He also coined the name Homo sapiens for humanity and flipped Anders Celsius's upside-down thermometer scale so water boiled at 100.
Today the abbreviation "L." trailing thousands of plant names still credits his binomial taxonomy.
questions.whyExplanation: Carl Linnaeus formalized binomial nomenclature in Systema Naturae, classifying thousands of organisms and famously naming the smelly herb Siegesbeckia after a detractor.

questions.prompt: Studying speckled purple-and-yellow Indian corn kernels in Cold Spring Harbor solitude, this cytogeneticist proved genes physically hop around chromosomes—winning the solo 1983 Medicine Nobel.
clues: When colleagues greeted her 1951 lecture on mobile genetic elements with baffled silence, she stopped publishing details for years yet kept working.
Her "jumping genes"—formally transposons—turned out to make up nearly half of the entire human genome.
questions.whyExplanation: Barbara McClintock discovered genetic transposition ("jumping genes") in maize at Cold Spring Harbor, earning an unshared 1983 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

questions.prompt: Arriving at Tanzania's Gombe Stream in 1960 without a degree—and naming chimps instead of numbering them—she saw David Greybeard craft a termite twig, forcing science to redefine "human."
clues: Upon reading her telegram about chimpanzee toolmaking, mentor Louis Leakey wired back that humanity must redefine tools, redefine man, or accept chimps as humans.
Cambridge University later admitted her directly into a PhD program without an undergraduate degree.
questions.whyExplanation: Jane Goodall's landmark Gombe Stream study shattered the notion that only humans make tools and transformed primatology and wildlife conservation.

questions.prompt: Braving chemical-industry smears, this marine biologist's 1962 book Silent Spring proved DDT was thinning bald eagle eggshells—igniting modern environmentalism and helping birth the EPA.
clues: Secretly battling breast cancer while testifying before Congress, she had earlier topped bestseller lists with The Sea Around Us.
Her poetic warning of a springtime devoid of birdsong led directly to the 1972 U.S. ban on agricultural DDT.
questions.whyExplanation: Rachel Carson's 1962 book Silent Spring exposed the ecological toll of indiscriminate pesticides like DDT, catalyzing modern environmental regulation.

questions.prompt: After roughly 15 journals rejected her bold 1967 manuscript, this evolutionary maverick convinced modern biology that mitochondria and chloroplasts began as free-living bacteria swallowed by ancient host cells.
clues: Her endosymbiotic theory was clinched once DNA sequencing proved mitochondria carry their own circular bacterial-style genomes.
Once married to Carl Sagan, she later teamed with James Lovelock to co-develop the Gaia hypothesis.
questions.whyExplanation: Lynn Margulis championed serial endosymbiotic theory in 1967, demonstrating that eukaryotic mitochondria and plastids evolved from engulfed symbiotic bacteria.

questions.prompt: Born into Missouri slavery and barred from his first college, this Tuskegee agricultural botanist rescued depleted Southern cotton soils by promoting crop rotation with peanuts and sweet potatoes.
clues: He outfitted a horse-drawn "Jesup Agricultural Wagon" as a rolling classroom to teach sharecroppers soil conservation across Alabama.
Though myth wrongly credits him with inventing peanut butter, he cataloged over 300 commercial uses for legumes to create demand for the crop.
questions.whyExplanation: Tuskegee scientist George Washington Carver promoted crop rotation with nitrogen-fixing peanuts and sweet potatoes to revitalize exhausted Southern farmland.

questions.prompt: Feverish with malaria on Ternate in 1858, this self-taught beetle collector independently cracked natural selection—and drew the faunal boundary dividing Asian monkeys from Australian marsupials.
clues: He lost four years of priceless Amazon specimens when his homeward ship caught fire and sank in the Atlantic in 1852.
His namesake line snakes through the deep Lombok Strait between Bali and Lombok.
questions.whyExplanation: Alfred Russel Wallace co-discovered evolution by natural selection in 1858 and founded evolutionary biogeography, demarcating the famous Wallace Line.

questions.prompt: Blinded in his right eye by a boyhood fishing fin—leaving his left razor-sharp for tiny creatures—this Harvard naturalist became the world's top ant expert and popularized "biodiversity" and "sociobiology."
clues: Two-time Pulitzer Prize winner (for On Human Nature and The Ants), he proposed protecting Half-Earth to halt mass extinction.
Along with Robert MacArthur, he co-authored the classic 1967 Theory of Island Biogeography.
questions.whyExplanation: Harvard myrmecologist Edward O. Wilson won two Pulitzers, pioneered island biogeography and sociobiology, and championed global biodiversity conservation.

questions.prompt: Grinding pinhead-sized glass beads to inspect cloth threads, this self-taught Dutch draper stunned London's Royal Society in the 1670s by spying swimming "animalcules"—bacteria—in rainwater.
clues: He jealously guarded his lens-making secret to the grave, yet his single-lens brass paddles magnified up to 275 times.
He was also the first human ever to witness red blood cells, protozoa, and sperm cells.
questions.whyExplanation: Delft textile merchant Antonie van Leeuwenhoek crafted high-power single-lens microscopes and discovered bacteria and protozoa ("animalcules") in the 1670s.

questions.prompt: The first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate, this Kenyan veterinary anatomist launched the Green Belt Movement in 1977—planting over 50 million trees and winning the 2004 Nobel Peace Prize.
clues: She was beaten and jailed by Daniel arap Moi's regime while defending Nairobi's Uhuru Park from a planned 60-story skyscraper.
Her 2004 Nobel honor made her the first African woman—and first environmentalist—to win the Peace Prize.
questions.whyExplanation: Biologist Wangari Maathai founded Kenya's Green Belt Movement, mobilizing rural women to reforest degraded land and earning the 2004 Nobel Peace Prize.

questions.prompt: Mocked by geologists after 1912 for lacking a driving mechanism, this German meteorologist matched fossil ferns and jigsaw coastlines into Pangaea—before perishing on Greenland's ice sheet.
clues: Before proposing continental drift, he set a 1906 hot-air balloon endurance record of 52 hours aloft with his brother Kurt.
Seafloor-spreading magnetic stripes finally vindicated his theory in the 1960s as plate tectonics.
questions.whyExplanation: Meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift and supercontinent Pangaea in 1912; decades after his 1930 death in Greenland, plate tectonics vindicated him.

questions.prompt: Analyzing a 1909 Croatian earthquake near Zagreb, a seismologist noticed shockwaves suddenly accelerating deep underground—pinpointing this sharp boundary separating Earth's crust from the denser mantle.
clues: Sitting just 5 to 10 kilometers beneath ocean floors yet up to 70 kilometers under Tibet, it was the target of 1960s Project Mohole.
Geologists mercifully shorten this tongue-twisting Croatian boundary name to four letters: the Moho.
questions.whyExplanation: Discovered in 1909 by Andrija Mohorovičić via seismic wave refraction, the Mohorovičić discontinuity (Moho) marks the boundary between Earth's crust and mantle.

questions.prompt: Carved where the ancient Pacific Plate dives beneath a tiny microplate, this western Pacific abyss sinks nearly 11 kilometers—deep enough to drown Mount Everest with over two kilometers of dark water to spare.
clues: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh first reached its Challenger Deep floor in January 1960 aboard the bathyscaphe Trieste.
Film director James Cameron repeated the solo descent in 2012 inside his lime-green Deepsea Challenger.
questions.whyExplanation: The Mariana Trench hosts Challenger Deep (~10,920–10,984 m), the deepest known point in Earth's oceans, first reached by Trieste in 1960.

questions.prompt: Taking its Greek name from "turning" because relentless convection churns clouds inside it, this lowest atmospheric layer packs nearly 80 percent of Earth's air mass and virtually all weather.
clues: Unlike the ozone-warmed layer directly above it, air here generally cools by about 6.5 degrees Celsius for every kilometer you climb.
Stretching roughly 18 kilometers thick at the equator and barely 8 at the poles, it ends at the jet-stream-lined tropopause.
questions.whyExplanation: The troposphere (Greek tropos, "turning") is Earth's lowest atmospheric layer, containing roughly 75–80 percent of total atmospheric mass and almost all weather.

questions.prompt: Stretching 40,000 kilometers like a tectonic horseshoe around the Pacific basin, this arc of subduction trenches generates roughly 75 percent of Earth's active volcanoes and 90 percent of its earthquakes.
clues: It stitches together Mount Fuji, Mount St. Helens, Pinatubo, Krakatoa, and the towering Andean stratovolcanoes.
Johnny Cash sang a famous 1963 hit sharing this exact fiery three-word phrase.
questions.whyExplanation: The Pacific Ring of Fire is a 40,000-kilometer arc of convergent plate boundaries responsible for the vast majority of Earth's earthquakes and active volcanism.

questions.prompt: Spotting faint echoes from a 1929 New Zealand quake inside a textbook "shadow zone," this Danish seismologist proved in 1936 that Earth hides a solid inner core inside its molten metal.
clues: She titled her groundbreaking 1936 paper with the shortest title in geophysics history—just two characters: P'.
Living to age 104, she was later honored with the American Geophysical Union's prestigious medal for Earth-mantle and core studies.
questions.whyExplanation: Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann inferred Earth's solid inner core in 1936 by explaining anomalous P-wave reflections from the 1929 Murchison earthquake.

questions.prompt: Computed by hand by a Serbian civil engineer—partly while interned in Budapest during World War I—these slow periodic shifts in Earth's orbital stretch, tilt, and wobble pace the rhythm of Ice Ages.
clues: They combine a 100,000-year eccentricity pulse, a 41,000-year axial obliquity nod, and a 26,000-year precession wobble.
Deep-sea sediment cores analyzed in 1976 confirmed these astronomical rhythms steer Pleistocene glaciations.
questions.whyExplanation: Milutin Milanković calculated how periodic changes in Earth's eccentricity, axial tilt, and precession alter high-latitude sunlight and pace Ice Age cycles.

questions.prompt: Triggered roughly 2.4 billion years ago by photosynthetic cyanobacteria, this planetary upheaval rusted ocean iron into banded rock strata and poisoned anaerobic microbes with free O2.
clues: Stripping heat-trapping methane from the early air, it ushered in the 300-million-year Huronian glaciation.
Also called the Oxygen Catastrophe, it simultaneously paved the way for complex oxygen-breathing eukaryotes—and eventually us.
questions.whyExplanation: The Great Oxidation Event (~2.4 Ga) marked the rise of biologically produced O2 in Earth's atmosphere, transforming geology, climate, and the trajectory of life.

questions.prompt: Named by Peruvian fishermen for the Christ Child because warm Pacific waters rolled in around Christmas, this ocean-atmosphere reversal chokes South American fisheries and scrambles weather worldwide.
clues: When Pacific trade winds slacken, pooled warm water sloshes eastward toward Ecuador, dampening Atlantic hurricanes while drenching California.
Paired with its cool counterpart, it forms the warm phase of the climate oscillation abbreviated ENSO.
questions.whyExplanation: El Niño (Spanish for "the little boy," referring to the Christ Child) is the warm phase of ENSO, weakening Pacific trade winds and reshaping global weather.

questions.prompt: Built in 1812 from ten everyday scratch-test benchmarks running from soapy talc to diamond, this Austrian geologist's ranking is strictly ordinal—corundum at 9 is nowhere near nine-tenths as hard as 10.
clues: A human fingernail registers around 2.5, a copper penny about 3.5, and common window glass sits near 5.5 on this geologist's yardstick.
Quartz holds rank 7 and topaz holds rank 8 on this classic mineral-identification ladder.
questions.whyExplanation: Friedrich Mohs created his 1-to-10 scratch hardness scale in 1812 (talc=1 to diamond=10); its steps are relative rather than linear in absolute indentation hardness.

questions.prompt: Hidden beneath Yucatán limestone until oil-survey gravity maps and flooded cenote rings gave it away, this 180-kilometer scar marks the asteroid strike that ended the Cretaceous.
clues: Geophysicists Glen Penfield and Antonio Camargo noticed its concentric underwater arcs in 1978, linking it to the global iridium layer a decade later.
Its Mayan name—borrowed from a nearby coastal Mexican town—is often translated whimsically as "tail of the devil."
questions.whyExplanation: The 180-kilometer Chicxulub crater in Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula preserves the impact of the ~10 km asteroid that triggered the end-Cretaceous mass extinction.

questions.prompt: Calculated by a Hungarian-American aerospace theorist as the altitude where air grows too thin for airplane wings to generate lift below orbital speed, this 100-kilometer threshold divides sky from outer space.
clues: Recognized by the international aviation body FAI (though the U.S. Air Force uses 50 miles), crossing it earns private passengers astronaut wings.
It is named for Jet Propulsion Laboratory co-founder Theodore von ...
questions.whyExplanation: Named after aerodynamicist Theodore von Kármán, the Kármán line at 100 kilometers (62 miles) altitude is the standard international boundary of outer space.

questions.prompt: Split into two peninsulas bridged since 1957 by the Mackinac Strait's five-mile suspension span, which U.S. state touches four of the five Great Lakes?
clues: Its Upper Peninsula was awarded in 1837 to settle the bloodless Toledo Strip dispute with Ohio.
Its Lower Peninsula famously resembles a mitten bounded by Lakes Huron, Erie, and its namesake inland sea.
questions.whyExplanation: Michigan comprises both Upper and Lower Peninsulas linked by the Mackinac Bridge and borders Lakes Superior, Michigan, Huron, and Erie—missing only Lake Ontario.

questions.prompt: Cut off from North America's highway grid by glaciers and steep fjords, which mainland U.S. state capital can be reached only by airplane or ferry?
clues: Founded during an 1880 gold rush along the Gastineau Channel, it replaced Sitka as territorial seat in 1906.
By land area, this Panhandle municipality is larger than the entire state of Delaware.
questions.whyExplanation: Hemmed in by the Coast Mountains and vast icefields, Juneau has no road link to the rest of Alaska or Canada, forcing every visitor and vehicle to arrive by air or sea.

questions.prompt: Thanks to California's sharp southeastward slant, this neon-lit Silver State casino city lies roughly 100 miles farther west in longitude than Los Angeles.
clues: Its famous downtown arch has long billed it as 'The Biggest Little City in the World.'
Perched along the Truckee River just east of Lake Tahoe, it became a 1930s capital of quick six-week divorces.
questions.whyExplanation: Reno sits at about 119.8° W longitude, noticeably west of Los Angeles at 118.2° W, because the Pacific coast bends steeply southeast from Cape Mendocino.

questions.prompt: Perched 90 miles from Havana—closer to Cuba's capital than to Miami—which coral-island U.S. city marks the end of U.S. Route 1?
clues: In 1982 its residents staged a tongue-in-cheek secession as the 'Conch Republic' to protest a Border Patrol roadblock.
Ernest Hemingway kept six-toed cats at his Whitehead Street house near the continental U.S. Southernmost Point buoy.
questions.whyExplanation: Connected to the mainland by the Overseas Highway, Key West sits at the western end of the Florida Keys, roughly 90 miles north of Havana and 126 miles southwest of Miami.

questions.prompt: Quoddy Head's eastward jut makes this pine-covered state both the U.S. state closest to Africa and the only one bordering just a single other state.
clues: Its sole land border with another U.S. state runs along the Piscataqua River and New Hampshire.
Entered the Union in 1820 under the Missouri Compromise after splitting off from Massachusetts.
questions.whyExplanation: On a globe, Quoddy Head in Maine lies roughly 3,154 miles from El Beddouza, Morocco—hundreds of miles closer than Florida—and Maine touches only New Hampshire domestically.

questions.prompt: Nicknamed 'The Equality State' after its 1869 territorial legislature granted women full suffrage, which least-populous U.S. state forms a near-perfect latitude-longitude rectangle?
clues: In 1925 it inaugurated Nellie Tayloe Ross as the first female state governor in U.S. history.
Bounded strictly by meridians and parallels, its northwest corner holds most of Yellowstone.
questions.whyExplanation: Wyoming's territorial council legalized women's voting and officeholding in 1869, decades before the 19th Amendment, and its population remains the smallest of all 50 states.

questions.prompt: Born as 'Losantiville' in 1788, which Ohio River metropolis was renamed two years later for a Revolutionary officers' society honoring a Roman farmer-general?
clues: Territorial Governor Arthur St. Clair chose the classical name honoring Lucius Quinctius, who relinquished dictatorial power.
Its 19th-century meatpacking boom earned it the nickname 'Porkopolis' across the river from Covington, Kentucky.
questions.whyExplanation: Arthur St. Clair renamed Losantiville in 1790 after the Society of the Cincinnati, an organization of Continental Army officers named for Roman statesman Cincinnatus.

questions.prompt: Honoring a southern French city for Revolutionary War aid, which least-populous U.S. state capital is famously the only one without a McDonald's?
clues: Fewer than 8,500 residents live around its gold-domed granite State House along the Winooski River.
Its spelling drops one 'l' compared to the historic Languedoc university city in southern France.
questions.whyExplanation: With around 8,000 residents, Montpelier is the smallest U.S. state capital by population and remains the only state capital lacking a McDonald's franchise.

questions.prompt: Lying closer to San Diego than to Houston, which Rio Grande border metropolis is the largest Texas city operating on Mountain Time instead of Central Time?
clues: Framed by the Franklin Mountains, it forms a single binational urban basin with Ciudad Juárez.
Spanish explorers called the gap between two mountain ranges here 'the pass of the north.'
questions.whyExplanation: Positioned at Texas's far western tip, El Paso sits roughly 725 miles from San Diego versus 745 miles from Houston and uses Mountain Time alongside neighboring New Mexico.

questions.prompt: Sitting 2,342 miles from the Atlantic via the St. Lawrence Seaway, which Minnesota city shares the world's farthest-inland port accessible to oceangoing ships?
clues: Freighters hauling taconite iron ore pass beneath its iconic 1905 Aerial Lift Bridge at the tip of Lake Superior.
It faces its Wisconsin twin port, Superior, across a natural sandbar harbor on St. Louis Bay.
questions.whyExplanation: At the westernmost tip of Lake Superior, the Twin Ports of Duluth and Superior allow saltwater freighters to sail over 2,300 miles inland from the Atlantic Ocean.

questions.prompt: Stranded below the 49th parallel on Canada's Tsawwassen Peninsula, which Washington pene-exclave forces high-schoolers to cross international borders four times a day?
clues: Created by the 1846 Oregon Treaty's straight-line border, it covers just five square miles south of Vancouver.
Residents driving to the rest of Whatcom County must pass through British Columbia twice each round trip.
questions.whyExplanation: Because the 49th parallel sliced off the tip of the Tsawwassen Peninsula in 1846, Point Roberts is a U.S. community reachable by land only via British Columbia, Canada.

questions.prompt: Anchored on wooden alder piles driven across 118 marshy lagoon islands, which Adriatic city replaced roads with 150 canals linked by over 400 footbridges?
clues: Its S-shaped Grand Canal is crossed by the 16th-century Rialto Bridge and traversed by vaporetti.
Once the maritime 'Most Serene Republic,' its Piazza San Marco routinely floods during winter acqua alta tides.
questions.whyExplanation: Built atop dense timber pilings in a sheltered Adriatic lagoon, Venice grew into a maritime superpower whose 118 islands are tied together by canals and stone bridges.

questions.prompt: Named for 'Fair Winds' by 16th-century Spanish mariners, which South American capital gave birth to tango along the western shore of the Río de la Plata?
clues: Its colorful La Boca dockside quarter and wide Avenida 9 de Julio reflect waves of Italian and Spanish immigration.
The broad estuary fronting this Argentine metropolis separates it directly from Uruguay.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded as Nuestra Señora Santa María del Buen Ayre, Buenos Aires flourished on the Río de la Plata estuary and forged tango in its late-19th-century port neighborhoods.

questions.prompt: Norse settlers dubbed this harbor 'Smoky Bay' after seeing geothermal steam rise from hot springs; today it is the world's northernmost sovereign capital.
clues: Sitting near 64° N latitude on Faxaflói Bay, it heats nearly all of its homes and sidewalks with volcanic water.
Ingólfur Arnarson established Iceland's first permanent settlement here around 874 CE.
questions.whyExplanation: At 64°08' N, Reykjavik ('Smoky Bay' in Old Norse) is the northernmost capital of any independent country, outranking Helsinki and Oslo while Nuuk governs autonomous Greenland.

questions.prompt: Built in just 41 months to shift a nation's gravity inland, which planned capital was laid out by Lúcio Costa to resemble an airplane—or a soaring bird?
clues: Oscar Niemeyer designed its sweeping white-concrete cathedral, National Congress bowls, and presidential palace.
Inaugurated on April 21, 1960, it replaced coastal Rio de Janeiro as federal capital.
questions.whyExplanation: Conceived by President Juscelino Kubitschek, Brasília was carved out of central Brazil's highlands in under four years and remains the only 20th-century city listed by UNESCO.

questions.prompt: Circling a three-peaked hill Jacques Cartier named Mount Royal in 1535, which island metropolis hides a 32-kilometer climate-controlled underground city called RÉSO?
clues: Sitting at the confluence of the St. Lawrence and Ottawa rivers, it hosted Expo 67 and the 1976 Summer Olympics.
Its cobblestone Old Port and French-speaking majority make it Quebec's economic powerhouse.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded as Ville-Marie on an island in the St. Lawrence River, Montreal built its vast underground pedestrian network to connect metro stations and towers during harsh Canadian winters.

questions.prompt: Sprawling across an Andean valley 2,850 meters above sea level, which South American capital lies just 25 kilometers south of the Equator beneath Pichincha volcano?
clues: Visitors drive minutes north of downtown to straddle the Mitad del Mundo monument at zero degrees latitude.
Its intact Spanish colonial center was among the very first UNESCO World Heritage Sites designated in 1978.
questions.whyExplanation: Ecuador's constitutional capital, Quito is the world's second-highest capital city (behind Sucre/La Paz) and sits practically astride the Equator in the Andes.

questions.prompt: Long isolated as a coastal Croatian exclave cut off by Bosnia's Neum corridor until 2022, which walled Adriatic gem once ruled as the Republic of Ragusa?
clues: Its limestone Stradun promenade and terracotta roofs doubled as King's Landing in HBO's Game of Thrones.
The 2.4-kilometer Pelješac Bridge finally linked this 'Pearl of the Adriatic' directly to mainland Croatia.
questions.whyExplanation: Known historically as the maritime Republic of Ragusa, Dubrovnik's medieval walls overlook the Adriatic and were reunited overland with the rest of Croatia by the 2022 Pelješac Bridge.

questions.prompt: Laid out by Inca planners in the silhouette of a crouching puma, which high-altitude Peruvian city takes its Quechua name from a word meaning 'navel of the world'?
clues: Spanish builders raised the Convent of Santo Domingo directly atop the mortarless stone walls of its Coricancha sun temple.
Travelers acclimatize at 3,400 meters here before boarding trains through the Sacred Valley toward Machu Picchu.
questions.whyExplanation: Capital of the Tawantinsuyu empire, Cusco was rebuilt under Pachacuti in the shape of a sacred puma, with the fortress Sacsayhuamán forming its head and zig-zagging teeth.

questions.prompt: Tucked between the Martial Mountains and the Beagle Channel on Tierra del Fuego, which Argentine port serves as the main launchpad for Antarctic cruises?
clues: Beginning in 1896, Argentina built a notorious maximum-security penal colony here to cement its Patagonian claim.
Lying below 54° S latitude, it markets itself globally as 'El Fin del Mundo'—the southernmost city on Earth.
questions.whyExplanation: Situated on Tierra del Fuego's southern coast along the Beagle Channel, Ushuaia grew around a former Argentine prison and is now the world's primary gateway to the Antarctic Peninsula.

questions.prompt: Perched above 4,000 meters beneath the silver-veined Cerro Rico, which Bolivian boomtown rivaled London and Paris in population around 1600?
clues: Its royal mint struck millions of Spanish 'pieces of eight' that circulated from Europe to Ming China.
The Spanish idiom 'valer un...' still means 'to be worth a fortune' in memory of this Andean mountain's ore.
questions.whyExplanation: After silver was discovered in Cerro Rico in 1545, Potosí swelled past 160,000 inhabitants, funding the Habsburg Empire at immense human cost to Indigenous forced laborers.

questions.prompt: Once Prussian Königsberg—where Kant never left home and Euler solved the Seven Bridges puzzle—which Baltic port now anchors a Russian exclave between Poland and Lithuania?
clues: Annexed by the Soviet Union after the 1945 Potsdam Conference, it was renamed for the long-serving Chairman of the Supreme Soviet.
Sitting on the Pregolya River, it provides Russia's Baltic Fleet with a vital ice-free naval outpost.
questions.whyExplanation: Formerly East Prussia's capital Königsberg, it was renamed for Mikhail Kalinin in 1946 and became a detached Russian Baltic exclave after Lithuania's 1990 independence.

questions.prompt: Straddling the Bosporus Strait between the Black Sea and the Sea of Marmara, which megacity is the world's premier metropolis spanning both Europe and Asia?
clues: Known successively as Byzantium and Constantinople, it served as capital of the Roman, Byzantine, and Ottoman empires.
Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque crown its historic European peninsula overlooking the Golden Horn.
questions.whyExplanation: Istanbul occupies both the European Thracian shore and the Asian Anatolian shore of the Bosporus, making it the historic bridge between two continents and two seas.

questions.prompt: Japan's imperial seat for over a thousand years until the 1868 Meiji Restoration, which city of 1,600 Buddhist temples bears a name literally meaning 'Capital City'?
clues: Founded in 794 CE as Heian-kyō, its vermilion Fushimi Inari torii gates and golden Kinkaku-ji survived World War II intact.
In 1997 international delegates met here to adopt a landmark climate protocol curbing greenhouse emissions.
questions.whyExplanation: Established in 794 CE as Heian-kyō, Kyoto remained Japan's imperial residence until Emperor Meiji moved to Tokyo ('Eastern Capital') in 1868.

questions.prompt: Carved out of New South Wales sheep pastures in 1913 to end a bitter feud between Sydney and Melbourne, which planned city sits around man-made Lake Burley Griffin?
clues: Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin won the global competition to design its geometric avenues.
Its 1988 Parliament House is tucked beneath a grass-covered hillside topped by a towering stainless-steel flagpole.
questions.whyExplanation: Australia's Constitution mandated a federal capital at least 100 miles from Sydney; Canberra was chosen in 1908 as the inland compromise between Sydney and Melbourne.

questions.prompt: Its Sanskrit-derived name means 'Lion City'—even though lions never roamed the Malay Peninsula—for which sovereign island port guarding the Strait of Malacca?
clues: Sir Stamford Raffles established a British trading post here in 1819; it became independent after leaving Malaysia in 1965.
Its waterfront mascot, the Merlion, pairs a feline head with a fish tail near Marina Bay.
questions.whyExplanation: According to the Malay Annals, Prince Sang Nila Utama named the island Singapura ('Lion City') after mistaking a Malayan tiger or mythical beast for a lion around 1299.

questions.prompt: Funneling Roaring Forties gales through the Cook Strait earned which New Zealand harbor the title of world's southernmost capital of a sovereign nation?
clues: Perched at the southern tip of the North Island, it houses New Zealand's Beehive executive parliament building.
Replaced Auckland as national capital in 1865 for its central location between the North and South Islands.
questions.whyExplanation: At 41°17' S latitude on Cook Strait, Wellington is the southernmost sovereign national capital—farther south than Canberra, Buenos Aires, or Montevideo—and famously windy.

questions.prompt: Known historically as Kashi and Benares, which sacred Indian city lines the western curve of the Ganges with more than 80 stone riverfront steps called ghats?
clues: Its name derives from two tributary rivers, the Varuna and the Assi, that flank its ancient Uttar Pradesh core.
Hindu pilgrims travel here to bathe at Dashashwamedh Ghat and attend evening Ganga Aarti fire rituals.
questions.whyExplanation: One of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, Varanasi is Hinduism's holiest pilgrimage center along the Ganges, renowned for its riverside ghats and silk weaving.

questions.prompt: Formerly Tang Dynasty Chang'an at the eastern mouth of the Silk Road, which Shaanxi metropolis hit headlines in 1974 when well-diggers uncovered 8,000 clay soldiers?
clues: Ringed by intact 14th-century Ming fortifications, it was the capital of 13 imperial Chinese dynasties.
Qin Shi Huang's buried Terracotta Army stands guard roughly 35 kilometers east of its historic Drum Tower.
questions.whyExplanation: Ancient Chang'an—modern Xi'an—anchored the eastern Silk Road and lies near Emperor Qin Shi Huang's mausoleum, where farmers accidentally discovered the Terracotta Warriors in 1974.

questions.prompt: Timur transformed this Uzbek oasis into his glittering 14th-century capital, crowned today by the three turquoise-tiled madrasas surrounding Registan Square.
clues: Timur's astronomer-grandson Ulugh Beg built a giant marble sextant observatory on a hill at its edge in the 1420s.
Alexander the Great marveled at this Silk Road crossroads in 329 BCE when it was known as Marakanda.
questions.whyExplanation: Positioned in Uzbekistan's Zeravshan River valley, Samarkand thrived as a premier Silk Road crossroads and was rebuilt into an architectural showcase under Timur and Ulugh Beg.

questions.prompt: Drivers in this Himalayan valley capital still rely on a white-gloved police officer inside an ornate pagoda booth, because residents rejected its sole traffic light in 1995.
clues: Sitting at 2,334 meters along the Raidāk River, it replaced Punakha as Bhutan's permanent capital in 1961.
Its giant golden Buddha Dordenma gazes across the valley toward the fortress-monastery Tashichho Dzong.
questions.whyExplanation: Bhutan's capital, Thimphu, briefly installed a traffic signal in 1995 before removing it after citizens complained it felt impersonal, restoring hand-directed traffic at the main intersection.

questions.prompt: Unveiled secretly in 2005 with surreal 20-lane boulevards and a replica Shwedagon Pagoda, which planned city abruptly replaced Yangon as Myanmar's capital?
clues: Carved from rural scrubland 320 kilometers north of the coast, its Burmese name translates to 'Abode of the King.'
Covering over 7,000 square kilometers—more than four times Greater London—its ministries sit widely dispersed.
questions.whyExplanation: Myanmar's military junta unexpectedly shifted ministries north from Yangon to Naypyidaw in November 2005, creating one of the world's most expansive yet sparsely populated capitals.

questions.prompt: Where January highs average minus 38 degrees Celsius and apartment blocks stand on concrete stilts to keep from melting permafrost, which Siberian port crowns the Lena River?
clues: Capital of Russia's vast Sakha Republic, it sits near the world's richest diamond-mining basin.
Its summer temperatures can top 30°C, giving it one of the widest annual temperature swings of any city on Earth.
questions.whyExplanation: Built entirely on continuous permafrost along the Lena River, Yakutsk is widely recognized as the coldest major city on Earth, requiring elevated foundations and heated utility pipes.

questions.prompt: Founded by Fatimid conquerors in 969 CE as 'Al-Qahirah'—'The Victorious'—which Nile metropolis sits just south of where Africa's longest river fans into its delta?
clues: Its medieval Al-Azhar mosque and university remain among the foremost centers of Sunni Islamic scholarship.
Across the Nile's western bank, its urban sprawl reaches right to the footsteps of the Great Pyramids of Giza.
questions.whyExplanation: Established in 969 CE near the older garrison town of Fustat, Cairo sits at the apex of the Nile Delta and has grown into the Arab world's most populous urban area.

questions.l2Subcategory: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.prompt: So remote to 19th-century Europeans that its name became English shorthand for the ends of the Earth, which Malian desert city once housed hundreds of thousands of manuscripts?
clues: Perched 20 kilometers north of the Niger River, it grew wealthy swapping Saharan rock salt for West African gold.
Its mud-brick Sankore, Djinguereber, and Sidi Yahya mosques formed a renowned medieval center of Islamic learning.
questions.whyExplanation: During Mali's and Songhai's golden ages, Timbuktu's libraries preserved astronomy, law, and poetry manuscripts; its mythologized isolation made its name synonymous with faraway places.

questions.l2Subcategory: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.prompt: Cradled inside a natural stone amphitheater below flat-topped Table Mountain, which coastal metropolis serves as South Africa's legislative capital?
clues: Founded by Jan van Riebeeck in 1652 as a Dutch East India Company supply station en route to Asia.
Offshore in its bay lies Robben Island, where Nelson Mandela spent 18 of his 27 years in prison.
questions.whyExplanation: South Africa splits its national branches across three cities: Pretoria (executive), Bloemfontein (judicial), and Cape Town (legislative), watched over by Table Mountain.

questions.l2Category: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.l2Subcategory: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.prompt: Carved straight into rose-pink sandstone cliffs by Nabataean caravan masters, which hidden Jordanian city greets visitors through a narrow gorge called the Siq?
clues: Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt reintroduced its rock-cut Treasury (Al-Khazneh) to the West in 1812.
Its engineers built flash-flood dams and ceramic cisterns to supply water in the arid mountains south of the Dead Sea.
questions.whyExplanation: Nicknamed the 'Rose City,' Petra served as the wealthy Nabataean kingdom's capital from roughly the 4th century BCE until Roman annexation and shifting trade routes eclipsed it.

questions.l2Category: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.l2Subcategory: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.prompt: Empress Taytu Betul named this 2,355-meter-high Ethiopian capital 'New Flower' in 1886; today its avenues host the headquarters of the African Union.
clues: Resting at the foot of Mount Entoto, it is Africa's highest national capital by elevation.
Its National Museum houses the 3.2-million-year-old fossil skeleton of Australopithecus afarensis known as Lucy.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded by Emperor Menelik II and Empress Taytu near geothermal springs in 1886, Addis Ababa became the diplomatic capital of Africa when the OAU—now the African Union—opened there in 1963.

questions.l2Category: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.l2Subcategory: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.prompt: Behind its blue Bab Bou Jeloud gate lies the world's largest car-free urban zone—a labyrinth of 9,000 alleys where Fatima al-Fihri founded al-Qarawiyyin in 859 CE.
clues: Donkeys and handcarts still haul hides to its open-air Chouara Tannery vats inside this Moroccan imperial city.
A cylindrical red felt cap worn across the late Ottoman Empire took its name from this Maghreb craft center.
questions.whyExplanation: Fez's walled medina, Fes el-Bali, remains completely pedestrianized and houses the University of al-Qarawiyyin, recognized by UNESCO as the oldest continually operating degree-granting university.

questions.l2Category: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.l2Subcategory: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.prompt: Gazing across a four-kilometer stretch of the Congo River directly at Brazzaville, which megacity forms half of the world's closest pair of sovereign capitals?
clues: Called Léopoldville until 1966, it surpassed Paris to become the world's largest Francophone metropolitan area.
In October 1974 its Stade Tata Raphaël staged Muhammad Ali and George Foreman's 'Rumble in the Jungle.'
questions.whyExplanation: Separated from the Republic of the Congo's capital Brazzaville only by the wide Malebo Pool of the Congo River, Kinshasa is the Democratic Republic of the Congo's booming capital.

questions.l2Category: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.l2Subcategory: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.prompt: Safavid Shah Abbas I made this central Iranian jewel so splendid that Persians coined the rhyming boast 'Nesf-e Jahan'—literally 'Half the World.'
clues: Its colossal Naqsh-e Jahan Square is framed by the cobalt Shah Mosque, Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque, and Ali Qapu Palace.
Thirty-three arched bays carry the Si-o-se-pol bridge across its seasonal Zayanderud River.
questions.whyExplanation: After Shah Abbas I moved the Safavid capital to Isfahan in 1598, its tiled mosques, bazaars, and bridges earned it the enduring Persian epithet 'Isfahan is half the world.'

questions.l2Category: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.l2Subcategory: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.prompt: Guarded by the 16th-century Portuguese twin forts Al-Jalali and Al-Mirani, which whitewashed Gulf of Oman port commands the approach to the Strait of Hormuz?
clues: Strict civic laws forbid garish skyscrapers here, keeping Oman's capital framed by jagged dark volcanic hills.
Its waterfront Muttrah Souq has traded frankincense, spices, and curved khanjar daggers for centuries.
questions.whyExplanation: Nestled in a sheltered rocky cove on the Gulf of Oman, Muscat was fortified by the Portuguese in the 1580s and remains the low-rise, historic capital of the Sultanate of Oman.

questions.l2Category: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.l2Subcategory: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.prompt: Built virtually from scratch in the mid-1960s so newly independent Botswana would no longer be governed from Mafikeng across the border in South Africa, what is its capital?
clues: Named for a 19th-century Batlokwa chief, it sits beside the Notwane River just 15 kilometers from South Africa.
Before 1965, the Bechuanaland Protectorate was one of the rare territories administered from a capital outside its own borders.
questions.whyExplanation: Because colonial Bechuanaland was administered from Mafikeng inside South Africa, Botswana constructed Gaborone in 1964–1966 to serve as its sovereign domestic capital.

questions.l2Category: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.l2Subcategory: Cities of Africa & the Middle East
questions.prompt: Taking its Berber name from 'place of the winds,' which Saharan Atlantic capital grew from a tiny fishing village after Mauritania chose it over Senegal-based Saint-Louis in 1958?
clues: Designed initially for 15,000 people, it swelled past a million after severe 1970s Sahel droughts pushed nomads coastward.
Sand dunes constantly encroach on its eastern avenues while colorful wooden pirogues crowd its Atlantic fish beach.
questions.whyExplanation: Like Botswana, colonial Mauritania was run from outside its borders—in Saint-Louis, Senegal—prompting leaders to build Nouakchott from scratch along the windswept Atlantic coast starting in 1958.

questions.prompt: Revered in Tibetan as Chomolungma and in Nepali as Sagarmatha, which Himalayan giant was fixed at 8,848.86 meters by a joint China-Nepal survey in 2020?
clues: The British Great Trigonometrical Survey initially labeled it Peak XV before naming it for retired Surveyor General George.
Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay first stood on its summit ridge on May 29, 1953.
questions.whyExplanation: Earth's highest mountain above sea level, Mount Everest sits on the Nepal-Tibet frontier and was officially recalibrated to 8,848.86 meters in December 2020.

questions.prompt: Carved by glaciers into four razor-sharp faces above Zermatt, which pyramidal Alpine peak graced Toblerone chocolate bars until 2023 and claimed four lives on its 1865 first ascent?
clues: Known as Monte Cervino on its Italian side, its silhouette rises 4,478 meters along the Pennine Alps frontier.
British illustrator Edward Whymper survived when a hemp rope snapped during the descent from his historic triumph.
questions.whyExplanation: Straddling the Swiss-Italian border, the Matterhorn's iconic chiseled horn was first climbed by Edward Whymper's party on July 14, 1865, in a triumph marred by a fatal fall.

questions.prompt: Modern alpinism was born on August 8, 1786, when crystal hunter Jacques Balmat and doctor Michel-Gabriel Paccard summited which 4,806-meter Western European roof?
clues: Swiss scientist Horace-Bénédict de Saussure offered a cash prize to whoever first reached its snow-capped dome.
An 11.6-kilometer road tunnel bores straight beneath its granite massif to link Chamonix, France, with Courmayeur, Italy.
questions.whyExplanation: Rising above Chamonix on the French-Italian border, Mont Blanc is Western Europe's highest mountain, and its 1786 conquest ignited mountaineering as a formal pursuit.

questions.prompt: Still answering to an 1856 survey notation because it stood too remote for a single local name, which 8,611-meter Karakoram pyramid earned the dread epithet 'Savage Mountain'?
clues: Lying on the Pakistan-China border, it was first summited in July 1954 by Italians Achille Compagnoni and Lino Lacedelli.
It remained the very last 8,000-meter peak to be climbed in winter until a Nepali team succeeded in January 2021.
questions.whyExplanation: Surveyor Thomas Montgomerie labeled Karakoram's peaks K1, K2, and so on from afar; K2—Earth's second-highest peak—kept its alphanumeric code and fierce climbing reputation.

questions.prompt: Topping out at 6,961 meters in Argentina's Mendoza province, which Andean titan is both the highest peak outside Asia and the tallest mountain in the Western Hemisphere?
clues: Unlike many neighboring Andean giants, it is a tectonic uplifted massif rather than an active or dormant volcano.
Swiss guide Matthias Zurbriggen completed its first recorded ascent in January 1897 near the Chilean frontier.
questions.whyExplanation: Rising 6,961 meters in Argentina's Principal Cordillera, Aconcagua is the highest summit in both the Americas and the Southern Hemisphere and one of the Seven Summits.

questions.prompt: Climbers nicknamed its sheer 1,800-meter North Face 'Mordwand'—'Murder Wall'—before a German-Austrian quartet finally scaled which Bernese Alps peak in July 1938?
clues: Standing beside the Mönch and Jungfrau above Grindelwald, its name translates loosely to 'Ogre.'
A cogwheel railway tunnels right inside its limestone flank, letting tourists peer through cliffside windows.
questions.whyExplanation: Though only 3,967 meters tall, the Eiger's concave, storm-swept North Face defied mountaineers for years until Anderl Heckmair, Ludwig Vörg, Heinrich Harrer, and Fritz Kasparek climbed it in 1938.

questions.prompt: Polish explorer Paweł Strzelecki named mainland Australia's 2,228-meter high point in 1840 after a compatriot who designed West Point's Revolutionary War defenses.
clues: Its gently rounded Snowy Mountains summit can be reached on foot along a nine-kilometer boardwalk trail.
When surveys later proved a neighbor was taller, New South Wales simply swapped the two peaks' names so the hero kept the crown.
questions.whyExplanation: Strzelecki named Australia's highest mainland peak for Polish-American hero Tadeusz Kościuszko because its profile reminded him of the Kościuszko Mound in Kraków.

questions.prompt: Three years before Everest fell, French climbers Maurice Herzog and Louis Lachenal braved frostbite in June 1950 to make which 8,091-meter Nepali peak the first 8,000er ever summited?
clues: Named for a Hindu goddess of harvest and plenty, it remains among the deadliest of the fourteen 8,000-meter summits.
Herzog dictated his bestselling mountaineering memoir from a hospital bed after losing all his fingers and toes on the descent.
questions.whyExplanation: On June 3, 1950, Maurice Herzog and Louis Lachenal reached the 8,091-meter top of Annapurna I, achieving the first human ascent of any peak exceeding 8,000 meters.

questions.prompt: Unspotted until a 1958 U.S. Navy reconnaissance flight over the Ellsworth Mountains, which 4,892-meter peak completes the Seven Summits as Antarctica's highest point?
clues: It honors a long-serving Georgia congressman who championed U.S. naval power and Antarctic exploration.
American mountaineer Nicholas Clinch led the ten-man team that first stood on its frigid crest in December 1966.
questions.whyExplanation: Named after U.S. Representative Carl Vinson, Vinson Massif rises 4,892 meters in Antarctica's Sentinel Range, roughly 1,200 kilometers from the South Pole.

questions.prompt: Known also as Carstensz Pyramid after a Dutch navigator mocked for claiming he saw equatorial snow in 1623, which 4,884-meter New Guinea spire is Earth's highest island summit?
clues: Rising in Indonesia's Papua province, its limestone wall is the technical climbing alternative to Kosciuszko in the Seven Summits.
Its vanishing equatorial glaciers sit just four degrees south of the Equator near the colossal Grasberg mine.
questions.whyExplanation: At 4,884 meters in western New Guinea, Puncak Jaya (Carstensz Pyramid) is the tallest mountain on any island on Earth and the highest peak in Oceania.

questions.prompt: Because Bhutan banned mountaineering above 6,000 meters out of spiritual respect in 1994, which 7,570-meter Himalayan peak remains the highest unclimbed mountain on Earth?
clues: Its Dzongkha name translates to 'White Peak of the Three Spiritual Brothers' along the Bhutan-Tibet frontier.
Four international expeditions in 1985 and 1986 were turned back by blizzards and ridges before the royal ban sealed its summit.
questions.whyExplanation: Following Bhutan's 1994 ban on climbing peaks over 6,000 meters—and a total mountaineering ban in 2003—7,570-meter Gangkhar Puensum stands as the world's highest untouched mountain.

questions.prompt: Banished from Iceland for manslaughter around 982 CE, Erik the Red gave this ice-capped landmass an enticingly verdant name to lure Norse colonists across the North Atlantic.
clues: Covered roughly 80 percent by an ice sheet up to three kilometers thick, it is Earth's largest non-continental island.
An autonomous territory of Denmark, its capital Nuuk sits near the mouth of a sprawling southwest fjord.
questions.whyExplanation: According to Icelandic sagas, Erik the Red dubbed the Arctic giant Greenland hoping a pleasant name would persuade settlers to follow him; geographically it is the world's largest island.

questions.prompt: Drifting free of Gondwana roughly 88 million years ago turned which fourth-largest island on Earth into an evolutionary ark where all wild lemurs live exclusively?
clues: Separated from Mozambique by a 400-kilometer Indian Ocean channel, its red laterite soils earned it the 'Great Red Island' nickname.
Its first human settlers arrived not from nearby mainland Africa, but by outrigger canoes from Borneo across the Indian Ocean.
questions.whyExplanation: Isolated from mainland Africa and India for tens of millions of years, Madagascar evolved extraordinary endemism—over 90 percent of its wildlife, including every wild lemur species, occurs nowhere else.

questions.prompt: Cold Humboldt Current upwellings allow penguins to nest right on the Equator in which volcanic Ecuadorian archipelago visited by HMS Beagle in 1835?
clues: Spanish sailors named the chain after its giant saddle-backed tortoises, whose shell shapes varied island by island.
Charles Darwin's study of its mockingbirds and finches helped crystallize his theory of natural selection.
questions.whyExplanation: Lying roughly 1,000 kilometers off Ecuador's coast, the Galápagos Islands are cooled by the Humboldt and Cromwell Currents, enabling equatorial penguins alongside marine iguanas and giant tortoises.

questions.prompt: Earth's third-largest island holds a unique political distinction: which rainforest-draped landmass is the only island shared by three sovereign nations?
clues: Indonesia administers its southern Kalimantan provinces, while Malaysia governs Sabah and Sarawak alongside tiny oil-rich Brunei.
Mount Kinabalu towers 4,095 meters above its ancient dipterocarp jungles—the last stronghold of wild orangutans outside Sumatra.
questions.whyExplanation: While New Guinea and Hispaniola are each split between two countries, Borneo is divided among Indonesia, Malaysia, and the Sultanate of Brunei.

questions.prompt: Dutch captain Jacob Roggeveen named this isolated Pacific speck off Chile for the Christian holiday on which he sighted it on April 5, 1722.
clues: Known in Polynesian as Rapa Nui, it is governed by Chile more than 3,500 kilometers west of the South American mainland.
Nearly 900 volcanic tuff statues called moai—many with buried torsos—were quarried at Rano Raraku crater.
questions.whyExplanation: Sighted on Easter Sunday in 1722, Easter Island (Rapa Nui) sits at the southeastern vertex of the Polynesian Triangle and is world-famous for its monumental carved moai.

questions.prompt: Governed by Norway under a 1920 treaty granting visa-free residency to citizens of over 40 signatory nations, which high-Arctic archipelago safeguards humanity's backup crop seeds?
clues: Its main island, Spitsbergen, hosts the Global Seed Vault tunneled deep inside permafrost near Longyearbyen.
Polar bears outnumber residents across parts of this icy chain, where carrying a rifle outside town is legally required.
questions.whyExplanation: The 1920 Svalbard Treaty recognizes Norwegian sovereignty while demilitarizing the archipelago and guaranteeing equal economic and residential access to treaty signatories.

questions.prompt: Resting in Ontario's Lake Huron, which Ojibwe-sacred landmass is Earth's largest freshwater lake island—and holds its own record lake on a lake island?
clues: Spanning 2,766 square kilometers, it is larger than Luxembourg and harbors more than 100 inland lakes of its own.
Some of those interior lakes even hold tiny islets, creating rare third-order 'islands within lakes within an island.'
questions.whyExplanation: Manitoulin Island separates Georgian Bay from Lake Huron proper; its 2,766 sq km make it the world's largest freshwater lake island, cradling Lake Manitou inside.

questions.prompt: Over a third of its flora exists nowhere else on Earth—including umbrella-shaped dragon's blood trees bleeding crimson resin—on which Yemeni island in the Arabian Sea?
clues: Separated from the Horn of Africa by the Guardafui Channel, it has been nicknamed 'the Galápagos of the Indian Ocean.'
Ancient Greek and Roman traders prized its frankincense, aloe, and red cinnabar-like sap.
questions.whyExplanation: Part of Yemen despite lying closer to Somalia, Socotra's long isolation produced surreal endemic plants like Dracaena cinnabari, the umbrella-crowned dragon's blood tree.

questions.prompt: With no airstrip and the nearest inhabited neighbor 2,400 kilometers away on St. Helena, which South Atlantic volcanic speck holds the record as Earth's remotest inhabited archipelago?
clues: Its roughly 250 British citizens live in the single village of Edinburgh of the Seven Seas beneath Queen Mary's Peak.
A 1961 volcanic eruption forced the entire population to evacuate to England for two years before almost everyone voted to return.
questions.whyExplanation: Accessible only by a week-long voyage from Cape Town, Tristan da Cunha is the most remote permanently inhabited archipelago on Earth, governed as a British Overseas Territory.

questions.prompt: Under the 1659 Treaty of the Pyrenees, which tiny uninhabited condominium in the Bidasoa River peacefully swaps sovereignty between France and Spain every six months?
clues: Louis XIV met his Spanish bride Maria Theresa on this narrow 200-meter strip between Hendaye and Irun in 1660.
Navies of both nations hold brief twice-yearly handover ceremonies on February 1 and August 1.
questions.whyExplanation: Pheasant Island (Île des Faisans / Isla de los Faisanes) is the world's oldest surviving condominium, rotating cleanly between Spanish administration (Feb–Jul) and French administration (Aug–Jan).

questions.prompt: Nicknamed 'Tomorrow' and 'Yesterday,' which pair of rocky Bering Strait specks sit barely four kilometers apart yet straddle the International Date Line nearly a full calendar day apart?
clues: Vitus Bering sighted them on August 16, 1728—the Russian Orthodox feast day of a Greek martyr.
The larger western isle belongs to Russia's Chukotka region, while the smaller eastern isle hosts an Inupiat village in Alaska.
questions.whyExplanation: Big Diomede (Russia) and Little Diomede (United States) lie just 3.8 kilometers apart across the Bering Strait, divided by both the U.S.–Russia border and the International Date Line.

questions.prompt: Pliny the Younger's eyewitness letters describing its pine-tree ash cloud gave volcanology the term 'Plinian eruption' after which Italian peak buried Pompeii in 79 CE?
clues: Looming over the Bay of Naples, it is the only active volcano on mainland Europe.
Its 79 CE pyroclastic surges entombed both Pompeii and neighboring Herculaneum, while killing Pliny the Elder.
questions.whyExplanation: Mount Vesuvius erupted catastrophically in 79 CE; Pliny the Younger's detailed letters to Tacitus became the founding text of modern volcanology.

questions.prompt: Immortalized in Katsushika Hokusai's 'Thirty-Six Views,' which symmetrical 3,776-meter Japanese stratovolcano last dusted Edo in ash during its 1707 Hōei eruption?
clues: Rising on Honshu about 100 kilometers southwest of Tokyo, its snow-trimmed cone sits atop three stacked volcanic edifices.
Its 1707 blast struck just 49 days after one of the strongest megathrust earthquakes in Japanese history.
questions.whyExplanation: Japan's tallest mountain at 3,776 meters, Mount Fuji is classified as an active stratovolcano despite lying quiet since the 1707–1708 Hōei eruption.

questions.prompt: Three merged cones—Kibo, Mawenzi, and Shira—lift this dormant Tanzanian stratovolcano to 5,895 meters, making it both Africa's roof and Earth's tallest free-standing mountain.
clues: Climbers trek through rainforest, moorland, and alpine desert without technical gear to reach Uhuru Peak.
Ernest Hemingway immortalized its rapidly shrinking equatorial icefields in a famous 1936 short story.
questions.whyExplanation: Not part of a continuous mountain range, Mount Kilimanjaro rises roughly 4,900 meters directly from the East African plains, crowned by the dormant Kibo cone.

questions.prompt: On May 18, 1980, a magnitude-5.1 quake triggered a lateral blast that blew 400 meters off the summit of which Washington Cascade peak in the deadliest U.S. eruption?
clues: Volcanologist David A. Johnston radioed 'Vancouver! Vancouver! This is it!' moments before the pyroclastic surge struck.
Before 1980, its symmetrical cone had earned it the nickname 'the Fuji of America' north of Portland.
questions.whyExplanation: Mount St. Helens unleashed the largest landslide in recorded history alongside a sideways blast on May 18, 1980, flattening 600 square kilometers of forest and claiming 57 lives.

questions.prompt: Ancient Greeks imagined the blacksmith god Hephaestus hammering lightning bolts beneath which hyperactive Sicilian peak, Europe's tallest active volcano?
clues: Towering above Catania and Taormina, frequent summit outbursts keep its height shifting around 3,357 meters.
Its fertile volcanic slopes support renowned vineyards and pistachio orchards despite centuries of lava flows.
questions.whyExplanation: Sitting above the subduction of the African plate beneath Sicily, Mount Etna is Europe's highest and most continuously active volcano, celebrated in Greek myth as the forge of Hephaestus.

questions.prompt: Its August 27, 1883 paroxysm in Indonesia's Sunda Strait was heard 4,800 kilometers away on Rodrigues Island and painted skies worldwide crimson—possibly inspiring Edvard Munch's 'The Scream.'
clues: Positioned between Java and Sumatra, its collapse spawned 30-meter tsunamis that destroyed coastal towns.
A new volcanic cone named 'Anak'—literally 'Child'—emerged from its submerged caldera in 1927.
questions.whyExplanation: The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa produced the loudest sound in modern history, ruptured eardrums 64 kilometers away, and lofted fine volcanic dust that created fiery twilight skies across Europe.

questions.prompt: Measured from its base on the Pacific Ocean floor rather than sea level, which dormant Hawaiian shield volcano stretches over 10,200 meters—surpassing Everest by more than a kilometer?
clues: Its Hawaiian name translates to 'White Mountain,' honoring the winter snow that dusts its 4,207-meter Big Island summit.
Dry, stable high-altitude air makes its peak home to major astronomical facilities including the twin Keck telescopes.
questions.whyExplanation: Although Mauna Kea stands 4,207 meters above sea level, roughly 6,000 meters of its massive shield lie underwater, making it Earth's tallest mountain from base to peak.

questions.prompt: Its colossal April 1815 VEI-7 eruption on Sumbawa chilled global summers so severely that 1816's wet, gloomy 'Year Without a Summer' drove Mary Shelley indoors to draft 'Frankenstein.'
clues: The largest volcanic eruption in recorded human history sheared over 1,400 meters off this Indonesian island peak.
Global crop failures in 1816 triggered famine across Europe and inspired J.M.W. Turner's luminous yellow sunsets.
questions.whyExplanation: Mount Tambora's April 1815 blast ejected over 150 cubic kilometers of tephra and sulfate aerosols into the stratosphere, depressing Northern Hemisphere temperatures throughout 1816.

questions.prompt: Because Earth bulges outward at the Equator, the 6,263-meter glacier-clad crest of which Ecuadorian stratovolcano stands farther from Earth's center than the top of Everest?
clues: Sitting just one degree south of the Equator, its summit clears Earth's core by roughly 6,384 kilometers—two kilometers beyond Everest.
Alexander von Humboldt's 1802 climb up its icy slopes pioneered the study of altitude-based plant zones.
questions.whyExplanation: Earth's oblate spheroid shape gives the Equator a 21-kilometer wider radius than the poles, placing Ecuador's Chimborazo farther from Earth's center—and closer to the stars—than Mount Everest.

questions.prompt: News anchors stumbled over its 16-letter name in April 2010 when this glacier-capped Icelandic volcano shut down European airspace for six days, grounding over 100,000 flights.
clues: Its Icelandic compound name translates literally to 'island-mountain glacier' near the southern coast.
Meltwater colliding with magma shattered lava into fine abrasive glass shards that posed a severe hazard to jet engines.
questions.whyExplanation: Eyjafjallajökull's subglacial eruption in April 2010 injected glass-rich ash straight into the jet stream over northern Europe, causing the largest peacetime airspace closure since World War II.

questions.prompt: Named in 1841 after one of James Clark Ross's bomb vessels, which 3,794-meter Ross Island peak is Earth's southernmost active volcano and cradles a permanent convecting lava lake?
clues: Steam escaping its vents freezes into eerie hollow 'ice fumarole' towers up to 20 meters tall across Antarctica.
Its sister vessel lent its name to an adjacent dormant cone on the same McMurdo Sound island.
questions.whyExplanation: Towering above McMurdo Station on Ross Island, Mount Erebus has sustained a rare exposed phonolite lava lake since at least 1972 and emits tiny crystals of metallic gold in its gas plumes.

questions.prompt: Carrying a fifth of all river water that reaches Earth's oceans—more than the next seven rivers combined—which South American giant remarkably has zero bridges crossing its main stem?
clues: Seasonal rains swell its width from a few kilometers to over 40 kilometers across soft rainforest floodplains.
Near Manaus, its sandy-colored Solimões channel flows alongside the dark Rio Negro for six kilometers without mixing.
questions.whyExplanation: The Amazon accounts for roughly 20 percent of global river discharge, yet seasonal flooding, shifting soft banks, and sparse road demand mean no highway bridge spans its main channel.

questions.prompt: Formed where its White and Blue branches merge at Khartoum, which northward-flowing 6,650-kilometer lifeline drains eleven African nations before fanning into a Mediterranean delta?
clues: Greek historian Herodotus famously called ancient Egypt 'the gift' of its annual silt-rich summer floods.
Completed in 1970, the Aswan High Dam tamed its seasonal inundations and created sprawling Lake Nasser.
questions.whyExplanation: Fed by East Africa's Great Lakes via the White Nile and Ethiopia's Lake Tana via the Blue Nile, the Nile River winds northward through Sudan and Egypt to the Mediterranean Sea.

questions.prompt: Rising in Germany's Black Forest and emptying into the Black Sea, which waterway flows through ten countries and four national capitals—more sovereign nations than any other river?
clues: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, and Belgrade all sit directly along its winding central European course.
Johann Strauss II celebrated it in an 1867 waltz whose title gave the river a famous—if rarely accurate—color.
questions.whyExplanation: Touching Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova, and Ukraine, the Danube crosses or borders ten nations—more than any other river on Earth.

questions.prompt: Beginning as a shallow stream emerging from Minnesota's Lake Itasca—named from the Latin 'veritas caput' for 'true head'—which mighty waterway drains 31 U.S. states?
clues: Explorer Henry Schoolcraft trimmed the first and last letters off the Latin phrase in 1832 to coin its source lake's name.
Its winding delta below New Orleans feeds the Gulf of Mexico after gathering the Missouri, Ohio, and Arkansas.
questions.whyExplanation: Starting at Lake Itasca in northern Minnesota, the Mississippi River runs roughly 3,766 kilometers to the Gulf of Mexico, draining over 40 percent of the contiguous United States.

questions.prompt: Running 6,300 kilometers from the Tibetan Plateau to Shanghai's East China Sea delta, which Asian titan is Earth's longest river lying entirely within a single country?
clues: Known in China as Chang Jiang ('Long River'), it divides the nation's northern wheat belt from its southern rice paddies.
Its middle reaches power the Three Gorges Dam, the world's largest hydroelectric station by installed capacity.
questions.whyExplanation: The Yangtze is Asia's longest river and the third-longest on Earth, flowing exclusively within China from Qinghai glaciers through the Three Gorges to Shanghai.

questions.prompt: Plunging deeper than 220 meters in its rock-walled lower canyons, which central African giant is both the world's deepest river and the only major river to cross the Equator twice?
clues: Known as the Zaire River from 1971 to 1997, its colossal arc sweeps north through Kisangani before curving back south.
Second only to the Amazon in water discharge, its churning rapids near Inga harbor rare blind cave-adapted fish.
questions.whyExplanation: Carving submarine-like trenches over 220 meters deep, the Congo River arcs north across the Equator and then south across it again before pouring into the Atlantic Ocean.

questions.prompt: Rising in China as the Lancang before threading six Southeast Asian nations, which 4,350-kilometer river swells so heavily in monsoons that it reverses Cambodia's Tonlé Sap?
clues: Its fertile southern delta in Vietnam is called Cuu Long—'Nine Dragons'—for its distributary branches entering the South China Sea.
Giant freshwater stingrays and critically endangered giant catfish inhabit its deep muddy pools.
questions.whyExplanation: Flowing through China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam, the Mekong drives an extraordinary seasonal hydrological reversal into Cambodia's Tonlé Sap lake.

questions.prompt: Europe's longest waterway never reaches any ocean; instead, which 3,530-kilometer Russian artery empties into the landlocked Caspian Sea 28 meters below global sea level?
clues: Affectionately called 'Matushka' ('Little Mother'), it links Moscow, Kazan, and Volgograd—the site of Stalingrad.
Its broad delta at Astrakhan makes it the largest river on Earth draining into an endorheic basin.
questions.whyExplanation: Rising in the Valdai Hills northwest of Moscow, the Volga flows 3,530 kilometers solely within Russia into the enclosed Caspian Sea, supplying roughly 80 percent of the sea's inflow.

questions.prompt: Along the Zambia-Zimbabwe border, this 2,574-kilometer southern African river plunges into a narrow basalt chasm known locally as Mosi-oa-Tunya—'The Smoke That Thunders.'
clues: David Livingstone encountered its mile-wide curtain of spray in November 1855 and named the cataract for Queen Victoria.
Downstream from the falls, the massive Kariba Dam impounds one of the world's largest man-made reservoirs.
questions.whyExplanation: Southern Africa's largest river flowing into the Indian Ocean, the Zambezi tumbles over Victoria Falls (Mosi-oa-Tunya) before coursing through Mozambique to the sea.

questions.prompt: Born as Tibet's Yarlung Tsangpo, which Himalayan powerhouse bends sharply around Namcha Barwa to carve Earth's deepest canyon before joining the Ganges in Bangladesh?
clues: Its Sanskrit name uniquely makes it one of the rare major Indian rivers cast in the masculine, honoring the Hindu creator god's son.
Its braided Assam valley shelters Majuli, one of the largest inhabited river islands in the world.
questions.whyExplanation: Running east across Tibet as the Yarlung Tsangpo, the Brahmaputra hooks south through the 5,500-meter-deep Tsangpo Canyon into India's Assam and joins the Ganges to form the Sundarbans delta.

questions.prompt: Alexander von Humboldt stunned European geographers in 1800 by proving the natural Casiquiare Canal siphons water straight out of this Venezuelan river into the Amazon basin.
clues: Sweeping 2,250 kilometers in a giant arc along Colombia and Venezuela, it ranks among Earth's top four rivers by volume.
Christopher Columbus spotted its massive freshwater plume in 1498 and realized he had reached a continent, not an island.
questions.whyExplanation: Through the Casiquiare bifurcation, the upper Orinoco River naturally splits part of its flow into the Rio Negro—forming the world's largest natural link between two major river systems.

questions.prompt: Holding over 20 percent of Earth's unfrozen surface freshwater inside a 1,642-meter-deep Siberian rift, which crescent lake is also the only freshwater home of an endemic seal?
clues: Estimated at 25 million years old, it is both the world's oldest lake and its deepest.
Over 330 rivers pour into its crystal-clear waters, yet only one—the Angara—flows out.
questions.whyExplanation: Tucked into southern Siberia, Lake Baikal is Earth's deepest (1,642 m) and most voluminous freshwater lake, harboring the endemic nerpa freshwater seal and over 1,000 unique species.

questions.prompt: Covering 82,100 square kilometers—roughly the size of Austria—which cold North American basin holds more water than all four of its Great Lakes siblings combined?
clues: November gales across its open waters sank the ore freighter SS Edmund Fitzgerald on November 10, 1975.
French explorers named it 'le lac supérieur' simply because it lay higher in elevation above Lake Huron.
questions.whyExplanation: Lake Superior is the world's largest freshwater lake by surface area and contains roughly 10 percent of the planet's surface freshwater, draining through the St. Marys River into Lake Huron.

questions.prompt: Roughly ten times saltier than the open ocean, which rift-valley body between Israel, the West Bank, and Jordan laps Earth's lowest exposed land surface 430 meters below sea level?
clues: Fed mainly by the Jordan River with no outlet, relentless evaporation lets swimmers float effortlessly on their backs.
Caves at Qumran along its arid northwest cliffs yielded priceless ancient biblical manuscripts starting in 1947.
questions.whyExplanation: At more than 430 meters below sea level, the Dead Sea's shoreline is Earth's lowest dry land; its 34 percent salinity prevents fish and macroscopic plants from surviving in its waters.

questions.prompt: Explorer John Hanning Speke reached its southern shore in 1858 and named Africa's largest lake—shared by Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania—after Britain's reigning monarch.
clues: Covering 59,947 square kilometers across a shallow plateau, it is the world's largest tropical lake by area.
Introducing the predatory Nile perch in the 1950s wiped out hundreds of its native cichlid fish species.
questions.whyExplanation: Known locally as Nyanza or Nalubaale, Lake Victoria is Africa's largest lake by surface area and serves as the principal headwater reservoir of the White Nile.

questions.prompt: Surrounded by five countries—Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran, and Azerbaijan—which brackish inland expanse is technically the largest lake on Earth by both area and volume?
clues: Ancient Romans called it a sea after tasting its salty waters, which lie 28 meters below global ocean level.
Its waters harbor the prized Beluga sturgeon, source of the world's most expensive caviar.
questions.whyExplanation: Covering roughly 371,000 square kilometers with no natural connection to the world ocean, the Caspian Sea is Earth's largest enclosed inland water body—roughly four times the area of Lake Superior.

questions.prompt: Floating at 3,812 meters in the Andes between Peru and Bolivia, which sacred Inca basin is Earth's highest lake navigable by large commercial steamers?
clues: The Indigenous Uros people still weave buoyant totora reeds into artificial islands, homes, and crescent boats here.
Its Isla del Sol is venerated in Andean tradition as the birthplace of the sun god Inti and the first Inca.
questions.whyExplanation: Straddling the Peruvian-Bolivian Altiplano at 3,812 meters, Lake Titicaca is South America's largest lake by volume and supports commercial ferry traffic across its deep cold waters.

questions.prompt: Stretching 673 kilometers north-to-south along Africa's Western Rift, which trench-like basin is the world's longest freshwater lake and second only to Baikal in depth?
clues: Divided among Tanzania, the DR Congo, Burundi, and Zambia, its bottom plunges 1,470 meters deep.
Near its eastern shore at Ujiji in 1871, Henry Morton Stanley greeted missing explorer David Livingstone.
questions.whyExplanation: Lake Tanganyika reaches 1,470 meters in depth and spans 673 kilometers end to end, holding roughly 16 percent of Earth's available freshwater and hundreds of colorful endemic cichlids.

questions.prompt: Narrowing to barely 2.8 kilometers in the Phillips Channel south of Singapore, which vital 900-kilometer waterway separates Sumatra from the Malay Peninsula?
clues: Carrying roughly a quarter of all global seaborne trade, it is the shortest sea route linking India and East Asia.
Its name derives from a prosperous 15th-century Malay sultanate captured by Portuguese admiral Afonso de Albuquerque in 1511.
questions.whyExplanation: Funneling tens of thousands of tankers and container ships annually between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, the Strait of Malacca is one of Earth's premier maritime chokepoints.

questions.prompt: Sealed beneath nearly four kilometers of East Antarctic ice for at least 15 million years, which Ontario-sized liquid freshwater lake was finally pierced by Russian drillers in 2012?
clues: Geothermal heat from below and crushing pressure from the overlying glacier keep its water liquid at minus 3 degrees Celsius.
It takes its name from the nearby Soviet polar station—itself named for Fabian von Bellingshausen's 1820 sloop.
questions.whyExplanation: Discovered via airborne radar in the 1970s and confirmed in 1996, subglacial Lake Vostok is studied by astrobiologists as an earthly analog for the buried oceans of Europa and Enceladus.

questions.prompt: Once Earth's fourth-largest lake between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, Soviet cotton-irrigation diversions of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya shrank which inland basin by 90 percent?
clues: Rusting fishing trawlers stranded miles from water near Moynaq turned its dried seabed into a haunting environmental symbol.
Kazakhstan's 2005 Kok-Aral Dam has helped revive its smaller northern lobe, bringing fish back to Aralsk.
questions.whyExplanation: Starting in the 1960s, Soviet canals siphoned the rivers feeding the Aral Sea to irrigate desert cotton, causing one of the 20th century's worst ecological collapses.

questions.prompt: Up to 28 lightning bolts per minute flicker almost nightly where Andean winds collide above warm waters over which oil-rich Venezuelan tidal bay-lake?
clues: Known as the Catatumbo lightning, its nearly constant storms give this South American basin Earth's highest lightning density.
Connected to the Gulf of Venezuela via the Tablazo Strait, its stilt villages inspired Amerigo Vespucci to name the country 'Little Venice.'
questions.whyExplanation: Linked to the Caribbean by a narrow channel, Lake Maracaibo is South America's largest brackish bay-lake and Earth's lightning capital, lighting up around 297 nights every year.

questions.prompt: Signed into law by Ulysses S. Grant on March 1, 1872, which geothermal wonderland spanning Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho became the world's very first national park?
clues: Sitting atop an active supervolcano caldera, it protects more than half of all the geysers on Earth.
Reintroducing 14 gray wolves here in 1995 triggered a famous trophic cascade that restored riverside aspens and beavers.
questions.whyExplanation: Created by Congress in 1872 'as a public park or pleasuring-ground for the benefit and enjoyment of the people,' Yellowstone launched the modern global national park movement.

questions.prompt: Derived from a Maasai word meaning 'endless plains,' which northern Tanzanian reserve stages Earth's largest terrestrial mammal migration of over a million wildebeest?
clues: Bordering Kenya's Maasai Mara to the north, its savannahs are dotted with granite kopje outcrops favored by lions.
Herds brave Nile crocodiles each dry season as they plunge across the Grumeti and Mara rivers in search of fresh grass.
questions.whyExplanation: Established as a national park in 1951, Tanzania's Serengeti anchors an ancient circular ecosystem sustaining the Great Migration of wildebeest, zebras, and Thomson's gazelles.

questions.prompt: Born in 1885 after Canadian Pacific Railway workers quarreled over ownership of bubbling sulfur springs, which Rocky Mountain gem became Canada's first national park?
clues: Glacial rock flour tints its iconic Lake Louise and Moraine Lake a vivid milky turquoise beneath Victoria Glacier.
