Prime Minister John A. Macdonald reserved 26 square kilometers around Cave and Basin to create a railway resort magnet.
questions.whyExplanation: Created in 1885 around the Cave and Basin hot springs in Alberta, Banff National Park became Canada's inaugural national park and now draws millions to the Canadian Rockies.

questions.prompt: Abraham Lincoln signed an 1864 wartime land grant protecting this glaciated California Sierra valley, whose 900-meter granite monolith El Capitan later became a rock-climbing mecca.
clues: Scottish-born naturalist John Muir camped in its meadows with President Theodore Roosevelt in 1903 to expand federal protection.
Half Dome, Bridalveil Fall, and the ancient Mariposa Grove of giant sequoias draw visitors from across the globe.
questions.whyExplanation: The 1864 Yosemite Grant set a historic precedent for preserving scenic public lands, leading to full national park status in 1890 under John Muir's tireless advocacy.

questions.prompt: Founded in 1898 as the Sabie Game Reserve to halt uncontrolled trophy hunting, which nearly 20,000-square-kilometer South African stronghold shelters all of Africa's Big Five?
clues: Stretching 360 kilometers along South Africa's Limpopo and Mpumalanga frontier with Mozambique, it rivals Israel in size.
It was renamed in 1926 for the former Transvaal Republic president who first proclaimed the reserve.
questions.whyExplanation: Named after President Paul Kruger, Kruger National Park is South Africa's flagship wildlife sanctuary, famed for pioneering modern park management and protecting rhinos, lions, and elephants.

questions.prompt: Beneath rolling Kentucky hills lies Earth's longest known labyrinth—more than 420 miles of surveyed limestone corridors—protected inside which UNESCO World Heritage park?
clues: Enslaved guide Stephen Bishop mapped miles of its subterranean canyons and crossed the 'Bottomless Pit' by lantern light in 1838.
Eyeless blind cavefish and albino crayfish inhabit its pitch-black underground Green River tributaries.
questions.whyExplanation: With over 426 miles of interconnected passages—nearly twice the length of its nearest rival—Kentucky's Mammoth Cave National Park preserves the longest cave system discovered on Earth.

questions.prompt: Three sheer granite needles whose Tehuelche name means 'blue' pierce Patagonian storm clouds above turquoise glacial lakes in which flagship Chilean national park?
clues: Trekkers brave fierce southern winds along its famous 'W' and 'O' circuits past Grey Glacier and the Cuernos horns.
Guanacos and pumas prowl its windswept steppe near the southern tip of the Andes in Magallanes.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded in 1959 in southern Chilean Patagonia, Torres del Paine ('Towers of Blue') protects jagged granite spires, glaciers, and abundant puma populations.

questions.prompt: Living mosses and algae precipitate calcium carbonate into natural travertine dams that staircase 16 emerald karst pools in which oldest Croatian national park?
clues: Wooden boardwalks wind across crystal-clear cascades spanning over 130 vertical meters between its upper and lower basins.
Proclaimed in 1949 in the Dinaric Alps, its barriers slowly grow and reshape the waterfalls every single year.
questions.whyExplanation: Plitvice Lakes National Park showcases dynamic karst hydro-geology where biochemically formed tufa barriers separate 16 terraced lakes fed by underground streams.

questions.prompt: Over 3,000 weathered quartz-sandstone pillars soaring above misty ravines in China's Hunan province inspired the floating Hallelujah Mountains of James Cameron's 'Avatar.'
clues: Established in 1982 as China's first national forest park, it forms the heart of the UNESCO Wulingyuan scenic area.
Visitors ascend 326 meters up one vertical cliff face in the Bailong Elevator, the world's tallest outdoor lift.
questions.whyExplanation: Physical erosion of ancient quartz-sandstone joints sculpted Zhangjiajie's gravity-defying spires, one of which local officials playfully nicknamed 'Avatar Hallelujah Mountain' in 2010.

questions.prompt: Carving Milford Sound and Doubtful Sound into New Zealand's rainy southwest coast, which largest Kiwi national park hid the 'extinct' flightless takahē until its 1948 rediscovery?
clues: Receiving up to seven meters of annual rain, its sheer glacier-cut walls tumble straight into the Tasman Sea.
Physician Geoffrey Orbell stunned ornithologists by tracking down a surviving colony of purple-blue rail birds in its Murchison Mountains.
questions.whyExplanation: Covering 12,600 square kilometers of South Island wilderness, Fiordland National Park anchors the Te Wahipounamu World Heritage Area and sheltered the presumed-extinct takahē for half a century.

questions.prompt: Spanning 972,000 square kilometers across the frozen crown of Earth's largest island—bigger than all but 29 sovereign countries—which Arctic sanctuary is the largest land national park?
clues: Patrolled by the Danish Navy's elite Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, it has no permanent civilian population.
Established in 1974, its tundra and fjords shelter roughly 40 percent of the world's wild muskoxen.
questions.whyExplanation: Covering nearly half of the island's interior and northeastern fjords, Northeast Greenland National Park spans 972,000 sq km—more than twice the size of California—making it Earth's largest terrestrial park.

questions.prompt: Originally assigned a two-letter 1930s weather-station code, Southern California's busiest Pacific gateway simply tacked an 'X' onto the end in 1947 to create which iconic three-letter code?
clues: The parabolic white concrete arches of its 1961 Theme Building became a Googie-architecture landmark.
Its first two letters stand plainly for Los Angeles, paired with a dummy final letter shared by Portland's PDX.
questions.whyExplanation: When North American airports expanded from two-letter National Weather Service codes to three-letter IATA identifiers in 1947, Los Angeles ('LA') simply appended 'X' to form LAX.

questions.prompt: Before honoring World War II flying ace Edward 'Butch' O'Hare in 1949, Chicago's main airfield was built beside Orchard Place—leaving which seemingly mismatched IATA code?
clues: Douglas Aircraft originally constructed its wartime runways here as Orchard Field to build C-54 Skymaster transports.
United and American Airlines both operate colossal Midwest hubs beneath this three-letter identifier.
questions.whyExplanation: Chicago O'Hare International Airport began as Orchard Field in 1942; even after being renamed for Medal of Honor aviator Butch O'Hare in 1949, it kept the legacy code ORD.

questions.prompt: Progressive rock trio Rush tapped the Morse code for this Toronto Pearson identifier into the opening rhythm of their Grammy-nominated 1981 instrumental.
clues: Like nearly every major Canadian hub, it opens with 'Y'—signifying 'Yes' to an on-site weather and radio beacon.
The final two letters came from the nearby Malton railway telegraph station outside Ontario's capital.
questions.whyExplanation: Neil Peart and Alex Lifeson heard Toronto's Malton radio beacon tapping out its distinctive dot-and-dash Morse rhythm and turned Toronto Pearson's IATA code, YYZ, into a classic rock instrumental.

questions.prompt: Although Ho Chi Minh City officially took its modern name in 1976, travelers flying into Tan Son Nhat International still see which three-letter reminder of its former name on luggage tags?
clues: Vietnam's busiest airport still preserves the consonants of the historic South Vietnamese capital.
Its legacy naming parallels Mumbai's BOM and Chennai's MAA, where IATA codes outlived municipal renamings.
questions.whyExplanation: Tan Son Nhat International Airport retains SGN—short for Saigon—because IATA rarely alters long-established airport codes after a city changes its official name.

questions.prompt: Honoring daredevil aviator John Moisant—who crashed to his death in 1910—and the cattle pens that once stood on its site, which quirky IATA code belongs to New Orleans?
clues: Its letters abbreviate 'Moisant Stock Yards' rather than jazz great Louis Armstrong, for whom the terminal was named in 2001.
Located in suburban Kenner west of Lake Pontchartrain, it serves Louisiana's Crescent City.
questions.whyExplanation: New Orleans's airport opened as Moisant Field on the site of the Moisant Stock Yards, yielding the enduring code MSY even after its 2001 renaming for Louis Armstrong.

questions.prompt: Theme-park visitors landing in Orlando see no 'O' at the start of their baggage tag because its IATA code preserves McCoy Air Force Base—named for a B-47 bomber commander killed in 1957.
clues: During the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, U-2 spy planes flew vital reconnaissance sorties directly from its runways.
The letters abbreviate Colonel Michael N.W. McCoy's surname after the base transitioned to civilian jets in the 1970s.
questions.whyExplanation: Orlando International Airport occupies the former McCoy Air Force Base, retaining MCO while smaller downtown Orlando Executive Airport holds the older ORL code.

questions.prompt: St. Petersburg voters restored their city's imperial name in 1991, yet Pulkovo Airport still stamps boarding passes with which Soviet-era three-letter IATA code?
clues: Its letters abbreviate the Bolshevik-era name the Neva River metropolis carried from 1924 to 1991.
Located 23 kilometers south of Palace Square, it serves Russia's historic 'Window to the West.'
questions.whyExplanation: Pulkovo Airport's code LED derives from Leningrad—the city's name when commercial aviation codes were assigned—and remained unchanged after the USSR dissolved.

questions.prompt: Opened in 1962 as 'DIA,' Eero Saarinen's sweeping Virginia jetport inverted its own initials six years later to stop baggage handlers confusing handwritten tags with 'DCA.'
clues: Passengers famously rode giant stilt-legged 'mobile lounges' between its sculptural terminal and midfield concourses.
Rearranging 'Dulles International Airport' into 'International Airport Dulles' created its permanent 1968 identifier.
questions.whyExplanation: Because handwritten DIA tags too closely resembled Washington National's DCA, Dulles flipped its IATA code to IAD in 1968 to prevent misrouted luggage across the Potomac.

questions.prompt: Home to UPS's colossal automated Worldport sorting hub, Louisville's Muhammad Ali International Airport still carries which IATA code honoring 1941 benefactor Elisha Standiford?
clues: Built by the Army Corps of Engineers as Standiford Field, it sat above the catastrophic 1937 Ohio River floodline.
Hundreds of brown cargo jets descend here nightly, making this Kentucky airfield one of Earth's busiest freight hubs.
questions.whyExplanation: Although renamed for hometown boxing legend Muhammad Ali in 2019, Louisville's airport keeps SDF from its original 1941 name, Standiford Field.

questions.prompt: Rio de Janeiro's main international airport on Governador Island bears which three-letter IATA code echoing a 1663 Portuguese galleon—'Galeão'—built right on its shoreline?
clues: Its official name honors bossa nova composer Antônio Carlos Jobim, contrasting with smaller downtown Santos Dumont (SDU).
The letters come from 'Galeão' plus 'Ilha do Governador' in Guanabara Bay.
questions.whyExplanation: Rio de Janeiro/Galeão International Airport takes GIG from Praia do Galeão on Ilha do Governador, where the giant Portuguese galleon Padre Eterno was launched in 1663.

questions.prompt: Immortalized in the Broadway musical 'Come From Away' after sheltering 38 diverted transatlantic airliners on September 11, 2001, Gander International in Newfoundland uses which IATA code?
clues: During the 1940s and 1950s, its wide concrete runways made it 'the Crossroads of the World' for prop planes crossing the Atlantic.
Its prefix is Canada's universal 'Y,' followed by two letters inherited from an old eastern Newfoundland radio beacon.
questions.whyExplanation: Once an indispensable refueling stop for early transatlantic flights, Gander International Airport (YQX) received 38 diverted jets and nearly 6,700 stranded travelers during Operation Yellow Ribbon.

questions.prompt: Built atop Coca-Cola founder Asa Candler's abandoned 1909 automobile racetrack, which Georgia megahub has ranked as Earth's busiest airport by passenger count almost every year since 1998?
clues: An underground Plane Train shuttles millions of Delta connecting passengers across seven parallel concourses.
Its hyphenated title honors two pioneering local mayors who championed southern aviation and civil rights.
questions.whyExplanation: Occupying the site of Candler's 1909 Atlanta Speedway, Hartsfield-Jackson serves over 100 million travelers a year because roughly 80 percent of the U.S. population lives within a two-hour flight.

questions.prompt: Originally called Idlewild after a Queens golf course until its emotional December 1963 renaming, which New York gateway boasts Eero Saarinen's bird-winged TWA Flight Center?
clues: The Beatles stepped off Pan Am Flight 101 onto its windy Jamaica Bay tarmac in February 1964 to screaming crowds.
Its AirTrain connects Manhattan-bound rail riders directly to six sprawling international terminals.
questions.whyExplanation: Opened in 1948 as New York International Airport—popularly Idlewild—the Queens hub was renamed for President John F. Kennedy on December 24, 1963, one month after his assassination.

questions.prompt: Crowned by a peaked white fiberglass roof mimicking snow-dusted Rockies—and greeted by a glowing-eyed 32-foot blue mustang statue—which 53-square-mile hub is America's largest by land area?
clues: Opened in 1995 to replace crowded Stapleton, its vast prairie footprint could swallow Manhattan twice over.
A notorious automated baggage-system breakdown delayed its debut by 16 months, fueling endless conspiracy theories about its tunnels.
questions.whyExplanation: Covering roughly 33,531 acres on Colorado's high plains, Denver International Airport is North America's largest airport by land area and features Luis Jiménez's dramatic sculpture 'Blue Mustang.'

questions.prompt: In 1934, New York's fiery mayor refused to step off a TWA flight that landed in Newark because his ticket read 'New York'—prompting him to build which Flushing Bay airport?
clues: Opened in 1939 with a Marine Air Terminal for Pan Am flying-boat Clippers, it sits just eight miles from Midtown Manhattan.
Its crisp $8 billion modernization erased decades of jokes comparing its old concourses to a relic of the 1960s.
questions.whyExplanation: Fiorello La Guardia forced TWA to fly him from Newark to Brooklyn's Floyd Bennett Field in 1934 and then championed a brand-new Queens airfield, which opened in 1939 bearing his name.

questions.prompt: Carved across 27 square miles of north Texas prairie—larger than Manhattan—which twin-city megahub is so self-contained it has its own ZIP code (75261), police force, and fire department?
clues: Its five semicircular terminals straddle a central north-south spine highway, serving as American Airlines' global fortress.
In 1974 it replaced Love Field and Greater Southwest as the compromise commercial gateway between two rival metro centers.
questions.whyExplanation: Spanning 17,207 acres midway between its namesake Texas cities, Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport operates effectively like a municipality with seven runways and dedicated ZIP code 75261.

questions.prompt: Built atop reclaimed bay tidelands in San Mateo County, which foggy Northern California gateway pioneered America's first museum-accredited airport gallery and pairs runways just 750 feet apart?
clues: Low summer marine fog routinely halts simultaneous side-by-side approaches onto its closely spaced Runways 28L and 28R.
Passengers strolling its terminals can view rotating historical exhibits and even greet Wag Brigade therapy pigs and dogs.
questions.whyExplanation: Opened in 1927 as Mills Field, San Francisco International Airport houses the SFO Museum (accredited in 1999) and is known nationwide for marine-layer flow delays caused by its tight parallel runways.

questions.prompt: Perched 2,230 meters above sea level in a sinking former lakebed where thin mountain air steals jet lift, which bustling hub honors 19th-century Zapotec president Benito Juárez?
clues: Ringed tightly by dense neighborhoods, its two parallel runways cannot be operated independently at the same time.
Heavy widebody flights bound for Europe sometimes had to stop for fuel or trim payload because of the valley's high density altitude.
questions.whyExplanation: Located on the eastern edge of the ancient Lake Texcoco basin, Benito Juárez Mexico City International Airport is one of the busiest gateways in Latin America despite elevation and urban crowding.

questions.prompt: Named officially for Governor André Franco Montoro when it opened on an old air-force base in 1985, which hub northeast of Brazil's financial engine is South America's busiest airport?
clues: Its Terminal 3 opened just in time for the 2014 FIFA World Cup to handle massive long-haul widebody traffic.
Travelers transferring from tight downtown Congonhas routinely ride helicopters or buses out to this sprawling suburb.
questions.whyExplanation: Handling over 40 million passengers annually, São Paulo/Guarulhos (GRU) serves as South America's premier international aviation crossroads and LATAM's primary Brazilian hub.

questions.prompt: Taking its name from the Muisca legend of a gold-dusted chief, which 2,548-meter-high Colombian gateway ranks as Latin America's busiest cargo airport, airlifting cut roses worldwide?
clues: Opened in 1959 on Bogotá's Sabana plateau, it is the primary base for Avianca—the Americas' oldest operating airline.
Ahead of Valentine's Day and Mother's Day, hundreds of freighters depart here packed with fresh Andean carnations and roses.
questions.whyExplanation: Bogotá's El Dorado International Airport moves more air freight than any other airport in Latin America, led by Colombia's massive perishable cut-flower export industry.

questions.prompt: Sunbathers on St. Maarten's Maho Beach duck beneath the deafening jetwash of landing widebodies skimming barely ten meters overhead before touching down at which Dutch Caribbean airport?
clues: Opened as a wartime airstrip in 1943, it bears the name of the Dutch royal who visited the island the following year.
Warning signs along the perimeter fence caution thrill-seekers not to cling to the wire during full-throttle jet blast.
questions.whyExplanation: Because St. Maarten's short 2,300-meter runway begins immediately past a narrow road and Maho Beach, arriving jets fly dramatically low over tourists at Princess Juliana International Airport.

questions.prompt: At 4,061 meters above sea level on Bolivia's Altiplano, which sky-high La Paz gateway demands a four-kilometer runway and special aircraft modifications to cope with thin Andean air?
clues: As the highest major international airport in the Americas, Boeing and Airbus routinely fly prototype jets here for high-altitude testing.
A dramatic urban cable-car network—Mi Teleférico—drops passengers 400 meters down from its plateau rim into the canyon capital below.
questions.whyExplanation: Sitting above 13,300 feet on the plateau overlooking La Paz, El Alto International Airport is one of the highest commercial airports on Earth, requiring extended takeoff rolls and oxygen-equipped terminals.

questions.prompt: Named after a rural Middlesex hamlet leveled for runways in 1944, which West London titan handles more international traffic than any other European gateway on just two runways?
clues: Its Terminal 2 honors Queen Elizabeth II, while Richard Rogers's sweeping Terminal 5 anchors British Airways.
Operating at nearly 99 percent runway capacity for years, debates over building a third runway have spanned decades.
questions.whyExplanation: Built over the demolished village of Heath Row and opened for civil aviation in 1946, London Heathrow consistently ranks as Europe's busiest airport despite having only two parallel runways.

questions.prompt: Passengers in its circular 1974 Terminal 1 ride futuristic crisscrossing glass escalator tubes across an open central void at which flagship hub northeast of Paris?
clues: Also known simply as Roissy for its commune, it opened in 1974 to honor France's wartime leader and Fifth Republic founder.
Air France's global fortress links directly into France's high-speed TGV rail network right beneath Terminal 2.
questions.whyExplanation: Designed in part by architect Paul Andreu, Paris–Charles de Gaulle Airport is France's largest aviation hub and Europe's premier high-speed rail-to-air interchange.

questions.prompt: Repeatedly crowned the world's finest airport, which Southeast Asian showcase added Moshe Safdie's toroidal glass Jewel dome in 2019—home to the 40-meter Rain Vortex indoor waterfall?
clues: Opened in 1981 on reclaimed eastern coastal land, its terminals also pamper transit flyers with a butterfly garden and rooftop pool.
Its Skytrain tracks pass visibly right beside the lush terraced indoor forest surrounding the waterfall.
questions.whyExplanation: Singapore Changi Airport transformed transit hubs into architectural destinations, featuring the world's tallest indoor waterfall—the 40-meter HSBC Rain Vortex—inside its Jewel complex.

questions.prompt: Positioned within an eight-hour flight of two-thirds of humanity, which Persian Gulf colossus—home base of Emirates—has led the world in international passenger volume since 2014?
clues: Its cavernous Terminal 3 was engineered specifically around the double-deck Airbus A380 fleet.
It opened in 1960 with a tiny compacted-sand runway before oil wealth and global transit hubs turned it into an intercontinental crossroads.
questions.whyExplanation: Capitalizing on geography linking Europe, Asia, and Africa, Dubai International Airport surpassed Heathrow in 2014 as Earth's busiest airport for international travelers.

questions.prompt: Its runways sit roughly three meters below sea level atop the drained bed of Haarlemmermeer lake—whose stormy waves earned this Dutch hub a name meaning 'ship's grave.'
clues: Opened as a military airfield in 1916, it became KLM's home hub and Europe's pioneering single-terminal complex.
Transit passengers strolling Holland Boulevard can visit a free annex of the Rijksmuseum right between security gates.
questions.whyExplanation: Built inside a 19th-century reclaimed polder three meters below sea level, Amsterdam Airport Schiphol takes its name from a treacherous corner of the former Haarlemmermeer where ships sank.

questions.prompt: Sitting on a reclaimed Tokyo Bay peninsula just 15 kilometers south of Ginza, which historic 1931 airfield regained long-haul slots to outpace distant Narita as Japan's busiest hub?
clues: After Narita opened in 1978 to absorb international traffic, this closer-in base remained Japan's colossal domestic powerhouse.
Opening its fourth runway on a man-made offshore pier in 2010 sparked a dramatic international renaissance.
questions.whyExplanation: Far closer to central Tokyo than Narita, Tokyo Haneda International Airport handles over 80 million travelers annually, ranking consistently among the five busiest airports in the world.

questions.prompt: Once a base for Zeppelin airships before launching supply flights during the 1948–1949 Berlin Airlift, which Rhine-Main giant is Germany's busiest air hub and Lufthansa's home?
clues: Its long-distance railway station—AIRail Terminal—sends ICE bullet trains speeding straight to Cologne and Stuttgart.
Historically serving more direct country destinations than almost any rival, it flanks the wooded Stadtwald.
questions.whyExplanation: Opened in 1936 as an airplane and Zeppelin base, Frankfurt Airport served as a vital western staging hub for the Berlin Airlift and grew into continental Europe's leading cargo and connecting gateway.

questions.prompt: Constructed on reclaimed tidal flats fusing Yeongjong and Yongyu islands in the Yellow Sea, which South Korean showpiece opened in 2001 to relieve crowded Gimpo?
clues: A dramatic 21-kilometer cable-stayed sea bridge links its island runways directly toward Seoul's Songdo district.
Inside its airy concourses, travelers encounter Korean royal court parades, traditional craft studios, and an indoor skating rink.
questions.whyExplanation: Reclaiming shallow tidal land between two Yellow Sea islands allowed South Korea to open noise-free, 24-hour Incheon International Airport in March 2001 as Seoul's main global gateway.

questions.prompt: For decades, cars entering this tiny Mediterranean territory had to halt behind railway-style boom barriers whenever a jet rolled straight across Winston Churchill Avenue's active runway.
clues: Its single 1,776-meter strip hugs the northern base of a towering limestone Rock just yards from the Spanish frontier.
A four-lane underground road tunnel finally diverted normal automobile traffic beneath the tarmac in March 2023.
questions.whyExplanation: Sandwiched between Spain and the sheer Rock, Gibraltar International Airport famously intersected the peninsula's main road at grade for decades until the Kingsway Tunnel opened in 2023.

questions.prompt: Tucked inside a narrow 2,235-meter Himalayan valley walled by 5,500-meter peaks, which sole international gateway to Bhutan permits only a couple dozen specially certified pilots to land?
clues: With no radar-guided instrument approach possible around its mountains, aircraft must bank sharply at 45 degrees by eye in daylight.
Passengers look right past terraced rice paddies and hillside monasteries moments before touching down along its namesake river.
questions.whyExplanation: Surrounded by jagged Himalayan peaks and reachable only via visual maneuvering through a winding gorge, Bhutan's Paro International Airport is universally ranked among Earth's most challenging approaches.

questions.prompt: Twin Otter turboprops time their flight schedules by the Atlantic tide table at which Scottish Outer Hebrides oddity—the only airport on Earth with scheduled landings on a sandy beach?
clues: Three triangular runways marked by wooden poles across Traigh Mhor bay disappear completely underwater twice every day.
Before each landing, a windsock alerts cockle pickers to clear the wide wet shell-sand foreshore.
questions.whyExplanation: Opened in 1936 on the Isle of Barra in Scotland's Outer Hebrides, Barra Airport is the world's only commercial airfield using a tidal beach as its active runway surface.

questions.prompt: Layers of darkened varnish long tricked viewers into thinking this 1642 Rembrandt civic-guard portrait unfolded at midnight rather than in broad daylight.

distractors.text: The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp
The Syndics of the Drapers' Guild

clues: In 1715, Amsterdam officials trimmed all four edges so the huge canvas could fit between two doors in the Town Hall.
Its formal title names Captain Frans Banninck Cocq's militia company; a 1940s cleaning revealed the sunlit street.
questions.whyExplanation: Rembrandt's 1642 militia portrait earned its nocturnal nickname from centuries of darkened grime and varnish; it anchors the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.

questions.prompt: Painted from an asylum window in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence in 1889, this Van Gogh swirl invents an idealized Dutch-style church steeple absent from the real view.
clues: A towering dark cypress anchors the left foreground while eleven luminous celestial orbs wheel across the Provençal sky.
Vincent sent it to his brother Theo in Paris, calling it a failure; it has hung at MoMA in New York since 1941.
questions.whyExplanation: Van Gogh painted The Starry Night in June 1889 from his barred east-facing window at Saint-Paul-de-Mausole, blending Provence's Alpilles hills with memories of Brabant.

questions.prompt: A Carpenter Gothic window spotted on a tiny farmhouse in Eldon, Iowa inspired Grant Wood to paint his sister and his dentist as this dour 1930 pitchfork-toting pair.
clues: The stern man holds a three-pronged fork whose vertical tines echo the stitching on his denim overalls.
Dentist Byron McKeeby and Wood's sister Nan posed separately for the Art Institute of Chicago icon.
questions.whyExplanation: Grant Wood envisioned 'the kind of people I fancied should live in that house' in Eldon, Iowa; American Gothic won a $300 bronze medal in Chicago in 1930.

questions.prompt: Unveiled at the 1937 Paris Expo, this monochrome Picasso protest canvas stayed exiled at New York's MoMA for decades under orders not to return to Spain until democracy did.
clues: A gored horse, a stoic bull, and a jagged light bulb scream across 25 feet of black, white, and gray oil paint.
Named for a Basque market town bombed by Luftwaffe and Italian planes in April 1937, it moved to Madrid in 1981.
questions.whyExplanation: Picasso painted Guernica in response to the April 26, 1937 bombing of the Basque town; following Franco's death and Spain's democratic transition, it arrived in Madrid in 1981.

questions.prompt: In this 1656 courtly puzzle at the Prado, King Philip IV and Queen Mariana appear only as fuzzy reflections in a far wall mirror while Velázquez paints right beside their daughter.
clues: Infanta Margaret Theresa stands at center surrounded by maids of honor, court dwarves, and a sleepy Spanish mastiff.
The red Cross of the Order of Santiago on the artist's chest was reportedly added after his 1659 knighthood.
questions.whyExplanation: Diego Velázquez's 1656 masterpiece Las Meninas ('The Ladies-in-Waiting') turns the viewer into the royal couple's standpoint, making it a cornerstone of Western art theory.

questions.prompt: Inspired by Camembert cheese softening in the Catalan sun, this diminutive 1931 Dalí oil—barely larger than a sheet of paper—drapes limp pocket watches over Cap de Creus cliffs.
clues: Swarms of ants crawl across an orange closed timepiece while a fleshy profile of the artist sleeps beneath a draped dial.
First sold in New York for $250, the Surrealist icon measures just 9.5 by 13 inches at MoMA.
questions.whyExplanation: Salvador Dalí completed The Persistence of Memory in 1931 on a tiny 24-by-33 cm canvas; its melting timepieces visually echoed Einsteinian anxieties over rigid clock time.

questions.prompt: Above a convex mirror reflecting two unseen guests entering a Bruges bedchamber, Jan van Eyck signed 'I was here' in legalistic Latin calligraphy on this 1434 double panel.

distractors.text: Portrait of a Man in a Red Turban

clues: A single burning chandelier candle, cast-off wooden pattens, and a tiny Brussels griffon terrier pack the oak panel with symbols.
Hanging in London's National Gallery, it depicts a wealthy Lucchese merchant and his wife clasping hands.
questions.whyExplanation: Jan van Eyck's 1434 Arnolfini Portrait pioneered luminous oil glazes and bears the famous Latin inscription 'Johannes de eyck fuit hic 1434' above its tiny convex mirror.

questions.prompt: Georges Seurat spent two years layering tiny contrasting dots of pure pigment to populate this 1886 Seine riverbank scene—including a fashionably bustled woman walking a pet monkey.
questions.answerCorrect: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte
clues: Its optical-mixing technique, dubbed pointillism or divisionism, inspired a 1984 Stephen Sondheim Broadway musical.
Nearly ten feet wide, the Neo-Impressionist landmark anchors the Art Institute of Chicago.
questions.whyExplanation: Seurat worked from 1884 to 1886 on A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, applying color theory to depict Parisian leisure along the suburban Seine.

questions.prompt: Stretched diagonally across the tiled floor of Hans Holbein's 1533 Tudor double portrait lies a warped blur that snaps into a crisp human skull only when viewed from a sharp side angle.
clues: Between two French envoys sit a broken-stringed lute, globes, sundials, and a Lutheran hymnal hinting at religious schism.
Painted in London for Jean de Dinteville and Georges de Selve, this anamorphic memento mori hangs in the National Gallery.
questions.whyExplanation: Holbein's 1533 painting The Ambassadors depicts French diplomats Jean de Dinteville and Georges de Selve flanking Renaissance instruments and a famous anamorphic skull.

questions.prompt: To prepare for this towering 1819 Romantic canvas, Théodore Géricault sketched severed limbs from a Paris morgue and interviewed starving survivors of an 1816 frigate wreck off Mauritania.
clues: A towering pyramid of desperate castaways culminates in a Black sailor waving a cloth toward a speck-sized rescue ship.
The French frigate's incompetent aristocratic captain sparked a national scandal; the 23-foot painting dominates the Louvre.
questions.whyExplanation: Géricault's 1818-1819 masterpiece The Raft of the Medusa dramatized the 1816 French naval disaster in which only 15 of 147 adrift passengers survived, launching French Romanticism.

questions.prompt: Closed, its grisaille shutters show Earth on the third day of Creation; opened at the Prado, this triptych's hellish right wing hides playable musical notation inked onto a sinner's rear.
clues: Giant strawberries, translucent glass orbs, and a bird-headed demon devouring souls fill its sprawling oak panels.
Painted by Hieronymus Bosch around 1500, it later became a prized obsession of Spain's King Philip II.
questions.whyExplanation: Hieronymus Bosch's triptych The Garden of Earthly Delights (c. 1490-1510) progresses from Eden through teeming sensuality to musical torment; modern scholars even transcribed its 'butt music'.

questions.prompt: Art historians still debate the plot of this enigmatic c. 1508 Venetian landscape, where 1939 X-rays revealed Giorgione originally painted a bathing nude beneath the standing halberdier.
clues: A lightning bolt splits storm clouds over ruined columns while a nursing woman sits opposite a soldier across a stream.
Housed in Venice's Gallerie dell'Accademia, it is hailed as Western art's first landscape where weather upstages human drama.
questions.whyExplanation: Giorgione's The Tempest (La Tempesta, c. 1508) defies consensus iconography, and X-radiography proved he altered the left foreground figure from a seated nude to a standing man.

questions.prompt: Begun around 1190 by King Philip II as a riverside medieval fortress, this Parisian institution suffered its most famous heist in 1911 when a former glazier smuggled out a small Da Vinci portrait.
clues: Visitors descend beneath I. M. Pei's 1989 glass-and-steel pyramid to reach its Denon, Richelieu, and Sully wings.
Vincenzo Peruggia walked out of its Salon Carré with the Mona Lisa hidden under his white smock.
questions.whyExplanation: Originally a Capetian fortress and royal palace before opening as a public museum in 1793, the Louvre saw the Mona Lisa stolen in August 1911 and recovered in Florence in 1913.

questions.prompt: Giorgio Vasari designed this horseshoe-shaped Florentine complex in 1560 as Medici administrative offices, linking it to Palazzo Pitti across the Arno via an elevated private corridor.
clues: Its Italian name literally translates to 'offices,' and its sunlit top floor was converted to showcase Medici art.
Botticelli's Primavera and The Birth of Venus headline its Renaissance rooms.
questions.whyExplanation: Commissioned by Cosimo I de' Medici in 1560, the Uffizi opened to visitors on request by 1591 and holds the world's premier Renaissance collection, linked by the Vasari Corridor.

questions.prompt: Originally built in Madrid as a neoclassical natural history cabinet by Juan de Villanueva, this national showcase opened in 1819 to house the Spanish crown's vast trove of Velázquez and Goya.
clues: Napoleon's cavalry stabled horses inside the unfinished structure during the Peninsular War before Ferdinand VII turned it into a gallery.
Goya's Black Paintings, Bosch's triptychs, and Titian's royal portraits line its grand Madrid boulevard halls.
questions.whyExplanation: Inaugurated on November 19, 1819, the Museo del Prado occupies Juan de Villanueva's 1785 neoclassical building and anchors Madrid's Golden Triangle of Art.

questions.prompt: Born in 1764 when Catherine the Great snapped up over 200 European paintings from a cash-strapped Berlin merchant, this Neva-side institution sprawls through Saint Petersburg's Winter Palace.
clues: Dozens of pest-hunting palace cats have patrolled its basements since Empress Elizabeth's 1745 decree.
With over three million items, its holdings stretch from Scythian gold to Matisse's The Dance.
questions.whyExplanation: The State Hermitage Museum traces its 1764 founding to Catherine the Great's purchase of Johann Ernst Gotzkowsky's collection and occupies six historic buildings led by the Winter Palace.

questions.prompt: Pierre Cuypers's 1885 neo-Gothic Amsterdam landmark splits neatly down its middle to let cyclists pedal through a vaulted public tunnel directly below its Gallery of Honour.
clues: After a decade-long renovation reopened in 2013, cyclists won a fierce municipal dispute to keep riding through its archway.
Its national Golden Age collection culminates in Rembrandt, Vermeer, and Frans Hals.
questions.whyExplanation: Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum opened in Pierre Cuypers's grand 1885 building featuring the famous bicycle passage; its Gallery of Honour leads straight to Rembrandt's Night Watch.

questions.prompt: Empty gilt frames still hang across this Venetian-style Boston palazzo after two thieves disguised as police stole 13 works—including Vermeer's The Concert—in March 1990.
clues: Its eccentric founder's will strictly forbade rearranging her galleries, turning the bare walls into placeholders for the missing art.
Still unsolved, the $500 million robbery also claimed Rembrandt's only known seascape, The Storm on the Sea of Galilee.
questions.whyExplanation: On March 18, 1990, the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum suffered history's costliest art theft; its empty frames remain mounted both as a tribute to the founder's will and in hope of return.

questions.prompt: Saved from demolition in the 1970s, this Left Bank Paris showcase opened in 1986 inside a Beaux-Arts railway terminal originally constructed for the 1900 Exposition Universelle.
clues: Gae Aulenti's interior redesign preserved the giant gilt station clocks overlooking the Seine.
Chronologically bridging the Louvre and Pompidou, it holds the world's finest collection of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist art.
questions.whyExplanation: Opened in December 1986 inside Victor Laloux's former Gare d'Orsay train station (1900), the Musée d'Orsay houses iconic works by Monet, Manet, Degas, Renoir, and Van Gogh.

questions.prompt: Frank Gehry's 1997 titanium-sheathed flagship beside Spain's Nervión River revived a rusty industrial port so dramatically that urban planners named an economic phenomenon after its host city.
clues: Jeff Koons's towering floral sculpture Puppy guards the entrance alongside Louise Bourgeois's bronze spider Maman.
More than 33,000 paper-thin titanium sheets shimmer in shifting Basque weather above its boat-like atrium.
questions.whyExplanation: Opening in October 1997, Frank Gehry's Guggenheim Museum Bilbao sparked the 'Bilbao Effect,' turning a declining Basque steel-and-shipbuilding city into a global cultural magnet.

questions.prompt: Argyrol patent-medicine fortune funded this quirky gallery's wall 'ensembles,' pairing 181 Renoirs and 69 Cézannes with wrought-iron hinges before a bitter court fight moved it to Philadelphia in 2012.
clues: Its eccentric founder banned color reproductions and stipulated his Merion mansion's layout never be altered.
Architects Tod Williams and Billie Tsien recreated the exact room dimensions on the Benjamin Franklin Parkway.
questions.whyExplanation: Albert C. Barnes established the Barnes Foundation in Merion, Pennsylvania in 1922; after a fiercely contested legal battle over his trust, its exact wall ensembles reopened in Philadelphia in 2012.

questions.prompt: Opened in 1891 on Vienna's Ringstrasse to showcase Habsburg imperial treasures, this domed palace holds the largest trove of Pieter Bruegel the Elder and Cellini's stolen-and-recovered gold Salt Cellar.
clues: Its symmetrical twin across Maria-Theresien-Platz is Austria's Natural History Museum.
Gustav Klimt painted murals in its grand marble stairwell, while Bruegel's The Hunters in the Snow headlines the galleries.
questions.whyExplanation: Emperor Franz Joseph opened Vienna's Kunsthistorisches Museum in 1891; Benvenuto Cellini's gold Saliera was famously stolen from it in 2003 and recovered buried in a forest in 2006.

questions.prompt: Built in the 1630s as a classical Dutch residence for colonial governor Johan Maurits of Nassau, this intimate Hague jewel box safeguards Vermeer's View of Delft and Girl with a Pearl Earring.
clues: Sitting right beside the Binnenhof parliament complex, it also displays Carel Fabritius's poignant little painting The Goldfinch.
Jacob van Campen designed its graceful brick-and-sandstone facade along the Hofvijver pond.
questions.whyExplanation: Opened as a royal picture gallery in 1822 inside Johan Maurits's 1644 Hague palace, the Mauritshuis holds barely 800 paintings yet packs an unmatched concentration of Dutch Golden Age gems.

questions.prompt: Tucked deep inside the Netherlands' Hoge Veluwe National Park alongside free white bicycles and a vast sculpture garden, this museum holds the world's second-largest Van Gogh trove.
clues: Collector Helene amassed nearly 90 paintings and over 180 drawings by Vincent long before the art market caught up.
Its Otterlo galleries house Café Terrace at Night and Country Road in Provence by Night.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded by art patron Helene Kröller-Müller and opened in 1938 in Otterlo, the Kröller-Müller Museum trails only Amsterdam's Van Gogh Museum in works by Vincent van Gogh.

questions.prompt: Originally titled The Poet to depict Dante brooding atop Auguste Rodin's unfinished doorway The Gates of Hell, this hunched bronze nude first gained its own monumental casting in 1904.
clues: One of more than two dozen authorized casts sits over Rodin's own grave at his estate in Meudon, France.
Resting chin on right hand with tense muscles, the figure embodies contemplation rather than relaxed repose.
questions.whyExplanation: Auguste Rodin conceived the figure in 1880 as the crowning centerpiece of The Gates of Hell representing Dante Alighieri before enlarging it into an independent bronze icon in 1904.

questions.prompt: Newly imported synthetic Prussian blue ink gave Katsushika Hokusai's c. 1831 woodblock print its electric sea spray, framing a snow-capped volcano behind three oared boats braving claw-like foam.
clues: Opening the series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, it was printed thousands of times in Edo for roughly the price of two bowls of noodles.
Its sweeping blue crest inspired Claude Debussy's orchestral score La Mer and became Japan's most recognizable ukiyo-e image.
questions.whyExplanation: Hokusai's c. 1831 polychrome woodblock print Under the Wave off Kanagawa leveraged newly affordable Berlin blue pigment imported via Dutch traders at Nagasaki.

questions.prompt: Discovered in two halves by peasant Yorgos Kentrotas on an Aegean island in 1820, this Parian marble Aphrodite lost her inscribed base—pointing to sculptor Alexandros of Antioch—soon after reaching Paris.
clues: Art historians suspect her vanished left hand once held a golden apple from the Judgment of Paris.
French naval officer Olivier Voutier spotted her excavation on Melos, launching a scramble to ship her to King Louis XVIII.
questions.whyExplanation: Carved around 150-125 BCE and unearthed on Melos in 1820, the Venus de Milo lost her plinth bearing Alexandros of Antioch's signature—conveniently letting the Louvre tout her as Praxiteles.

questions.prompt: Kept locked in climate-controlled darkness at Venice's Gallerie dell'Accademia except for rare showings, this c. 1490 Leonardo ink drawing matches human proportions to a circle and square.
clues: Leonardo's left-handed mirror script above and below the figure quotes a Roman architect from the first century BCE.
The navel centers the circle while the groin anchors the square in this Renaissance emblem of harmony.
questions.whyExplanation: Drawn around 1490, Leonardo da Vinci's Vitruvian Man illustrates De architectura by Roman engineer Marcus Vitruvius Pollio and is far too light-sensitive for permanent display.

questions.prompt: Unearthed in more than 100 marble shards on a northern Aegean island in 1863, this headless Hellenistic goddess alights on a carved battleship prow atop the Louvre's grand Daru staircase.
clues: Her wet-look carved chiton clings to her body as if battered by sea gales celebrating a Rhodian naval triumph.
Her right wing is actually a plaster mirror-copy of the surviving left wing, crafted during 1880s restoration.
questions.whyExplanation: Created around 190 BCE for the Sanctuary of the Great Gods on Samothrace, the Nike of Samothrace was pieced together after French diplomat Charles Champoiseau's 1863 discovery.

questions.prompt: Stopping on a rainy whim in Nipomo, California in March 1936, Dorothea Lange snapped six frames of 32-year-old pea-picker Florence Owens Thompson—then later retouched a ghostly thumb from prints.
clues: Two children bury their faces in their parent's shoulders while an infant sleeps in her lap inside a tattered tent.
Commissioned by the Farm Security Administration, the portrait became the haunting face of America's Great Depression.
questions.whyExplanation: Dorothea Lange's 1936 FSA photograph Migrant Mother prompted emergency food shipments to Nipomo within days, though Thompson later resented receiving no royalties from its fame.

questions.prompt: Inside Rome's Cornaro Chapel, Gian Lorenzo Bernini concealed an overhead skylight behind gilded bronze rays to bathe this 1652 marble vision of a smiling angel piercing a Carmelite mystic's heart.
clues: Carved members of the patron Cornaro family lean out of sculpted theater boxes along both side walls like opera spectators.
Floating on rough-hewn marble clouds, the Spanish nun's swooning expression drew raised eyebrows from Baroque critics.
questions.whyExplanation: Completed in 1652 for Santa Maria della Vittoria in Rome, Bernini's Ecstasy of Saint Teresa fused sculpture, architecture, and hidden theatrical lighting into a High Baroque triumph.

questions.prompt: Commissioned to honor six medieval French volunteers who offered their lives to England's King Edward III in 1347, this Rodin bronze shocked city elders by setting gaunt figures at street level.
clues: Draped in sackcloth with hangman's nooses around their necks, Eustache de Saint-Pierre and five peers trudge toward surrender.
Municipal officials ignored the sculptor's wishes for decades, perching the 1889 group on a tall pedestal until 1924.
questions.whyExplanation: Rodin's The Burghers of Calais (completed 1889) rejected heroic triumphalism by portraying the six Hundred Years' War hostages gripped by fear and anguish at ground level.

questions.prompt: When Roman diggers struck this writhing Hellenistic marble trio in a vineyard in 1506, Pope Julius II rushed Michelangelo to the pit—where Pliny's account of a doomed Trojan priest confirmed the find.
clues: Two massive sea serpents coil around a bearded priest and two boys who warned Troy against dragging in the wooden horse.
Archaeologist Ludwig Pollak finally spotted the father's genuine bent right arm in a Roman stonemason's shop in 1906.
questions.whyExplanation: Unearthed near Rome's Domus Aurea on January 14, 1506 and verified from Pliny the Elder's Natural History, Laocoön and His Sons reshaped Michelangelo's anatomy and anchors the Vatican Museums.

questions.prompt: Albrecht Dürer packed this dense 1514 copper engraving with a brooding winged genius, a truncated polyhedron, and a 4-by-4 magic square whose bottom center cells spell out the year it was cut.

distractors.text: The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse

clues: Every row, column, and diagonal of the engraved grid sums to 34, while scattered carpentry tools lie idle around a compass.
Alongside two companion prints, it represents the intellectual temperament linked to Saturn in Renaissance humor theory.
questions.whyExplanation: Dürer's 1514 master engraving Melencolia I embeds the date '15 14' in the bottom row of its Jupiter magic square and remains one of the most analyzed prints in art history.

questions.prompt: When photographer Edward Steichen imported Constantin Brâncuși's gleaming abstract bronze in 1926, U.S. Customs taxed it as raw kitchenware—sparking a landmark 1928 trial redefining modern art.

distractors.text: Unique Forms of Continuity in Space

clues: Customs officials insisted a duty-free artwork must imitate a natural object, slapping a 40% industrial metal tariff on the tapered shaft.
Judge Byron S. Waite ruled in the sculptor's favor, recognizing the streamlined vertical flight form as fine sculpture.
questions.whyExplanation: Brâncuși v. United States (1928) centered on the gleaming bronze Bird in Space, establishing U.S. legal precedent that non-representational modern sculptures qualify as duty-free fine art.

questions.prompt: Too politically incendiary for Restoration Spain, Francisco Goya's 82 stark aquatint etchings exposing Peninsular War atrocities sat unprinted until the Royal Academy issued an edition in 1863.
clues: Etched between 1810 and 1820, plates carry biting captions like 'Yo lo vi' ('I saw it') and 'Tampoco' ('Nor this').
Unlike heroic Napoleonic propaganda, the portfolio condemned both French occupiers and Spanish guerrilla brutality alike.
questions.whyExplanation: Goya's Los Desastres de la Guerra—82 etchings created during and after Napoleon's invasion of Spain—was published posthumously in 1863, 35 years after the artist's death.

questions.prompt: Born in the 1140s when Abbot Suger rebuilt the choir of Saint-Denis outside Paris, this soaring style traded thick stone walls for pointed arches, ribbed vaults, and flying buttresses.
clues: Renaissance critic Giorgio Vasari coined its name as a slur, blaming northern 'barbarians' for abandoning Roman forms.
Flooding tall naves with stained-glass light, it reached dizzying heights at Amiens, Reims, and Cologne.
questions.whyExplanation: Gothic architecture originated at France's Basilica of Saint-Denis in the 1140s, engineering skeletal stone frames that lifted cathedrals skyward and opened walls to luminous stained glass.

questions.prompt: Named retroactively after a dazzling 1925 Paris decorative-arts exposition, this Jazz Age movement crowned Manhattan's Chrysler Building and Miami's South Beach with sunbursts and stepped chevrons.
clues: Blending machine-age speed with ancient Egyptian motifs unearthed in Tutankhamun's 1922 tomb, it embraced chrome and terracotta.
Radio City Music Hall and the Empire State Building lobby showcase its bold geometric glamour.
questions.whyExplanation: Art Deco took its name from Paris's 1925 Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes, defining interwar skyscrapers, ocean liners, and cinemas.

questions.prompt: Launched by Walter Gropius in Weimar in 1919 before moving to a curtain-walled Dessau campus, this movement fused fine art with industrial design until Nazi pressure shuttered its Berlin rooms in 1933.
clues: Marcel Breuer's tubular-steel Wassily chair and Marianne Brandt's geometric teapots emerged from its workshops.
Its German name reverses the word for house-building, championing flat roofs, steel frames, and form following function.
questions.whyExplanation: Operating from 1919 to 1933 under Walter Gropius, Hannes Meyer, and Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, the Bauhaus revolutionized modernist architecture, typography, and industrial furniture.

questions.prompt: Championed by Counter-Reformation Rome and master showmen like Bernini and Borromini, this 17th-century style shattered Renaissance stillness with undulating walls, oval domes, and theatrical gilding.
clues: Its name likely descends from a Portuguese jeweler's term for an irregularly shaped pearl.
Saint Peter's sweeping colonnade and San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane epitomize its kinetic drama.
questions.whyExplanation: Emerging in late-16th-century Italy to awe Counter-Reformation worshippers, Baroque architecture replaced balanced symmetry with sculptural curves, trompe-l'oeil ceilings, and dramatic light.

questions.prompt: Despite its harsh-sounding name, this postwar movement descends from the French phrase 'béton brut' for raw poured concrete, defining Boston City Hall and London's Barbican Estate.
clues: Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation in Marseille inspired British architects Alison and Peter Smithson to champion its honesty.
Unpainted board-formed surfaces, blocky cantilevers, and civic monumentality make it both fiercely loathed and cultishly beloved.
questions.whyExplanation: Brutalism derives from Le Corbusier's 'béton brut' (raw concrete) rather than English 'brutal'; flourishing from the 1950s to 1970s, it prized exposed structure and unadorned materials.

questions.prompt: Flourishing across Europe around 1890 to 1910, this whiplash-curved movement reshaped Victor Horta's Brussels townhouses and Hector Guimard's vine-like cast-iron Paris Métro entrances.
clues: Rejecting stiff historical revivals, its designers drew asymmetric stems, irises, and dragonfly wings into glass and iron.
Its French title echoed Samuel Bing's influential Paris gallery that showcased the 'new' turn-of-the-century aesthetic.
questions.whyExplanation: Art Nouveau swept Europe at the fin de siècle through architects like Victor Horta, Hector Guimard, and Antoni Gaudí, uniting architecture and furnishings in organic, sinuous lines.

questions.prompt: Born around turn-of-the-century Chicago, this distinctly American movement mirrored the flat Midwest horizon with low hipped roofs, sweeping eaves, open interiors, and horizontal bands of art glass.
clues: Frank Lloyd Wright's Robie House in Hyde Park stands as its purest residential manifesto.
Marion Mahony Griffin and George Grant Elmslie also shaped its earth-hugging, hearth-centered domestic spaces.
questions.whyExplanation: Flourishing roughly 1900-1916 in the American Midwest, the Prairie School rejected boxy Victorian parlors in favor of horizontal lines echoing the surrounding flat plains.

questions.prompt: Exported to Gilded Age America by graduates of Paris's premier state art academy, this grand neoclassical mode produced Grand Central Terminal, the New York Public Library, and the 1893 White City.
clues: Firms like McKim, Mead & White paired rusticated stone bases with paired columns, sculptural garlands, and axial lobbies.
Paris's Opéra Garnier and Grand Palais served as its French templates.
questions.whyExplanation: Taught at Paris's École des Beaux-Arts, Beaux-Arts architecture blended classical Roman discipline with Baroque richness to give American cities monumental civic terminals and museums.

questions.prompt: Codified in a 1570 treatise by a Venetian master, this symmetrical temple-front movement swept 18th-century British country estates and directly shaped Thomas Jefferson's Monticello and University of Virginia.
clues: Inigo Jones imported it to Stuart England with the Queen's House in Greenwich and London's Banqueting House.
Signature hallmarks include musical mathematical ratios, pedimented porticoes, and arched central windows flanked by flat-topped lights.
questions.whyExplanation: Inspired by Andrea Palladio's I quattro libri dell'architettura (1570) and villas like Villa Rotonda, Palladianism became the foundation of Georgian British and early American civic design.

questions.prompt: Crystallized in a provocative 1988 MoMA exhibition curated by Philip Johnson and Mark Wigley, this movement shattered neat right angles with tilted planes and fractured volumes by Gehry, Eisenman, and Hadid.
clues: Drawing loosely on philosopher Jacques Derrida and early Soviet Constructivism, it made buildings appear caught mid-collision.
Daniel Libeskind's jagged Jewish Museum Berlin and Seattle's Central Library embody its tilted geometry.
questions.whyExplanation: The 1988 MoMA exhibition 'Deconstructivist Architecture' grouped seven boundary-breaking architects—including Frank Gehry, Rem Koolhaas, and Zaha Hadid—whose colliding geometries upended modernist boxes.

questions.prompt: Unveiled at the 1960 Tokyo World Design Conference by Kenzo Tange's young disciples, this postwar Japanese movement envisioned biological megastructures with replaceable living pods like Nakagin Capsule Tower.
clues: Kisho Kurokawa, Kiyonori Kikutake, and Fumihiko Maki proposed floating marine cities that could grow and shed cells.
Its 1972 Tokyo tower of 140 bolt-on concrete rooms—each fitted with a circular washing-machine window—was dismantled in 2022.
questions.whyExplanation: Japanese Metabolism merged postwar reconstruction urgency with biological renewal metaphors, imagining permanent urban spines fitted with swappable modular pods.

questions.prompt: Named for the delicate metalwork of Spanish silversmiths, this early-16th-century Iberian Renaissance mode draped Salamanca's university facade in dense stone filigree—including a famous hidden frog.
clues: Students in Salamanca still hunt for the tiny sculpted amphibian perched atop a skull on the intricately carved doorway for exam luck.
Its Spanish root 'platero' reflects how medallioned pilasters and crests encrusted Gothic building frames like chased silver.
questions.whyExplanation: Flourishing in Spain roughly 1490-1560, Plateresque ('silversmith-like') architecture fused Italian Renaissance ornament with late Gothic and Mudéjar exuberance, peaking at the University of Salamanca.

questions.prompt: Built in just five years under Emperor Justinian by physicists Anthemius and Isidore, this 537 Byzantine marvel floated a colossal dome on four spherical pendentives above Istanbul's skyline.
clues: After serving as Eastern Orthodoxy's premier cathedral for nearly a millennium, Mehmed II converted it into an imperial mosque in 1453.
Turned into a secular museum by Atatürk in 1935, it resumed worship as a mosque in 2020.
questions.whyExplanation: Dedicated in 537 CE as the Church of Holy Wisdom, Hagia Sophia pioneered the pendentive dome over a square bay and reigned as the world's largest cathedral for nearly 1,000 years.

questions.prompt: Using upside-down chains weighted with birdshot to calculate its branching stone vaults, Antoni Gaudí devoted his final 15 years to this Barcelona basilica—still unfinished a century after his 1926 tram death.
clues: When finished, eighteen soaring towers will represent the twelve Apostles, four Evangelists, Mary, and Jesus.
Spanish Civil War anarchists torched Gaudí's plaster models in 1936, forcing successors to reconstruct his math from fragments.
questions.whyExplanation: Begun in 1882 and taken over by Antoni Gaudí in 1883, Barcelona's Basílica de la Sagrada Família uses catenary arches modeled from inverted weighted strings and remains the world's longest-running church build.

questions.prompt: Unlike most Khmer sanctuaries facing the rising sun, this sprawling 12th-century Cambodian complex looks west—built by King Suryavarman II for Vishnu before gradually becoming a Buddhist shrine.
clues: Its five lotus-bud towers symbolize mythical Mount Meru and appear on Cambodia's national flag.
Ringed by a rectangular moat more than three miles around, its outer gallery bears the Churning of the Ocean of Milk relief.
questions.whyExplanation: Constructed in the early 12th century under Suryavarman II, Angkor Wat is the world's largest religious monument; its westward orientation likely reflects Vishnu's association or funerary use.

questions.prompt: Neglected after Revolutionary vandals beheaded its stone kings, this Île de la Cité Gothic landmark owed its 19th-century rescue partly to Victor Hugo's 1831 bestseller—and reopened in 2024 after a 2019 blaze.
clues: Eugène Viollet-le-Duc's 1859 oak-and-lead spire toppled on live television in April 2019 before artisans rebuilt it identically.
Its twin square west towers and grotesque chimeras overlook Point Zero of France's highway network.
questions.whyExplanation: Begun in 1163, Notre-Dame de Paris gained popular urgency from Victor Hugo's 1831 novel, underwent Viollet-le-Duc's major restoration, and reopened in December 2024 after five years of post-fire rebuilding.

questions.prompt: Its gaping 148-foot octagonal opening sat roofless for decades because no forest held enough timber for scaffolding—until Filippo Brunelleschi vaulted it in 1436 with a double herringbone-brick shell.
clues: Also called Santa Maria del Fiore, its white, green, and pink marble facade faces Lorenzo Ghiberti's bronze Gates of Paradise.
Brunelleschi invented a three-speed ox-driven hoist to lift sandstone and marble rings high above the Tuscan skyline.
questions.whyExplanation: Filippo Brunelleschi solved Renaissance architecture's greatest engineering puzzle by constructing the self-supporting double masonry dome of Florence Cathedral (1420-1436) without wooden centering.

questions.prompt: A forest of 856 recycled Roman and Visigothic columns topped by red-and-white striped horseshoe arches gained an intrusive Renaissance choir planted right inside its center in the 1500s.
clues: Emperor Charles V reportedly scolded the builders who carved out its middle, saying they had ruined something unique in the world.
Begun by Umayyad exile Abd al-Rahman I in 785, its glittering Byzantine-tesserae mihrab remains an Andalusian crown jewel.
questions.whyExplanation: Built in stages from 785 to 987 under Spain's Umayyad rulers, the Mezquita-Catedral of Córdoba became a cathedral after the 1236 Reconquista and had a full Christian nave inserted in 1523.

questions.prompt: After an 1194 fire spared its prized Tunic of the Virgin relic, French masons raised this High Gothic icon in 26 years, preserving cobalt glass and mismatched spires.
clues: Its plain 12th-century south tower contrasts dramatically with Jehan de Beauce's lacy Flamboyant north spire added in 1513.
An 11-circuit stone labyrinth inlaid into its nave floor still draws modern pilgrims southwest of Paris.
questions.whyExplanation: Rebuilt swiftly after the 1194 fire, Chartres Cathedral retains over 150 original 13th-century stained-glass windows famed for 'Chartres blue' cobalt pigment and asymmetrical spires.

questions.prompt: Erected in 691 under Umayyad Caliph Abd al-Malik atop Jerusalem's Haram al-Sharif, this gilded octagonal monument is actually a commemorative shrine rather than a congregational mosque.
clues: Suleiman the Magnificent replaced its weather-worn Byzantine exterior glass mosaics with turquoise Ottoman tiles in the 1500s.
Its interior encircles the Foundation Stone linked to Abraham's sacrifice and Muhammad's Night Journey.
questions.whyExplanation: Completed in 691-692 CE, Jerusalem's Dome of the Rock is the oldest surviving masterpiece of Islamic architecture, built as a pilgrim shrine over the sacred Foundation Stone.

questions.prompt: Pierced by bundles of protruding palm-wood sticks that act as permanent scaffolding, this soaring West African mud-brick sanctuary gets replastered by the entire town during an annual festival.
clues: Built in its present Sudano-Sahelian form in 1907 along Mali's Bani River, it stands as the planet's largest adobe building.
Its festive spring resurfacing, known as the Crépissage, pits masons and neighborhoods in a lively race before rainy season.
questions.whyExplanation: Completed in 1907 on the site of a 13th-century precursor in Mali, the Great Mosque of Djenné is the world's largest mud-brick structure, studded with palm-wood toron beams for annual repairs.

questions.prompt: Stacked in Central Java around 800 CE without a drop of mortar, this nine-tiered Buddhist stone mountain wraps over 2,600 relief panels beneath 72 bell-shaped perforated stupas housing seated Buddhas.
clues: Hidden beneath volcanic ash and jungle growth for centuries, it was rediscovered in 1814 under British governor Stamford Raffles.
Pilgrims ascend clockwise from earthly desire through formless enlightenment atop its volcanic-stone terraces.
questions.whyExplanation: Built by the Sailendra dynasty in the 8th-9th centuries in Indonesia, Borobudur is the world's largest Buddhist temple, interlocked from two million volcanic andesite blocks without mortar.

questions.prompt: King Louis IX paid more for the Crown of Thorns than for this entire 1248 Parisian royal reliquary, whose Rayonnant engineers dissolved nearly its whole upper stone wall into 15 glowing stained-glass lancets.
clues: Tucked inside the Palais de la Cité courtyard, its dark low lower chapel served palace staff while royals climbed to the jewel box above.
More than 1,100 biblical scenes shimmer across 6,400 square feet of 13th-century glass held together by concealed iron rods.
questions.whyExplanation: Consecrated in 1248 to house relics Louis IX bought from Baldwin II of Constantinople for 135,000 livres, Sainte-Chapelle is the pinnacle of Rayonnant Gothic architecture.

questions.prompt: Instead of stacking blocks upward, 8th-century Rashtrakuta artisans carved this monolithic Hindu sanctuary at India's Ellora Caves from the top down out of a single basalt cliff.
clues: Excavating roughly 200,000 tons of volcanic rock without mortar, sculptors left full-scale stone elephants and a courtyard tower standing.
Designated Cave 16 in Maharashtra, it honors Shiva's Himalayan abode under King Krishna I.
questions.whyExplanation: Commissioned by Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna I in the mid-8th century, Ellora's Kailasa Temple (Cave 16) is the largest monolithic rock-cut structure on Earth, chiselled downward from one cliff face.

questions.prompt: Bankrupting himself on a fairytale homage to Richard Wagner, Bavaria's King Ludwig II fitted this 19th-century Alpine fantasy with flushing toilets and telephone lines—yet lived inside it for barely 172 days.
clues: Set designer Christian Jank drafted its dramatic storybook turrets before architects translated his theater sketches into limestone.
Opened to paying tourists just weeks after Ludwig's mysterious 1886 drowning, it inspired Walt Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle.
questions.whyExplanation: Begun in 1869 by Bavaria's 'Swan King' Ludwig II, Neuschwanstein blended medieval revival fantasy with cutting-edge 1880s central heating and plumbing before his deposition in 1886.

questions.prompt: Crowning Granada's Sabika hill as Iberia's last Nasrid royal seat, this fortified palace dazzles with honeycomb muqarnas vaults and a courtyard fountain borne by twelve marble lions.
clues: Sultan Boabdil surrendered its keys to Ferdinand and Isabella in January 1492, inspiring Washington Irving's romantic 1832 tales.
Its Arabic nickname refers to the sun-baked red clay of its outer ramparts above the Sierra Nevada foothills.
questions.whyExplanation: Built primarily by Granada's Nasrid sultans Yusuf I and Muhammad V in the 14th century, the Alhambra ('The Red One') epitomizes Moorish court architecture, water engineering, and plasterwork.

questions.prompt: In a covert 1929 skyscraper race against rival 40 Wall Street, William Van Alen secretly built a 185-foot steel spire inside this Manhattan tower and hoisted it up in 90 minutes.
clues: Hood-ornament eagle gargoyles and hubcap brickwork celebrate its automaker patron across its terraced sunburst crown.
It reigned as the world's tallest building for just 11 months before a crosstown competitor overtook it in May 1931.
questions.whyExplanation: Van Alen's stealth 'Vertex' lifted the Chrysler Building to 1,046 feet in October 1929—beating H. Craig Severance's 40 Wall Street until the Empire State Building opened in 1931.

questions.prompt: After its designer died of tetanus and his son was paralyzed by decompression sickness, Emily Warren Roebling spent eleven years steering this 1883 steel-wire East River suspension span to completion.
clues: To calm nervous New Yorkers after a deadly 1883 stampede, P. T. Barnum paraded 21 elephants—including Jumbo—across its roadway.
Its pointed Gothic granite towers linked two once-separate cities fifteen years before Greater New York consolidated.
questions.whyExplanation: Completed on May 24, 1883, the Brooklyn Bridge was the first steel-wire suspension bridge; Emily Warren Roebling mastered higher math and cable engineering to become its de facto chief engineer.

questions.prompt: Cantilevering Edgar Kaufmann's 1930s Pennsylvania retreat directly over Bear Run's cascade rather than facing it, Frank Lloyd Wright watched nervous engineers sneak extra rebar into its slabs.
clues: A glass-enclosed hatch opens straight down to the rushing creek, and a native boulder erupts right through the living-room hearth.
Its soaring ochre concrete terraces sagged measurably over decades until a 2002 post-tensioning cable rescue stabilized them.
questions.whyExplanation: Built 1936-1939 in Mill Run, Pennsylvania, Frank Lloyd Wright's Fallingwater told Kaufmann to live 'with the waterfall, not just look at it,' becoming a landmark of organic modernism.

questions.prompt: Expanded from Louis XIII's brick hunting lodge to 2,300 rooms, this French estate's 73-meter Hall of Mirrors hosted both the 1871 German Empire proclamation and the 1919 peace treaty.
clues: Landscape genius André Le Nôtre sculpted its formal fountains while Charles Le Brun gilded its Sun King ceilings.
Louis XIV moved France's government here in 1682 to keep scheming nobles busy competing over dressing-room privileges.
questions.whyExplanation: Transformed under Louis XIV by Louis Le Vau and Jules Hardouin-Mansart, the Palace of Versailles anchored French royal rule until 1789 and witnessed key 1871 and 1919 diplomatic milestones.

questions.prompt: Rising 13 stories and over 1,000 rooms atop Marpo Ri hill in Lhasa, this winter seat of the Dalai Lamas began its White Palace in 1645 with rammed earth and molten-copper joints.
clues: Perched at 12,100 feet above sea level, its crimson central Red Palace houses gilded stupa tombs of past spiritual leaders.
The 14th Dalai Lama fled its walls in 1959, and the landmark now operates as a UNESCO World Heritage museum.
questions.whyExplanation: Built between 1645 and 1694 atop Lhasa's Red Hill, the Potala Palace combines Tibetan fortress walls with sacred chapels and remains the highest ancient palace in the world.

questions.prompt: Spanning southern France's misty Tarn Gorge since 2004, this graceful seven-mast cable-stayed highway crossing designed by Michel Virlogeux and Norman Foster tops out at 343 meters—taller than the Eiffel Tower.
clues: Its 2,460-meter steel deck was hydraulically pushed out over concrete piers using GPS-guided jacks from both hillsides.
Motorists driving from Paris toward Barcelona often glide above a solid carpet of valley clouds on the A75 motorway.
questions.whyExplanation: Inaugurated in December 2004 by President Jacques Chirac, the Millau Viaduct holds the record as the world's tallest bridge structure, with Pier 2 and its mast reaching 343 meters.

questions.prompt: Pioneering Manhattan's setback public plaza on Park Avenue in 1958, Mies van der Rohe's bronze-and-glass tower bolted decorative exterior I-beams on after fire codes hid the steel.
clues: Whisky heiress Phyllis Lambert convinced her father Samuel Bronfman to reject a mediocre design and hire the German modernist master.
Its 38 stories cost so much per square foot that New York City briefly tried to assess an extra 'prestige tax' on it.
questions.whyExplanation: Completed in 1958 at 375 Park Avenue, the Seagram Building codified International Style skyscraper design and directly prompted New York's 1961 zoning bonus for public plazas.

questions.prompt: Coated in flame-retardant white plaster that earned it the nickname 'White Heron,' this 17th-century Japanese hilltop fortress escaped both World War II firebombing and the 1995 Kobe earthquake unscathed.
clues: An Allied incendiary bomb actually landed on its top floor in 1945—and miraculously failed to detonate.
Comprising 83 wooden buildings linked by spiral defensive mazes, it is Japan's finest surviving original feudal keep.
questions.whyExplanation: Expanded to its iconic form by Ikeda Terumasa between 1601 and 1609 in Hyōgo Prefecture, Himeji-jō ('White Heron Castle') survives intact with its original wooden structure and fireproof plaster.

questions.prompt: Built in Poissy in 1931 as Le Corbusier's manifesto of his Five Points of Architecture, this white residence on pilotis curved its ground-floor glass wall to a 1920s car's turning radius.
clues: A continuous interior ramp rises from the chauffeur-friendly entry all the way to a sculpted rooftop solarium in Poissy.
Its leaking flat roof so infuriated the wealthy owners that they threatened to sue the architect before war intervened.
questions.whyExplanation: Built 1928-1931 in Poissy, France, Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye exemplified pilotis, roof garden, free plan, ribbon windows, and free facade—despite notorious early rain leaks.

questions.prompt: Spared by retreating German troops in 1944 when every other Arno span fell, this medieval Florence bridge banished butchers for goldsmiths in 1593 on Grand Duke Ferdinando I's orders.
clues: The Medici's private elevated Vasari Corridor threads right across the upper story of its overhanging timber-propped stalls.
Built in 1345 with three daringly flat segmental stone arches, it remains Europe's oldest closed-spandrel segmental bridge.
questions.whyExplanation: Rebuilt in 1345, Florence's Ponte Vecchio banished tanners and butchers in 1593 so foul odors would not waft up into the Medici's Vasari Corridor; German commanders instead rubble-blocked its approaches in 1944.

questions.prompt: Bedridden in a full-body plaster cast after an iron bus handrail impaled her in Mexico City in 1925, this painter began her unflinching self-portraits using a mirror hung on her bed canopy.
clues: Her tempestuous twin marriages to muralist Diego Rivera anchored Coyoacán's cobalt-blue Casa Azul.
Tehuana skirts, pet spider monkeys, and fractured spines recur across her 55 introspective self-portraits.
questions.whyExplanation: Following a near-fatal September 1925 trolley-bus crash at age 18, Frida Kahlo abandoned medical studies for painting, turning physical agony and Mexican folk iconography into iconic self-portraiture.

questions.prompt: Severe cataracts in his eighties skewed this Giverny founder of Impressionism toward murky reds and yellows—prompting him to destroy many late garden canvases once 1923 surgery restored blues.
clues: A hostile 1874 critic mocked his foggy Le Havre harbor sunrise to coin the entire movement's name.
He diverted the Epte River to build his Japanese footbridge and painted roughly 250 water-lily studies.
questions.whyExplanation: Diagnosed with bilateral cataracts in 1912, Claude Monet painted increasingly reddish, blurred Japanese-bridge scenes at Giverny until 1923 lens surgery let him finish his vast Orangerie water-lily murals.

questions.prompt: Carving his giant Florence David from a narrow marble block abandoned by two earlier sculptors, this grumpy Tuscan genius signed only one work in his entire career—across the Virgin's sash.
clues: Overhearing Lombards credit his 1499 Vatican Pietà to a Milanese rival, he snuck in by night with a chisel to carve his name.
Despite insisting 'I am not a painter,' he spent four grueling years aloft on scaffolding frescoing the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
questions.whyExplanation: Michelangelo Buonarroti sculpted David (1501-1504) from an Agostino di Duccio cast-off block and famously inscribed 'MICHELANGELVS BONAROTVS FLORENTINVS FACIEBAT' solely on St. Peter's Pietà.

questions.prompt: While photographer husband Alfred Stieglitz encouraged Freudian readings of her magnified poppies and desert cow skulls, this Ghost Ranch modernist tartly insisted a flower was just a flower.
clues: She packed bleached New Mexico bones into barrels and mailed them east to paint under Manhattan's Shelton Hotel skyline.
Her 1932 canvas Jimson Weed/White Flower No. 1 set a record auction price for a female artist in 2014.
questions.whyExplanation: Pioneering American modernism, Georgia O'Keeffe moved permanently to New Mexico after Stieglitz's 1946 death, transforming Abiquiú mesas, adobe walls, and close-cropped blooms into austere abstractions.

questions.prompt: Fleeing Rome under a papal death warrant after stabbing Ranuccio Tomassoni in a 1606 brawl, this hot-tempered pioneer of dramatic tenebrist lighting painted on the run from Naples to Malta.
clues: He cast Roman street brawlers and sex workers as saints in The Calling of Saint Matthew and Judith Beheading Holofernes.
He died at 38 in Porto Ercole in 1610 while traveling back to Rome expecting a papal pardon.
questions.whyExplanation: Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio revolutionized Baroque painting through theatrical spotlight-and-shadow tenebrism, though his violent temper kept him an exile across southern Italy until his 1610 death.

questions.prompt: Around the 1440s, this Florentine trailblazer cast Renaissance Europe's first freestanding life-sized nude bronze since antiquity—a lithe young shepherd in a laurelled hat resting a foot on Goliath's head.
clues: His shallow-relief technique 'schiacciato' created atmospheric perspective in marble barely millimeters deep.
Later in life he shocked Florence with an emaciated, toothless carved-wood Penitent Magdalene.
questions.whyExplanation: Donato di Niccolò di Betto Bardi—Donatello—revived classical contrapposto in his bronze David for the Medici courtyard and shaped a century of Renaissance sculpture from Florence to Padua.

questions.prompt: In 1616 she became the first woman admitted to Florence's prestigious Accademia delle Arti del Disegno, bringing visceral Baroque grit to biblical heroines like Judith and Susanna.
clues: Trained in Rome by her Caravaggist painter father Orazio, she later worked at Charles I's London court.
Unlike timid contemporary versions, her Uffizi canvas shows Judith and her maidservant aggressively pinning down Holofernes.
questions.whyExplanation: After enduring an infamous 1612 Roman trial against her rapist Agostino Tassi, Artemisia Gentileschi forged an acclaimed pan-European career famed for fearless, psychologically sharp Baroque canvases.

questions.prompt: Trained as a mechanical engineer before wowing Paris avant-gardists with a miniature suitcase wire circus, this American sculptor invented balanced hanging kinetic works Marcel Duchamp dubbed 'mobiles.'
clues: A 1930 visit to Piet Mondrian's studio inspired him to set primary-colored geometric cutouts drifting in mid-air.
His grounded, motionless monumental steel abstractions earned the contrasting nickname 'stabiles' from Jean Arp.
questions.whyExplanation: Combining engineering balance with playful modernist color, Alexander Calder transformed sculpture from static mass into weightless motion, leaving soaring mobiles in museums and airports worldwide.

questions.prompt: Born to Parisian tapestry restorers, this sculptor waited until age 70 for her first MoMA retrospective in 1982—then cast 30-foot bronze spiders titled Maman to honor her patient weaver mother.
clues: In 2000, her towering steel-and-marble arachnid became the inaugural Turbine Hall commission at London's Tate Modern.
