Psychological 'Cells' packed with mirrors, antique perfume bottles, and stitched fabric defined her fierce late-life surge.
questions.whyExplanation: Working quietly in New York for decades before late-career acclaim, French-American sculptor Louise Bourgeois turned childhood trauma and maternal memory into monumental bronzes like Maman (1999).

questions.prompt: Born Doménikos Theotokópoulos in Venetian Crete and schooled in Venice's glowing colorism, this eccentric Mannerist settled in Toledo in 1577 to stretch saints into flickering, acid-lit flames.
clues: He baffled Philip II with his unconventional Martyrdom of Saint Maurice yet triumphed with The Burial of the Count of Orgaz.
Dismissed for centuries as astigmatic, his stormy View of Toledo thrilled 20th-century Expressionists and Picasso alike.
questions.whyExplanation: Signing canvases in Greek letters even in Spain, El Greco merged Byzantine icon austerity, Venetian brushwork, and Mannerist elongation to become Toledo's most visionary Golden Age painter.

questions.prompt: Scandalizing the 1783 Paris Salon by painting Marie Antoinette in a casual muslin chemise, this royal portraitist fled the Revolution in disguise to paint across Naples and Russia.
clues: She completed more than 30 portraits of the French queen, helping soften Marie Antoinette's public image as a devoted mother.
One of just four women admitted to France's Royal Academy in 1783, she painted over 660 portraits across a 70-year career.
questions.whyExplanation: Favorite painter of Marie Antoinette, Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun escaped Paris in October 1789 and won international renown across Vienna, Rome, and St. Petersburg with luminous Rococo-Neoclassical portraits.

questions.prompt: Pioneering unpainted monochrome limewood altarpieces in Late Gothic Würzburg, this master woodcarver and city councilor was imprisoned and tortured in 1525 for refusing to back crushing the Peasants' War.
clues: His breathtaking Holy Blood Altarpiece in Rothenburg ob der Tauber lets bare wood grain catch shifting church candlelight.
Legends claim the Prince-Bishop broke his sculpting hands in Marienberg Fortress; either way, he took no major commissions afterward.
questions.whyExplanation: One of northern Europe's supreme Late Gothic sculptors, Tilman Riemenschneider revolutionized German limewood carving before his political defense of rebellious peasants ended his career in 1525.

questions.prompt: Surviving a tragic 1914 Taliesin blaze, this American modernist spent 16 years spiraling concrete up Fifth Avenue—only to die six months before New York's Guggenheim opened.
clues: His 1923 Tokyo Imperial Hotel famously withstood the Great Kantō Earthquake on floating mud-layer foundations.
From Oak Park's Unity Temple to Johnson Wax's lily-pad columns, he championed 'organic architecture' fused to landscape.
questions.whyExplanation: Designing over 1,000 structures across seven decades, Frank Lloyd Wright invented the Prairie House and completed designs for New York's spiral Guggenheim Museum shortly before dying at 91 in April 1959.

questions.prompt: Enduring Parisian outrage from critics who called his 1989 Louvre courtyard glass pyramid a 'gadget' and an 'eyesore,' this Cantonese-born Pritzker laureate lived to see it rival the Eiffel Tower in popularity.
clues: His crisp triangular geometry shaped Hong Kong's Bank of China Tower, Cleveland's Rock Hall, and Washington's East Building.
At age 91, he came out of retirement to design Doha's sunlit limestone Museum of Islamic Art.
questions.whyExplanation: Ieoh Ming Pei (1917-2019) overcame fierce opposition to President François Mitterrand's Grand Louvre commission, crafting an iconic 71-foot steel-and-glass pyramid that transformed museum circulation.

questions.prompt: Dismissed early as a 'paper architect' whose swooping forms seemed unbuildable, this Baghdad-born visionary became the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize in 2004.
clues: Her breakout built commission was the jagged 1993 Vitra Fire Station in Weil am Rhein, Germany.
Later projects spanned Rome's MAXXI museum, London's 2012 Aquatics Centre, and Guangzhou's flowing Opera House.
questions.whyExplanation: Mathematician turned radical spatial visionary, Dame Zaha Hadid (1950-2016) pioneered parametric curves in steel and concrete, shattering glass ceilings with the 2004 Pritzker Prize.

questions.prompt: Originally an Oxford astronomy professor and Royal Society co-founder, this polymath pivoted after the 1666 Great Fire of London to rebuild 51 City churches and crown St. Paul's Cathedral.
clues: He cleverly built St. Paul's lofty dome using a hidden brick cone sandwiched between an inner plaster shell and outer lead roof.
Buried inside his own cathedral crypt, his plain Latin epitaph instructs: 'Reader, if you seek his monument, look around you.'
questions.whyExplanation: Sir Christopher Wren reshaped London's skyline after the 1666 fire, dedicating 35 years to St. Paul's Cathedral alongside Greenwich's Royal Naval College and Hampton Court's baroque south wing.

questions.prompt: Declaring he was drawn not to rigid right angles but to 'the free-flowing, sensual curve' of his homeland's mountains and rivers, this centenarian Brazilian shaped Brasília's soaring concrete Cathedral.
clues: Collaborating with urban planner Lúcio Costa, he designed the saucer-and-bowl National Congress for Brazil's brand-new capital in 1960.
Working well past age 100 before dying at 104 in 2012, he also crafted Niterói's flying-saucer art museum.
questions.whyExplanation: Oscar Niemeyer (1907-2012) liberated reinforced concrete from boxy grids, winning the 1988 Pritzker Prize for landmark civic sculptures in Brasília and helping design New York's UN Headquarters.

questions.prompt: Submitted anonymously as entry #1026 for a Yale senior class assignment in 1981, this 21-year-old student's stark black-granite V-shaped wall beat 1,420 rivals to become the Vietnam Veterans Memorial.
clues: Her architecture professor gave her initial class sketch only a B, yet the national competition jury unanimously chose it.
Polished Indian gabbro slabs list over 58,000 fallen Americans chronologically while reflecting visitors' own faces.
questions.whyExplanation: Still a Yale undergraduate in 1981, Maya Lin weathered intense controversy over her minimalist sunken design before its November 1982 dedication made it Washington's most emotionally resonant memorial.

questions.prompt: Resigning in 1966 amid a bitter clash with New South Wales officials over soaring costs, this Danish architect never returned to see his white-tiled Sydney Opera House completed.
clues: Legend says peeling an orange gave him his breakthrough geometric solution: cutting every soaring roof vault from a single giant sphere.
Reconciled late in life, he won the 2003 Pritzker Prize and saw his landmark named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007.
questions.whyExplanation: Danish architect Jørn Utzon won the 1957 Sydney Opera House competition with freehand sketches, solved its spherical shell geometry with Ove Arup, yet left in 1966 and died in 2008 without ever visiting the finished hall.

questions.prompt: Conscripted as a Christian youth from Anatolia into the Ottoman Janissary corps, this imperial chief architect built over 300 structures—hailing Edirne's Selimiye Mosque as his supreme masterpiece at age 85.
clues: Serving sultans Suleiman the Magnificent, Selim II, and Murad III, he mastered bridge engineering during military campaigns.
His Süleymaniye Mosque dominates Istanbul's Third Hill, using hollow acoustic jars tucked inside its dome to carry voices.
questions.whyExplanation: Serving as Chief Imperial Architect for half a century, Mimar Sinan (c. 1489-1588) perfected the centrally domed Ottoman mosque, finally surpassing Hagia Sophia's span at Edirne's Selimiye Mosque.

questions.prompt: Famed for asking a brick 'what it wanted to be,' this Estonian-born master designed La Jolla's Salk Institute and Dhaka's Parliament before dying unidentified in Penn Station in 1974.
clues: He had crossed out his home address on his passport, delaying identification of his body for three days after a heart attack.
His Kimball Art Museum in Fort Worth bathes galleries in natural Texas daylight filtered through concrete cycloid vaults.
questions.whyExplanation: Louis I. Kahn (1901-1974) united monumental Roman ruin poetry with raw modernist concrete and travertine, producing late-life masterpieces from California's Salk Institute to Bangladesh's Jatiya Sangsad.

questions.prompt: An Irish lacquer artist turned furniture pioneer, she built the 1929 Côte d'Azur modernist villa E-1027—only for a jealous Le Corbusier to paint uninvited murals across her white walls.
clues: Her chrome-and-glass adjustable side table and Bibendum armchair remain twentieth-century design staples.
Its coded villa name intertwined her own initial with lover Jean Badovici's alphabetical positions (10=J, 2=B, 7=G).
questions.whyExplanation: Eileen Gray (1878-1976) designed both the Roquebrune-Cap-Martin house E-1027 and its ingenious built-in furnishings; overshadowed for decades by Le Corbusier's intrusion, she is now revered as a modernist giant.

questions.prompt: A self-taught former truck driver and professional boxer from Osaka with zero formal university training, he won the 1995 Pritzker Prize for meditative raw-concrete sanctuaries like the Church of the Light.
clues: In his 1989 Ibaraki chapel, a simple cruciform slot cut cleanly through the altar wall lets dawn sunlight form a glowing cross.
Carpenters finish his shuttered concrete forms so smoothly that visitors compare the grey walls to cool silk.
questions.whyExplanation: Teaching himself architecture from books and travels after fighting professionally under the ring name Great Ando, Tadao Ando pioneered poetic minimalist concrete spaces shaped by shadow, water, and wind.

questions.prompt: The first woman admitted to Paris's École des Beaux-Arts architecture section, this California engineer designed over 700 buildings—spending 28 years shaping Hearst Castle at San Simeon.
clues: Her reinforced-concrete bell tower at Mills College rode out the devastating 1906 San Francisco earthquake without a single crack.
In 2014 she became the first female architect posthumously awarded the AIA Gold Medal.
questions.whyExplanation: Licensed in California in 1904, Julia Morgan (1872-1957) blended Arts and Crafts rigor with seismic concrete mastery across YWCAs, churches, and Hearst Castle's Neptune Pool and twin towers.

questions.prompt: A trained concert pianist who co-invented the Zone System of tonal exposure, he mounted an 8-by-10 camera atop his station wagon to immortalize Yosemite's Half Dome and Hernandez moonrises.
clues: He famously compared a camera negative to a musical score and the darkroom print to its live performance.
His Sierra Club activism helped persuade Congress to establish Kings Canyon National Park in 1940.
questions.whyExplanation: Ansel Adams (1902-1984) brought Group f/64 razor sharpness and masterful darkroom dodging-and-burning to black-and-white American wilderness photography.

questions.prompt: Born in 1928 to Rusyn immigrants in Pittsburgh, this commercial shoe illustrator turned his silver-foil Manhattan loft 'The Factory' into a silkscreen assembly line of soup cans and Marilyns.
clues: After surviving a near-fatal 1968 shooting by Valerie Solanas, he launched Interview magazine and painted Mao portraits.
He predicted everyone would be world-famous for 15 minutes while managing The Velvet Underground's banana-cover debut.
questions.whyExplanation: By adopting commercial photo-silkscreen printing in 1962, Andy Warhol erased the boundary between fine art and mass consumer imagery, defining American Pop Art.

questions.prompt: Captivated by Moorish tilework during a 1936 visit to Spain's Alhambra, this Dutch printmaker drew mathematically impossible looping staircases, waterfalls, and interlocking lizards.
clues: Though he insisted he had zero formal mathematical training, topologists and crystallographers flocked to his 1954 Amsterdam show.
Drawing Hands, Relativity, and Ascending and Descending turned optical paradox into dorm-poster immortality.
questions.whyExplanation: Maurits Cornelis Escher (1898-1972) fused tessellations, hyperbolic geometry, and Penrose stairs into meticulous woodcuts and mezzotints beloved by mathematicians and illusion fans alike.

questions.prompt: On December 8, 1980, this Rolling Stone chief photographer snapped a naked John Lennon curled around a clothed Yoko Ono—just five hours before Lennon was murdered outside Manhattan's Dakota.
clues: She also photographed a pregnant Demi Moore on Vanity Fair's 1991 cover and Queen Elizabeth II at Buckingham Palace.
Her bold, hyper-staged celebrity portraits helped define Vanity Fair and Vogue over four decades.
questions.whyExplanation: Annie Leibovitz's intimate Polaroid-tested December 1980 portrait of John Lennon and Yoko Ono ran on Rolling Stone's January 1981 cover without headlines and was voted the best magazine cover of the prior 40 years.

questions.prompt: Co-founding Magnum Photos in 1947 while prowling streets with a tape-blackened 35mm Leica, this French master coined 'the decisive moment' after catching a man mid-leap over a puddle behind Gare Saint-Lazare.
clues: He refused to crop his prints, insisting full-frame black borders proved his split-second composition needed no darkroom rescue.
Escaping a German POW camp on his third try in 1943, he photographed Mahatma Gandhi just hours before his 1948 assassination.
questions.whyExplanation: Father of modern street photojournalism, Henri Cartier-Bresson captured unposed geometric harmony with his compact Leica, publishing his landmark 1952 monograph The Decisive Moment.

questions.prompt: Serving as director, stylist, makeup artist, and sole model, this artist shot 70 black-and-white Untitled Film Stills between 1977 and 1980 evoking B-movies that never existed.
clues: MoMA bought the complete 69-print set in 1995, while her color Centerfolds and History Portraits parodied Renaissance masters.
Despite appearing in nearly every single frame she sells, she insists her chameleonic work is never autobiographical self-portraiture.
questions.whyExplanation: MacArthur Fellow Cindy Sherman transformed postmodern photography by staging herself across cinematic clichés, dissecting gender roles and media stereotypes without ever repeating a single persona.

questions.prompt: An Edo fire warden turned ukiyo-e poet of rain, snow, and twilight, this Japanese printmaker created Fifty-Three Stations of the Tōkaidō—woodblocks Van Gogh directly copied in oil.
clues: His parting 1856-1858 masterpiece One Hundred Famous Views of Edo used radical close-up foreground branches and bokeh-like depth.
Monet collected dozens of his woodblocks at Giverny, admiring his gradated 'bokashi' indigo skies.
questions.whyExplanation: Utagawa Hiroshige (1797-1858) brought lyrical weather and everyday travelers to Japanese woodblock printing, igniting European Japonisme and inspiring both Monet and Van Gogh.

questions.prompt: Walking away from glossy magazine fashion shoots, she aimed a square-format twin-lens Rolleiflex at identical twins in Roselle, New Jersey and a wide-eyed boy clutching a toy hand grenade in Central Park.
clues: Her haunting 1967 twin portrait directly inspired Stanley Kubrick's eerie hallway sisters in The Shining.
Following her 1971 suicide, she became the first photographer featured at the Venice Biennale in 1972.
questions.whyExplanation: Diane Arbus (1923-1971) used direct eye contact and harsh daylight flash to photograph marginalized performers, eccentrics, and everyday New Yorkers with unsettling intimacy.

questions.prompt: Her 150,000 dazzling mid-century Chicago and New York street negatives sat unseen by anyone until real-estate historian John Maloof bought a delinquent storage locker box at a 2007 auction for $380.
clues: She worked privately for forty years as a fiercely guarded North Shore nanny, often shooting reflections of herself in shop glass.
Most of her rolls of Kodak Tri-X film were still undeveloped when she died nearly penniless in 2009.
questions.whyExplanation: Posthumously celebrated as one of the 20th century's finest street photographers, reclusive Chicago nanny Vivian Maier concealed over 100,000 Rolleiflex negatives that were rescued at a 2007 auction.

questions.prompt: Born Emmanuel Radnitzky in Philadelphia, this Paris Dadaist stumbled onto camera-less photograms he immodestly dubbed 'rayographs'—and painted cello f-holes onto Kiki de Montparnasse's bare back.
clues: Alongside darkroom assistant Lee Miller, he accidentally turned overexposed solarization into a sleek Surrealist halo technique.
His 1924 visual pun Le Violon d'Ingres set a record $12.4 million photography auction price in 2022.
questions.whyExplanation: The lone American core member of Paris Dada and Surrealism, Man Ray (1890-1976) reinvented experimental photography through camera-less rayographs, solarization, and iconic avant-garde portraits.

questions.prompt: Buying his first camera at a Seattle pawnshop for $7.50, he became Life's first Black staff photographer—famed for a 1942 shot of charwoman Ella Watson with a mop before a U.S. flag—and later directed Shaft.
clues: On a 1942 Farm Security Administration fellowship in Washington, D.C., he explicitly subverted Grant Wood's farm painting.
A true Renaissance polymath, he also wrote The Learning Tree and documented Harlem gangs, Malcolm X, and Muhammad Ali.
questions.whyExplanation: Gordon Parks (1912-2006) wielded his camera as 'a weapon of choice' against racism and poverty across FSA Washington, Life magazine photo essays, and pioneering Hollywood cinema.

questions.prompt: Though this 18th-century Venetian architect built barely a single church, his moody etchings of impossible cavernous vaults and dangling chains—Carceri d'invenzione—shaped Gothic horror and modern set design.
clues: His crisp souvenir Vedute (Views of Rome) lured generations of Grand Tour travelers to Italy's ruins.
Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Edgar Allan Poe, and M. C. Escher all drew dizzying inspiration from his Imaginary Prisons.
questions.whyExplanation: Giovanni Battista Piranesi (1720-1778) revolutionized architectural printmaking with his towering Vedute di Roma and 16 nightmare copperplate etchings of labyrinthine Imaginary Prisons.

questions.prompt: Published in Amsterdam in 1725 alongside four descriptive sonnets likely penned by Antonio Vivaldi himself, this quartet of violin concertos mimics barking sheepdogs, buzzing flies, and chattering icy teeth.
clues: Known as 'The Red Priest' for his flame-colored hair, Vivaldi tucked these four works inside his Op. 8 collection.
Its brisk E-major Spring opening and stormy G-minor Summer finale rank among the earliest masterpieces of program music.
questions.whyExplanation: Antonio Vivaldi's Le quattro stagioni (1725) pioneered vivid programmatic storytelling in the Baroque solo concerto, printing lines of accompanying poetry right above specific violin passages.

questions.prompt: So deaf by his Ninth Symphony's May 1824 Vienna premiere that he kept conducting after the final chord, this titan had to be turned around by contralto Caroline Unger to see the cheers.
clues: He famously scratched Napoleon's name off the Eroica title page in fury after Bonaparte crowned himself emperor in 1804.
His Ninth was the first major symphony to weld human voices and Friedrich Schiller's poetry into an orchestral finale.
questions.whyExplanation: Despite progressive hearing loss starting in his late twenties, Ludwig van Beethoven bridged Classicism and Romanticism, conducting alongside Michael Umlauf at the rapturous 1824 premiere of his Choral Ninth.

questions.prompt: Opening with a strained high solo bassoon before plunging into stomping polyrhythmic chords, Stravinsky's 1913 pagan ballet score sparked fistfights and catcalls on its Paris debut.
clues: Vaslav Nijinsky's pigeon-toed, earth-pounding choreography for the Ballets Russes appalled tuxedoed patrons at Théâtre des Champs-Élysées.
Conductor Pierre Monteux kept the orchestra playing straight through whistling and flying vegetables on May 29, 1913.
questions.whyExplanation: Igor Stravinsky's Le Sacre du printemps exploded 19th-century tonal and metric conventions on May 29, 1913, instantly ushering orchestral music into jagged 20th-century modernism.

questions.prompt: Commissioned secretly by Count Franz von Walsegg—who planned to pass the funeral mass off as his own composition—this 35-year-old Salzburg prodigy died in December 1791 leaving its Lacrimosa unfinished.
clues: His widow Constanze secretly hired pupil Franz Xaver Süssmayr to complete the D-minor score so she could collect the balance.
A century of lurid rumors falsely blamed Viennese court rival Antonio Salieri for poisoning him.
questions.whyExplanation: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart died on December 5, 1791 just eight bars into the Lacrimosa of his Requiem in D minor, commissioned via an anonymous messenger by eccentric nobleman Franz von Walsegg.

questions.prompt: Channeling obsessive unrequited love for Irish actress Harriet Smithson, Hector Berlioz wrote this 1830 opium-fueled symphony whose beloved recurring melody marches to the guillotine.
clues: Its five movements climax in a 'Witches' Sabbath' where shrill E-flat clarinet mocks the tender theme amid Dies Irae chimes.
Astonishingly, Smithson eventually heard the piece in 1832, realized she was its muse, and married the composer in 1833.
questions.whyExplanation: Premiered in Paris in December 1830 when Berlioz was just 26, Symphonie fantastique introduced the unifying 'idée fixe' leitmotif and expanded Romantic orchestration to theatrical extremes.

questions.prompt: Commissioned by dancer Ida Rubinstein in 1928, Maurice Ravel dismissively called this hypnotic 15-minute orchestral crescendo 'a piece for orchestra without music'—yet its relentless snare drum made him rich.
clues: A solo snare drummer repeats the exact same two-bar Spanish rhythm 169 times as instruments layer onto a single melody.
At its Paris Opéra premiere, a shocked woman reportedly shouted 'Madman!'—to which Ravel smiled, 'She understood the piece!'
questions.whyExplanation: Maurice Ravel's 1928 one-movement ballet Boléro proved pure orchestration and gradual dynamic build could mesmerize listeners without harmonic development—until a lone abrupt modulation near the end.

questions.prompt: Composed in 1893 while Antonín Dvořák directed Manhattan's National Conservatory, his E-minor Ninth's English-horn Largo drew on spirituals—and Neil Armstrong took a tape of it to the Moon.
clues: Student Harry Burleigh introduced the Czech visitor to spirituals like 'Swing Low, Sweet Chariot,' inspiring its pentatonic melodies.
Premiered at Carnegie Hall in December 1893, its mournful second movement later acquired lyrics as the song 'Goin' Home.'
questions.whyExplanation: Antonín Dvořák's Symphony No. 9 in E minor, 'From the New World' (1893), urged American composers to build a national sound on African American and Indigenous melodies, becoming an Apollo 11 soundtrack.

questions.prompt: Shaped around astrological personalities rather than astronomy, Gustav Holst's 1918 seven-movement orchestral suite omitted Earth—and he stubbornly refused to add newly discovered Pluto in 1930.
clues: Its menacing 5/4 opening 'Mars, the Bringer of War' echoed across film scores from Star Wars to Gladiator.
Its haunting finale 'Neptune, the Mystic' fades into silence as an offstage wordless women's chorus vanishes behind a closing door.
questions.whyExplanation: Completed in 1916 and premiered privately in 1918, Gustav Holst's Op. 32 suite The Planets moves from Mars to Neptune by astrological character, leaving Colin Matthews to add a 'Pluto' appendix in 2000.

questions.prompt: Smuggled out of wartime Russia on microfilm in 1942, Dmitri Shostakovich's Seventh was premiered inside a starving besieged city by musicians given extra bread rations and broadcast toward German trenches.
clues: Its infamous first-movement 'invasion theme' repeats a banal march 12 times over a relentless snare drum like a twisted Boléro.
Soviet artillery bombarded Nazi batteries into silence on August 9, 1942 just so Karl Eliasberg's gaunt orchestra could play.
questions.whyExplanation: Completed in December 1941 and performed inside the blockaded city on August 9, 1942, Shostakovich's Seventh ('Leningrad') became an electrifying international symbol of endurance—even landing him on Time's cover.

questions.prompt: Determined to wake drowsy London aristocrats after heavy dinners in 1792, Joseph Haydn planted a sudden fortissimo timpani crash inside the whisper-quiet slow movement of his Symphony No. 94.
clues: Biographers report the witty composer chuckled that his sudden chord 'will make the ladies jump!'
In German it goes by 'Mit dem Paukenschlag'—literally 'with the kettledrum stroke'—part of his twelve London Symphonies.
questions.whyExplanation: Premiered at London's Hanover Square Rooms on March 23, 1792, Joseph Haydn's Symphony No. 94 in G major earned its nickname from the explosive chord punctuating its gentle Andante theme.

questions.prompt: Modest Mussorgsky dashed off this 1874 piano suite after touring a memorial exhibit of friend Viktor Hartmann's sketches, before Maurice Ravel's 1922 orchestration made it a symphonic staple.
clues: A stately asymmetrical 11/4 'Promenade' theme portrays the heavy-set composer strolling between watercolor frames.
Vignettes range from 'Ballet of the Unhatched Chicks' and 'Baba Yaga's Hut' to a thunderous finale at 'The Great Gate of Kiev.'
questions.whyExplanation: Written in June 1874 to honor architect-painter Viktor Hartmann, Mussorgsky's solo piano suite Pictures at an Exhibition achieved global symphonic fame after Serge Koussevitzky commissioned Ravel's 1922 orchestration.

questions.prompt: After Queen Victoria sang 'Italien' at Buckingham Palace in 1842 praising it as her favorite piece by Felix, he had to blushingly confess this brilliant older sister—author of the Easter Sonata—wrote it.
clues: Warned by her banker father that music could be only 'an ornament' for a woman, she published six early songs under her brother's name.
Her 1828 Easter Sonata was misattributed to Felix for over a century until scholars verified her signed manuscript in 2010.
questions.whyExplanation: Composing over 460 works including the piano cycle Das Jahr, Fanny Mendelssohn Hensel (1805-1847) defied 19th-century gender barriers, finally publishing under her own name in 1846 before her sudden death.

questions.prompt: Georges Bizet died of a heart attack at 36 just three months after this 1875 Opéra-Comique debut horrified respectable Paris families with cigarette-factory brawlers, smugglers, and an onstage stabbing.
clues: Adapted from Prosper Mérimée's novella, its seductive 'Habanera' actually reworked a melody by Spanish composer Sebastián Iradier.
Bullfighter Escamillo's swaggering 'Toreador Song' and fatal Seville love triangle soon made it one of opera's most staged works.
questions.whyExplanation: Premiering March 3, 1875 to shocked Parisian critics, Bizet's Carmen triumphed in Vienna months after his June death and won fervent praise from Tchaikovsky, Brahms, and Nietzsche.

questions.prompt: Staged in a rowdy suburban Vienna theater two months before Mozart's death, this 1791 Singspiel weaves Masonic three-fold symbolism around bird-catcher Papageno and the Queen of the Night's blistering high F.
clues: Librettist Emanuel Schikaneder wrote the feathered comic role of Papageno specifically for himself to perform.
Prince Tamino must pass trials of silence, fire, and water alongside Sarastro to win Pamina's hand.
questions.whyExplanation: Premiering September 30, 1791 at Theater auf der Wieden, Mozart's Die Zauberflöte blended popular Viennese fairytale comedy with Enlightenment Masonic ideals and soaring coloratura fireworks.

questions.prompt: Giacomo Puccini's 1896 weepie of freezing Left Bank Paris artists inspired Jonathan Larson's rock musical Rent a century later—trading Rodolfo's garret stove for an East Village loft and tuberculosis for HIV.
clues: In Act I, poet Rodolfo and seamstress Mimì meet by candlelight when her wick blows out and she drops her room key in the dark.
Arturo Toscanini conducted its Turin premiere despite stiff early competition from Ruggero Leoncavallo's rival version of Henri Murger's book.
questions.whyExplanation: Adapted from Henri Murger's Scènes de la vie de bohème, Puccini's La Bohème (1896) became a verismo cornerstone and the exact structural blueprint for Broadway's 1996 hit Rent.

questions.prompt: Gioachino Rossini allegedly dashed off this 1816 comic gem in under three weeks—only for opening night in Rome to turn chaotic when a stray cat wandered onstage, a singer tripped, and rival fans hissed.
clues: Its frantic patter aria 'Largo al factotum' introduces the town's indispensable fixer, later parodied endlessly by Bugs Bunny.
Serving as a prequel to Mozart's Marriage of Figaro, it follows Count Almaviva disguising himself to woo guarded ward Rosina.
questions.whyExplanation: Composed at breakneck speed in early 1816 from Beaumarchais's comedy, Rossini's Il barbiere di Siviglia rebounded from a calamitous Rome opening night to become the pinnacle of opera buffa.

questions.prompt: Though popular myth links it to the 1869 Suez Canal opening, Giuseppe Verdi actually premiered this Egyptian tragedy in Cairo on Christmas Eve 1871—commissioning custom five-foot valved trumpets for its march.
clues: French Egyptologist Auguste Mariette drafted the scenario of a captive Ethiopian princess torn between fatherland and commander Radamès.
Trapped alive inside a sealed stone vault beneath the Temple of Vulcan, the doomed lovers sing their tender final duet.
questions.whyExplanation: Commissioned by Khedive Ismail Pasha for Cairo's Khedivial Opera House (delayed by the Franco-Prussian War trapping sets in Paris), Verdi's Aida opened December 24, 1871 to thunderous acclaim.

questions.prompt: Unfolding across less than 24 hours inside three real Roman landmarks—Sant'Andrea della Valle, Palazzo Farnese, and Castel Sant'Angelo—Puccini's 1900 thriller ends with a diva leaping from the battlements.
clues: Jealous opera singer Floria stabs sadistic police chief Baron Scarpia with a dinner knife after praying through 'Vissi d'arte.'
Discovering her painter lover Mario Cavaradossi's 'mock' firing squad used live bullets, she cries 'O Scarpia, avanti a Dio!'
questions.whyExplanation: Adapted from Victorien Sardou's stage vehicle for Sarah Bernhardt, Puccini's Tosca premiered in Rome on January 14, 1900, grounding operatic melodrama in exact Napoleonic-era Roman geography.

questions.prompt: To stage his 15-hour four-part mythic epic properly, Richard Wagner built a custom Bayreuth festival house with a sunken hooded orchestra pit so audiences could hear leitmotifs without seeing musicians.
clues: Spanning 26 years of composition, its four nights run from Das Rheingold through Die Walküre and Siegfried to Götterdämmerung.
A stolen gold hoard cursed by dwarf Alberich dooms gods, Valkyries, and dragons before Valhalla burns.
questions.whyExplanation: Premiered as a complete four-evening cycle at the inaugural Bayreuth Festival in August 1876, Wagner's Ring cycle fused Norse Eddas and the Nibelungenlied into a revolutionary Gesamtkunstwerk.

questions.prompt: Verdi called its 1853 Venice opening 'a fiasco'—partly because robust soprano Fanny Salvini-Donatelli drew chuckles while supposedly wasting away from consumption as Violetta Valéry.
clues: Based on Alexandre Dumas fils's scandal-tinged La Dame aux camélias, it opens with the sparkling champagne toast 'Libiamo.'
Audiences at La Fenice also balked at seeing contemporary 1850s evening dress onstage rather than safe historical costumes.
questions.whyExplanation: Verdi's La Traviata ('The Fallen Woman') recovered swiftly in an 1854 Venetian revival with a new cast and now stands among the most frequently performed operas worldwide.

questions.prompt: At its April 1926 La Scala premiere, conductor Arturo Toscanini halted the orchestra right after slave girl Liù's funeral, turned to the hall, and announced 'Here the Maestro laid down his pen.'
clues: Puccini died of throat cancer in Brussels in 1924 with 36 pages of sketches left for Franco Alfano to finish from night two onward.
Prince Calaf stakes his head on solving three riddles before unleashing the triumphal tenor showstopper 'Nessun dorma.'
questions.whyExplanation: Giacomo Puccini's final opera Turandot premiered posthumously at Milan's La Scala on April 25, 1926, with Toscanini stopping at the exact bar where Puccini's own manuscript ended.

questions.prompt: His 1607 Mantuan court drama L'Orfeo stands as the earliest opera still regularly performed today, using a rich Baroque orchestra and expressive recitative to bridge Renaissance madrigals and theater.
clues: Later appointed maestro di cappella at Venice's St. Mark's Basilica, he penned the late masterpiece L'incoronazione di Poppea at age 75.
His bold dissonances sparked a famous print feud with conservative theorist Giovanni Artusi over 'seconda pratica.'
questions.whyExplanation: Claudio Monteverdi (1567-1643) transformed opera from an elite Florentine experiment into gripping musical drama with L'Orfeo (1607), Il ritorno d'Ulisse, and L'incoronazione di Poppea.

questions.prompt: Adapting Georg Büchner's unfinished play after wartime barracks trauma, Alban Berg spent seven years on this 1925 atonal Berlin opera about a barber-soldier fed only peas by a mad doctor.
clues: Its 15 terse scenes are secretly built atop strict classical structures—including a passacaglia, a symphony, and six inventions.
Driven over the brink when Marie betrays him for a strutting Drum Major, the protagonist drowns beside a blood-red pond.
questions.whyExplanation: Premiered in Berlin on December 14, 1925 under Erich Kleiber, Alban Berg's Wozzeck became the landmark atonal opera of the Second Viennese School, proving expressionist dissonance could pack devastating pathos.

questions.prompt: Premiered on Broadway in 1935 and waiting until 1985 to reach New York's Met, George Gershwin's Charleston 'folk opera' mandated an all-Black classically trained cast on Catfish Row.
clues: Adapted from DuBose Heyward's novel set on Catfish Row, it opens with Clara soothing her infant to the immortal lullaby 'Summertime.'
Todd Duncan and Anne Brown originated the title lovers opposite drug dealer Sportin' Life singing 'It Ain't Necessarily So.'
questions.whyExplanation: Fusing symphonic leitmotifs with jazz, blues, and spirituals, George and Ira Gershwin and DuBose Heyward's Porgy and Bess (1935) finally entered the Metropolitan Opera repertoire in February 1985.

questions.prompt: Opening at Broadway's Majestic Theatre in January 1988 with a plummeting crystal chandelier, this Andrew Lloyd Webber Gothic smash ran 35 years and 13,981 performances before lowering its curtain in April 2023.
clues: Michael Crawford and Sarah Brightman originated its haunted Palais Garnier leads in London's West End in 1986.
Adapted from Gaston Leroux's 1910 French novel, it remains Broadway's all-time longest-running show by thousands of dates.
questions.whyExplanation: Directed by Harold Prince with Maria Björnson's iconic chandelier and subterranean boat, The Phantom of the Opera dominated Broadway from January 1988 to April 2023, grossing over $1.4 billion in New York alone.

questions.prompt: Sparked when Lin-Manuel Miranda grabbed Ron Chernow's hefty 2004 biography at an airport for beach reading, this sung-through hip-hop musical swept 11 Tonys and the 2016 Pulitzer Prize for Drama.
clues: Its first song debuted in May 2009 at a White House poetry evening, drawing stunned cheers from Barack and Michelle Obama.
Packing over 20,000 words into two acts, it casts actors of color as America's Founding Fathers.
questions.whyExplanation: Moving from the Public Theater to Broadway's Richard Rodgers Theatre in August 2015, Lin-Manuel Miranda's Hamilton reimagined Treasury founder Alexander Hamilton's life through rap, R&B, and Broadway showmanship.

questions.prompt: First pitched by Jerome Robbins in 1949 as a Catholic-versus-Jewish Easter-Passover clash in Manhattan, this 1957 Bernstein-Sondheim masterpiece recast Romeo and Juliet as Jets and Sharks.
clues: Arthur Laurents wrote the book and a 27-year-old Stephen Sondheim made his Broadway lyricist debut with 'Something's Coming.'
Its unsettling tritone interval threads from the opening finger snaps straight through 'Maria' and 'Cool.'
questions.whyExplanation: Premiering September 26, 1957, West Side Story fused Jerome Robbins's explosive athletic dance, Leonard Bernstein's symphonic jazz score, and contemporary Puerto Rican migration tensions into Broadway history.

questions.prompt: Julie Taymor became the first woman to win the Tony for Best Direction of a Musical in 1998 by turning Disney's savanna hit into visible Balinese-inspired puppetry, towering stilts, and soaring woven gazelles.
clues: Its unforgettable opening 'Circle of Life' sends life-sized elephants and cheetahs marching straight down the theater aisles.
Adding Lebo M's choral African arrangements to Elton John and Tim Rice's songs, it became Broadway's all-time top-grossing musical.
questions.whyExplanation: Opening at the New Amsterdam Theatre in November 1997, Julie Taymor's staging of The Lion King revolutionized theatrical puppetry and has grossed more worldwide than any other stage production.

questions.prompt: Opening on March 31, 1943 with a lone woman churning butter—ditching Broadway's noisy chorus-girl curtain-raiser—Rodgers and Hammerstein's debut welded Agnes de Mille's dream ballet directly into plot.
clues: Before triumphing in Boston, the show flopped in early New Haven tryouts under the bland title Away We Go!
Based on Lynn Riggs's play Green Grow the Lilacs, it earned a special 1944 Pulitzer citation and ran 2,212 performances.
questions.whyExplanation: Oklahoma! inaugurated the modern 'integrated book musical' where every song and dance advanced character and story, launching Richard Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein II's legendary partnership.

questions.prompt: Brushed off by several New York critics upon its October 2003 Gershwin Theatre debut—and upset for Best Musical by puppet spoof Avenue Q—this Stephen Schwartz prequel soared into an emerald juggernaut.
clues: Idina Menzel and Kristin Chenoweth originated its unlikely Shiz University roommates from Gregory Maguire's 1995 revisionist novel.
Act I climaxes with a green-skinned outcast levitating on a cherry-picker lift while belting 'Defying Gravity.'
questions.whyExplanation: Despite mixed 2003 reviews and losing the Best Musical Tony to Avenue Q, Winnie Holzman and Stephen Schwartz's Wicked became one of Broadway's four billion-dollar blockbusters.

questions.prompt: Born as a 1980 French concept album before producer Cameron Mackintosh expanded it for London's Barbican in 1985, this barricade epic spins its cast on a giant revolving stage around convict 24601.
clues: Claude-Michel Schönberg and Alain Boublil adapted Victor Hugo's massive 1862 novel with English lyrics by Herbert Kretzmer.
Colm Wilkinson originated Jean Valjean, whose fugue with Inspector Javert and 'One Day More' anchor its sung-through score.
questions.whyExplanation: Though London critics initially panned its 1985 RSC premiere, Les Misérables sparked record box-office demand, became the West End's longest-running musical, and swept eight 1987 Tonys on Broadway.

questions.prompt: After Bob Fosse's cynical 1975 original lost all 11 Tonys it was nominated for to A Chorus Line, its stripped-down 1996 Encores! revival grew into Broadway's longest-running American musical.
clues: John Kander and Fred Ebb adapted Maurine Dallas Watkins's 1926 Jazz Age play about celebrity murderesses Roxie Hart and Velma Kelly.
Its 1996 staging leaves the band tiered center-stage in black while Ann Reinking's Fosse-style choreography unfolds in front.
questions.whyExplanation: Overshadowed by A Chorus Line in 1975-1976, Kander and Ebb's vaudeville satire Chicago found immortality through Walter Bobbie's sleek 1996 concert-turned-Broadway revival.

questions.prompt: Shocking 1927 Broadway audiences weaned on escapist fluff, Jerome Kern and Oscar Hammerstein II tackled racism, miscegenation laws, and spousal abandonment aboard the Mississippi riverboat Cotton Blossom.
clues: Florenz Ziegfeld nervously feared the serious drama would flop until opening-night applause at the Ziegfeld Theatre stunned him.
Paul Robeson later immortalized its stevedore bass anthem 'Ol' Man River,' originally introduced by Jules Bledsoe.
questions.whyExplanation: Opening December 27, 1927 from Edna Ferber's novel, Show Boat bridged operetta and serious American musical drama, confronting Jim Crow tragedy across forty years on the Mississippi.

questions.prompt: Drawn from Christopher Bond's 1973 play rather than raw Victorian penny dreadfuls, Stephen Sondheim's 1979 Grand Guignol thriller pairs a wrongly exiled Fleet Street barber with Mrs. Lovett's suspicious pies.
clues: Angela Lansbury and Len Cariou won 1979 Tonys harmonizing darkly over cannibal puns in the waltz 'A Little Priest.'
A piercing industrial factory whistle opens and closes Harold Prince's bleak Industrial Revolution staging.
questions.whyExplanation: Subtitled The Demon Barber of Fleet Street, Stephen Sondheim and Hugh Wheeler's 1979 musical thriller won eight Tonys and crosses frequently into grand opera houses worldwide.

questions.prompt: Distilled from choreographer Michael Bennett's late-night 1974 tape-recorded confessions with real Broadway dancers, this mirror-lined audition drama ran 6,137 performances and won the 1976 Pulitzer Prize.
clues: Marvin Hamlisch and Edward Kleban turned real backstage memories of puberty, surgery, and injury into 'At the Ballet' and 'What I Did for Love.'
Instead of glamorous headliners, its final glittering gold-tuxedo kickline 'One' intentionally erases every dancer's individuality.
questions.whyExplanation: Workshopped at Joseph Papp's Public Theater from hours of real 'gypsy' interviews, A Chorus Line opened at the Shubert in 1975, sweeping nine Tonys and holding Broadway's run record until 1997.

questions.prompt: Scuttling a conventional linear plot for a 35th-birthday collage of New York bachelor Bobby observing five married couples, Stephen Sondheim and George Furth's 1970 landmark birthed the modern concept musical.

distractors.text: Sunday in the Park with George

clues: Elaine Stritch stopped shows nightly with her raspy toast 'The Ladies Who Lunch' amid Boris Aronson's chrome-and-elevator set.
Its 2021 gender-swapped Broadway revival reimagined protagonist Bobby as Bobbie, winning Katrina Lenk and Patti LuPone Tonys.
questions.whyExplanation: Directed by Harold Prince in April 1970, Company traded linear romance for sharp vignettes on modern commitment, culminating in 'Being Alive' and defining Broadway's concept-musical era.

questions.prompt: When mechanical shark 'Bruce' chronically shorted out in Martha's Vineyard saltwater, Steven Spielberg relied on yellow barrels and John Williams's two-note ostinato to invent the 1975 summer blockbuster.

distractors.text: Close Encounters of the Third Kind

clues: Roy Scheider improvised the immortal warning 'You're gonna need a bigger boat' while staring down the great white.
Based on Peter Benchley's bestseller, it became the first movie ever to surpass $100 million at the domestic box office.
questions.whyExplanation: Broken hydraulic props forced Steven Spielberg to keep his predator mostly unseen in Jaws (1975), ratcheting suspense so effectively that Universal's wide June release reshaped Hollywood's calendar forever.

questions.prompt: Paramount nearly fired Francis Ford Coppola and resisted Marlon Brando until he stuffed tissues in his cheeks for a test—and a stray lot cat walked straight onto Brando's lap in this 1972 opener.

distractors.text: Once Upon a Time in America

clues: The purring stray was so loud in the wedding study scene that sound editors had to re-loop several of Don Corleone's lines.
Al Pacino beat out studio favorites like Robert Redford to play reluctant heir Michael Corleone.
questions.whyExplanation: Despite chaotic Paramount interference during production, Francis Ford Coppola's 1972 adaptation of Mario Puzo's The Godfather broke box-office records and swept Best Picture, Actor, and Adapted Screenplay.

questions.prompt: Stunned by Industrial Light & Magic's 1992 computer-generated dinosaur test, stop-motion legend Phil Tippett sighed 'I've just become extinct'—a line Steven Spielberg promptly wrote into this 1993 smash.
clues: Effects crew plucked a guitar string taped inside a car dashboard to make ripples dance across a glass of water.
Though Spielberg used CGI for wide shots, Stan Winston built a full-sized animatronic T. rex that shook uncontrollably when rain-soaked.
questions.whyExplanation: Released in June 1993 from Michael Crichton's novel, Jurassic Park combined Stan Winston's practical creatures with groundbreaking ILM computer graphics to become cinema's highest-grossing film of its era.

questions.prompt: Winning the 1994 Palme d'Or at Cannes with a scrambled timeline, this Quentin Tarantino crime mosaic revived John Travolta's career while keeping its glowing gold briefcase contents forever unexplained.
clues: Uma Thurman and John Travolta twist barefoot at Jack Rabbit Slim's shortly before an adrenaline-needle crisis.
Samuel L. Jackson's hitman recites a fictionalized Ezekiel 25:17 speech and debates European burger names.
questions.whyExplanation: Produced on an $8 million budget and grossing over $213 million worldwide, Pulp Fiction (1994) won Best Original Screenplay and transformed 1990s American independent filmmaking.

questions.prompt: Despite Anthony Hopkins appearing onscreen for barely 16 minutes, this 1991 Jonathan Demme thriller became only the third film ever to sweep the Oscar 'Big Five'—and the lone horror Best Picture winner.
clues: Jodie Foster plays FBI trainee Clarice Starling trading childhood confessions with an imprisoned psychiatrist to catch Buffalo Bill.
Released unusually early in February, it survived nearly a full year in Academy voters' memories to sweep March 1992's ceremony.
questions.whyExplanation: Joining It Happened One Night and One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest in the Oscar Big Five club, The Silence of the Lambs (1991) won Picture, Director, Actor, Actress, and Adapted Screenplay.

questions.prompt: Opening their 1996 Minnesota kidnapping noir with a solemn 'This is a true story' title card, Joel and Ethan Coen later cheerfully confessed that the entire wood-chipper plot was pure invention.
clues: Pregnant Brainerd police chief Marge Gunderson tracks inept hired thugs while politely exclaiming 'Oh, yah!'
William H. Macy plays desperate car salesman Jerry Lundegaard, whose botched ransom scheme snowballs across frozen plains.
questions.whyExplanation: Though borrowing a fake documentary disclaimer to coax audiences into accepting absurd black comedy, Fargo (1996) won Oscars for Frances McDormand and the Coen brothers' original screenplay.

questions.prompt: Shot in just 23 days on a $4.5 million Blumhouse budget, this razor-sharp 2017 suburban satire grossed $255 million and made Jordan Peele the first Black winner of the Best Original Screenplay Oscar.
clues: A silver teacup and spoon send photographer Chris Washington spiraling helplessly into the paralyzing 'Sunken Place.'
Daniel Kaluuya visits his white girlfriend's liberal upstate family only to uncover the horrifying Coagula brain-transplant plot.
questions.whyExplanation: Jordan Peele's directorial debut Get Out (2017) blended social thriller, comedy, and horror to become a cultural touchstone, earning four Oscar nods including Best Picture and winning Original Screenplay.

questions.prompt: Crowned Best Picture at the 2017 Oscars only after an envelope mix-up interrupted La La Land's acceptance speeches, Barry Jenkins's $1.5 million triptych traces a Miami boy across three ages.
clues: Three separate actors play Little, Chiron, and Black—kept deliberately apart during shooting so they wouldn't mimic one another.
Mahershala Ali won Best Supporting Actor as compassionate drug dealer Juan teaching a shy boy to float in the Atlantic.
questions.whyExplanation: Adapted from Tarell Alvin McCraney's unproduced play, Barry Jenkins's Moonlight (2016) won three Oscars including Best Picture after PwC's infamous backstage envelope error briefly named La La Land.

questions.prompt: Screenwriter Robert Towne fought fiercely with director Roman Polanski to save Evelyn Mulwray—until Polanski forced this 1974 water-wars noir's bleak street finale and immortal fatalistic closing line.
clues: Jack Nicholson's private eye Jake Gittes sports a taped slit nostril for much of the film after an encounter with a switchblade.
Inspired loosely by the California Water Wars, John Huston's ruthless tycoon Noah Cross whispers that he owns the future.
questions.whyExplanation: Winning Robert Towne the Best Original Screenplay Oscar, Chinatown (1974) remains a screenwriting gold standard, capped by associate Walsh telling Gittes to forget the corrupt neighborhood.

questions.prompt: Filmed on one scorching Bedford-Stuyvesant block in 1988, Spike Lee's racial powder keg missed a Best Picture nod—prompting presenter Kim Basinger to protest the snub live onstage at the 1990 Oscars.
clues: A dispute over Sal's Famous Pizzeria's Wall of Fame boils over alongside Radio Raheem's booming 'Fight the Power' cassette.
Closing with paired quotes from Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X, it lost Screenplay while Driving Miss Daisy took Picture.
questions.whyExplanation: Written, directed by, and starring Spike Lee as pizza courier Mookie, Do the Right Thing (1989) captured simmering urban tensions on Brooklyn's hottest day and entered the National Film Registry in 1999.

questions.prompt: Built on an independent A24 budget with hot-dog fingers, a cosmic bagel black hole, and googly-eyed boulders, Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert's 2022 laundromat saga swept seven Academy Awards.

distractors.text: Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind

clues: Ke Huy Quan staged an emotional Hollywood comeback as kindly fanny-pack-wielding husband Waymond Wang.
Audited by Jamie Lee Curtis's IRS inspector, stressed mother Evelyn Wang leaps across parallel universes to reconnect with her daughter.
questions.whyExplanation: Everything Everywhere All at Once (2022) won seven of its eleven Oscar nominations—including Picture, Director, Original Screenplay, and three acting trophies—becoming A24's biggest commercial hit.

questions.prompt: Before directing Arrival and Dune, Québécois filmmaker Denis Villeneuve adapted Wajdi Mouawad's stage tragedy into this 2010 Canadian drama whose chilling equation '1 + 1 = 1' shatters twin siblings.
clues: After their mother Nawal dies in Montreal, twins Jeanne and Simon carry sealed letters to a war-scarred Middle Eastern country.
Radiohead's 'You and Whose Army?' opens this Oscar-nominated Foreign Language contender from Quebec.
questions.whyExplanation: Nominated for the Best Foreign Language Film Oscar representing Canada, Denis Villeneuve's Incendies (2010) weaves generational trauma and civil war into one of modern cinema's starkest final revelations.

questions.prompt: Built around an architect's minimalist mansion set in Seoul, Bong Joon-ho's 2019 class-warfare dark comedy made Oscars history as the first non-English-language film ever to win Best Picture.
clues: After infiltrating the wealthy Park household as tutors and drivers, the destitute Kim family uncovers a hidden bunker secret.
Fuzzy peach allergies, Morse-code stairway lights, and 'ram-don' steak noodles drive its razor-sharp Palme d'Or triumph.
questions.whyExplanation: Sweeping four major trophies at the 92nd Academy Awards—Picture, Director, Original Screenplay, and International Feature—Bong Joon-ho's Parasite (2019) broke Hollywood's 'one-inch-tall barrier of subtitles.'

questions.prompt: Drawn by Hayao Miyazaki without a finished script as a gift for a friend's ten-year-old daughter, this 2001 Studio Ghibli bathhouse odyssey became the first hand-drawn anime to win Best Animated Feature.
clues: After her greedy parents turn into pigs at an abandoned theme park, young Chihiro must work for witch Yubaba to save them.
A masked gold-conjuring specter named No-Face and a coal-hauling six-armed boiler man populate its supernatural resort.
questions.whyExplanation: Winning both the Berlin Golden Bear and the 2003 Best Animated Feature Oscar, Miyazaki's Spirited Away (Sen to Chihiro no Kamikakushi) held Japan's all-time box-office record for nineteen years.

questions.prompt: So far over budget that Toho Studios shut production down twice, Akira Kurosawa's 1954 mud-soaked epic invented the 'assembling a misfit team' blueprint later remade as a 1960 Hollywood Western.
clues: Desperate 16th-century farmers hire masterless ronin paid solely in white rice to defend their harvest from forty bandits.
Kurosawa used multi-camera telephoto shots during its torrential rain climax so actors couldn't tell which lens caught them.
questions.whyExplanation: Running 207 minutes at its premiere, Akira Kurosawa's Seven Samurai (Shichinin no Samurai, 1954) established modern action editing and inspired countless remakes from Westerns to A Bug's Life.

questions.prompt: Climbing straight atop auditorium seatbacks after Sophia Loren shouted his name at the 1999 Oscars, Italian comic Roberto Benigni swept Best Actor and Foreign Film for this 1997 concentration-camp fable.
clues: Bookshop owner Guido invents an elaborate point-scoring game—promising a real tank as first prize—to shield his young son Joshua.
Benigni's own father had survived two years in a German labor camp, shaping the film's daring blend of slapstick and grief.
questions.whyExplanation: La vita è bella (1997) won the Cannes Grand Prix and three Oscars, making Roberto Benigni only the second performer ever to direct himself to a Best Actor Academy Award.

questions.prompt: Turning down Hollywood funding from David O. Selznick because the mogul insisted on casting Cary Grant, Vittorio De Sica hired real factory worker Lamberto Maggiorani for this 1948 Neorealist landmark.
clues: Desperate Roman poster-hanger Antonio Ricci combs flea markets with his son Bruno after losing the lone vehicle keeping his family fed.
Shot entirely on postwar city streets with non-professional faces, it won an Honorary Oscar before the Foreign Film category existed.
questions.whyExplanation: Ladri di biciclette (1948) epitomized Italian Neorealism by filming working-class poverty on real Roman locations with untrained actors, profoundly influencing Satyajit Ray and the French New Wave.

questions.prompt: Featuring wire-work duels gliding atop swaying Anji bamboo treetops, Ang Lee's 2000 Mandarin wuxia drama earned $128 million in North America—still the top-grossing foreign-language release in U.S. history.
clues: Chow Yun-fat, Michelle Yeoh, and Zhang Ziyi chase the stolen jade sword Green Destiny across Qing-dynasty rooftops and deserts.
Cellist Yo-Yo Ma performed Tan Dun's Oscar-winning score while Yuen Woo-ping choreographed its weightless martial ballet.
questions.whyExplanation: Nominated for ten Academy Awards and winning four—including Best Foreign Language Film—Ang Lee's Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (2000) brought Chinese wuxia cinema into the global mainstream.

questions.prompt: Turning Montmartre's Café des 2 Moulins into a shrine, Jean-Pierre Jeunet's 2001 whimsy starts when Audrey Tautou's shy waitress discovers a hidden tin treasure box behind a bathroom tile.
clues: Armed with Yann Tiersen's accordion waltzes, she plots covert acts of joy—including mailing her father's stolen garden gnome around the globe.
Its quirky heroine delights in cracking crème brûlée crusts with a spoon and tracking down a photo-booth scrap collector.
questions.whyExplanation: Le Fabuleux Destin d'Amélie Poulain (2001) swept the César Awards, earned five Oscar nods, and became one of the highest-grossing French-language movies ever released worldwide.

questions.prompt: Declining doubled Hollywood budgets to keep his script strictly in Spanish, Guillermo del Toro cast contortionist Doug Jones as both the mossy Faun and the hand-eyed Pale Man in this 2006 Franco-era fable.
clues: In 1944 fascist Spain, bookish young Ofelia escapes her brutal Falangist stepfather Captain Vidal through three mythic underworld trials.
Its 22-minute standing ovation at Cannes heralded three craft Oscars for cinematography, art direction, and makeup.
questions.whyExplanation: El laberinto del fauno (2006) merged Spanish Civil War brutality with grim Grimm-style dark fantasy, leaving viewers to debate whether Ofelia's underground kingdom was magic or refuge.

questions.prompt: Barred from Cannes in 1958 for savaging stale French cinema in print, critic François Truffaut returned one year later to win Best Director with a boyhood debut ending in an iconic beach freeze-frame.
clues: Fourteen-year-old Jean-Pierre Léaud debuted as misunderstood Parisian truant Antoine Doinel, whom he would revisit across four sequels.
Its English title translates the French idiom 'faire les quatre cents coups'—meaning to raise hell or run wild.
questions.whyExplanation: Les Quatre Cents Coups (1959) detonated the French New Wave with handheld Paris location shooting and Antoine Doinel's haunting final stare straight into the camera beside the sea.

questions.prompt: Shot over 15 agonizing months without a finished script by Wong Kar-wai and Christopher Doyle, this 2000 Hong Kong romance drifts past slow-motion noodle-stall stairs to Shigeru Umebayashi's haunting waltz.
clues: In 1962 cramped boarding rooms, Tony Leung and Maggie Cheung realize their unseen spouses are having an affair—and vow never to be like them.
Cheung wore more than twenty tailored silk cheongsams before Leung whispers his unspoken secret into a hollow stone at Angkor Wat.
questions.whyExplanation: Celebrated as one of the 21st century's supreme films, Wong Kar-wai's In the Mood for Love (Fa yeung nin wa, 2000) turned cigarette smoke, rain, and restraint into intoxicating cinematic longing.

questions.prompt: Pawning his wife's jewelry and borrowing against life insurance to film on weekends over three years, Satyajit Ray turned this 1955 Bengali village drama into India's international arthouse breakthrough.
clues: Launching the acclaimed Apu Trilogy, it follows young siblings Apu and Durga racing through white kans-grass fields to see their first steam train.
Sitar master Ravi Shankar recorded its improvised musical score in a single marathon eleven-hour studio session.
questions.whyExplanation: Rescued mid-shoot by a West Bengal government loan recorded under 'road improvement,' Satyajit Ray's Pather Panchali ('Song of the Little Road,' 1955) won Best Human Document at Cannes.

questions.prompt: After a Mosfilm lab blunder ruined nearly the entire original Kodak negative shot in Estonia, Andrei Tarkovsky rewrote and reshot this hypnotic 1979 sci-fi allegory of guides leading men into a forbidden Zone.
clues: Loosely adapted from Arkady and Boris Strugatsky's Roadside Picnic, the Writer and Professor throw cloth-tied metal nuts ahead to test invisible traps.
Toxic chemical runoff along the Jägala River filming location was later tragically suspected of contributing to the director's fatal cancer.
questions.whyExplanation: Comprising only 142 long meditative shots shifting from sepia to rich color, Andrei Tarkovsky's Stalker (1979) quests toward a mysterious Room said to grant a pilgrim's deepest secret desire.

questions.prompt: Given an unheard-of final-cut deal by RKO at age 25, Orson Welles saw William Randolph Hearst's newspapers ban ads for this 1941 debut after spotting San Simeon's reflection in Xanadu.
clues: Cinematographer Gregg Toland sawed holes in soundstage floors to shoot low-angle ceilings in groundbreaking deep focus.
Though nominated for nine Oscars, it won only Original Screenplay for Welles and Herman J. Mankiewicz's 'Rosebud' puzzle.
questions.whyExplanation: Citizen Kane (1941) revolutionized screen grammar with overlapping sound, deep-focus lenses, and fractured chronology, rising from box-office disappointment under Hearst's boycott to film history's pinnacle.

questions.prompt: Screenplay pages arrived so late during 1942 shooting that Ingrid Bergman never knew which man Ilsa would leave with—and nobody ever actually utters 'Play it again, Sam' inside Rick's Café Américain.
clues: Dooley Wilson couldn't actually play piano, so studio pianist Elliot Carpenter synced 'As Time Goes By' from behind a curtain.
Released hastily to capitalize on the November 1942 Allied North Africa landings, Michael Curtiz's wartime romance swept Best Picture.
questions.whyExplanation: Adapted from the unproduced play Everybody Comes to Rick's, Casablanca (1942) welded Humphrey Bogart, Ingrid Bergman, and Claude Rains into Golden Age Hollywood's most quoted wartime melodrama.

questions.prompt: Cycling through four directors and losing original Tin Man Buddy Ebsen to aluminum-dust makeup, MGM's lavish 1939 Technicolor gamble didn't turn a theatrical profit until its 1949 re-release.

distractors.text: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs

clues: Studio bosses nearly cut 'Over the Rainbow' three separate times, fearing the slow ballad dragged down the sepia Kansas opening.
Margaret Hamilton suffered severe burns during a trapdoor fire gag, while Judy Garland stepped seamlessly from sepia into Munchkinland.
questions.whyExplanation: Directed primarily by Victor Fleming before he left for Gone with the Wind, MGM's 1939 adaptation of L. Frank Baum's fantasy achieved eternal family-classic status through annual CBS broadcasts starting in 1956.

questions.prompt: Buying up every copy of Robert Bloch's novel he could find and ordering theaters to lock doors after screenings began in 1960, Alfred Hitchcock stunned viewers by killing his billed star 47 minutes in.
clues: Shot on a thrifty TV-crew budget in black-and-white—using Bosco chocolate syrup in the drain—it showed Hollywood's first flushing toilet.
Bernard Herrmann persuaded the director to drop his plan for a silent shower murder by scoring it with shrieking muted violins.
questions.whyExplanation: Starring Anthony Perkins and Janet Leigh, Alfred Hitchcock's Psycho (1960) shattered moviegoing etiquette and censorship taboos, turning an $800,000 gamble into the blueprint for modern slasher cinema.

questions.prompt: Gene Kelly danced his soggy street-lamp anthem with a 103-degree fever—while teenage Debbie Reynolds ironically had parts of her own voice dubbed while playing a vocal double in this 1952 MGM musical.
clues: Donald O'Connor spent days recovering in bed after backflipping off studio walls for 'Make 'Em Laugh'—only to reshoot when film spoiled.
Betty Comden and Adolph Green built its Hollywood talkie-transition satire around Nacio Herb Brown and Arthur Freed's back-catalog songs.
questions.whyExplanation: Co-directed by Stanley Donen and Gene Kelly, Singin' in the Rain (1952) satirized 1927's chaotic shift from silent films to sound and regularly tops polls of the greatest movie musicals ever made.

questions.prompt: Opening with a dead screenwriter floating face-down in a Beverly Hills pool—filmed via a sunken mirror—Billy Wilder's 1950 noir lured real silent-era queen Gloria Swanson back as delusional Norma Desmond.
clues: Erich von Stroheim played devoted butler Max, screening clips from his own real unfinished 1929 Swanson vehicle Queen Kelly.
Studio chief Louis B. Mayer raged at Wilder after the premiere, screaming he had disgraced the industry that fed him.
questions.whyExplanation: Starring William Holden as hack scribe Joe Gillis and Gloria Swanson declaring 'I am big; it's the pictures that got small,' Sunset Boulevard (1950) remains Hollywood's sharpest self-autopsy.

questions.prompt: Shot in 19 days inside one sweltering Manhattan jury room in 1957, Sidney Lumet steadily swapped to longer telephoto lenses and lower angles so the walls visually closed in around holdout Henry Fonda.
clues: Only two of the twelve deliberations participants ever share their actual names—and only on the courthouse steps at the very end.
Adapted from Reginald Rose's 1954 Studio One teleplay, Juror 8 flips an 11-to-1 murder vote using a duplicate switchblade.
questions.whyExplanation: Produced by and starring Henry Fonda alongside Lee J. Cobb and E. G. Marshall, Sidney Lumet's directorial debut 12 Angry Men (1957) transformed claustrophobic chamber dialogue into masterclass tension.

questions.prompt: Constructed on a towering Paramount soundstage spanning 31 Greenwich Village apartments with working wiring, Alfred Hitchcock's 1954 thriller locks leg-cast photographer Jimmy Stewart inside a single room.
clues: Grace Kelly scales a fire escape in a billowing Edith Head gown to snag a dead wife's wedding ring from Raymond Burr's salesman.
Hitchcock directed distant apartment actors through tiny hidden radio earpieces from Stewart's cramped vantage point.
questions.whyExplanation: Adapted from Cornell Woolrich's short story, Rear Window (1954) turns moviegoing voyeurism itself into the suspense engine, using telephoto lenses and flashbulbs as weapons against killer Lars Thorwald.

questions.prompt: Holding the Oscar benchmark of 14 nominations since 1950—including rival Best Actress nods for Bette Davis and Anne Baxter—Joseph L. Mankiewicz's theater satire drew on a real fan's scheming takeover.
clues: Young Marilyn Monroe steals a cocktail-party scene as aspiring 'graduate of the Copacabana School of Dramatic Arts' Miss Caswell.
Acidic critic Addison DeWitt unmasks the sweet understudy plotting to usurp aging Broadway queen Margo Channing.
questions.whyExplanation: Inspired by Mary Orr's short story about actress Elisabeth Bergner's manipulative assistant, All About Eve (1950) won six Oscars including Best Picture and remains the lone film with four nominated female performances.

questions.prompt: Scouting bombed-out Vienna in 1949, Carol Reed heard busker Anton Karas play zither in a tavern—scrapping an orchestra to pair that lone twanging instrument with Orson Welles's sewer chase.
clues: Pulp writer Holly Martins arrives to find friend Harry Lime supposedly dead—until a doorway spotlight catches a smug grin.
Aboard Vienna's giant Riesenrad Ferris wheel, Welles improvised his famous monologue contrasting Renaissance Italy with Swiss cuckoo clocks.
questions.whyExplanation: Written by Graham Greene and filmed in tilted Dutch angles by Oscar-winner Robert Krasker, The Third Man (1949) won the Cannes Grand Prix and turned Anton Karas's zither tune into a global chart-topper.

questions.prompt: Clashing bitterly with co-writer Raymond Chandler, Billy Wilder still turned James M. Cain's pulp insurance plot into this 1944 noir benchmark—dodging Hays Code bans on real murder blueprints.
clues: Bleeding into an office Dictaphone, Fred MacMurray confesses how Barbara Stanwyck's ankle bracelet lured him into staging a train-jump scam.
Edward G. Robinson plays sharp claims investigator Barton Keyes, whose 'little man' inside his stomach smells every phony claim.
questions.whyExplanation: Inspired by the 1927 Ruth Snyder murder case, Double Indemnity (1944) crystallized American film noir's venetian-blind shadows, cynical voiceover, and lethal femme fatale—despite winning zero of its seven Oscar nods.

questions.prompt: Nearly bankrupting Germany's UFA studio in 1927, Fritz Lang's towering futuristic fable lost a quarter of its runtime for 81 years until a scratched 16mm print surfaced in a Buenos Aires museum in 2008.
clues: Brigitte Helm plays both peace-preaching Maria and the gleaming metallic 'Maschinenmensch' robot that inspired C-3PO.
Its famous intertitle declares 'The mediator between head and hands must be the heart' above subterranean clockwork workers.
questions.whyExplanation: Released in Weimar Berlin in January 1927 and brutally slashed by distributors, Fritz Lang's Metropolis saw 25 lost minutes recovered in Argentina's Museo del Cine in 2008 and restored to nearly full length.

questions.prompt: Holding cinema's record with 21 Oscar nods across accents from Polish to Danish, she famously left her first statuette sitting on a ladies'-room floor after winning for Kramer vs. Kramer.
clues: She captured Best Actress trophies nearly thirty years apart for Sophie's Choice (1982) and Margaret Thatcher in The Iron Lady (2011).
From icy fashion tyrant Miranda Priestly to chef Julia Child, her vocal precision made her a Yale Drama legend.
questions.whyExplanation: With three wins and 21 Academy Award nominations—plus nine Golden Globes—Meryl Streep holds the modern benchmark for American screen acting versatility.

questions.prompt: Becoming only the second actor after Spencer Tracy to claim consecutive Best Actor Oscars—in 1994 and 1995—this antique-typewriter collector first won hearts jumping from sitcom Bosom Buddies to Big.
clues: Back-to-back trophies honored his AIDS-discrimination lawyer in Philadelphia and feather-chasing Alabamian Forrest Gump.
He also voiced pull-string cowboy Woody across Toy Story films and starred in five collaborations with Steven Spielberg.
questions.whyExplanation: Tom Hanks joined Spencer Tracy as the only back-to-back Best Actor Academy Award winners (1993-1994), anchoring beloved epics from Apollo 13 to Saving Private Ryan and Cast Away.

questions.prompt: Winning Oscars on opposite sides of morality in Glory and Training Day, this Fordham-trained titan quietly paid young Chadwick Boseman's Oxford summer theater tuition anonymously through Phylicia Rashad.
clues: Spike Lee cast him in four iconic collaborations including Malcolm X, Mo' Better Blues, and He Got Game.
Holding ten Academy Award nominations—the most of any Black actor—he also won a 2010 Tony for August Wilson's Fences.
questions.whyExplanation: A two-time Oscar winner (Glory, 1990; Training Day, 2002) and nine-time acting nominee, Denzel Washington was revealed years later as the mystery patron who funded Howard University students' 1998 Oxford program.

questions.prompt: After four widely memed Oscar losses stretching from What's Eating Gilbert Grape to The Wolf of Wall Street, he finally seized Best Actor in 2016 after eating raw bison liver on a freezing frontier shoot.
clues: Martin Scorsese made him a modern muse across six features, including The Aviator, The Departed, and Killers of the Flower Moon.
Named after da Vinci because he kicked in the womb before an Uffizi painting, he skyrocketed to teen stardom aboard Titanic.
questions.whyExplanation: Following nominations for Gilbert Grape, The Aviator, Blood Diamond, and The Wolf of Wall Street, Leonardo DiCaprio clinched the 2016 Best Actor Oscar for Alejandro G. Iñárritu's The Revenant.

questions.prompt: A Canadian Mickey Mouse Club alum alongside Justin Timberlake and Britney Spears, he spent two months building his own kitchen table to prepare for The Notebook before unleashing 'Kenergy' in Barbie.
clues: He earned Oscar nominations for Half Nelson, La La Land, and singing 'I'm Just Ken' in pink sparkles at the 2024 ceremony.
Equally at home in stoic neon thrillers like Drive and Blade Runner 2049, he won a Golden Globe for playing jazz pianist Sebastian.
questions.whyExplanation: Born in London, Ontario, Ryan Gosling evolved from 1990s Disney variety kid into one of cinema's premier chameleons, earning three Academy Award nominations across drama, musical, and comedy.

questions.prompt: Entering cinema's ultra-rare club of three-time Best Actress winners via Fargo, Three Billboards, and Nomadland, she also grabbed a fourth Oscar statuette the same night as Nomadland's producer.
clues: She popularized the term 'inclusion rider' during her electric 2018 Academy Awards acceptance speech.
Completing the Triple Crown of Acting with an Emmy for Olive Kitteridge and a Tony for Good People, she is married to Joel Coen.
questions.whyExplanation: Frances McDormand became only the second performer after Katharine Hepburn to win three Best Actress Oscars—and the first person ever to win both acting and producing Oscars for the same film in 2021.

questions.prompt: Joining the elite EGOT club in 2023 with a Grammy for narrating her memoir Finding Me, this Juilliard-trained powerhouse earlier won a Tony and an Oscar playing Rose Maxson in Fences.
clues: In 2015 she became the first Black woman to win the Lead Actress in a Drama Emmy for law professor Annalise Keating.
Her blistering ten-minute confrontation with Meryl Streep in Doubt earned her first Academy Award nomination in 2009.
questions.whyExplanation: Winning two Tonys (King Hedley II, Fences), an Emmy (How to Get Away with Murder), an Oscar (Fences), and a 2023 Audiobook Grammy, Viola Davis became the 18th competitive EGOT laureate.

questions.prompt: Born in Beirut and raised in Toronto as a teenage hockey goalie, this quietly generous action icon gifted Harley-Davidson motorcycles to his Matrix stunt crew before fueling four John Wick rampages.
clues: Before dodging bullets as Neo, he time-traveled in a phone booth as Ted 'Theodore' Logan and rode a rigged city bus in Speed.
His Hawaiian first name means 'cool breeze over the mountains,' and he plays bass in the alt-rock trio Dogstar.
questions.whyExplanation: Canadian actor Keanu Reeves parlayed slacker charm in Bill & Ted into generational action franchises—Point Break, Speed, The Matrix, and John Wick—while earning renown for understated off-screen kindness.

questions.prompt: Vanishing completely behind Truman Capote's reedy drawl to sweep the 2006 Best Actor Oscar, this luminous character chameleon anchored The Master, Doubt, and Synecdoche, New York before his death at 46.
clues: Director Paul Thomas Anderson cast him in five consecutive early films—from Boogie Nights' boom operator to Magnolia's nurse.
On Broadway he earned three Tony nominations starring in True West, Long Day's Journey into Night, and Death of a Salesman.
questions.whyExplanation: Widely regarded as the finest American character actor of his generation, Philip Seymour Hoffman (1967-2014) earned four Oscar nominations and won Best Actor for Capote (2005).

questions.prompt: An Ottawa-born trailblazer who became the first Asian performer to host the Golden Globes and win multiple trophies there, she jumped from Grey's Anatomy's Cristina Yang to Killing Eve's obsessive MI5 spy.
clues: In 2018 she became the first actress of Asian descent nominated for the Lead Actress in a Drama Emmy.
Her breakout cinema role as fiery winemaker Stephanie in Alexander Payne's Sideways preceded ten seasons in Seattle scrubs.
questions.whyExplanation: Canadian-American star Sandra Oh earned twelve Primetime Emmy nominations across Grey's Anatomy and Killing Eve alongside two Golden Globes, smashing representation barriers in North American TV and film.

questions.prompt: Appearing in just five feature films before dying at 42 in 1978, this fragile-eyed character legend holds a spotless Hollywood record: every single movie he ever made earned a Best Picture nod.
clues: He played tragic middle brother Fredo Corleone, Al Pacino's bank-robbery partner Sal, and Gene Hackman's audio aide Stan.
Robert De Niro paid his medical insurance personally so he could complete his final scenes in The Deer Hunter alongside fiancée Meryl Streep.
questions.whyExplanation: John Cazale's spotless five-film filmography—The Godfather, The Conversation, The Godfather Part II, Dog Day Afternoon, and The Deer Hunter—all received Best Picture Oscar nominations, with three winning.

questions.prompt: Despite five towering decades anchoring M*A*S*H, Klute, Don't Look Now, and The Hunger Games, this velvety-voiced Canadian giant never earned a competitive Oscar nod before his 2017 Honorary trophy.
clues: He originated wise-cracking Korean War surgeon Hawkeye Pierce onstage for Robert Altman before playing tyrannical President Snow.
His bone-chilling finger-pointing final shriek closes 1978's Invasion of the Body Snatchers; his son Kiefer starred in 24.
questions.whyExplanation: Canadian screen legend Donald Sutherland (1935-2024) appeared in nearly 200 works—including The Dirty Dozen and Pride & Prejudice—and was widely cited as the greatest actor never nominated for a competitive Oscar.

questions.prompt: The sole performer to win three Best Actor Oscars, this fiercely immersive Anglo-Irish method master stayed in a wheelchair throughout My Left Foot and apprenticed with a Florence cobbler between roles.
clues: His other two statuettes honored a ruthless oil prospector in There Will Be Blood and Spielberg's tall, reedy Abraham Lincoln.
Son of an Anglo-Irish Poet Laureate, he paused acting after 2017's Phantom Thread before reuniting onscreen with his son Ronan.
questions.whyExplanation: Sir Daniel Day-Lewis set the unmatched benchmark of three Best Actor Oscars (1990, 2008, 2013), famed for living completely inside characters from Hawkeye to Bill the Butcher.

questions.prompt: A Welsh baker's son knighted in 1993, he became the oldest acting Oscar winner in history at age 83 for The Father—skipping the 2021 ceremony to stay home painting in Wales before waking to the news.
clues: He won his first Academy Award thirty years earlier with an unblinking, chilling performance as cannibal psychiatrist Hannibal Lecter.
From restrained butler Stevens in The Remains of the Day to Richard Nixon and Odin, his range spans six decades.
questions.whyExplanation: Sir Anthony Hopkins won Best Actor in 1992 (The Silence of the Lambs) and again in 2021 (The Father), surpassing Christopher Plummer's age record while honoring fellow nominee Chadwick Boseman from Wales.

questions.prompt: Drilled from age six in punishing Peking Opera acrobatics alongside Sammo Hung, this Hong Kong dynamo broke his nose, ribs, and skull turning Buster Keaton slapstick into no-double martial arts.
clues: His signature closing-credits blooper reels proved his death-defying clock-tower drops and mall-pole slides in Police Story were real.
After Drunken Master and Rumble in the Bronx broke globally, he teamed with Chris Tucker in Rush Hour and won a 2016 Honorary Oscar.
questions.whyExplanation: Born Chan Kong-sang in Hong Kong in 1954, Jackie Chan fused kung fu, prop comedy, and perilous stunt work across over 150 films, becoming Asia's most recognizable global action star.

questions.prompt: At 33 she became the youngest actor ever to log six Oscar nods—finally winning for The Reader after enduring icy Titanic water tanks and later holding her breath over seven minutes for Avatar: The Way of Water.
clues: Breaking out in Peter Jackson's Heavenly Creatures and Sense and Sensibility, she also starred in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind.
Her gritty Pennsylvania detective in HBO's Mare of Easttown earned her a second Primetime Emmy alongside Mildred Pierce.
questions.whyExplanation: English actress Kate Winslet won Best Actress for The Reader (2008) after five earlier nominations, and shattered Tom Cruise's underwater filming breath-hold record during James Cameron's 2022 Avatar sequel.
