questions.l2Subcategory: Pro Basketball, Hockey, Baseball & Rugby Clubs
questions.prompt: Originally nicknamed the 'Trolley Dodgers' because 19th-century Brooklyn pedestrians had to leap out of the way of streetcars, this club moved west with the Giants in 1958 to bring MLB to California.
clues: Long known as 'Dem Bums' after losing five World Series to the Yankees, they finally broke through in 1955 before leaving Ebbets Field.
Since moving to Chavez Ravine, they have added seven more World Series crowns, including 2020 and 2024.
questions.whyExplanation: The Dodgers' 1958 relocation from Brooklyn to Los Angeles ended MLB's East-Midwest monopoly and opened baseball to the Pacific Coast.

questions.l2Subcategory: Pro Basketball, Hockey, Baseball & Rugby Clubs
questions.prompt: Winning six NBA championships across two perfect three-peats in the 1990s without ever letting a Finals reach Game 7, Phil Jackson's triangle-offense juggernaut went 72-10 in 1995-96.
clues: Michael Jordan, Scottie Pippen, and Dennis Rodman turned their crimson jerseys into the most recognized sportswear on Earth.
Their roaring pregame introductions to the Alan Parsons Project's 'Sirius' shook the United Center.
questions.whyExplanation: The 1990s Chicago Bulls went 6-0 in NBA Finals series (1991-93 and 1996-98), popularizing basketball globally as never before.

questions.l2Subcategory: Pro Basketball, Hockey, Baseball & Rugby Clubs
questions.prompt: Winning four Rugby World Cups—more than any other nation—and uniting a post-apartheid country in 1995 when Nelson Mandela wore Captain Francois Pienaar's No. 6 green jersey, this team represents South Africa.
clues: Named for a nimble southern African antelope, their 1995 triumph at Ellis Park inspired the film Invictus.
Captain Siya Kolisi lifted back-to-back Webb Ellis Cups for them in 2019 and 2023.
questions.whyExplanation: South Africa's Springboks turned rugby from a symbol of division into a vessel of national unity in 1995 and now lead the world with four Rugby World Cup titles.

questions.l2Subcategory: Pro Basketball, Hockey, Baseball & Rugby Clubs
questions.prompt: Founded in 1934 after Babe Ruth's barnstorming tour ignited baseball fever in Japan, this Tokyo club—often called 'the Yankees of Japan'—has captured a record 22 Japan Series crowns.
clues: Home-run legend Sadaharu Oh smashed 868 career homers in their orange-and-black uniform, including nine straight Japan Series titles (1965-1973).
Owned by Japan's largest daily newspaper, they play beneath the inflatable roof of the Tokyo Dome.
questions.whyExplanation: The Yomiuri Giants are Nippon Professional Baseball's oldest and most decorated franchise, anchored by icons Sadaharu Oh and Shigeo Nagashima.

questions.prompt: Guido van Rossum began coding this indentation-driven language over a quiet 1989 Christmas week in Amsterdam—naming it after a British sketch-comedy troupe rather than a venomous snake.
clues: Its official philosophy—accessible via "import this"—prizes readability and one obvious way to do a task.
Named for Monty's Flying Circus, it became the dominant language of modern AI and data science.
questions.whyExplanation: Guido van Rossum created Python in December 1989 at CWI Amsterdam, naming it for Monty Python's Flying Circus while designing clean whitespace syntax.

questions.prompt: Helsinki student Linus Torvalds originally wanted to christen his 1991 hobby kernel "Freax," until an FTP server admin uploaded it under this punning folder name instead.
clues: Its chubby penguin mascot, Tux, was inspired by a friendly nip Torvalds got at an Australian zoo.
Paired with GNU utilities, this open-source kernel quietly runs almost all top supercomputers and cloud servers.
questions.whyExplanation: FTP administrator Ari Lemmke renamed Torvalds's 1991 "Freax" kernel directory to Linux, launching the open-source operating system powering the modern cloud.

questions.prompt: Netscape's Brendan Eich hammered out the first working prototype of this web scripting tongue in just ten days in May 1995—dubbing it Mocha and LiveScript before a fateful marketing rebrand.
clues: Despite sharing half its name with Sun's popular 1990s coffee-named platform, the two languages are famously as unrelated as ham and hamster.
Standardized as ECMAScript, it now runs both inside every web browser and on servers via Node.
questions.whyExplanation: Brendan Eich built JavaScript in ten days at Netscape in 1995; its name was a co-marketing move alongside Sun Microsystems's unrelated Java platform.

questions.prompt: Born at Bell Labs in 1969 partly so Ken Thompson could keep playing his Space Travel game on an unused PDP-7, this streamlined OS took a cheeky punning name mocking the bloated Multics project.
clues: Rewritten in C in 1973, its philosophy of small tools linked by pipes became the direct ancestor of macOS and BSD.
Its 32-bit epoch clock began ticking at midnight UTC on January 1, 1970.
questions.whyExplanation: Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie created Unix at Bell Labs in 1969 (originally punned as Unics against Multics), inventing the foundation of modern operating systems.

questions.prompt: John Backus's IBM team stunned skeptics in 1957 by proving this pioneering high-level compiled language could match hand-tuned assembly speed on the IBM 704—and supercomputers still run it today.
clues: Its name contracts "Formula Translation" because it was crafted specifically for scientists and engineers crunching equations.
Even NASA's distant Voyager probes relied on legacy routines descended from this 1950s numerical workhorse.
questions.whyExplanation: Released by IBM in 1957 under John Backus, Fortran (Formula Translation) became the first widely adopted high-level language and remains a scientific computing staple.

questions.prompt: Shaped by Grace Hopper's FLOW-MATIC in 1959 so managers could read code like plain English prose, this verbose mainframe language still quietly processes trillions in daily ATM and banking traffic.
clues: During the 2020 pandemic, several U.S. states issued urgent pleas for retired programmers fluent in its 1960s syntax to patch unemployment systems.
Its five-letter acronym stands for Common Business-Oriented Language.
questions.whyExplanation: Designed in 1959 by CODASYL with strong influence from Grace Hopper, COBOL brought English-like readability to enterprise mainframes and still anchors global finance.

questions.prompt: Coded by Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina at the University of Illinois in 1993, this breakthrough web browser was the first to show inline images right beside text—turning the Web into a mass medium.
clues: Before it arrived from NCSA, early web readers opened pictures awkwardly in separate pop-up windows.
Its tiled-art name directly inspired both Netscape and Microsoft's licensed Internet Explorer codebase.
questions.whyExplanation: Released in 1993 by NCSA's Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina, Mosaic popularized the World Wide Web by rendering inline images alongside hypertext.

questions.prompt: Graydon Hoare began this memory-safe systems language in 2006 after a software-crashed apartment elevator forced him up 21 flights of stairs—naming it after a tough, hard-to-kill plant fungus.
clues: Sponsored by Mozilla starting in 2009, its strict borrow checker eliminates whole classes of memory leaks without a garbage collector.
Its unofficial crab mascot is named Ferris, a pun on the Latin word for iron.
questions.whyExplanation: Begun by Graydon Hoare in 2006 and backed by Mozilla, Rust uses compile-time ownership checks to guarantee memory safety and is named after resilient rust fungi.

questions.prompt: Andy Rubin originally founded a 2003 Palo Alto startup to build a smart OS for digital cameras before pivoting to phones—selling to Google in 2005 and naming early releases alphabetically after sweets.
clues: From Cupcake and Donut through KitKat and Oreo, its dessert codenames accompanied a friendly green robot logo.
Built atop a modified open-source kernel, it now commands roughly 70 percent of global smartphone shipments.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded in 2003 by Andy Rubin's team for cameras before pivoting to mobile, Android was acquired by Google in 2005 and grew into the world's most used phone OS.

questions.prompt: Paying Seattle Computer Products roughly $75,000 in 1981 for Tim Paterson's "Quick and Dirty" 86-DOS, Microsoft rebranded it to power the IBM PC—while cleverly keeping rights to license it to clones.
clues: Its blinking C:\> command prompt greeted an entire generation of 1980s personal computer users before graphical windows hid it.
IBM sold its nearly identical twin under the name PC DOS on the landmark 1981 IBM 5150.
questions.whyExplanation: Microsoft bought 86-DOS from Seattle Computer Products in 1981 and licensed it as MS-DOS to IBM and PC clone makers, laying the financial bedrock of Microsoft.

questions.prompt: Crafted at Xerox PARC in the 1970s by Alan Kay's team, this pure object-oriented language pioneered the Model-View-Controller pattern and ran the overlapping-window interface that dazzled Steve Jobs in 1979.
clues: In its radically unified design, even integers and code blocks are objects communicating strictly by sending messages.
Its casual, conversational two-word name belies its massive influence on Objective-C, Ruby, and modern IDEs.
questions.whyExplanation: Developed at Xerox PARC by Alan Kay, Dan Ingalls, and Adele Goldberg, Smalltalk pioneered modern object-oriented programming, MVC architecture, and windowed GUIs.

questions.prompt: Devised by MIT's John McCarthy in 1958, the second-oldest high-level language still in use became early AI's native tongue—and earned playful jokes about its dizzying forests of nested parentheses.
clues: Treating code and data as identical linked structures, it pioneered garbage collection, recursion, and dynamic typing.
Its four-letter name shortens "List Processing," though wags joked it stood for "Lots of Irritating Superfluous Parentheses."
questions.whyExplanation: John McCarthy created Lisp in 1958 at MIT as a mathematical notation for list processing, pioneering garbage collection and powering decades of AI research.

questions.prompt: Named in 1997 for a 10th-century Danish king who united warring Scandinavian tribes, this short-range wireless standard even fuses his two Nordic initials into its iconic angular blue-and-white logo.
clues: Intel's Jim Kardach suggested the Viking codename while reading a historical novel about King Harald Gormsson, expecting marketing to replace it later.
Its geometric symbol binds the Younger Futhark runes for H and B.
questions.whyExplanation: Bluetooth honors Danish King Harald "Bluetooth" Gormsson for uniting tech industries just as he united Denmark and Norway; its logo merges his runic initials.

questions.prompt: Born from Adobe co-founder John Warnock's 1991 "Camelot" memo dreaming of a paperless office, this self-contained document wrapper kept fonts and layouts identical on any printer—going open ISO in 2008.
clues: Initially Adobe charged $50 just for the reader app until giving Acrobat Reader away free sparked worldwide adoption.
Its ubiquitous three-letter extension stands for Portable Document Format.
questions.whyExplanation: Conceived in John Warnock's 1991 Camelot project and released by Adobe in 1993, Portable Document Format (PDF) became ISO 32000 in 2008.

questions.prompt: To fine-tune this psychoacoustic audio standard, Fraunhofer engineer Karlheinz Brandenburg replayed Suzanne Vega's a cappella "Tom's Diner" hundreds of times—earning the singer the title "Mother" of the format.
clues: By stripping away frequencies masked by the human ear, it shrank CD tracks by roughly 90 percent and fueled Napster and the iPod.
Its three-character name abbreviates MPEG-1 Audio Layer III.
questions.whyExplanation: Fraunhofer's Karlheinz Brandenburg used Suzanne Vega's sparse vocals on "Tom's Diner" to eliminate warbling artifacts while perfecting MP3 audio compression.

questions.prompt: Designed by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn in the 1970s to link networks via packets, this foundational protocol pair went live on ARPANET's January 1, 1983 "Flag Day"—the Internet's birthday.
clues: One half breaks data into numbered packets and checks for lost pieces; the other half stamps every packet with a destination address.
Its slashed five-letter name pairs Transmission Control Protocol with Internet Protocol.
questions.whyExplanation: Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn's TCP/IP suite replaced ARPANET's older NCP on January 1, 1983, creating the interoperable architecture of the modern Internet.

questions.prompt: When Unisys shocked webmasters in late 1994 by demanding royalties on GIF's LZW compression patent, open-source coders built this lossless, alpha-transparency image rival with a cheeky recursive-pun name.
clues: Officially standing for Portable Network Graphics, insiders affectionately expanded its three letters as "... Not GIF."
Unlike JPEG, it keeps crisp screenshots and transparent-background logos razor sharp without blocky compression smear.
questions.whyExplanation: Created in 1995 in response to Unisys patent enforcement on GIF, Portable Network Graphics (PNG) delivered patent-free lossless compression and full alpha transparency.

questions.prompt: Standardized in 1963 with seven bits mapping 128 letters, digits, and teletype commands—including code 7 to ring a physical bell—this classic character map still forms the opening slice of modern UTF-8.
clues: Creative early programmers arranged its printable punctuation marks into elaborate monochrome "art" banners on green-screen terminals.
Its five-letter acronym stands for American Standard Code for Information Interchange.
questions.whyExplanation: Published in 1963, 7-bit ASCII standardized 128 text and teletype control codes and remains completely backward-compatible with today's ubiquitous UTF-8 encoding.

questions.prompt: Forged in 1983 when rival synth makers Roland and Sequential Circuits bridged a Jupiter-6 and a Prophet-600 live onstage, this tiny 5-pin protocol carries zero actual sound—only digital sheet-music commands.
clues: Instead of bulky audio waveforms, it transmits compact messages like note pitch, key velocity, and sustain pedal timing.
Its four-letter acronym stands for Musical Instrument Digital Interface.
questions.whyExplanation: Spearheaded by Dave Smith and Ikutaro Kakehashi in 1983, MIDI standardized digital event messaging so synthesizers, drum machines, and computers could sync seamlessly.

questions.prompt: Unveiled by Netscape in 1994 to wrap ordinary web pages inside cryptographic tunnels over port 443, this five-letter protocol put a tiny padlock in browsers and made online shopping safe.
clues: Originally layered over SSL and now powered by TLS certificates, it verifies a website's identity while scrambling traffic against eavesdroppers.
Its name simply appends "Secure" to Tim Berners-Lee's foundational web-transfer acronym.
questions.whyExplanation: Introduced by Netscape in 1994, HTTPS encrypts HTTP traffic with SSL/TLS over TCP port 443, safeguarding passwords, payments, and privacy across the Web.

questions.prompt: By 1983, maintaining a single manual HOSTS.TXT directory for every computer on ARPANET had broken down—prompting Paul Mockapetris to invent this distributed hierarchy translating names into numeric IPs.
clues: Often dubbed the "phonebook of the Internet," its root zone is anchored globally by 13 named clusters of root servers labeled A through M.
Its three letters stand for Domain Name System.
questions.whyExplanation: Paul Mockapetris invented the Domain Name System (DNS) in 1983 to replace SRI's centralized HOSTS.TXT table with scalable, hierarchical domain-to-IP resolution.

questions.prompt: Finalized in 1992 by an imaging committee, this lossy photo workhorse trims file sizes sharply because human eyes notice brightness shifts far more than subtle color drops.
clues: Over-compressing it exposes its internal 8-by-8 pixel discrete cosine transform blocks as fuzzy square "mosquito noise" halos.
Its four-letter acronym stands for Joint Photographic Experts Group.
questions.whyExplanation: Standardized in 1992 by the Joint Photographic Experts Group, JPEG combines chroma subsampling with 8x8 discrete cosine transforms to make digital photography practical.

questions.prompt: Watching black and white stones on a lunchtime Go board gave Denso Wave engineer Masahiro Hara his 1994 spark for this high-speed 2D matrix—built to track Toyota auto parts before conquering restaurant menus.
clues: Its three corner finder squares let cameras lock onto its orientation instantly, while Reed-Solomon error correction lets it scan even when 30 percent damaged.
Denso Wave chose not to enforce its patent on this "Quick Response" square, fueling global smartphone adoption.
questions.whyExplanation: Masahiro Hara created the QR (Quick Response) code at Denso Wave in 1994 to scan automotive parts rapidly from any angle; Denso kept its use royalty-free.

questions.prompt: In a May 1973 Xerox PARC memo, Robert Metcalfe named his new office local-area cable standard after physics' long-discredited light-carrying medium—launching the wired backbone of modern LANs.
clues: Early versions shared a single thick yellow coaxial wire where colliding computers politely paused for random intervals before retransmitting.
Today its snap-in RJ45 twisted-pair cables link home routers and hyperscale data centers at multi-gigabit speeds.
questions.whyExplanation: Robert Metcalfe invented Ethernet at Xerox PARC in 1973, naming it for the luminiferous ether as a universal passive medium carrying data packets between computers.

questions.prompt: Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger launched this site in January 2001 merely as an informal wiki feeder for their expert-reviewed Nupedia—only for the lively side project to swallow its parent within weeks.
clues: Its iconic unfinished puzzle-sphere logo displays glyphs from over a dozen world scripts, symbolizing knowledge forever in progress.
Combining the Hawaiian word for "quick" with "encyclopedia," it remains one of the few top global websites with zero ads.
questions.whyExplanation: Launched January 15, 2001 as a rough-draft feeder for slow-moving Nupedia, Wikipedia rapidly became humanity's largest crowdsourced encyclopedia.

questions.prompt: Built in 2008 around Linus Torvalds's distributed version-control tool—and fronted by a quirky feline-cephalopod mascot named Octocat—this open-source code hub sold to Microsoft for $7.5 billion in 2018.
clues: Its "pull request" workflow turned social code review into the standard way millions of developers collaborate on software.
It also launched AI pair-programmer Copilot in 2021 using billions of lines of public repositories.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded in 2008 around Git version control, GitHub popularized pull-request collaboration and became a cornerstone Microsoft subsidiary in 2018.

questions.prompt: Tim Sweeney personally wrote roughly 90 percent of its 1998 first-person shooter debut at Epic Games; today this 3D powerhouse renders both Fortnite and the wraparound LED movie sets of The Mandalorian.
clues: Its fifth generation introduced Nanite virtualized geometry and Lumen real-time global illumination for photorealistic graphics.
Named after Epic's lush 1998 sci-fi shooter, it competes head-to-head with Unity across games and cinema.
questions.whyExplanation: Created by Epic Games's Tim Sweeney for 1998's Unreal, Unreal Engine evolved into an industry-standard real-time 3D platform for video games and film virtual production.

questions.prompt: Pivoting swiftly after their video dating-site pitch "Tune In Hook Up" flopped in early 2005, three ex-PayPal staffers launched this video giant with a 19-second elephant clip filmed at the San Diego Zoo.
clues: Co-founder Jawed Karim uploaded its historic first clip, "Me at the zoo," on April 23, 2005.
Google snapped it up just 18 months later in October 2006 for $1.65 billion in stock.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded in February 2005 by Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, and Jawed Karim after abandoning a dating-site concept, YouTube debuted with "Me at the zoo" before Google bought it in 2006.

questions.prompt: Descending directly from Michael Stonebraker's 1986 UC Berkeley follow-up to Ingres, this elephant-logoed open-source database won engineers' hearts with ironclad SQL compliance and custom data types.
clues: Its mascot, an elephant named Slonik, nods to the proverb that elephants never forget.
Its 10-letter name fuses "Post" (after Ingres) with "SQL"—and powers geographic extensions like PostGIS.
questions.whyExplanation: PostgreSQL evolved from Michael Stonebraker's 1986 Berkeley POSTGRES project into the world's premier open-source object-relational database system.

questions.prompt: Borrowing its name from animated dog Mr. Peabody's cartoon time-travel device, this Internet Archive service launched in 2001 to rescue hundreds of billions of vanished web pages from digital rot.
clues: Founded by Brewster Kahle in San Francisco, its crawlers let anyone inspect what Apple's or Yahoo's homepage looked like in 1996.
Courts, journalists, and patent examiners routinely cite its timestamped snapshots to verify deleted online claims.
questions.whyExplanation: Launched publicly by the Internet Archive in 2001 and named after Rocky and Bullwinkle's WABAC Machine, the Wayback Machine archives the historical World Wide Web.

questions.prompt: Co-founded in 2008 by bloggers Jeff Atwood and Joel Spolsky and named by readers after a classic runaway-recursion crash, this reputation-driven Q&A hub rescued coders from paywalled tech forums.
clues: Its iconic logo shows crisp horizontal bars spilling out of an open-topped gray container.
Generations of software developers have joked that half their career consists of copying its top green-checkmarked answers.
questions.whyExplanation: Created by Jeff Atwood and Joel Spolsky in 2008, Stack Overflow took its name from a call-stack memory crash and became the go-to programming Q&A network.

questions.prompt: Built in Copenhagen in 2005 solely for Mac OS X after three founders' marble game GooBall flopped, this cross-platform engine grew to power Hollow Knight, Cuphead, and Pokémon GO.
clues: Developers script its gameplay predominantly in C# inside an intuitive scene editor that exports to mobile, console, and VR.
Its single-word name evokes togetherness and is represented by a sleek isometric cube logo.
questions.whyExplanation: Launched in 2005 for Mac OS X after its creators' debut game underperformed, Unity expanded cross-platform to power a vast share of mobile and indie games.

questions.prompt: Italian programmer Salvatore Sanfilippo wrote this blazingly fast in-memory key-value store in 2009 just to stop his live web-analytics startup from choking—naming it after Remote Dictionary Server.
clues: Holding data structures like hashes, sorted sets, and streams directly in RAM lets it serve requests in sub-millisecond latency.
Its crimson logo stacks cubes into a stylized cylinder, and its five-letter name starts with "Re" and ends with "dis."
questions.whyExplanation: Salvatore Sanfilippo created Redis (Remote Dictionary Server) in 2009 to scale his analytics startup; it became a staple in-memory cache and message broker.

questions.prompt: Begun in 1995 as a plain-text San Francisco email list of local arts and tech happenings, this famously bare-bones classifieds giant spurned slick redesigns and banner ads for decades to keep pages zippy.
clues: Its refusal to monetize most free listings upended the multi-billion-dollar newspaper classified-ad business across America.
A purple peace-sign icon still accompanies this directory named for founder Newmark's first name.
questions.whyExplanation: Started in 1995 by Craig Newmark as a Bay Area email list, Craigslist kept an ultra-minimalist hyperlinked layout while transforming local online classifieds.

questions.prompt: D. Richard Hipp built this tiny, serverless C database in 2000 for U.S. Navy guided-missile destroyers so shipboard software needed zero admin—now it ships silently inside virtually every phone and browser.
clues: Storing an entire relational database inside a single ordinary disk file, its source code is dedicated outright to the public domain.
With trillions of active deployments worldwide, its six-letter name pairs structured query language with a featherweight suffix.
questions.whyExplanation: Created by D. Richard Hipp in 2000 for U.S. Navy destroyer software, public-domain SQLite is embedded in iOS, Android, browsers, and aircraft, making it the most deployed database engine.

questions.prompt: Created at LinkedIn in 2011 to pipe billions of real-time event streams, this open-source distributed log was named by co-creator Jay Kreps after a famous Prague novelist because it was "optimized for writing."
clues: Rather than deleting messages upon first read like classic queues, it appends immutable streams to partitioned topics that many services replay.
Its literary namesake penned The Metamorphosis and The Trial.
questions.whyExplanation: Built at LinkedIn by Jay Kreps, Neha Narkhede, and Jun Rao in 2011, Apache Kafka was named for author Franz Kafka as a distributed event-streaming log optimized for high-throughput writing.

questions.prompt: Cracking Enigma ciphers at Bletchley Park after defining computability with an imaginary tape machine in 1936, this British genius faced tragic 1952 prosecution before a 2013 royal pardon.
clues: His 1950 "Imitation Game" paper proposed an interactive conversation benchmark for testing machine intelligence.
Computing's highest annual honor—the ACM's "Nobel Prize of Computer Science"—bears his surname.
questions.whyExplanation: Alan Turing formalized algorithms and computability in 1936, broke WWII Enigma ciphers at Bletchley Park, and founded theoretical computer science and AI.

questions.prompt: Poet Lord Byron's math-drilled daughter appended a landmark 1843 algorithm for Bernoulli numbers to notes on Charles Babbage's unbuilt Analytical Engine—visioning a machine that could compose music too.
clues: Her mother steered her fiercely toward geometry and logic to suppress any trace of her estranged father's poetic madness.
Often hailed as the first computer programmer, she inspired the U.S. Defense Department's 1980 programming language.
questions.whyExplanation: Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace, published Note G in 1843 detailing a step-by-step algorithm for Babbage's Analytical Engine and glimpsing general-purpose computing.

questions.prompt: Handing out foot-long copper wires to show audiences how far electricity travels in a nanosecond, this U.S. Navy rear admiral pioneered compilers and helped popularize "debugging" after a 1947 relay moth.
clues: Her team taped that unlucky Harvard Mark II moth right into their logbook as the "first actual case of bug being found."
Her English-syntax FLOW-MATIC system directly shaped COBOL, and a Navy guided-missile destroyer bears her name.
questions.whyExplanation: Rear Admiral Grace Hopper built early compiler/linker tools, shaped COBOL, made "nanosecond" wires famous in lectures, and cemented "debugging" in computing lore.

questions.prompt: His CERN boss scribbled "Vague, but exciting" atop his March 1989 hypertext proposal—yet this Briton went on to code the first web server, browser, HTML, and HTTP, then gave the whole Web away royalty-free.
clues: He taped a sticky note reading "This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!" onto his black NeXTcube computer in Geneva.
During the 2012 London Olympics opening ceremony, he live-tweeted "This is for everyone" from center stage.
questions.whyExplanation: Sir Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989–1990 (HTML, HTTP, URLs) and persuaded CERN to release it royalty-free in 1993.

questions.prompt: Cruising Bell Labs hallways while juggling on a unicycle, this "Father of Information Theory" proved in a 1937 master's thesis that Boolean algebra maps onto electric switches—and popularized the "bit."
clues: He also built a playful mechanical "Ultimate Machine" whose sole purpose was reaching out of its box to switch itself back off.
His landmark 1948 paper defined information entropy and set the mathematical speed limit of every modem, Wi-Fi chip, and 5G tower.
questions.whyExplanation: Claude Shannon's 1937 thesis founded digital circuit design and his 1948 paper created information theory, establishing the mathematical framework behind all digital communication.

questions.prompt: Her MIT team's asynchronous priority software saved Apollo 11 from aborting during 1202 computer overload alarms—and she helped coin "software engineering" to win coding equal respect.
clues: An iconic 1969 photograph captures her standing beside a towering stack of printed Apollo Guidance Computer code as tall as she is.
President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016 for her lunar-landing code.
questions.whyExplanation: Margaret Hamilton directed MIT's Apollo flight software division; her fault-tolerant priority scheduling kept Apollo 11's lander flying through 1202 alarms and established software engineering.

questions.prompt: Pausing his multi-volume magnum opus The Art of Computer Programming for a decade just to fix ugly math typesetting—creating TeX—this Stanford legend famously mails $2.56 checks to anyone who spots a book typo.
clues: Why $2.56? Because in base-16 computing math, 256 pennies equals "one hexadecimal dollar."
He won the 1974 Turing Award for algorithm analysis and famously warned that "premature optimization is the root of all evil."
questions.whyExplanation: Stanford computer scientist Donald Knuth authored The Art of Computer Programming, invented TeX, and famously awards "hexadecimal dollar" ($2.56) checks for errata.

questions.prompt: Sipping coffee at an Amsterdam café in 1956, this blunt Dutchman spent 20 minutes sketching his shortest-path graph algorithm—and later penned "Go To Statement Considered Harmful."
clues: His 1956 routing method still guides GPS sat-navs and internet routers around congested streets and networks.
He won the 1972 Turing Award and quipped that computer science is no more about computers than astronomy is about telescopes.
questions.whyExplanation: Edsger W. Dijkstra devised the classic shortest-path algorithm, championed structured programming against GOTO spaghetti code, and pioneered concurrency concepts like semaphores.

questions.prompt: Dying quietly one week after Steve Jobs in October 2011 with a fraction of the media fanfare, this Bell Labs titan co-created Unix and invented the C language powering modern systems.
clues: With Brian Kernighan, he co-authored the slim 1978 "K&R" manual that introduced millions of coders to "hello, world."
He shared the 1983 Turing Award with longtime Bell Labs partner Ken Thompson.
questions.whyExplanation: Dennis Ritchie invented the C programming language and co-created Unix at Bell Labs—laying the quiet software foundation beneath modern operating systems, embedded chips, and Apple's own macOS.

questions.prompt: Electrifying a San Francisco crowd in December 1968 with "The Mother of All Demos," this visionary unveiled the wooden mouse, hypertext, video calling, and live co-editing in 90 minutes.
clues: His SRI lab's original 1964 pointer used two perpendicular metal wheels inside a carved pine block—nicknamed for its tail-like cord.
He won the 1997 Turing Award for human-computer interaction, though his mouse patent expired before the device went mainstream.
questions.whyExplanation: Douglas Engelbart's 1968 "Mother of All Demos" showcased the mouse, hypertext, windowing, and collaborative editing decades before personal computers caught up.

questions.prompt: One of America's first women with a computer science PhD, this MIT professor won the 2008 Turing Award for CLU—and lends her surname to the "L" in object-oriented design's SOLID rules.
clues: Her famous Substitution Principle states that objects of a subtype must behave safely anywhere a supertype is expected.
She also co-invented Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance, a consensus cornerstone used in distributed databases and blockchains.
questions.whyExplanation: MIT's Barbara Liskov won the 2008 Turing Award for pioneering abstract data types, the CLU language, and the Liskov Substitution Principle of object-oriented design.

questions.prompt: Driving across America chasing cryptography despite NSA pushback, he teamed with Martin Hellman in 1976 to publish public-key exchange—letting strangers share secrets in full view.
clues: Their breakthrough paper "New Directions in Cryptography" solved the centuries-old courier problem and earned them the 2015 Turing Award.
Using modular exponentiation, their shared-secret protocol underpins the handshake of modern encrypted web traffic.
questions.whyExplanation: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman revolutionized cryptography in 1976 with public-key key exchange, enabling secure communication across open networks like the Internet.

questions.prompt: Arriving in New York in 1884 with four cents and a glowing letter to Edison, this Serbian-American genius built AC induction motors before dying broke in Hotel New Yorker Room 3327.
clues: His polyphase alternating-current system beat direct current in the War of the Currents and lit the 1893 Chicago World's Fair.
The SI unit of magnetic flux density—and a famous electric carmaker—now carry his surname.
questions.whyExplanation: Nikola Tesla pioneered polyphase alternating current, the induction motor, and high-voltage coils, shaping the global power grid despite dying in debt in 1943.

questions.prompt: Borrowing heavily from Johann Fust to perfect oil-based ink and movable metal type around 1450, this Mainz goldsmith lost his workshop in a 1455 lawsuit just as his 42-line Bible finished.
clues: Adapting a Rhineland screw winepress, his workshop slashed the cost of books and lit the fuse for the Reformation and Scientific Revolution.
Only 49 mostly complete copies of his monumental Latin Bible survive today.
questions.whyExplanation: Johannes Gutenberg combined movable metal type, oil-based ink, and a mechanical screw press in Mainz around 1450, launching Europe's print revolution.

questions.prompt: Asked to fix a University of Glasgow scale model of Newcomen's sluggish steam pump in 1765, this Scotsman hit upon the separate condenser—and invented "horsepower" to sell engines to skeptical brewers.
clues: His separate condenser slashed coal waste by roughly 75 percent, making steam power practical far from coal mines.
Partnering with Matthew Boulton in Birmingham, he lent his surname to the SI unit of electrical and mechanical power.
questions.whyExplanation: Scottish engineer James Watt's separate condenser (1765) and rotary steam improvements powered the Industrial Revolution and inspired both "horsepower" and the watt.

questions.prompt: Between starring in Hollywood hits like Samson and Delilah, this Austrian-born actress teamed with composer George Antheil to patent 1942 frequency-hopping radio guidance—a forerunner of Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
clues: Inspired by synchronized player-piano paper rolls, their spread-spectrum patent aimed to stop Axis warships from jamming Allied radio torpedoes.
Ignored by the Navy during World War II, the concept was finally deployed during the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis.
questions.whyExplanation: Actress Hedy Lamarr and composer George Antheil patented frequency-hopping spread-spectrum communication in 1942, laying conceptual groundwork for secure wireless tech.

questions.prompt: Defying physicists who insisted radio waves would shoot straight into space off Earth's curve, this Italian caught the three Morse dots of the letter "S" across the Atlantic in Newfoundland in December 1901.
clues: Unbeknownst to him at the time, Earth's upper ionosphere had bounced his long-wave signal from Cornwall over the horizon.
His shipboard wireless operators later helped summon rescue ships to the sinking Titanic, and he shared the 1909 Physics Nobel.
questions.whyExplanation: Guglielmo Marconi pioneered long-distance wireless telegraphy, famously claiming the first transatlantic radio signal in 1901 and sharing the 1909 Physics Nobel.

questions.prompt: Amassing 1,093 U.S. patents at his Menlo Park "invention factory," he stunned 1877 onlookers when a tinfoil cylinder echoed "Mary Had a Little Lamb"—two years before his practical carbon lightbulb.
clues: Before lighting Manhattan's Pearl Street Station in 1882, he pioneered the kinetoscope motion-picture viewer and the first industrial research lab.
Known nationwide as the "Wizard of Menlo Park," he championed direct current against Nikola Tesla's AC grid.
questions.whyExplanation: Thomas Alva Edison invented the phonograph, practical incandescent lighting system, and early cinema equipment while creating the modern team-based R&D laboratory.

questions.prompt: Teaching deaf students—including his future wife Mabel—inspired this Scotsman to beat rival Elisha Gray to the U.S. Patent Office in February 1876 before summoning assistant Thomas Watson by wire.
clues: He actually disliked keeping his most famous invention in his own study, fearing its incessant ringing would disrupt his work.
Later in life he tested hydrofoils in Nova Scotia and lent his surname to the decibel loudness scale.
questions.whyExplanation: Alexander Graham Bell patented the practical telephone in 1876 (just ahead of Elisha Gray's caveat), transmitting his famous first sentence to Thomas Watson on March 10.

questions.prompt: In a towering stovepipe hat despite standing barely five feet tall, this Victorian giant built Britain's Great Western Railway, Clifton Suspension Bridge, and the cable-laying SS Great Eastern.
clues: His colossal 1858 iron steamship SS Great Eastern was six times larger than any vessel afloat—and finally laid the lasting 1866 transatlantic telegraph cable.
In a 2002 BBC poll of the Greatest Britons ever, this civil engineer stunned observers by ranking second—behind only Winston Churchill.
questions.whyExplanation: Victorian civil and marine engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel revolutionized railways, bridges, tunnels, and iron steamships including SS Great Britain and SS Great Eastern.

questions.prompt: After knockoffs drained profits from his 1793 cotton gin, this Yale grad won a 1798 federal musket contract championing interchangeable parts—even though his demo locks were hand-fitted.
clues: His wire-toothed roller stripped seeds from short-staple cotton fifty times faster by hand—unintentionally entrenching plantation slavery across the American South.
His New Haven armory nevertheless helped launch the precision "American system" of mechanized manufacturing.
questions.whyExplanation: Eli Whitney invented the cotton gin in 1793 and popularized the vision of interchangeable-part mass manufacturing through his 1798 U.S. government musket contract.

questions.prompt: Son of parents who escaped Virginia slavery, this self-taught draftsman drew Alexander Graham Bell's 1876 telephone patent sketches before patenting a longer-lasting carbon lightbulb filament process in 1881.
clues: He oversaw electric streetlamp installations from New York to Montreal and London, and wrote the first engineering textbook on incandescent lighting.
He became the sole Black charter member of the elite "Edison Pioneers" organization.
questions.whyExplanation: Lewis Howard Latimer drafted Bell's telephone patent, invented an improved carbon-filament manufacturing process in 1881, and helped electrify major cities.

questions.prompt: Plowing neat rows across an Idaho potato field at age 14 sparked this farm boy's epiphany of scanning pictures line by line with electrons—demonstrating all-electronic TV in 1927 before fierce RCA patent wars.
clues: His high-school chemistry teacher's testimony—backed by a 1922 chalkboard sketch he had saved—helped him defeat corporate giant RCA in court.
Even his futuristic animated namesake professor on Futurama pays playful tribute to this inventor.
questions.whyExplanation: Philo T. Farnsworth invented the image dissector camera tube and demonstrated the first all-electronic television transmission in San Francisco in September 1927.

questions.prompt: Brewing a cloudy, watery polymer solution at DuPont in 1965 that technicians almost refused to spin for fear of clogging jets, this chemist yielded golden aramid threads five times stronger than steel—Kevlar.
clues: She was actually hunting for lightweight radial-tire reinforcements to save gasoline during a looming oil crunch—not body armor.
Her liquid-crystal fiber discovery has since saved thousands of police officers' and soldiers' lives in bulletproof vests.
questions.whyExplanation: DuPont chemist Stephanie Kwolek discovered liquid-crystalline aramid solutions in 1965, leading directly to Kevlar—used in body armor, aerospace composites, and suspension cables.

questions.prompt: When published lift tables failed them, these Dayton bicycle makers built a six-foot wind tunnel and cracked three-axis wing warping—flying 12 seconds at Kitty Hawk in December 1903.
clues: A coin toss on December 14 gave Wilbur the first try, which stalled—leaving younger brother Orville at the controls for the historic December 17 liftoff.
A tiny square of muslin fabric from their 1903 Flyer hitched a ride to Mars aboard NASA's Ingenuity helicopter in 2021.
questions.whyExplanation: Orville and Wilbur Wright achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered heavier-than-air flight on December 17, 1903 near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.

questions.prompt: Irritated after crossing the Atlantic as a 1928 passenger—grousing she felt like "a sack of potatoes"—she flew solo to a Northern Ireland cow pasture in 1932, five years before vanishing over the Pacific.
clues: Piloting a crimson Lockheed Vega 5B through icy storms and a cracked exhaust manifold, she became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic.
She and navigator Fred Noonan disappeared in July 1937 while trying to locate tiny Howland Island on an around-the-world flight.
questions.whyExplanation: Amelia Earhart completed the first solo transatlantic flight by a woman in May 1932 before vanishing over the central Pacific during her 1937 circumnavigation attempt.

questions.prompt: Kept strictly anonymous as the Soviet Union's "Chief Designer" until his 1966 death, this Kolyma Gulag survivor turned the R-7 missile into the rocket that launched Sputnik, Laika, and Yuri Gagarin.
clues: When the Nobel committee inquired whom to honor for Sputnik, Nikita Khrushchev refused to reveal his identity for state-security reasons.
His basic R-7 cluster design lives on more than six decades later in Russia's Soyuz crew launchers.
questions.whyExplanation: Sergei Korolev directed the early Soviet space program in total secrecy, masterminding Sputnik 1, Vostok 1, and the first spacewalk before his death in 1966.

questions.prompt: Running Lockheed's secret Burbank "Skunk Works" under 14 brisk rules, he built America's first operational jet fighter in 143 days—then fathered the U-2 and Mach 3.2 SR-71 Blackbird.
clues: To stop Mach-3 air friction from melting his Blackbird, he turned to titanium—which the CIA quietly bought through shell companies from the Soviet Union itself.
His famous nickname actually began as a schoolboy taunt over his Swedish-immigrant pronunciation of his real first name, Clarence.
questions.whyExplanation: Clarence "Kelly" Johnson founded Lockheed's Skunk Works and designed over 40 landmark aircraft, including the P-38 Lightning, P-80, U-2, and SR-71 Blackbird.

questions.prompt: Before his 1939 VS-300 nailed the modern single-rotor helicopter layout, this Kyiv-born emigre built the world's first four-engine airplane in Russia and Pan Am's Flying Clipper boats.
clues: After fleeing the Bolshevik Revolution to America nearly broke, he received crucial early startup funding from fellow Russian emigre pianist Sergei Rachmaninoff.
He always test-flew his experimental rotorcraft wearing his trademark dark fedora hat—and built the Black Hawk's corporate lineage.
questions.whyExplanation: Igor Sikorsky built the first four-engine aircraft, pioneered transoceanic flying boats, and created the first mass-produced single-rotor helicopters in Connecticut.

questions.prompt: Wary of NASA's new IBM mainframe before his 1962 Friendship 7 flight, John Glenn famously ordered, "If she says they're good, then I'm ready to go"—trusting this Langley mathematician's math.
clues: Starting as a "human computer" in Langley's segregated West Area Computing unit, she later computed critical Apollo 11 lunar-rendezvous trajectories.
Portrayed by Taraji P. Henson in Hidden Figures, she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015 at age 97.
questions.whyExplanation: NASA orbital-mechanics mathematician Katherine Johnson verified the Friendship 7 re-entry trajectory for John Glenn and helped calculate trajectories for Mercury and Apollo.

questions.prompt: Nursing two broken ribs—and using a sawed-off broomstick to lock his orange Bell X-1 hatch—this West Virginian shattered the sound barrier over California's Mojave Desert in October 1947.
clues: He named his bullet-shaped rocket plane Glamorous Glennis after his wife and kept his cracked ribs secret so flight surgeons would not ground him.
Tom Wolfe immortalized his cool Appalachian drawl—copied by generations of airline pilots—in The Right Stuff.
questions.whyExplanation: On October 14, 1947, test pilot Chuck Yeager flew the Bell X-1 past Mach 1 in level flight, becoming the first human confirmed to break the sound barrier.

questions.prompt: Mocked by a 1920 New York Times editorial sneering that rockets cannot push against space's vacuum, this Worcester professor fired the first liquid-fueled rocket from his aunt's snowy cabbage farm in 1926.
clues: His spindly 1926 contraption climbed just 41 feet in 2.5 seconds—yet proved liquid oxygen and gasoline propulsion worked.
The New York Times finally printed a sheepish correction on July 17, 1969, the day after Apollo 11 left for the Moon.
questions.whyExplanation: Robert H. Goddard launched the world's first liquid-propellant rocket on March 16, 1926 in Auburn, Massachusetts, earning recognition as the Father of Modern Rocketry.

questions.prompt: Moving from Nazi Germany's V-2 program at Peenemünde to surrendering to U.S. troops in 1945, this controversial architect later led NASA's Marshall Center in forging the colossal Saturn V.
clues: In the 1950s he teamed with Walt Disney on prime-time TV specials to sell the American public on orbital stations and Mars voyages.
His Redstone rocket also lofted Explorer 1—America's first satellite—and Mercury astronaut Alan Shepard.
questions.whyExplanation: Wernher von Braun led German V-2 development during WWII before immigrating under Operation Paperclip to lead the U.S. Saturn V Moon rocket program.

questions.prompt: After circling Paris's Eiffel Tower in a motorized blimp in 1901—inspiring Louis Cartier to craft him a pioneering wristwatch—this dapper Brazilian flew Europe's first official powered airplane hop in 1906.
clues: He used to tether his personal airship right outside his favorite Paris café while stopping in for lunch.
His box-kite-winged 14-bis lifted off on its own wheels without a catapult in October 1906, cementing him as Brazil's "Father of Aviation."
questions.whyExplanation: Brazilian aviation pioneer Alberto Santos-Dumont flew powered dirigibles around Paris in 1901, sparked the Cartier Santos wristwatch, and made Europe's first public powered plane flight in 1906.

questions.prompt: Using featherweight composites and canard wings in Mojave, California, this maverick designed both the nonstop round-the-world Voyager aircraft and SpaceShipOne, winner of the $10 million X Prize.
clues: His brother Dick and co-pilot Jeana Yeager circled Earth nonstop without refueling in 1986 inside his flying fuel tank of a plane.
Five of his radical canard-wing creations now hang in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum.
questions.whyExplanation: Aerospace designer Burt Rutan pioneered composite canard aircraft at Scaled Composites, engineering both the 1986 Voyager circumnavigator and 2004's SpaceShipOne.

questions.prompt: Rejected by every U.S. flight school over race and gender, this Chicago manicurist learned French and sailed to France to win a pilot's license in 1921—two years ahead of Amelia Earhart.
clues: Nicknamed "Queen Bess" for her daring loop-the-loops and wing-walking barnstorming shows, she refused to perform at segregated airfields.
She was the first woman of African American and Native American descent to hold a pilot's license.
questions.whyExplanation: Bessie Coleman trained at France's Caudron Brothers' aviation school to earn her FAI pilot's license in June 1921, dazzling 1920s crowds as a trailblazing stunt pilot.

questions.prompt: Sketched over coffee at a San Jose Denny's in 1993 by Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem, this 3D graphics-chip upstart rode its CUDA software platform into the multi-trillion-dollar AI engine.
clues: Its founders fused "NV" (for "next version") with the Roman Latin root for "envy"—inspiring its signature green eye emblem.
Its GeForce cards first conquered PC gaming before its Hopper and Blackwell silicon began training frontier AI models.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded at a San Jose Denny's in 1993, Nvidia invented the modern GPU (GeForce 256) and CUDA parallel computing, becoming the dominant hardware backbone of modern AI.

questions.prompt: Launched in Hsinchu in 1987 by 55-year-old ex-Texas Instruments executive Morris Chang, this Taiwanese titan invented the pure-play semiconductor foundry—fabricating flagship chips for Apple, AMD, and Nvidia.
clues: By promising never to design its own rival consumer chips, it freed "fabless" Silicon Valley firms from building billion-dollar factories.
Its four-letter ticker abbreviates Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company.
questions.whyExplanation: Morris Chang founded TSMC in 1987 to pioneer the dedicated pure-play foundry model; today it manufactures the vast majority of the world's most advanced logic chips.

questions.prompt: Spun out of Philips inside a leaky Dutch shed in Veldhoven in 1984, this monopoly giant builds bus-sized EUV machines that zap falling tin droplets 50,000 times a second to print sub-3-nanometer chips.
clues: Each of its newest High-NA extreme-ultraviolet lithography tools costs roughly $380 million and takes multiple Boeing 747 cargo jets to ship.
Its four-letter name originally stood for Advanced Semiconductor Materials Lithography.
questions.whyExplanation: Headquartered in Veldhoven, Netherlands, ASML is the sole global manufacturer of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems essential for cutting-edge microchips.

questions.prompt: Founded in Kyoto in 1889 by Fusajiro Yamauchi to paint hanafuda cards—and later dabbling in taxis and instant rice—this Japanese icon pivoted to video games and revived consoles in 1985.
clues: Its earliest toy-department wizard Gunpei Yokoi later created both the directional D-pad and the pocket-sized Game Boy.
Shigeru Miyamoto's Mario and Zelda adventures turned this 19th-century card shop into gaming's most enduring brand.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded in Kyoto in 1889 making handmade hanafuda cards, Nintendo experimented with taxis and toys before transforming global video gaming with the NES, Game Boy, and Switch.

questions.prompt: Formed on April Fools' Day 1976 with forgotten third co-founder Ronald Wayne selling his 10 percent stake 12 days later for $800, this Cupertino juggernaut reshaped personal tech from the Mac to the iPhone.
clues: Its very first hand-drawn emblem depicted Isaac Newton reading underneath a fruit tree—before Rob Janoff crafted its sleek bitten silhouette.
Launched by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak out of Los Altos, it became the first U.S. public company to cross $1 trillion, $2 trillion, and $3 trillion.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded April 1, 1976 by Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne (who promptly exited for $800), Apple pioneered personal computers, digital music, and modern smartphones.

questions.prompt: Originally hyphenated when Seattle friends Bill Gates and Paul Allen founded it in Albuquerque in 1975 to code Altair BASIC, this software titan grew from desktop OSes to Azure cloud.
clues: Its 1995 desktop launch licensed the Rolling Stones' "Start Me Up" and turned its four-pane window icon into an office staple.
Headquartered in Redmond, Washington, it also created Excel, Xbox, and became OpenAI's primary cloud partner.
questions.whyExplanation: Bill Gates and Paul Allen founded "Micro-Soft" in Albuquerque in 1975 before relocating to Washington state, building Windows, Office, Xbox, and Azure.

questions.prompt: Leaving Fairchild in 1968, Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore nearly named their startup "Moore Noyce"—until realizing it sounded like static—picking a contraction of "Integrated Electronics."
clues: Its 1971 4004 became the world's first commercial single-chip microprocessor, originally designed for a Japanese desktop calculator.
Its iconic five-note sonic chime accompanied the x86 "Inside" stickers pasted on hundreds of millions of PCs.
questions.whyExplanation: Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore founded Intel ("Integrated Electronics") in 1968 after nixing "Moore Noyce," launching the microprocessor revolution with the 4004 and x86 family.

questions.prompt: Born in 1946 inside a war-damaged Tokyo department store fixing radios and failing with a wooden electric rice cooker, Masaru Ibuka and Akio Morita's firm later redefined portable culture with the 1979 Walkman.
clues: Rebranding in 1958 from Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo, it fused the Latin word sonus ("sound") with 1950s American slang "sonny boy."
Beyond cassette players and Trinitron TVs, its Ken Kutaragi-led PlayStation division transformed console gaming in 1994.
questions.whyExplanation: Masaru Ibuka and Akio Morita founded Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo in 1946—later renamed Sony—going from pocket transistor radios and the 1979 Walkman to PlayStation.

questions.prompt: Spun out of Britain's Acorn Computers in Cambridge in 1990 without owning a single chip factory, this design licensor's lean RISC instruction architecture quietly runs inside nearly every smartphone on Earth.
clues: Its original 1980s acronym stood for Acorn RISC Machine before broadening to Advanced RISC Machines.
Apple's M-series Mac silicon, iPhone chips, and Raspberry Pi boards all license its energy-sipping processor blueprints.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded in Cambridge in 1990 from Acorn Computers (backed by Apple and VLSI), ARM licenses low-power RISC processor architectures powering almost all modern smartphones.

questions.prompt: Forged in 1911 as the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company making meat slicers, scales, and punch-card sorters, Thomas Watson Sr. rebranded "Big Blue" in 1924 to build mainframes, Deep Blue, and Watson AI.
clues: Its Armonk, New York research labs have minted five Nobel Prize winners and invented the hard disk drive, floppy disk, and relational database.
Its iconic striped three-letter logo was designed by graphic legend Paul Rand.
questions.whyExplanation: Formed in 1911 as CTR before Thomas Watson Sr. renamed it International Business Machines in 1924, IBM built the System/360 mainframe, the 1981 PC, and Deep Blue.

questions.prompt: Co-founder Marc Randolph later debunked the famous $40 Apollo 13 late-fee origin myth—yet this 1997 Scotts Valley DVD-by-mail pioneer still outlasted Blockbuster after pivoting boldly to streaming in 2007.
clues: In 2000 it famously offered to sell itself to Blockbuster for $50 million—only to be laughed out of the room.
Its bright red mailing envelopes gave way to original hits starting with House of Cards and Stranger Things.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded in 1997 by Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph as a DVD rental site, Netflix launched streaming in 2007 and grew into the world's largest subscription video platform.

questions.prompt: Launched in Weinheim in 1972 by five ex-IBM engineers after their boss killed their real-time accounting software project, this Walldorf giant became Europe's dominant enterprise resource planning powerhouse.
clues: Its R/3 client-server platform in 1992 revolutionized how global Fortune 500 firms tracked supply chains, payroll, and inventory live.
Its three-letter German acronym originally translated to System Analysis and Program Development.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded in 1972 by five former IBM engineers in Germany, SAP pioneered real-time enterprise resource planning (ERP) software and became Europe's largest software company.

questions.prompt: After three consecutive Falcon 1 failures left it days from bankruptcy in 2008, this Hawthorne aerospace upstart nailed Flight 4, won a $1.6 billion NASA lifeline, and revolutionized orbital booster landings.
clues: In December 2015 its Falcon 9 first stage touched down upright at Cape Canaveral—proving orbital rockets did not have to be thrown into the sea.
It also operates the Crew Dragon astronaut capsule and the global Starlink satellite-internet constellation.
questions.whyExplanation: SpaceX survived three Falcon 1 failures to reach orbit in September 2008, secure NASA's CRS contract, and pioneer reusable orbital-class Falcon 9 boosters.

questions.prompt: Started in Seattle in 1916 as Pacific Aero Products by a timber heir building floatplanes in a boathouse, this aviation colossus later birthed the B-17, the 707, and the twin-deck 747.
clues: Its 1969 "Queen of the Skies" jumbo jet was assembled in an Everett, Washington factory that remains the world's largest building by volume.
In 1997 it absorbed longtime American airliner rival McDonnell Douglas.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded in Seattle in 1916 by timber magnate William E. Boeing as Pacific Aero Products, Boeing shaped modern commercial aviation with the 707, 737, and 747.

questions.prompt: Formed as a European consortium in 1970 to break American airliner dominance, it flew the world's first twin-engine widebody A300 in 1972—then pioneered digital fly-by-wire controls on the A320 and giant A380.
clues: To ferry giant wings and fuselage sections between Britain, Germany, Spain, and France, it built a fleet of whale-headed Beluga cargo jets.
Its final-assembly hub in Toulouse, France anchors Boeing's sole global widebody airliner rival.
questions.whyExplanation: Established in 1970 by European aerospace partners, Airbus introduced the twin-aisle A300 and fly-by-wire A320 family to become the world's largest airliner builder by deliveries.

questions.prompt: Growing out of Sakichi Toyoda's automatic cotton looms, this Japanese automaker tweaked one letter of the family surname to eight lucky brush strokes in 1937—and gave global industry lean kanban manufacturing.
clues: Its "just-in-time" Production System let any assembly-line worker yank an andon cord to halt the line the moment a defect appeared.
From the Corolla to the hybrid Prius, it became the world's highest-volume carmaker.
questions.whyExplanation: Spun off from Toyoda Automatic Loom Works in 1937 with a lucky 8-stroke Japanese spelling change, Toyota revolutionized manufacturing via its lean Production System and kaizen.

questions.prompt: Founded in Brooklyn in 1849 by two German cousins selling almond-toffee antiparasitic lozenges, this pharma giant scaled D-Day penicillin before partnering with BioNTech in 2020.
clues: Its wartime fermentation vats supplied roughly 90 percent of the penicillin carried ashore by Allied medics on Normandy beaches.
In the late 1990s an unexpected side effect during a heart-angina trial handed it one of pharmacology's biggest accidental blockbusters—Viagra.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded in Brooklyn in 1849 by Charles Pfizer and Charles Erhart, Pfizer scaled deep-tank penicillin production for WWII and co-delivered the first authorized COVID-19 mRNA vaccine.

questions.prompt: Rooted in a 1922 Danish couple's Atlantic voyage to license Toronto's brand-new insulin, this Bagsværd pharma leader surged past LVMH to become Europe's most valuable firm on GLP-1 drugs Ozempic and Wegovy.
clues: Nobel laureate August Krogh and his diabetic physician wife Marie brought insulin manufacturing home to Copenhagen, launching a century-long diabetes focus.
Its explosive semaglutide export boom briefly outsized the entire rest of Denmark's annual GDP growth in 2023.
questions.whyExplanation: Born from August and Marie Krogh's 1922 insulin license in Denmark, Novo Nordisk dominated diabetes care for a century before semaglutide (Ozempic/Wegovy) transformed obesity medicine.

questions.prompt: Started in a Berlin courtyard in 1847 making pointer telegraphs—and stringing an 11,000-kilometer London-to-Calcutta wire by 1870—this German giant now builds trains, MRI scanners, and grids.
clues: Its founder Werner discovered the dynamo-electric principle in 1866 and demonstrated the world's first electric passenger railway in Berlin in 1879.
Today its headquarters sits in Munich, and its name also marks the SI unit of electrical conductance.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded in Berlin in 1847 by Werner von Siemens and Johann Georg Halske, Siemens evolved from telegraph lines and dynamos into Europe's largest industrial engineering group.

questions.prompt: Forged in 1892 when J. P. Morgan merged Edison's electric firm with Thomson-Houston, it was the last original 1896 Dow stock until 2018—and split into three separate companies by 2024.
clues: Under CEO Jack Welch it ballooned into a sprawling conglomerate spanning jet engines, NBC television, medical scanners, and finance.
Its historic 2024 breakup carved it into HealthCare, energy-focused Vernova, and jet-engine powerhouse Aerospace.
questions.whyExplanation: Created by J. P. Morgan in 1892 from Edison's company and Thomson-Houston, General Electric was the longest-tenured original Dow component before its 2024 three-way split.

questions.prompt: Sparked by a 1904 Manchester hotel lunch pairing aristocratic racer Charles with engineer Henry, this British name now spins Trent jet turbines—completely separate from BMW's luxury cars.
clues: Its iconic Merlin piston engine powered both the Spitfire and the P-51 Mustang during World War II.
After a 1971 bankruptcy over RB211 carbon-fiber fan blades, its aerospace-engine parent permanently split from the car division in 1973.
questions.whyExplanation: Founded by Charles Rolls and Henry Royce in 1904, Rolls-Royce Holdings today is a leading aero-engine and naval-propulsion manufacturer independent of BMW's Rolls-Royce Motor Cars.

questions.prompt: Five Minnesota investors founded this firm in 1902 to mine corundum that proved worthless rock—pivoting to sandpaper, Scotch tape, and Spencer Silver's "failed" glue for Post-it Notes.
clues: Its famous "15 percent rule" lets engineers spend part of work hours chasing blue-sky side ideas—giving Art Fry time to stick bookmark notes in his church hymnal.
Headquartered in Maplewood near St. Paul, its two-character name shortens Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing.
questions.whyExplanation: After its 1902 corundum mine failed, Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing (3M) reinvented itself into a materials-science powerhouse behind Scotch tape, N95 respirators, and Post-it Notes.

questions.prompt: Blending "modified" and "RNA" into its name and NASDAQ ticker, this Cambridge, Massachusetts biotech had never shipped a single approved drug before delivering its COVID-19 vaccine in December 2020.
clues: Co-founded in 2010 by stem-cell biologist Derrick Rossi and MIT's Robert Langer, it designed its mRNA-1273 sequence just two days after SARS-CoV-2's genome was posted.
It partnered directly with the NIH's Vaccine Research Center to launch Spikevax.
questions.whyExplanation: Moderna (NASDAQ: MRNA, from "modified RNA") went from a decade-old clinical-stage biotech with zero approved products to delivering one of the world's premier COVID-19 vaccines.

questions.prompt: Beginning as an 1898 Danish village blacksmith shop that pivoted from kitchen appliances and farm trailers during the 1979 oil shock, this Aarhus manufacturer grew into a global colossus of wind turbines.
clues: Its 1945 brand name shortened VEstjysk STaalteknik A/S—West Jutland Steel Technology—before wind power took over the entire business.
It has installed more than 175 gigawatts of onshore and offshore wind capacity across over 85 countries.
questions.whyExplanation: Tracing its roots to an 1898 Danish smithy, Vestas pivoted to wind turbines during the 1979 energy crisis and became one of the world's largest wind-power manufacturers.

questions.prompt: Built on an old Hewlett-Packard site where a 12-year-old Steve Jobs once begged Bill Hewlett for frequency-counter parts, Apple Park's mile-around glass ring anchors this Silicon Valley city.
clues: Long before tech campuses replaced its orchards, this Santa Clara Valley town was famed for prunes and apricots.
Its former Apple campus stood at the cheeky street address 1 Infinite Loop.
questions.whyExplanation: Apple moved to Cupertino, California in 1977 and opened its circular Apple Park headquarters there in 2017 on land formerly owned by Hewlett-Packard.

questions.prompt: Just across Lake Washington from Seattle, this leafy Pacific Northwest tech suburb hosts both Microsoft's sprawling corporate campus and—practically down the road—Nintendo of America's headquarters.
clues: Microsoft relocated here in 1986, eventually turning the town's name into journalistic shorthand for the Windows giant.
It is also nicknamed the "Bicycle Capital of the Northwest" and sits east of Lake Sammamish's northern tip.
questions.whyExplanation: Redmond, Washington has served as Microsoft's global headquarters since 1986 and also houses the North American headquarters of Nintendo.

questions.prompt: Transformed from a quiet 30,000-person border fishing town into China's first Special Economic Zone in 1980, this gleaming Guangdong hardware metropolis now headquarters Huawei, Tencent, DJI, and BYD.
clues: Sitting immediately north of Hong Kong across the Sham Chun River, its Huaqiangbei market is electronics prototyping heaven.
Often dubbed "China's Silicon Valley," its population surged past 17 million in barely four decades.
questions.whyExplanation: Designated a Special Economic Zone in 1980, Shenzhen grew rapidly into China's premier hardware and software hub, home to Huawei, Tencent, DJI, and EV leader BYD.

questions.prompt: Nicknamed "La Ville Rose" for its warm terracotta bricks, this southwestern French city watched Concorde's 1969 maiden flight and today anchors Airbus's primary commercial-airliner final assembly lines.
clues: In the 1920s, Aéropostale mail pilots like Antoine de Saint-Exupéry departed here on daring routes toward Africa and South America.
Its Blagnac airport hosts both Europe's largest aerospace cluster and the Aéroscopia aviation museum.
questions.whyExplanation: Toulouse, France is Europe's aerospace capital—birthplace of Concorde's French test flights and home to Airbus's final assembly hub and headquarters.

questions.prompt: Where Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach bolted an engine onto a carriage in 1885, this Swabian city now houses the global headquarters and museums of both Mercedes-Benz and Porsche.
clues: Its historic name traces back to an early medieval "stud garden" for warhorses—a prancing horse still crowns Porsche's crest.
Nestled amid steep vineyards in Baden-Württemberg, it is also home to automotive-supplier giant Bosch's region.
questions.whyExplanation: Stuttgart, Germany—birthplace of Daimler's 1885 internal-combustion innovations—remains the global headquarters of both Mercedes-Benz Group and Porsche.

questions.prompt: Crowned by an 18th-century UNESCO fortress just south of Seoul, this Gyeonggi city hosts "Samsung Digital City," the global corporate headquarters and R&D nerve center of Samsung Electronics.
clues: Over 35,000 engineers and staff work inside its sprawling 390-acre semiconductor and mobile-research complex.
Located roughly 30 kilometers south of Seoul, it is the provincial capital of Gyeonggi-do.
questions.whyExplanation: Suwon, South Korea—famed for Hwaseong Fortress—serves as the global corporate headquarters of Samsung Electronics at its massive Samsung Digital City campus.

questions.prompt: Bordering Helsinki along the Gulf of Finland, this coastal tech city hosts the global headquarters of Nokia—descended from an 1865 wood-pulp mill—alongside Angry Birds creator Rovio.
clues: Its Otaniemi district anchors Aalto University and Finland's premier startup accelerator hub.
Though Nokia took its name from a river near Tampere, Finland's second-largest city became its modern corporate home.
questions.whyExplanation: Espoo, Finland's second-largest city just west of Helsinki, is the longtime headquarters of telecom pioneer Nokia as well as game studio Rovio.

questions.prompt: Spread across 14 Baltic islands, this Nordic capital has punched far above its size as Europe's "unicorn factory," birthing Spotify, Klarna, Minecraft maker Mojang, and Skype's co-founding roots.
clues: A 1998 Swedish home-PC tax break and early municipal fiber broadband helped turn its teenagers into world-class coders.
Its Kista suburb also serves as Ericsson's wireless-telecom headquarters.
questions.whyExplanation: Stockholm, Sweden ranks among the world's top producers of billion-dollar tech startups per capita, hosting Spotify, Klarna, Mojang, and Ericsson.

questions.prompt: Straddling the Rhine where Switzerland meets France and Germany, this 19th-century synthetic silk-dye hub reinvented itself as Europe's pharma capital—headquartering both Novartis and Hoffmann-La Roche.
clues: Chemists at local firm Sandoz famously synthesized LSD here in 1938 before Sandoz merged with Ciba-Geigy into Novartis in 1996.
Roche's gleaming stepped white towers now dominate this northern Swiss city's skyline.
questions.whyExplanation: Basel, Switzerland evolved from 19th-century textile dye chemistry into one of Earth's foremost pharmaceutical clusters, headquartering both Novartis and Roche.

questions.prompt: Just west of Detroit lies Henry Ford's birthplace—still home to Ford Motor Company's 1956 "Glass House" headquarters, the colossal River Rouge complex, and Greenfield Village's relocated Wright bicycle shop.
clues: Its iconic Rouge factory once took raw iron ore and rubber in one end and rolled finished cars out the other.
Today its world-class Henry Ford Museum preserves Rosa Parks's bus and Abraham Lincoln's theater chair.
questions.whyExplanation: Dearborn, Michigan is Henry Ford's hometown and has anchored Ford Motor Company's global headquarters, River Rouge factory, and Henry Ford Museum for generations.

questions.prompt: In 1964, Thomas Watson Jr. moved IBM out of Manhattan to this quiet Westchester hamlet 35 miles north of Midtown—still "Big Blue's" leafy corporate headquarters six decades later.
clues: Just 15 miles up the road in Yorktown Heights sits IBM's famed Thomas J. Watson Research Center.
Its six-letter name comes from a Mohican word for "fishing place" inside the town of North Castle.
questions.whyExplanation: IBM relocated its global headquarters from Manhattan to Armonk, New York in 1964, making the small Westchester hamlet synonymous with Big Blue.

questions.prompt: Nicknamed Taiwan's "Windy City," this coastal hub opened a landmark 1980 Science Park that now headquarters TSMC, MediaTek, and UMC—making it the geopolitical heart of global silicon manufacturing.
clues: Flanked by National Tsing Hua and Yang Ming Chiao Tung universities, its park was modeled directly on Stanford's Silicon Valley.
Roughly an hour southwest of Taipei by high-speed rail, it produces the lion's share of Earth's leading-edge microchips.
questions.whyExplanation: Hsinchu, Taiwan's Science Park (founded 1980) hosts TSMC, MediaTek, and UMC, forming the world's most critical advanced semiconductor manufacturing cluster.

questions.prompt: Stretching up to ten inches in flight from Mach 2 friction heat and tilting a hinged "droop snoot" nose so pilots could see the runway, this Anglo-French airliner crossed the Atlantic in under three hours.
clues: Pilots used to wedge their flight caps into a widened cockpit console gap that vanished once the supersonic fuselage cooled on landing.
Operated solely by British Airways and Air France from 1976 to 2003, its spelling sparked a cheeky British-French row over the final E.
questions.whyExplanation: The Anglo-French Concorde cruised at Mach 2.04 for 27 years, featuring a droop nose for visibility and thermal expansion that noticeably lengthened its fuselage mid-flight.

questions.prompt: Leaking JP-7 jet fuel across the runway until Mach 3.2 aerodynamic heating expanded its titanium panels tight, this stealthy spy plane outran roughly 4,000 enemy missiles without losing a single jet in combat.
clues: Cruising at 85,000 feet where pilots wore full astronaut pressure suits, its standard evasion tactic against incoming missiles was simply accelerating.
Built by Kelly Johnson's Skunk Works, it still holds the 1976 absolute airspeed record for a jet-powered aircraft at 2,193 mph.
questions.whyExplanation: Lockheed's titanium-bodied SR-71 Blackbird cruised past Mach 3.2 above 85,000 feet, intentionally designed with loose cold-skin tolerances that sealed shut at supersonic heat.

questions.prompt: Towering 363 feet tall and roaring off Florida with 7.5 million pounds of thrust from five F-1 engines, this three-stage Apollo behemoth sent 24 humans to the Moon without a single mission loss.
clues: Its 13th and final flight in 1973 hoisted the entire Skylab space station into orbit in a single launch.
Designed under Wernher von Braun in Huntsville, Alabama, its Roman-numeral name honors the ringed sixth planet.
questions.whyExplanation: The 363-foot Saturn V launched all nine crewed Apollo lunar missions plus Skylab (1967–1973), remaining the only launch vehicle to carry humans beyond low Earth orbit.

questions.prompt: Built in 28 months by Joe Sutter's "Incredibles" with an upper-deck hump designed so its nose could hinge open for freighters, this 1969 widebody shrank global airfares as "Queen of the Skies."
clues: When supersonic airliners failed to take over, airlines filled that iconic upstairs hump with swanky piano lounges and first-class cabins.
Producing 1,574 airframes over 54 years—including two famous Air Force One jets—its final freighter left Everett in January 2023.
questions.whyExplanation: First flown in February 1969, the Boeing 747 invented the widebody jumbo-jet era; its signature upper hump came from placing the cockpit clear of a swinging cargo nose.

questions.prompt: Flashing the historic signal "Underway on nuclear power" in January 1955, Admiral Hyman Rickover's pioneering atomic submarine became the first vessel ever to cross the North Pole submerged in 1958.
clues: Borrowing its name from Captain Nemo's fictional electric sub in Jules Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas, it freed subs from snorkeling for air.
Decommissioned in 1980, hull SSN-571 now rests as a museum ship in Groton, Connecticut.
questions.whyExplanation: Commissioned in 1954 as the world's first nuclear-powered submarine, USS Nautilus (SSN-571) completed the first submerged transit of the geographic North Pole in August 1958.

questions.prompt: Stripped of a front windshield to cram extra gas tanks ahead of the pilot—forcing him to peek forward through a periscope—this custom Ryan monoplane crossed the Atlantic solo in May 1927.
clues: Built in San Diego in just 60 days, its 223-horsepower Wright Whirlwind engine carried Charles Lindbergh 33.5 sleepless hours to Paris.
Backed by Missouri financiers, it now hangs proudly in the Smithsonian's Milestones of Flight hall.
questions.whyExplanation: Charles Lindbergh's Ryan NYP monoplane, Spirit of St. Louis, traded forward visibility for fuel capacity to achieve the first solo nonstop transatlantic flight in May 1927.

questions.prompt: Playfully named for Han Solo's fictional freighter and its cluster of nine Merlin engines, this workhorse rocket made spaceflight history in December 2015 by landing an orbital booster back upright.
clues: Its reused first stages touch down either on concrete Florida pads or autonomous ocean drone ships named after Iain M. Banks sci-fi craft.
Single boosters in its fleet have now flown to orbit and returned safely more than 20 times apiece.
questions.whyExplanation: SpaceX's two-stage Falcon 9 achieved the first vertical landing of an orbital-class booster in December 2015 and transformed commercial launch economics through rapid reuse.

questions.prompt: Despite a mocking wood-and-waterfowl newspaper nickname Howard Hughes hated, his colossal 320-foot-wingspan H-4 Hercules flying boat was built almost entirely of laminated birch—and flew just once in 1947.
clues: Conceived during wartime aluminum rationing to haul 750 troops over U-boats, it lifted 70 feet above Long Beach Harbor for a single surprise mile.
After decades hidden in an air-conditioned California hangar, it now anchors Oregon's Evergreen Aviation Museum.
questions.whyExplanation: Howard Hughes's wooden H-4 Hercules—derisively dubbed the Spruce Goose though made mainly of birch—made its lone one-mile flight in Long Beach Harbor on November 2, 1947.

questions.prompt: Constructed in Belfast with a fourth smokestack added chiefly as a dummy for sleek symmetry and kitchen ventilation, this White Star liner went down in April 1912 after grazing an iceberg.
clues: Sixteen watertight compartments sounded reassuring until a 300-foot hull scrape flooded six—two more than it could survive.
Oceanographer Robert Ballard finally located its split two-piece wreck 3,800 meters beneath the North Atlantic in 1985.
questions.whyExplanation: Built at Harland and Wolff in Belfast with a largely cosmetic fourth funnel, RMS Titanic sank on April 15, 1912 on its maiden voyage from Southampton toward New York.

questions.prompt: Ditching a vertical tail completely in favor of quadruple fly-by-wire computers and radar-absorbing composites, this $2 billion Northrop flying-wing bomber can strike anywhere on Earth nonstop from Missouri.
clues: Its bat-like sawtooth silhouette shrinks its radar cross-section to roughly the size of a small bird despite a 172-foot wingspan.
Only 21 were ever built after Cold War defense cuts, with Whiteman Air Force Base hosting the fleet.
questions.whyExplanation: Northrop's tailless B-2 Spirit stealth bomber entered U.S. Air Force service in 1997, combining flying-wing aerodynamics with low-observable composites for global range.

questions.prompt: Launched at Portsmouth in 1906 with ten uniform 12-inch guns and steam turbines instead of reciprocating pistons, this revolutionary Royal Navy battleship rendered every older dread fleet obsolete overnight.
clues: Championed by reformist Admiral Jackie Fisher and built in a furious 366 days, it triggered a fierce Anglo-German naval arms race before World War I.
Ironically, its sole wartime ship kill came in 1915 when it rammed and sliced German submarine U-29 in half.
questions.whyExplanation: Commissioned in 1906, Britain's all-big-gun, turbine-powered HMS Dreadnought instantly defined a new class of capital ships and made earlier battleships "pre-dreadnoughts."
