questions.whyExplanation: John Steinbeck's 1939 novel The Grapes of Wrath won the 1940 Pulitzer Prize, took its title from 'The Battle Hymn of the Republic,' and sparked bans in California.

questions.prompt: Inspired by an 1856 newspaper clipping about fugitive mother Margaret Garner, this 1987 Pulitzer-honored novel opens at 124 Bluestone Road with the flat declaration that the house is spiteful.
clues: Former Sweet Home captives Sethe and Paul D confront a mysterious young woman with a scar across her throat.
Its single-word title mirrors the sole word Sethe could afford to have carved on a headstone.
questions.whyExplanation: Toni Morrison's 1987 novel Beloved—winner of the 1988 Pulitzer Prize—was inspired by Margaret Garner's story and opens: '124 was spiteful. Full of a baby's venom.'

questions.prompt: Originally drafted as The Hours, this 1925 modernist classic follows a Westminster society hostess buying flowers herself across one June day, shadowed by shell-shocked veteran Septimus Warren Smith.
clues: Big Ben's leaden circles dissolving in the air punctuate its stream-of-consciousness London walks.
Clarissa prepares for an evening party attended by the Prime Minister and her old suitor Peter Walsh.
questions.whyExplanation: Virginia Woolf's 1925 novel Mrs. Dalloway—originally titled The Hours—unfolds over a single June day in London, pairing Clarissa's party with Septimus Warren Smith's trauma.

questions.prompt: Siphoning current from Monopolated Light & Power to burn exactly 1,369 bulbs in a Harlem cellar, the unnamed narrator of this 1952 National Book Award-winning novel recalls a brutal Battle Royal.

distractors.text: Go Tell It on the Mountain

clues: Ralph Ellison's only novel published in his lifetime traces its protagonist from a Southern college to the Brotherhood.
Unlike H. G. Wells's sci-fi title with a definite article, this narrator's vanishing is purely social.
questions.whyExplanation: Ralph Ellison's 1952 masterpiece Invisible Man opens in a cellar lit with 1,369 stolen-current lightbulbs, symbolizing society's refusal to see its unnamed Black narrator.

questions.prompt: Smuggled into America after Sylvia Beach's Paris bookshop printed it in 1922, this single-day Dublin odyssey won a landmark 1933 Judge John Woolsey ruling lifting its U.S. obscenity ban.
clues: Its 18 episodes map June 16, 1904 onto Homeric trials, culminating in Molly Bloom's unpunctuated soliloquy.
James Joyce's modernist monument follows ad canvasser Leopold Bloom and Stephen Dedalus through Dublin.
questions.whyExplanation: Published by Sylvia Beach's Shakespeare and Company in 1922, James Joyce's Ulysses was cleared of obscenity in United States v. One Book Called Ulysses (1933).

questions.prompt: Borrowing its title from Macbeth's bleak speech about life as a tale told by an idiot, this 1929 Yoknapatawpha novel opens on April 7, 1928 inside the fractured mind of Benjy Compson.
clues: Four perspectives—including suicidal Harvard student Quentin and steadfast servant Dilsey—recount Caddy's loss.
William Faulkner wanted Benjy's time-jumping chapter printed in different colors of ink.
questions.whyExplanation: William Faulkner's 1929 novel The Sound and the Fury takes its title from Macbeth Act V and opens on Benjy Compson's 33rd birthday, April 7, 1928.

questions.prompt: Subtitled A Study of Provincial Life and issued in eight installments across 1871 and 1872, this Victorian panoramic novel traps idealistic Dorothea Brooke in marriage to pedantic scholar Edward Casaubon.
clues: Casaubon wastes his life compiling an unfinished Key to All Mythologies while physician Tertius Lydgate falls into debt.
Virginia Woolf praised this George Eliot masterwork as one of the few English novels written for grown-up people.
questions.whyExplanation: George Eliot published Middlemarch in eight parts from 1871 to 1872, intertwining Dorothea Brooke's stifling marriage to Casaubon with Lydgate's medical ambitions.

questions.l2Category: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.l2Subcategory: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.prompt: After a pseudonymous rival named Avellaneda published a counterfeit sequel in 1614, the real author wrote the forgery directly into Part II of this 1605 Spanish landmark about Alonso Quixano.
clues: Its gaunt hidalgo rides the bony nag Rocinante and mistakes La Mancha windmills for thirty-odd giants.
Accompanied by squire Sancho Panza, the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance tilts for Dulcinea del Toboso.
questions.whyExplanation: Cervantes incorporated Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda's unauthorized 1614 sequel into Part II (1615) of Don Quixote, having his knight deliberately skip Zaragoza to spite the impostor.

questions.l2Category: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.l2Subcategory: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.prompt: Serialized in The Russian Messenger across 1866, this St. Petersburg psychological thriller follows an impoverished ex-student who tests his Napoleonic "extraordinary man" theory with an axe.
clues: Pawnbroker Alyona Ivanovna and her sister Lizaveta fall victim before cat-and-mouse magistrate Porfiry Petrovich closes in.
Feverish guilt drives Rodion Raskolnikov to confess to Sonya Marmeladova and accept Siberian penal servitude.
questions.whyExplanation: Serialized in 1866, Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment follows Rodion Raskolnikov as his hubristic murder of pawnbroker Alyona Ivanovna unravels under Porfiry Petrovich's questioning.

questions.l2Category: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.l2Subcategory: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.prompt: Composed in Tuscan vernacular rather than scholarly Latin around 1320, this 100-canto Italian masterpiece invented interlocking terza rima verse to chart a Good Friday pilgrim's three-realm journey.
clues: Roman poet Virgil guides the exiled Florentine through nine descending circles before Beatrice takes over in heaven.
Boccaccio later added the adjective 'Divine' to Dante Alighieri's Commedia.
questions.whyExplanation: Dante Alighieri finished his Commedia around 1320 in Tuscan Italian using interlocking ABA BCB terza rima across 100 cantos (Inferno, Purgatorio, Paradiso).

questions.l2Category: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.l2Subcategory: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.prompt: Famous for an opening sentence that leaps from a firing squad back to an afternoon discovering ice, this 1967 Colombian novel tracks seven generations of the Buendía clan in isolated Macondo.

distractors.text: Love in the Time of Cholera

clues: Gypsy sage Melquíades leaves Sanskrit parchments predicting the town's rise, insomnia plague, and apocalyptic wind.
Colonel Aureliano Buendía fights 32 armed uprisings in Gabriel García Márquez's magical-realist saga.
questions.whyExplanation: Published in Spanish in 1967, Gabriel García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude opens with Colonel Aureliano Buendía facing a firing squad and remembering the afternoon his father took him to discover ice.

questions.l2Category: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.l2Subcategory: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.prompt: Insisting that his publisher never depict the creature on the cover, Franz Kafka used the vague German word Ungeziefer—"vermin"—to describe traveling salesman Gregor Samsa's dawn ordeal in this 1915 novella.
clues: Initially worried only about catching the five o'clock train, the narrator later suffers an apple lodged in his back.
Known in German as Die Verwandlung, it ends with Gregor's sister Grete stretching her young body on a tram.
questions.whyExplanation: Franz Kafka's 1915 novella Die Verwandlung (The Metamorphosis) never names an exact insect species—calling Gregor Samsa 'ein ungeheures Ungeziefer'—and Kafka explicitly forbade showing the bug on the cover.

questions.l2Category: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.l2Subcategory: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.prompt: Written by Heian court lady-in-waiting Murasaki Shikibu around 1008, this 54-chapter Japanese classic follows the romantic entanglements of the "Shining Prince" and is widely called the world's first novel.

distractors.text: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter

clues: Its 795 waka poems and seasonal imagery capture the bittersweet aesthetic of mono no aware in Kyoto's imperial court.
Arthur Waley's 1925–1933 English translation first introduced this Heian epic to Western readers.
questions.whyExplanation: Composed c. 1008 by Murasaki Shikibu, The Tale of Genji spans 54 chapters and 795 poems tracing Hikaru Genji's life at the Heian court, earning recognition as the world's earliest full-length novel.

questions.l2Category: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.l2Subcategory: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.prompt: Put on trial for offenses against public morality in Paris in 1857 and acquitted, this realist novel by Gustave Flaubert dooms a Normandy doctor's romantic wife to crushing debts and arsenic.
clues: Bored with kindly physician Charles in Yonville-l'Abbaye, its heroine chases romance through Rodolphe and Léon.
Flaubert obsessed over le mot juste for five years while crafting Emma Rouault's provincial tragedy.
questions.whyExplanation: Gustave Flaubert stood trial for immorality in January 1857 after Madame Bovary was serialized in La Revue de Paris; his acquittal turned the novel into an overnight sensation.

questions.l2Category: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.l2Subcategory: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.prompt: Dying in 19 BCE with half-lines still unfinished, Virgil begged his executors to burn this 12-book Latin epic, only for Emperor Augustus to overrule the will and preserve "Arma virumque cano."
clues: Opening with 'I sing of arms and the man,' its Trojan survivor flees Carthage's Queen Dido to found Rome's lineage.
Its first six books echo the Odyssey's wanderings and its last six mirror the Iliad's Italian wars.
questions.whyExplanation: Before dying in 19 BCE, Virgil asked Varius Rufus and Plotius Tucca to destroy his unfinished Aeneid, but Emperor Augustus ordered it published intact.

questions.l2Category: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.l2Subcategory: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.prompt: Spanning seven French volumes and over a million words, this modernist masterwork hinges on involuntary memory triggered when a spoonful of lime-blossom tea softens a shell-shaped madeleine cake.
clues: Once known in English by C. K. Scott Moncrieff's Shakespearean rendering Remembrance of Things Past, it opens with Swann's Way.
Marcel Proust drafted its cork-lined bedroom meditation from Combray to the Guermantes salons.
questions.whyExplanation: Marcel Proust's seven-volume À la recherche du temps perdu (In Search of Lost Time, 1913–1927) famously unlocks childhood memories of Combray through a tea-dipped madeleine.

questions.l2Category: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.l2Subcategory: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.prompt: Concealed in a drawer for 26 years after its author's 1940 death under Stalin, this Soviet satire sends Satan—disguised as Professor Woland—and a vodka-swilling giant cat named Behemoth to Moscow.
clues: Opening at Patriarch's Ponds where an editor loses his head to a tram, it interweaves Pontius Pilate's Jerusalem.
Mikhail Bulgakov's suppressed masterpiece gave Russian literature the defiant motto 'Manuscripts don't burn.'
questions.whyExplanation: Written secretly from 1928 to 1940 by Mikhail Bulgakov and first serialized in censored form in 1966–1967, The Master and Margarita features Woland, Behemoth the cat, and 'Manuscripts don't burn.'

questions.l2Category: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.l2Subcategory: French, Russian, German, Spanish & World Classics
questions.prompt: Originally circulated in manuscript as The Story of the Stone in 18th-century Qing China, Cao Xueqin's sprawling family epic follows aristocrat Jia Baoyu, born clutching a glowing piece of jade.
clues: Its doomed love triangle links Baoyu to sickly poetess Lin Daiyu and pragmatic cousin Xue Baochai inside the Jia clan.
Recognized as one of China's Four Great Classical Novels, it spawned its own scholarly field called Redology.
questions.whyExplanation: Cao Xueqin's mid-18th-century masterpiece Hongloumeng (Dream of the Red Chamber, also called The Story of the Stone) traces Jia Baoyu and the decline of the Jia family.

questions.prompt: Sentenced to death over the Petrashevsky circle, this Russian novelist endured a staged 1849 firing-squad execution in St. Petersburg before a last-second imperial commutation sent him to Siberia.
clues: Four years in an Omsk prison camp inspired The House of the Dead and deepened his epileptic, existential fiction.
He later dictated The Gambler in 26 days to stenographer Anna Snitkina to dodge a predatory publisher.
questions.whyExplanation: On December 22, 1849, Tsar Nicholas I staged a mock execution of Fyodor Dostoevsky at Semyonov Square before commuting his sentence to hard labor in Siberia.

questions.prompt: Printing Sense and Sensibility in 1811 under the anonymous credit "By a Lady," this Hampshire clergyman's daughter supposedly left a Chawton cottage parlor door creaking so she could hide pages from visitors.
clues: Her brother Henry finally revealed her true authorship in a biographical notice after her 1817 death in Winchester.
She described her own sharp domestic ironies as painting on a 'little bit (two inches wide) of ivory.'
questions.whyExplanation: Jane Austen published her novels anonymously during her lifetime—starting with 'By a Lady' in 1811—and reportedly refused to oil the creaking door at Chawton Cottage so it would warn her of guests.

questions.prompt: After losing the use of his left hand to gunshot wounds at the 1571 Battle of Lepanto, this Spanish soldier spent five years held for ransom by Barbary corsairs in Algiers before turning to fiction.
clues: He later landed in a Seville jail over tax-collection shortfalls, where he reportedly conceived his chivalric parody.
He died in Madrid in April 1616, the same month and year as William Shakespeare.
questions.whyExplanation: Miguel de Cervantes suffered permanent damage to his left hand at Lepanto (1571) and survived five years of captivity in Algiers (1575–1580) before writing the quintessential Spanish novel.

questions.prompt: Excommunicated by the Russian Orthodox Holy Synod in 1901 over his radical pacifism, this aristocratic count freed his serfs' schools at Yasnaya Polyana and died at Astapovo railway station in 1910.
clues: His artillery service during the Siege of Sevastopol shaped the battlefield realism of War and Peace.
His nonviolent tract The Kingdom of God Is Within You profoundly influenced a young Mahatma Gandhi.
questions.whyExplanation: After publishing Resurrection and challenging church dogma, Count Leo Tolstoy was excommunicated in 1901; nine years later he fled Yasnaya Polyana and died at Astapovo station.

questions.prompt: Before becoming the first Black woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1993, this Lorain, Ohio native edited books by Muhammad Ali, Toni Cade Bambara, and Angela Davis at Random House.
clues: Born Chloe Ardelia Wofford, she wrote her 1970 debut novel The Bluest Eye in pre-dawn hours before commuting to work.
She later taught creative writing at Princeton and composed Song of Solomon and Jazz.
questions.whyExplanation: Born Chloe Wofford in Lorain, Ohio, Toni Morrison served as a pioneering senior editor at Random House before winning the 1993 Nobel Prize in Literature.

questions.prompt: Short of postage money in Mexico City in 1966, this Colombian journalist and his wife Mercedes pawned a hairdryer and heater to mail half of his breakthrough manuscript to Buenos Aires.
clues: Nicknamed Gabo, he grew up listening to his grandmother's deadpan ghost stories in the banana town of Aracataca.
He won the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature and also penned Chronicle of a Death Foretold.
questions.whyExplanation: When Gabriel García Márquez finished his famous Macondo manuscript in 1966, he and Mercedes Barcha had to mail it in two halves after pawning household appliances for postage.

questions.prompt: Buying a tabletop handpress in 1917 to found the Hogarth Press with her husband Leonard, this Bloomsbury modernist personally set type for T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land and argued for A Room of One's Own.
clues: Born Adeline Virginia Stephen, she drew on childhood summers in Cornwall for To the Lighthouse.
Her playful 1928 gender-shifting biography Orlando was a love letter to Vita Sackville-West.
questions.whyExplanation: Virginia and Leonard Woolf founded the Hogarth Press in 1917 with a handpress in Richmond, publishing early modernist landmarks including T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land alongside her own essays and novels.

questions.prompt: Running a Tokyo jazz club called Peter Cat in 1978, this future Japanese bestseller suddenly resolved to write his first novel at Meiji Jingu Stadium when Dave Hilton doubled for the Yakult Swallows.
clues: He translated F. Scott Fitzgerald and Raymond Chandler into Japanese while writing Wind-Up Bird Chronicle and Kafka on the Shore.
Cats, jazz records, subterranean wells, and Beatles references like Norwegian Wood recur throughout his fiction.
questions.whyExplanation: Haruki Murakami owned the Tokyo jazz bar Peter Cat until a 1978 Yakult Swallows game inspired him to buy a fountain pen and draft Hear the Wind Sing at his kitchen table.

questions.prompt: Appointed director of Argentina's National Library in 1955 just as hereditary blindness stole his sight, this Buenos Aires essayist celebrated the irony in poems and invented labyrinths in Ficciones.
clues: His dense, footnote-laced tales imagine an infinite hexagonal Library of Babel and an encyclopedic fake planet called Tlön.
In 'Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote,' he satirizes literary originality via word-for-word recreation.
questions.whyExplanation: Jorge Luis Borges became director of Argentina's National Library in 1955 while going blind—an irony of 'God's splendid irony, giving me at once books and the night.'

questions.prompt: Naming the three novels of his landmark Cairo Trilogy after actual Old Cairo thoroughfares, this Egyptian civil servant became the first Arabic-language writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988.
clues: Palace Walk, Palace of Desire, and Sugar Street chronicle three generations of the Abd al-Jawad family.
He survived a 1994 stabbing outside his Cairo home sparked by controversy over his allegory Children of Gebelawi.
questions.whyExplanation: Egyptian novelist Naguib Mahfouz won the 1988 Nobel Prize in Literature—the first Arabic-language laureate—celebrated for his Cairo Trilogy named after streets in Islamic Cairo.

questions.prompt: Born in war-torn Ukraine and raised in Recife, this Brazilian modernist stunned critics at age 23 with Near to the Wild Heart—its title lifted from James Joyce—and ended her career with The Hour of the Star.
clues: Her hallucinatory 1964 novel The Passion According to G.H. unfolds inside a maid's room over a crushed cockroach.
Her sharp cheekbones and enigmatic Portuguese prose made her a cult literary icon after her 1977 death.
questions.whyExplanation: Ukrainian-born Brazilian writer Clarice Lispector debuted at 23 with Near to the Wild Heart (1943) and completed The Hour of the Star shortly before her death in 1977.

questions.prompt: Originally sketched in his creator's notebook under the name "Sherrinford," this Baker Street consulting detective first met his roommate over a hemoglobin test in 1887's A Study in Scarlet.
clues: He keeps tobacco in the toe of a Persian slipper, plays a Stradivarius, and retires to keep bees in Sussex.
Arthur Conan Doyle reluctantly revived him after outraged fans protested his plunge at Reichenbach Falls.
questions.whyExplanation: Arthur Conan Doyle initially jotted down 'Sherrinford Holmes' before launching Sherlock Holmes in Beeton's Christmas Annual (1887) with A Study in Scarlet.

questions.prompt: Serving 19 years in Toulon's galleys after stealing a loaf of bread and attempting escape, Prisoner 24601 remakes himself as benevolent Mayor Madeleine after Bishop Myriel gifts him silver candlesticks.
clues: He rescues orphaned Cosette from the grasping Thénardiers and carries a wounded student through Paris sewers.
Victor Hugo's 1862 epic Les Misérables centers on his lifelong pursuit by a rigid police inspector.
questions.whyExplanation: In Victor Hugo's Les Misérables (1862), convict 24601 Jean Valjean is redeemed by Bishop Myriel's gift of silver candlesticks and adopts the alias Monsieur Madeleine.

questions.prompt: When asked to donate to charity in an 1843 London counting-house, this miserly partner of the dead Jacob Marley sneers, "Are there no prisons?" before three nocturnal spirits melt his frost.
clues: He begrudges clerk Bob Cratchit a single lump of coal on Christmas Eve before waking up to buy a prize turkey.
Charles Dickens made his surname an English synonym for a stingy holiday curmudgeon.
questions.whyExplanation: In Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol (1843), Ebenezer Scrooge dismisses charity collectors with 'Are there no prisons?' before Marley's ghost and three spirits reform him.

questions.prompt: Walking out of Boston's prison door cradling infant Pearl in 1642, this defiant Puritan seamstress wears a crimson letter embroidered in sumptuous gold thread rather than plain sackcloth.
clues: She refuses to name her lover, frail minister Arthur Dimmesdale, while her vengeful husband lurks as Roger Chillingworth.
Nathaniel Hawthorne's 1850 romance turns her stitched emblem of adultery into a badge meaning 'Able.'
questions.whyExplanation: In Nathaniel Hawthorne's The Scarlet Letter (1850), Hester Prynne steps onto the Boston scaffold with baby Pearl wearing an ornately gold-embroidered scarlet 'A'.

questions.prompt: Nicknamed "One-Shot" in his youth before putting down his rifle to practice law in Maycomb, Alabama, this widower shocks his children by felling a rabid dog with one bullet while defending Tom Robinson.
clues: He teaches daughter Scout that you never truly understand a person until you climb into their skin and walk around.
Harper Lee modeled this 1960 novel's Pulitzer-honored courtroom hero largely on her own father, Amasa.
questions.whyExplanation: In Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird (1960), Maycomb attorney Atticus Finch hides his legendary 'One-Shot' marksmanship until Sheriff Heck Tate begs him to shoot rabid dog Tim Johnson.

questions.prompt: Expelled from Pencey Prep after failing four of five subjects, this red-hunting-hatted runaway spends three December days wandering Manhattan, fretting over where Central Park's ducks go in winter.
clues: He brands almost every adult a 'phony' and dreams of standing at a cliff's edge in a field of rye.
J. D. Salinger's 1951 coming-of-age narrator finds fleeting peace watching little sister Phoebe on a carousel.
questions.whyExplanation: In J. D. Salinger's The Catcher in the Rye (1951), sixteen-year-old Holden Caulfield flees Pencey Prep in a red hunting hat and asks New York cabbies where the Central Park lagoon ducks winter.

questions.prompt: Framed on his betrothal day in Marseille by jealous rivals Fernand, Danglars, and Villefort, this young sailor endures 14 years inside the Château d'If until dying scholar Abbé Faria bequeaths him a fortune.
clues: Escaping by sewing himself into his dead mentor's burial sack, he unearths Spada treasure on a Tuscan islet.
Alexandre Dumas's 1844 revenge epic follows him reinvented as the enigmatic Count of Monte Cristo.
questions.whyExplanation: Betrayed in 1815 Marseille, Alexandre Dumas's Edmond Dantès spends 14 years in the Château d'If before Abbé Faria's secret treasure transforms him into the Count of Monte Cristo.

questions.prompt: Brought home to Yorkshire's desolate moors as a nameless Liverpool foundling by Mr. Earnshaw, this brooding outcast vanishes for three years and returns rich to exact generational ruin on two estates.
clues: Obsessed with Catherine Earnshaw even beyond the grave, he marries Edgar Linton's sister purely out of spite.
Emily Brontë's sole novel names its windswept manor Wuthering Heights and lets Lockwood hear a ghost at the window.
questions.whyExplanation: In Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights (1847), the orphaned foundling Heathcliff is brought from Liverpool to the Yorkshire moors and consumes two generations in vengeance over Catherine Earnshaw.

questions.prompt: Described by her creator as a heroine "whom no one but myself will much like," this meddlesome Hartfield heiress bungles Harriet Smith's courtships in Highbury while overlooking longtime friend Mr. Knightley.
clues: Her cruel Box Hill quip to impoverished chatterbox Miss Bates earns a stinging rebuke that finally humbles her.
Amy Heckerling's 1995 teen comedy Clueless transplanted her Highbury matchmaking to Beverly Hills.
questions.whyExplanation: Jane Austen famously said Emma Woodhouse (1815) was a heroine 'whom no one but myself will much like'—a self-satisfied matchmaker humbled after insulting Miss Bates at Box Hill.

questions.prompt: Defiantly tossing Samuel Johnson's dictionary out a carriage window as she leaves Miss Pinkerton's Academy, this penniless social climber schemes her way through Regency London and Waterloo.
clues: Subtitled A Novel without a Hero, William Makepeace Thackeray's 1848 satire contrasts her wit with timid Amelia Sedley.
She marries cavalry officer Rawdon Crawley only to be caught entertaining the wealthy Marquess of Steyne.
questions.whyExplanation: In William Makepeace Thackeray's Vanity Fair (1847–1848), audacious orphan Becky Sharp announces her rebellion by hurling Dr. Johnson's dictionary from the coach leaving Miss Pinkerton's school.

questions.prompt: In a green hunting cap pushing a New Orleans hot-dog cart, this medieval-obsessed malcontent rails against his "pyloric valve" and Boethius's Wheel of Fortune in Big Chief tablets.
clues: He lives with his long-suffering mother Irene on Constantinople Street and sparks a chaotic revolt at Levy Pants.
John Kennedy Toole's posthumous 1981 Pulitzer winner A Confederacy of Dunces immortalized this pompous slacker.
questions.whyExplanation: Ignatius J. Reilly is the gluttonous, medievalist antihero of John Kennedy Toole's posthumous Pulitzer-winning novel A Confederacy of Dunces (1980), set in 1960s New Orleans.

questions.prompt: Born from an 1816 Lake Geneva rainy-night ghost-story challenge alongside Lord Byron, this 1818 gothic milestone opens aboard Robert Walton's icebound Arctic vessel.
clues: Subtitled The Modern Prometheus, Mary Shelley's debut was published anonymously when she was only 20.
Its Ingolstadt anatomy student abandons an eight-foot sewn-together creature that educates itself on Paradise Lost.
questions.whyExplanation: Mary Shelley conceived Frankenstein (1818) during the rainy 'Year Without a Summer' at Villa Diodati in 1816, framing Victor's confession inside Captain Robert Walton's Arctic letters.

questions.prompt: Drafted on the rainy Scottish island of Jura under the working title The Last Man in Europe, this 1949 dystopia opens on a bright cold April day as clocks strike thirteen.
clues: Winston Smith alters back issues of The Times at the Ministry of Truth before Room 101 breaks him.
George Orwell gave English 'Big Brother,' 'Thoughtcrime,' and 'doublethink' in this Oceania nightmare.
questions.whyExplanation: Finishing the manuscript while dying of tuberculosis on Jura, George Orwell changed The Last Man in Europe to Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), whose famous first line notes clocks striking thirteen.

questions.prompt: Sparked by a single whimsical sentence an Oxford professor jotted on a blank exam-booklet page in the early 1930s, this 1937 fantasy sends a reluctant burglar east to Lonely Mountain.
clues: Thorin Oakenshield recruits Bilbo Baggins to reclaim Erebor's treasure hoard from the dragon Smaug.
J. R. R. Tolkien's famous opening line declares: 'In a hole in the ground there lived a...'
questions.whyExplanation: Grading School Certificate papers, J. R. R. Tolkien scribbled 'In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit' on a blank page, launching the 1937 fantasy classic The Hobbit.

questions.prompt: Rejected by over 20 New York publishers before Philadelphia auto-repair manual printer Chilton Books took a gamble in 1965, this desert-world epic became science fiction's top bestseller.
clues: Frank Herbert's ecology study of shifting Oregon coastal sands inspired the arid planet Arrakis and its spice melange.
Paul Atreides walks without rhythm among giant sandworms to lead the blue-eyed Fremen.
questions.whyExplanation: After more than twenty rejections, automotive-manual publisher Chilton Books released Frank Herbert's Dune in 1965, winning the inaugural Nebula Award and the 1966 Hugo.

questions.prompt: Assembled entirely from journals, ship logs, and phonograph cylinders, this 1897 gothic thriller drew inspiration from the real 1885 shipwreck of the Russian schooner Dmitry at Whitby.
clues: Solicitor Jonathan Harker travels to a Carpathian castle before the doomed vessel Demeter washes ashore in Yorkshire.
Bram Stoker pits Dutch polymath Abraham Van Helsing against a Transylvanian aristocrat buying London estates.
questions.whyExplanation: Bram Stoker researched Whitby folklore—including the 1885 wreck of the Dmitry—to craft his 1897 epistolary vampire novel Dracula.

questions.prompt: Borrowing its ironic title from Miranda's dazzled speech in The Tempest, this 1932 satire is set in Year of Our Ford 632, where citizens hatch in Hatcheries and soothe gloom with soma.
clues: Alpha-Plus psychologist Bernard Marx brings Shakespeare-quoting John 'the Savage' from a New Mexico reservation to London.
Aldous Huxley imagined a World State ruled not by pain and censorship, but by engineered pleasure and consumerism.
questions.whyExplanation: Aldous Huxley's 1932 dystopia Brave New World takes its title from Shakespeare's The Tempest and imagines a Fordist caste society pacified by the drug soma.

questions.prompt: Typed on coin-operated rental machines in UCLA's Powell Library basement for $9.80 in dimes, this 1953 dystopian classic imagines firemen who ignite books instead of dousing flames.
clues: Fireman Guy Montag hides stolen volumes after meeting teenage neighbor Clarisse McClellan and fleeing the Mechanical Hound.
Ray Bradbury named it for the supposed autoignition temperature of paper on an imperial scale.
questions.whyExplanation: Ray Bradbury drafted the expansion of 'The Fireman' into Fahrenheit 451 (1953) in nine days on coin-operated typewriters in UCLA's library basement at ten cents per half-hour.

questions.prompt: Opening with a famous simile comparing Chiba City's sky to "television, tuned to a dead channel," this 1984 debut became the first novel to sweep the Hugo, Nebula, and Philip K. Dick Awards.
clues: Washed-up console cowboy Case teams with mirror-shaded mercenary Molly Millions to hack an orbital AI named Wintermute.
William Gibson's cyberpunk blueprint popularized the term 'cyberspace' years before the World Wide Web.
questions.whyExplanation: William Gibson's 1984 debut Neuromancer won the science-fiction triple crown (Hugo, Nebula, Philip K. Dick Award) and coined modern cyberpunk imagery from its very first sentence.

questions.prompt: Sending Ekumen envoy Genly Ai across the frozen world of Gethen, this 1969 novel—winner of both the Hugo and Nebula Awards—explores a human society without fixed sex outside monthly "kemmer" cycles.
clues: Disgraced Karhide prime minister Estraven risks treason to haul a sledge across the Gobrin Ice beside the alien diplomat.
Ursula K. Le Guin drew its title from an imaginary Gethenian verse pairing light with shadow in Tormer's Lay.
questions.whyExplanation: Ursula K. Le Guin's 1969 Hainish Cycle milestone The Left Hand of Darkness pairs envoy Genly Ai with Estraven on ambisexual, icebound Gethen ('Winter').

questions.prompt: Published 25 years before Dracula in 1872, Sheridan Le Fanu's eerie Styrian novella follows young Laura as a seductive houseguest hides her ancient surname behind anagrams like Millarca and Mircalla.
clues: A century-old portrait dated 1698 exposes the languid visitor as Countess Karnstein of Austria.
This Irish gothic pioneer shaped lesbian vampire fiction and directly influenced Bram Stoker.
questions.whyExplanation: Serialized in The Dark Blue (1871–1872) by Irish writer Sheridan Le Fanu, Carmilla precedes Dracula by a quarter-century and reveals Countess Mircalla Karnstein via anagrammed aliases.

questions.prompt: In this 1961 Polish philosophical sci-fi classic, psychologist Kris Kelvin boards an orbital station where a sentient planetary ocean probes the crew's guilt by materializing his late wife Hari.
clues: Stanisław Lem questioned whether humanity can ever comprehend truly alien intelligence despite decades of academic study.
Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 Soviet film and Steven Soderbergh's 2002 remake both adapted its haunted space station.
questions.whyExplanation: Stanisław Lem's 1961 novel Solaris strands Kris Kelvin above a living oceanic planet that conjures physical 'visitors' from the crew's buried memories.

questions.prompt: Inspired by the 1932 Lindbergh kidnapping, this 1934 locked-room puzzle stalls a luxury Calais coach in a Yugoslav snowdrift with gangster Samuel Ratchett stabbed twelve times by uneven hands.
clues: Belgian sleuth Hercule Poirot presents two solutions to railway director Monsieur Bouc—one neat, one conspiratorial.
Twelve passengers tied to the tragic Daisy Armstrong case act as judge, jury, and executioner.
questions.whyExplanation: Agatha Christie modeled the fictional Armstrong kidnapping in Murder on the Orient Express (1934) on the Lindbergh case, staging a twelve-suspect conspiracy aboard a snowbound train.

questions.prompt: Originally titled The Inside of His Head to reflect its time-blurring staging, this 1949 Pulitzer tragedy ends with Linda Loman mourning at her traveling husband's grave after the last house payment.
clues: Willy Loman insists on being 'well liked' while sons Biff and Happy wrestle with his crumbling American Dream.
Arthur Miller's play gave American theater Linda's plea: 'Attention must be finally paid to such a person.'
questions.whyExplanation: Arthur Miller's 1949 Pulitzer-winning drama Death of a Salesman was first conceived as The Inside of His Head, tracing Willy Loman's final 24 hours across New York and Boston memories.

questions.prompt: Publicly burned by Nazi students in 1933 for "betraying the German soldier," this 1929 WWI novel kills narrator Paul Bäumer on an October 1918 day so calm the army dispatch gave the book its title.
questions.answerCorrect: All Quiet on the Western Front
clues: Erich Maria Remarque's Im Westen nichts Neues follows teenage schoolmates shattered by mud, gas, and trench shells.
Its 1930 Hollywood adaptation won Best Picture and Best Director for Lewis Milestone.
questions.whyExplanation: Erich Maria Remarque's 1929 antiwar novel All Quiet on the Western Front ends with Paul Bäumer dying on a tranquil October day summarized by the official communiqué of its title.

questions.prompt: When Humphrey Bogart's private eye calls a black enamel statuette "the stuff that dreams are made of," he borrows from The Tempest to sum up the gilded hoax at the heart of this 1930 Dashiell Hammett novel.
clues: San Francisco detective Sam Spade turns in murderous client Brigid O'Shaughnessy after his partner Miles Archer is shot.
Portly villain Kasper Gutman and Joel Cairo have chased the jewel-encrusted Knights of Rhodes tribute for 17 years.
questions.whyExplanation: Dashiell Hammett's 1930 hardboiled classic The Maltese Falcon pits Sam Spade against Kasper Gutman over a coveted black bird that proves to be lead.

questions.prompt: When Howard Hawks filmed this 1939 Raymond Chandler debut, the studio famously wired the author to ask who murdered the Sternwood family's chauffeur—and Chandler admitted he did not know either.
clues: It introduces cynical Los Angeles private investigator Philip Marlowe inside an orchid-filled Beverly Hills greenhouse.
Blackmailers, Carmen Sternwood's reckless secrets, and missing bootlegger Rusty Regan tangle in its rain-slick plot.
questions.whyExplanation: Raymond Chandler's 1939 debut The Big Sleep introduced Philip Marlowe; during the 1946 film adaptation, Chandler famously confessed he had forgotten who killed chauffeur Owen Taylor.

questions.prompt: Inspired by Cambridge Five double agent Kim Philby, this 1974 Cold War classic drags bespectacled spy George Smiley out of retirement to hunt a Soviet mole inside Britain's "Circus."

distractors.text: The Spy Who Came in from the Cold

clues: Control assigned nursery-rhyme code names to his top four deputies before dying in disgrace after a Czech ambush.
Former MI6 officer John le Carré modeled traitor Bill Haydon's betrayal on real British intelligence scandals.
questions.whyExplanation: John le Carré's 1974 espionage novel Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy draws directly on Kim Philby's real-life treason, tasking George Smiley with unmasking Soviet mole 'Gerald.'

questions.prompt: Blending semiotics with a 1327 Italian abbey whodunit, Umberto Eco's 1980 international sensation hinges on monks dying with blackened tongues after secretly reading Aristotle's lost treatise on comedy.
clues: Franciscan friar William of Baskerville—a clear nod to Holmes—and novice Adso of Melk map an octagonal labyrinth library.
Blind librarian Jorge of Burgos, an homage to Jorge Luis Borges, poisons the margins to suppress laughter.
questions.whyExplanation: Umberto Eco's 1980 medieval mystery The Name of the Rose pairs friar William of Baskerville and Adso of Melk inside a labyrinthine abbey where forbidden pages are laced with poison.

questions.prompt: Written by Patricia Highsmith in 1955, this icy psychological thriller tracks a New York con man sent to coastal Italy who kills jazz-loving shipping heir Dickie Greenleaf and simply assumes his identity.
clues: After bludgeoning Dickie in a Sanremo skiff, the smooth forger imitates his handwriting, wears his rings, and escapes scot-free.
Alain Delon in Purple Noon and Matt Damon in Anthony Minghella's 1999 film both played its charming sociopath.
questions.whyExplanation: Patricia Highsmith's 1955 novel The Talented Mr. Ripley follows Tom Ripley's chilling identity theft of Dickie Greenleaf in Italy and launched a five-book 'Ripliad.'

questions.prompt: Winner of the 2009 Booker Prize, Hilary Mantel's Tudor historical triumph reframes Putney blacksmith's son Thomas Cromwell from ruthless villain to shrewd architect of Henry VIII's break with Rome.
clues: Named for the Wiltshire seat of the Seymour family, it opens with brutal Walter Cromwell kicking his teenage son on cobblestones.
Its sequel Bring Up the Bodies made Mantel the first woman to win the Booker Prize twice.
questions.whyExplanation: Hilary Mantel's 2009 Booker winner Wolf Hall chronicles Thomas Cromwell's rise from Cardinal Wolsey's lawyer to Henry VIII's chief fixer, named after Jane Seymour's family estate.

questions.prompt: Praised by T. S. Eliot as the first and greatest English detective novel, Wilkie Collins's 1868 sensation follows Sergeant Cuff hunting a cursed Indian yellow diamond stolen on Rachel Verinder's birthday.
clues: Multiple eyewitnesses narrate the theft—including butler Gabriel Betteredge, who consults Robinson Crusoe like an oracle.
Its twist pioneered the opium-induced sleepwalking alibi and the 'least likely suspect' clue structure.
questions.whyExplanation: Serialized in Charles Dickens's All the Year Round in 1868, Wilkie Collins's The Moonstone established core whodunit tropes from the eccentric police detective to red herrings.

questions.prompt: Framed as a secret memoir buried to be read 1,900 years later, Robert Graves's 1934 historical novel follows a stammering, limping scholar who plays the fool to survive Livia's poisons and Caligula's court.
clues: Drawing heavily on Tacitus and Suetonius, it ends with Praetorian Guards discovering its reluctant narrator behind a palace curtain.
Derek Jacobi starred in the celebrated 1976 BBC miniseries adapting Graves's Julio-Claudian saga.
questions.whyExplanation: Robert Graves's 1934 novel I, Claudius presents the fictionalized autobiography of Rome's fourth emperor surviving family intrigue until the Praetorian Guard hails him ruler in 41 CE.

questions.prompt: So punctual on his afternoon walk through Königsberg that neighbors supposedly set their clocks by him, this 18th-century Prussian thinker never traveled far from home yet launched Critique of Pure Reason.
clues: He formulated the categorical imperative: act only on maxims you could will to become universal law.
He credited Scottish skeptic David Hume with waking him from his 'dogmatic slumber' before 1781.
questions.whyExplanation: Immanuel Kant lived his entire life in Königsberg, publishing Critique of Pure Reason in 1781 and founding deontological ethics via the categorical imperative.

questions.prompt: Writing "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman" in her groundbreaking 1949 study The Second Sex, this French existentialist co-founded the journal Les Temps modernes alongside Jean-Paul Sartre.
clues: She won the 1954 Prix Goncourt for The Mandarins and placed second behind Sartre on France's 1929 agrégation exam.
Her philosophical treatise analyzed how culture casts women as 'the Other' and ignited second-wave feminism.
questions.whyExplanation: French existentialist Simone de Beauvoir published Le Deuxième Sexe (The Second Sex) in 1949, shaping modern feminist philosophy with 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.'

questions.prompt: Expelled from Amsterdam's Portuguese-Jewish congregation by a harsh 1656 cherem writ for pantheistic heresy, this Dutch lens grinder laid out his Ethics like Euclid's geometry, equating God with Nature.
clues: His Latin slogan Deus sive Natura ('God or Nature') led Albert Einstein to profess belief in this thinker's God.
Silica dust from grinding optical lenses likely hastened his death in The Hague at age 44 in 1677.
questions.whyExplanation: Excommunicated in 1656 at age 23, Dutch rationalist Baruch Spinoza supported himself grinding lenses while composing his posthumous Ethics in geometric axiom-and-proof style.

questions.prompt: Watching Adolf Eichmann's 1961 Jerusalem war-crimes trial for The New Yorker, this German-born political theorist shocked readers by coining "the banality of evil" for a bureaucrat who failed to think.
clues: Earlier she analyzed Nazism and Stalinism together in her 1951 landmark The Origins of Totalitarianism.
A former student of Martin Heidegger who fled Europe in 1941, she later taught at The New School in New York.
questions.whyExplanation: Covering Eichmann's 1961 trial for The New Yorker, Hannah Arendt published Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963), introducing the famously debated phrase 'the banality of evil.'

questions.prompt: Complaining that his 1739 A Treatise of Human Nature "fell dead-born from the press," this Scottish Enlightenment empiricist challenged causality and miracles while befriending economist Adam Smith.
clues: He formulated the problem of induction and the is-ought guillotine separating factual statements from moral claims.
His radical skepticism about cause and effect famously roused Immanuel Kant from 'dogmatic slumber.'
questions.whyExplanation: Scottish empiricist David Hume lamented that his 1739 Treatise 'fell dead-born from the press,' yet its skepticism about induction and causality transformed modern philosophy.

questions.prompt: Publishing under playful pseudonyms like Johannes de Silentio after breaking off his engagement to Regine Olsen, this melancholy Copenhagen thinker launched Christian existentialism in Fear and Trembling.
clues: He distinguished aesthetic, ethical, and religious stages of life in Either/Or and championed the subjective 'leap' of faith.
Abraham's silent ascent of Mount Moriah anchors his critique of Hegelian rationalism.
questions.whyExplanation: Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard broke off his engagement to Regine Olsen in 1841 and used pseudonyms such as Johannes de Silentio to author Fear and Trembling (1843).

questions.prompt: Awaking from a vivid dream during China's Warring States period, this witty Daoist sage famously wondered whether he was a man who had dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming he was a man.
clues: His parables praise effortless harmony—wu wei—through Cook Ding, whose butcher knife stayed razor-sharp for 19 years.
He reportedly declined a royal prime-ministership by comparing himself to a tortoise happy wagging its tail in the mud.
questions.whyExplanation: Fourth-century BCE Daoist master Zhuangzi (Chuang Tzu) authored the famous Butterfly Dream parable questioning waking certainty alongside tales of spontaneous skill like Cook Ding.

questions.prompt: Drafting his terse Tractatus in WWI trenches—ending with "Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent"—this eccentric Austrian genius later dismantled his own theory at Cambridge.
clues: He gave away an immense Viennese steel fortune, taught village schoolkids, and once brandished a fireplace poker at Karl Popper.
His posthumous Philosophical Investigations (1953) replaced picture-theory logic with 'language games.'
questions.whyExplanation: Austrian-British philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein wrote the Tractatus (1921) during WWI before revolutionizing analytic philosophy a second time with Philosophical Investigations (1953).

questions.prompt: Six centuries before Descartes's cogito, this Persian polymath proposed the "Floating Man" thought experiment—a newly created person suspended in empty air—to prove self-awareness requires no bodily senses.
clues: Known in Arabic as Ibn Sina, he penned both The Book of Healing and The Canon of Medicine around 1025.
His medical encyclopedia remained a standard university textbook across medieval Europe for half a millennium.
questions.whyExplanation: Persian polymath Ibn Sina—known in the West as Avicenna (980–1037)—devised the Floating Man argument for an immaterial soul in The Book of Healing and authored The Canon of Medicine.

questions.prompt: Head of Alexandria's Neoplatonist school and praised by bishop Synesius for refining astrolabes and commentaries on Diophantus, this Roman Egyptian sage was brutally murdered by a mob of zealots in 415 CE.
clues: Daughter of mathematician Theon, she lectured openly to pagan and Christian pupils alike during Bishop Cyril's power struggle.
Her death became an enduring historical emblem of classical learning clashing with late-antique fanaticism.
questions.whyExplanation: Alexandrian Neoplatonist philosopher, astronomer, and mathematician Hypatia—daughter of Theon—was killed by a Christian mob in 415 CE amid political rivalry between Cyril and prefect Orestes.

questions.prompt: Asking readers to design society from an "original position" behind a "veil of ignorance" hiding wealth and status, this Harvard thinker revived political ethics in 1971's A Theory of Justice.
clues: His 'difference principle' allows economic inequalities only when they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged.
Colleague Robert Nozick soon countered his egalitarian blueprint with libertarian Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974).
questions.whyExplanation: Harvard philosopher John Rawls published A Theory of Justice in 1971, introducing the 'veil of ignorance' thought experiment to derive fair principles of social cooperation.

questions.prompt: Notoriously bequeathing his "second-best bed" to wife Anne Hathaway in his March 1616 will, this Warwickshire glover's son saw 18 of his plays saved from oblivion only by colleagues' 1623 First Folio.
clues: Actors John Heminges and Henry Condell gathered 36 of his comedies, histories, and tragedies seven years after his death.
Part-owner of the Globe Theatre, he retired to New Place in Stratford-upon-Avon after The Tempest.
questions.whyExplanation: William Shakespeare left his wife Anne Hathaway his 'second-best bed' in 1616; without the 1623 First Folio compiled by Heminges and Condell, plays like Macbeth and The Tempest might have vanished.

questions.prompt: Publishing barely a dozen altered verses in life, this white-clad Amherst recluse left sister Lavinia a locked bureau stuffed with 40 hand-sewn "fascicles" holding nearly 1,800 dash-filled lyrics.
clues: Almost all her lyrics fit common hymn meter, including 'Because I could not stop for Death' and 'Hope is the thing with feathers.'
Editors smoothed out her eccentric capitalization and punctuation until Thomas H. Johnson restored them in 1955.
questions.whyExplanation: After Emily Dickinson died in Amherst in 1886, her sister Lavinia discovered over 1,775 poems bound in hand-stitched booklets ('fascicles') inside a bedroom drawer.

questions.prompt: After a German star refused to play a mother leaving her children in 1880, this Norwegian dramatist reluctantly wrote a happier ending for A Doll's House before restoring Nora's famous slam.
clues: He bitterly called the watered-down German ending a 'barbaric outrage' against his 1879 realist landmark.
His later dramas Hedda Gabler and Ghosts solidified his reputation as the father of modern prose theater.
questions.whyExplanation: Henrik Ibsen briefly penned an alternate German ending for A Doll's House (1879) to protect his copyright against unauthorized edits, calling it a 'barbaric outrage' compared to Nora's famous door slam.

questions.prompt: Calling medicine his "lawful wife" and literature his "mistress," this Russian physician saw The Seagull bomb horribly in 1896 before Konstantin Stanislavski's Moscow Art Theatre revived his subtext-rich plays.
clues: He traveled across Siberia to survey Sakhalin's penal colony and gave drama the rule that a loaded rifle onstage must fire.
Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters, and The Cherry Orchard showcase his tragicomic blend of yearning and inertia.
questions.whyExplanation: Doctor-turned-dramatist Anton Chekhov famously joked that medicine was his lawful wife and literature his mistress; his four late plays defined modern psychological theater.

questions.prompt: Hailed by Plato as the "Tenth Muse," this seventh-century BCE lyricist from the island of Lesbos survives mostly in haunting fragments recovered from papyrus waste wrapped around Egyptian mummies.
clues: Her sole complete surviving poem, 'Hymn to Aphrodite,' begs the love goddess to descend in a sparrow-drawn chariot.
Both her island home and her own name gave English enduring words for love between women.
questions.whyExplanation: Archaic Greek poet Sappho of Lesbos was hailed as the 'Tenth Muse' in antiquity; modern scholars have recovered new fragments of her verse from Oxyrhynchus papyri and mummy cartonnage.

questions.prompt: Adopting his pen name from a banana tree planted outside his Edo river hut, this 17th-century Japanese wanderer distilled Zen stillness into a frog leaping into an old pond and Narrow Road to the Deep North.
clues: His 1689 five-month foot trek across northern Honshu yielded Oku no Hosomichi, a haibun blend of prose and verse.
He elevated the playful 5-7-5 hokku opening stanza into the serious solitary art later dubbed haiku.
questions.whyExplanation: Matsuo Bashō took his pen name from the banana plant (bashō) beside his Edo hut, elevating 17-syllable haiku in classics like The Narrow Road to the Deep North (Oku no Hosomichi).

questions.prompt: Executed by Nationalist militia in an olive grove near Granada in August 1936 at age 38, this Andalusian Generation of '27 poet fused gypsy ballads with stark rural tragedies like Blood Wedding.
clues: He toured rural Spain with his student troupe La Barraca and befriended Salvador Dalí and Luis Buñuel in Madrid.
His final play, The House of Bernarda Alba, was completed barely two months before his Spanish Civil War murder.
questions.whyExplanation: Spanish poet and dramatist Federico García Lorca—author of Gypsy Ballads, Blood Wedding, and The House of Bernarda Alba—was assassinated by Francoist forces near Granada in August 1936.

questions.prompt: Dropping out of high school at 15 after a teacher accused him of plagiarizing a Napoleon paper, this self-taught Pittsburgh playwright went on to win two Pulitzers and write a ten-play Century Cycle.
clues: Nine of his ten decade-by-decade plays unfold in Pittsburgh's Hill District, with Ma Rainey's Black Bottom set in Chicago.
Fences (1987) and The Piano Lesson (1990) earned him Pulitzer Prizes for Drama.
questions.whyExplanation: Self-educated at Pittsburgh's Carnegie Library after leaving school at 15, August Wilson chronicled every decade of 20th-century Black American life across his ten-play Pittsburgh Cycle.

questions.prompt: Opening his 1966 debut by vowing "Between my finger and my thumb / The squat pen rests. I'll dig with it," this Northern Irish 1995 Nobel laureate also penned a bestselling 1999 Beowulf.
clues: Raised on Mossbawn farm in County Derry, he evoked preserved Iron Age 'bog bodies' as metaphors for the Troubles.
His Anglo-Saxon epic translation famously rendered 'Hwæt!' with the Ulster conversational opener 'So.'
questions.whyExplanation: County Derry-born 1995 Nobel laureate Seamus Heaney began Death of a Naturalist (1966) with 'Digging' and won the 1999 Whitbread Book of the Year for his translation of Beowulf.

questions.prompt: Taking religious vows in 1669 mainly to pursue scholarship free from marriage, this Mexican Hieronymite nun amassed 4,000 books and defended women's intellect in her sharp 1691 Reply to Sor Filotea.
questions.answerCorrect: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
clues: Celebrated as New Spain's 'Tenth Muse,' she argued that Aristotle would have written even more had he cooked.
Her baroque masterpiece First Dream traces the soul's nocturnal flight toward cosmic knowledge.
questions.whyExplanation: Mexican baroque poet, dramatist, and scholar Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz (1648–1695) entered a convent to study, wrote Reply to Sor Filotea defending female learning, and was dubbed 'The Tenth Muse.'

questions.prompt: Editing poetry for Kraków's Życie Literackie for three decades while publishing fewer than 400 concise poems, this witty Polish 1996 Nobel laureate mourned a partner's death in "Cat in an Empty Apartment."
clues: She hated literary celebrity so deeply that friends joked about the 'Nobel Tragedy' when Stockholm called in 1996.
Her Nobel lecture praised the phrase 'I don't know' as the small wings that keep poets and scientists flying.
questions.whyExplanation: Polish ironist Wisława Szymborska won the 1996 Nobel Prize in Literature for her compact, razor-sharp lyrics such as 'Cat in an Empty Apartment' and 'View with a Grain of Sand.'

questions.prompt: After a taxi struck his infant son Theo in 1960, this former RAF fighter pilot teamed with a toymaker and neurosurgeon to co-invent a brain shunt before writing Matilda in a garden shed.
clues: The Wade-Dahl-Till shunt helped thousands of hydrocephalus patients while he created Willy Wonka and the BFG.
His sly taste for macabre twists also shone in adult tales like 'Lamb to the Slaughter.'
questions.whyExplanation: Before writing Charlie and the Chocolate Factory and Matilda in his Buckinghamshire writing hut, Roald Dahl co-invented the Wade-Dahl-Till valve to treat his injured son's hydrocephalus.

questions.prompt: Coined by accident in his 1941 story "Liar!"—which also debuted the Three Laws—the word "robotics" comes from this prolific biochemist who authored or edited nearly 500 books.
clues: Edward Gibbon's history of Rome inspired his galactic-empire saga Foundation and its fictional science psychohistory.
Born in Petrovichi, Russia and raised in a Brooklyn candy store, he suffered from acrophobia and hated flying.
questions.whyExplanation: Isaac Asimov coined 'robotics' in his 1941 story 'Liar!' (assuming the word already existed), authored Foundation and I, Robot, and published books in 9 of the 10 Dewey Decimal categories.

questions.prompt: Rejected by six London publishers over its small size, this Victorian mycologist self-printed 250 copies of a mischievous garden bunny's tale in 1901 and left 4,000 Lake District acres to conservation.
clues: Frederick Warne & Co. reconsidered in 1902, launching Jemima Puddle-Duck, Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle, and Mr. McGregor's pie threat.
Her delicate watercolor studies of fungi were dismissed by Kew Gardens' male botanists in the 1890s.
questions.whyExplanation: After six rejections, Beatrix Potter privately printed 250 copies of The Tale of Peter Rabbit in 1901; her royalties funded 14 Lake District farms bequeathed to the National Trust.

questions.prompt: Proposing geostationary relay satellites in a 1945 Wireless World paper long before Sputnik, this British futurist co-wrote 2001: A Space Odyssey and crafted three laws linking tech to magic.
clues: His 1951 story 'The Sentinel' grew into Stanley Kubrick's monolith epic featuring the mutinous computer HAL 9000.
Settling in Sri Lanka to indulge his love of scuba diving, he also wrote Childhood's End and Rendezvous with Rama.
questions.whyExplanation: Arthur C. Clarke outlined geostationary relay orbits in 1945 (now nicknamed the Clarke Orbit), co-wrote 2001: A Space Odyssey, and coined 'Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.'

questions.prompt: Inventing a super-strong red-haired orphan with a porch-dwelling horse to cheer her sick daughter Karin in 1941 Stockholm, this Swedish icon also sparked Sweden's 1988 animal-welfare law.
clues: Villa Villekulla, monkey Mr. Nilsson, and mismatched stockings made her rebellious nine-year-old a global favorite.
She also wrote The Brothers Lionheart and Ronia, the Robber's Daughter and now graces Sweden's 20-krona banknote.
questions.whyExplanation: Astrid Lindgren invented Pippi Longstocking in 1941 when her sick seven-year-old daughter Karin asked for a bedtime story about a name she made up on the spot.

questions.prompt: Originally titling his 1964 Caldecott Medal triumph Where the Wild Horses Are until admitting he drew horses poorly, this Brooklyn artist modeled Max's fanged monsters on his loud relatives.
clues: Sent to bed without supper in his wolf suit, young Max sails across an ocean to lead a wordless 'wild rumpus.'
He also illustrated Else Holmelund Minarik's Little Bear books and created In the Night Kitchen.
questions.whyExplanation: Maurice Sendak changed Where the Wild Horses Are to Where the Wild Things Are (1963) because he struggled drawing horses, basing the monsters' expressions on his Jewish immigrant aunts and uncles.

questions.prompt: Collecting 26 rejections because editors could not tell if her quantum-physics fantasy fit adult or children's shelves, she won the 1963 Newbery Medal with a tale introducing the tesseract.
clues: Opening with the cliché 'It was a dark and stormy night,' Meg Murry and Charles Wallace rescue their father from Camazotz.
Farrar, Straus & Giroux finally gambled on A Wrinkle in Time after her mother passed the manuscript to a friend.
questions.whyExplanation: Madeleine L'Engle endured 26 rejections for A Wrinkle in Time before its 1962 publication; the novel won the 1963 Newbery Medal and popularized the five-dimensional tesseract shortcut.

questions.prompt: Becoming the first science-fiction writer awarded a MacArthur "Genius" Fellowship in 1995, this Pasadena native wrote a 1979 time-travel masterpiece yanking a modern Black woman back to antebellum Maryland.
clues: Overcoming childhood dyslexia, she attended the Clarion workshop under Harlan Ellison and won Hugos for 'Speech Sounds' and 'Bloodchild.'
Her prescient 1993 novel Parable of the Sower imagines climate collapse and the Earthseed faith in 2020s California.
questions.whyExplanation: Octavia E. Butler won the MacArthur Fellowship in 1995—a first for science fiction—celebrated for Kindred (1979), Dawn, and the Earthseed novels Parable of the Sower and Parable of the Talents.

questions.prompt: Using the I Ching to steer plot twists in his 1963 Hugo winner The Man in the High Castle, this prolific California author saw his paranoia-soaked fiction become Blade Runner and Minority Report.
clues: His 1968 novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? tests empathy with the Voight-Kampff machine.
He churned out eleven novels in 1963–1964 alone while probing fake memories and simulated realities in Ubik.
questions.whyExplanation: Philip K. Dick consulted the I Ching while writing The Man in the High Castle (1962), and his short fiction and novels inspired Blade Runner, Total Recall, Minority Report, and A Scanner Darkly.

questions.prompt: First sketching a stubby white troll on an outhouse wall to tease her brother about Immanuel Kant, this Finnish-Swedish painter created a hippo-like fairytale valley beloved from Helsinki to Tokyo.
clues: Her 1945 wartime debut launched Snufkin, Little My, and a round cylindrical blue house on Finland's coast.
She won the 1966 Hans Christian Andersen Medal and also wrote the acclaimed adult gem The Summer Book.
questions.whyExplanation: Finnish-Swedish artist and writer Tove Jansson originally drew an 'ugly Kant' troll on a summer-island outhouse wall in the 1930s, which evolved into her beloved Moomin books and comic strips.

questions.prompt: Working as a software technical writer in Bellevue, Washington, this perfectionist won four Hugos and four Nebulas from barely two dozen stories, including the basis for Denis Villeneuve's Arrival.
clues: His 1998 novella 'Story of Your Life' links Fermat's principle of least time to an alien non-linear written language.
His two short-fiction collections—Stories of Your Life and Others and Exhalation—turned down a Hugo nomination once on principle.
questions.whyExplanation: Technical writer Ted Chiang has published fewer than twenty stories yet won four Hugos and four Nebulas, with 'Story of Your Life' adapted into the 2016 film Arrival.

questions.prompt: First angering Zeus at Mekone by disguising barren ox bones beneath gleaming fat, this cunning Titan later smuggled celestial fire to mortals inside a hollow stalk of giant fennel.
clues: Chained to a crag in the Caucasus, he suffered an eagle devouring his regenerating liver each day.
Heracles finally shot the bird and broke his fetters after the Titan traded a secret prophecy about Thetis.
questions.whyExplanation: In Hesiod's Theogony, Prometheus tricks Zeus with fat-wrapped bones at Mekone and steals fire in a fennel stalk (narthex), earning eternal torment on Mount Caucasus until Heracles frees him.

questions.prompt: After Zeus swallowed his pregnant first wife Metis to foil a prophecy, Hephaestus split the sky god's aching skull with a bronze axe so this fully armored grey-eyed goddess could leap forth.
clues: In a contest for Attica's patronage, her gift of a domesticated olive tree outvoted Poseidon's salty spring.
Known to the Romans as Minerva, she wore the Gorgon-bearing aegis and championed Odysseus.
questions.whyExplanation: Athena sprang full-grown and armed from Zeus's forehead after he swallowed Metis, later winning Athens's patronage by planting the first olive tree on the Acropolis.

questions.prompt: Having drowned out the Sirens' deadly song aboard the Argo with his golden lyre, this Thracian musician charmed even iron-teared Hades—only to break the sole rule before daylight touched his bride.
clues: Stones wept and Cerberus lay down as he sang to reclaim Eurydice after a viper's bite took her on her wedding day.
Glancing back a step too soon cost him his wife forever before Thracian Maenads tore him apart.
questions.whyExplanation: Mythic bard Orpheus saved the Argonauts from the Sirens and moved Hades to release Eurydice, losing her permanently when he looked back before both had exited the Underworld.

questions.prompt: Abducted through an earthly chasm after reaching for a miraculous hundred-blossom narcissus, this spring maiden tasted ruby pomegranate seeds in the Underworld and inadvertently invented winter.
clues: Called Kore ('the Maiden') before becoming Hades's queen, she spent part of each year below while her grieving mother froze the soil.
Her annual ascent and return formed the sacred core of the Eleusinian Mysteries.
questions.whyExplanation: In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, Persephone's abduction by Hades and consumption of pomegranate seeds forced her to split the year between Olympus and the Underworld, explaining the seasons.

questions.prompt: Born at dawn inside a Mount Cyllene cave, this precocious infant invented the lyre from a tortoise shell by noon and rustled fifty of Apollo's sacred cattle by evening, walking them backward to hide tracks.
clues: He settled his half-brother's fury by trading the stringed instrument for a golden herald's staff and cattle herds.
Winged sandals carried this trickster-messenger as psychopomp guiding dead souls to the Styx.
questions.whyExplanation: The Homeric Hymn to Hermes recounts how the newborn god built a tortoise-shell lyre and stole Apollo's cattle on his very first day of life, reconciling by gifting Apollo the lyre.

questions.prompt: Uniquely Roman with no direct Greek counterpart, this two-faced guardian of thresholds had bronze Forum temple doors left wide open in wartime and shut only during rare intervals of total imperial peace.
clues: Romans invoked his name at the start of every public prayer before Jupiter himself, honoring beginnings and endings.
He lends his name to the opening month of the modern calendar.
questions.whyExplanation: Janus was a uniquely Roman deity of doorways, transitions, and beginnings; the gates of his Forum temple stayed open whenever Rome waged war and closed only in complete peace.

questions.prompt: After outsmarting Thanatos with chains so that no mortal on earth could die, this sly king of Corinth hoodwinked Persephone herself into letting him leave Hades before earning Tartarus's most tedious hill.
clues: He told his wife Merope to omit his burial rites so he could beg the Underworld queen for a brief return to scold her.
Albert Camus later turned his endlessly rolling boulder into the ultimate emblem of absurd human defiance.
questions.whyExplanation: Corinth's founder Sisyphus cheated death twice—shackling Thanatos and tricking Persephone—prompting Zeus to sentence him to push a boulder up a Tartarus slope for eternity.

questions.prompt: Avenging his wife Aphrodite's affair with Ares by trapping them in bed under an invisible bronze net, this lame smith earlier built a golden throne that glued Hera fast until Dionysus intervened.
clues: Hurled from Olympus onto the volcanic isle of Lemnos, he forged Achilles's cosmic shield and Pandora's clay frame.
Romans equated this master metallurgist with their fire god Vulcan.
questions.whyExplanation: Master smith Hephaestus trapped Hera in a rigged golden throne and snared Aphrodite and Ares in an unbreakable net to expose their affair before the laughing Olympians.

questions.prompt: Spitting into her mouth—or retracting no gift once granted—Apollo punished this Trojan princess for rejecting his advances by twisting her flawless visions of the wooden horse into warnings nobody could trust.
clues: King Priam's daughter cried out in vain as Trojans breached their own walls and later foresaw her death at Mycenae.
Claimed as a war prize by Agamemnon, she walked knowingly into Clytemnestra's bloody ambush.
questions.whyExplanation: Trojan princess Cassandra accepted Apollo's gift of true prophecy but spurned him; unable to revoke a divine gift, Apollo cursed her so that no listener would ever believe her warnings.

questions.prompt: Challenging a goddess to a weaving duel in Lydia, this brash dyer's daughter filled her faultless tapestry with Olympian seductions like Europa's bull—provoking an enraged shred that birthed the first spider.
clues: Ovid's Metamorphoses tells how Athena could find zero flaw in the mortal's stitching, beating her with a boxwood shuttle instead.
Taxonomy honors her metamorphosis in the zoological class encompassing scorpions, mites, and eight-legged weavers.
questions.whyExplanation: In Ovid's Metamorphoses Book VI, Lydian weaver Arachne creates a flawless tapestry exposing Olympian abuses; furious at her hubris, Athena tears it and transforms her into a spider.

questions.prompt: After spending seven years as a woman for striking two mating snakes, this Theban seer lost his sight to Hera's wrath—yet received seven lifetimes of prophecy from Zeus to guide Oedipus and Odysseus.
clues: Summoned to settle whether men or women feel greater pleasure in love, his candid answer of nine-to-one infuriated Hera.
T. S. Eliot placed this blind, dual-sexed witness at the center of The Waste Land.
questions.whyExplanation: Theban prophet Tiresias experienced life as both man and woman after disturbing coupling snakes; blinded by Hera for siding with Zeus in their dispute, he gained unmatched foresight.

questions.prompt: Pledging an eye at Mímir's spring for cosmic foresight and hanging nine windy nights pierced by his own spear Gungnir to seize the runes, this one-eyed wanderer rides an eight-legged grey steed.
clues: Ravens Huginn ('Thought') and Muninn ('Memory') fly across Midgard each dawn to whisper news into his ear.
Old English speakers honored this Allfather in the middle weekday's name, Wednesday.
questions.whyExplanation: In the Poetic Edda's Hávamál, Odin sacrifices an eye at Mímir's well and hangs himself on Yggdrasil for nine nights to win runic wisdom, riding eight-legged Sleipnir.

questions.prompt: Once donning a bridal veil as Freyja to crash giant Þrymr's wedding and reclaim his stolen hammer, this red-bearded thunderer regularly roasts his two chariot goats for supper and revives them at dawn.
clues: He wears iron gloves Járngreipr and power belt Megingjörð to swing short-handled Mjölnir.
At Ragnarök he slays the World Serpent Jörmungandr before collapsing after nine poisoned steps.
questions.whyExplanation: In the Eddic poem Þrymskviða, Thor dons Freyja's bridal dress to recover Mjölnir from giant Þrymr; he also revives his eaten goats Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjóstr provided no bone is broken.

questions.prompt: Shapeshifting into a mare to lure giant stallion Svaðilfari—and birthing eight-legged Sleipnir—this blood-brother of Odin later slipped a harmless-looking mistletoe dart into blind Höðr's hand.
clues: Captured in salmon form for engineering Baldr's murder, he lies bound beneath a snake whose venom triggers earthquakes.
Sigyn holds a bowl over his face, though each time she empties it his writhing shakes Midgard.
questions.whyExplanation: Norse trickster Loki sabotaged Asgard's wall builder as a mare (birthing Sleipnir) and orchestrated Baldr's death with mistletoe, leading to his subterranean binding until Ragnarök.

questions.prompt: Merlin warned King Arthur that this legendary weapon's enchanted scabbard—keeping its bearer from bleeding to death—was worth ten times more than the blade Sir Bedivere twice hid in the reeds.
clues: On Bedivere's third trip to the lake after Camlann, a white-samite arm rose from the waves to catch and brandish it thrice.
Thomas Malory distinguished this Lady of the Lake gift from the earlier sword pulled from a churchyard anvil.
questions.whyExplanation: In Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, Merlin tells Arthur that Excalibur's scabbard is worth ten of the sword because its bearer loses no blood; after Camlann, Sir Bedivere finally returns the blade to the lake.

questions.prompt: Gnawed at its roots by corpse-eating dragon Níðhöggr while chatterbox squirrel Ratatoskr ferries insults up to a canopy eagle, this titanic evergreen ash binds all Nine Worlds.
clues: Three Norns—Urðr, Verðandi, and Skuld—water its trunk daily with white clay from the Well of Fate.
Its Old Norse name translates roughly to 'Odin's steed,' recalling the god's nine-night self-hanging on its boughs.
questions.whyExplanation: Yggdrasil is the cosmic ash tree of Norse cosmology uniting the Nine Worlds, with dragon Níðhöggr at its roots, an eagle in its crown, and squirrel Ratatoskr relaying barbs between them.

questions.prompt: Zooming through Russian forests inside an iron mortar steered with a pestle and sweeping away her tracks, this bony Slavic crone inhabits a spinning cottage perched on giant chicken legs.
clues: Her fence is topped with glowing human skulls, yet clever visitors like Vasilisa the Beautiful can earn fire or gifts from her.
Modest Mussorgsky immortalized her rickety fowl-legged hut in Pictures at an Exhibition.
questions.whyExplanation: Slavic folklore's ambivalent forest witch Baba Yaga flies in a mortar using a pestle as a rudder and lives in a turning hut on chicken legs, aiding or devouring heroes depending on their manners.

questions.prompt: Riding a chariot pulled by two cats and weeping tears of red gold, this Norse Vanir goddess owns the necklace Brísingamen and claims half the battle-slain for her meadow Fólkvangr.
clues: She also taught Odin the ecstatic shamanic magic called seiðr and owns a falcon-feather cloak enabling flight.
Though Valhalla gets the headlines, her hall Sessrúmnir takes the first half of fallen Viking warriors.
questions.whyExplanation: Norse goddess Freyja rides a cat-drawn chariot, wears Brísingamen, sheds golden tears, and receives half of all warriors slain in combat at Fólkvangr—sharing the dead equally with Odin.

questions.prompt: Accepting a solstice beheading wager at Camelot to spare his royal uncle, this courteous knight survives the Green Chapel with only a neck nick—penance for secretly keeping a lady's green girdle.
clues: A five-pointed golden pentangle painted on his crimson shield symbolizes five interlocking chivalric virtues.
An anonymous 14th-century alliterative Middle English poet turned his Lord Bertilak test into a masterpiece.
questions.whyExplanation: In the 14th-century poem Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, Arthur's nephew Sir Gawain accepts the Green Knight's axe game and earns a minor neck scratch for concealing Lady Bertilak's girdle.

questions.prompt: Portrayed by Geoffrey of Monmouth around 1150 as the benevolent chief of nine Avalon healers, Arthur's shapeshifting half-sister evolved in French romances and Malory into Camelot's wiliest rival.
clues: She steals Excalibur's healing scabbard for her lover Accolon yet still sails the barge that bears wounded Arthur to Avalon.
Her Italian name Fata Morgana lives on as the scientific term for towering horizon mirages over water.
questions.whyExplanation: Morgan le Fay began as a benevolent Avalon healer in Geoffrey of Monmouth's Vita Merlini before evolving into Arthur's complex sorceress half-sister—and inspiring the 'Fata Morgana' mirage.

questions.prompt: Born Sétanta before slaying smith Culann's watchdog with a hurley ball to guard the smithy himself, this Ulster teen triggered a monstrous warp-spasm to hold off Connacht's army alone.
clues: Wielding the barbed foot-thrown spear Gáe Bulg, he stars in the Irish cattle-raid epic Táin Bó Cúailnge.
Mortally wounded in his final battle, he tied himself upright to a standing stone so he would die facing his foes.
questions.whyExplanation: Irish hero Sétanta became Cú Chulainn ('Culann's Hound') after slaying Culann's guard dog with a sliotar and defended Ulster single-handedly via his berserk ríastrad ('warp-spasm') in the Táin.

questions.prompt: Aloft over Irish battlefields as a hooded crow or crouching beside a crimson ford rinsing a doomed warrior's bloody armor, this Celtic phantom queen embodies war, sovereignty, and inescapable doom.
clues: Often appearing as a triad alongside sisters Badb and Macha, she tried to seduce and later cursed Ulster's greatest champion.
Only when a raven landed on Cú Chulainn's shoulder at the standing stone did his enemies dare believe he was dead.
questions.whyExplanation: In Irish mythology, The Morrígan ('Phantom Queen') is a shapeshifting triple goddess of fate and battle who frequently manifests as a crow or the ominous Washer at the Ford.

questions.prompt: Presiding over the Hall of Two Truths with golden scales, this black-jackal-headed Egyptian embalmer weighs each soul's heart against Ma'at's ostrich feather while crocodile-lion Ammit waits nearby.
clues: Before Osiris took over the throne of the dead, this canine guardian was ancient Egypt's primary lord of necropoleis.
Priests wore his dark mask during mummification to evoke rich Nile silt and fertile rebirth.
questions.whyExplanation: Jackal-headed Egyptian god Anubis oversaw mummification and the Weighing of the Heart ceremony, balancing the deceased's heart against Ma'at's feather of truth while Ammit stood ready.

questions.prompt: Snapping off his own right tusk to use as an unbreakable pen so sage Vyasa could dictate the 100,000-verse Mahabharata nonstop, this elephant-headed Hindu lord of beginnings rides a humble mouse.
clues: Son of Shiva and Parvati, he is invoked before journeys, weddings, and manuscripts as the Remover of Obstacles.
Devotees offer him sweet modak dumplings during a vibrant ten-day autumn festival across Maharashtra.
questions.whyExplanation: According to Hindu tradition, Ganesha broke his right tusk to transcribe the Mahabharata without pause for sage Vyasa; the elephant-headed deity is revered as the Remover of Obstacles.

questions.prompt: Plunging the cosmos into darkness by sealing herself inside rock cave Ama-no-Iwato after brother Susanoo's vandalism, this Japanese sun goddess was coaxed out by bawdy laughter and a mirror.
clues: Goddess Ame-no-Uzume overturned a wooden tub for a bawdy dance until the curious deity peeked at her own reflection.
Shinto tradition reveres her at Ise Grand Shrine as the divine ancestress of Japan's imperial line.
questions.whyExplanation: When Susanoo desecrated her weaving hall, Shinto sun goddess Amaterasu hid in Ama-no-Iwato until Ame-no-Uzume's comedic dance and the bronze mirror Yata no Kagami lured light back to the world.

questions.prompt: Scouring Egypt's marshes to recover thirteen of her murdered husband Osiris's fourteen scattered body parts, this magic-working goddess fashioned a golden stand-in to conceive avenging son Horus.
clues: A Nile oxyrhynchus fish had swallowed the missing fourteenth piece after jealous Set sealed Osiris in a wooden chest.
Her mystery cult spread so far across the Roman Empire that temples honored her from Pompeii to London.
questions.whyExplanation: In the Osiris myth, Egyptian goddess Isis gathered thirteen of Osiris's fourteen dismembered pieces after Set scattered them, reviving him long enough to conceive Horus.

questions.prompt: Descending to bone-strewn Mictlán to steal ancestral remains from skeletal lord Mictlantecuhtli, this Mesoamerican Feathered Serpent bled onto the ground powder to shape modern humanity.
clues: Associated with wind, Venus as morning star, and priestly learning, he shares roots with the Maya deity Kukulkan.
A rival god later tricked him into drunkenness at Tollan, driving him to sail east on a raft of serpents.
