questions.prompt: John Conway's mental 'Doomsday' rule links matching dates like 4/4, 6/6, 8/8, 10/10, and 12/12 onto one weekday; if April 4 falls on a Monday, on what weekday does December 25 fall that same year?
clues: Because 4/4 and 12/12 always share the exact same Doomsday weekday, December 12 is also a Monday.
Add two full weeks to reach Monday, December 26—putting Christmas Day one slot earlier.
questions.whyExplanation: Both 4/4 and 12/12 are Conway Doomsdays, so if 4/4 is Monday then 12/12 and 12/26 are Mondays, making December 25 a Sunday.

questions.prompt: The Gregorian calendar's weekdays repeat identically every 400 years because that span contains exactly 97 leap years—making how many total days (an exact multiple of 7)?
clues: Start with 400 ordinary 365-day years (146,000 days) and add the 97 leap days (100 minus 3 skipped centuries).
Dividing your result by 7 yields exactly 20,871 whole weeks with zero remainder.
questions.whyExplanation: 400 × 365 + 97 = 146000 + 97 = 146097 days, which equals 20,871 × 7, forcing the Gregorian calendar to repeat every 400 years.

questions.prompt: Using modular month-offset arithmetic across all 14 possible Gregorian calendar layouts, every year has at least one Friday the 13th; what maximum number can strike in a single year?
clues: In a common year starting on Thursday (such as 2026), February, March, and November all open on Sunday—putting the 13th on Friday.
In a leap year starting on Sunday, January, April, and July match instead—yielding the exact same ceiling.
questions.whyExplanation: Checking all 14 Gregorian year types shows every year has 1 to 3 Friday the 13ths; the maximum is 3 (e.g., Feb, Mar, Nov in 2026).

questions.prompt: Leading Bletchley Park's Hut 8 against naval Enigma traffic, this Cambridge pioneer had already formalized algorithmic computation in 1936 with an imaginary tape-reading machine.
clues: His 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' proposed an imitation game to test machine thought.
Computer science's highest honor—widely called the Nobel Prize of computing—bears his surname.
questions.whyExplanation: Alan Turing defined the universal tape machine in his 1936 paper 'On Computable Numbers' and spearheaded naval Enigma cryptanalysis at Bletchley Park's Hut 8.

questions.prompt: Translating Luigi Menabrea's sketch of Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine in 1843, Lord Byron's daughter appended Note G—hailed as the first published computer algorithm—to compute Bernoulli numbers.
clues: She envisioned the mechanical engine weaving algebraic patterns 'just as the Jacquard loom weaves flowers and leaves.'
In 1980, the U.S. Department of Defense named a structured programming language after her first name.
questions.whyExplanation: Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace, published Note G in 1843 detailing a step-by-step Bernoulli-number algorithm for Babbage's Analytical Engine.

questions.prompt: Even after losing his sight completely in 1771, this Swiss giant dictated nearly half his 800-plus works—popularizing the symbols i, e, and f(x) while founding graph theory on seven Prussian bridges.
clues: His celebrated identity links five fundamental constants in one equation: e^(iπ) + 1 = 0.
Born in Basel, he solved the Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem in 1736 and served the St. Petersburg and Berlin Academies.
questions.whyExplanation: Leonhard Euler introduced modern function and constant notation, launched graph theory with the 1736 Königsberg bridges proof, and produced monumental work while blind.

questions.prompt: Working at Baghdad's 9th-century House of Wisdom, this Persian polymath titled a treatise Kitab al-Jabr—giving 'algebra' its name—while the Latinized form of his own name coined 'algorithm.'
clues: His systematic methods of 'completion and balancing' solved linear and quadratic equations geometrically.
European translators rendered his nisba from Khwarazm as 'Algoritmi' when introducing Hindu-Arabic numerals.
questions.whyExplanation: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote Kitab al-Jabr around 820 CE in Baghdad; 'algebra' stems from al-jabr and 'algorithm' derives from the Latinization Algoritmi.

questions.prompt: Mailing nine pages of startling modular identities from Madras to G. H. Hardy in 1913, this self-taught Indian prodigy later hailed taxi 1729 from a sickbed as the smallest sum of two cubes in two ways.
clues: He credited his leaps of intuition in partitions, mock theta functions, and rapid pi series to visions of the goddess Namagiri.
Hardy recalled 1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³ as the quintessential anecdote of his Cambridge collaborator.
questions.whyExplanation: Srinivasa Ramanujan sent his legendary 1913 letter to G. H. Hardy, moved to Trinity College Cambridge, and instantly recognized 1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³.

questions.prompt: Crowned the 'Prince of Mathematicians,' this Göttingen polymath published Disquisitiones Arithmeticae at age 24 in 1801 and predicted the lost dwarf planet Ceres's orbit using least-squares regression.
clues: His notebooks anticipated non-Euclidean geometry and elliptic functions years before peers published them.
Normal bell-curve distributions, magnetic-flux units, and modular arithmetic congruence notation (≡) all honor his name.
questions.whyExplanation: Carl Friedrich Gauss published Disquisitiones Arithmeticae in 1801 at age 24, formalized modular congruence, and located Ceres via least-squares orbit estimation.

questions.prompt: Praised by Albert Einstein as the most creative mathematical genius since women's higher education began, this Erlangen-born algebraist proved in 1918 that every continuous symmetry yields a conservation law.
clues: Recruited to Göttingen by David Hilbert and Felix Klein, she revolutionized abstract rings, ideals, and modules.
Her landmark 1918 theorem explains why time symmetry conserves energy and spatial symmetry conserves momentum.
questions.whyExplanation: Emmy Noether proved her celebrated 1918 symmetry-conservation theorem and reshaped modern abstract algebra, earning Albert Einstein's glowing 1935 New York Times tribute.

questions.prompt: Shattering David Hilbert's dream of a complete, self-certifying foundation for arithmetic, this Moravian-born logician published his 1931 Incompleteness Theorems before later befriending Einstein at Princeton.
clues: By encoding logical formulas as unique prime-factorization integers, he built an arithmetic sentence asserting its own unprovability.
He also discovered rotating-universe solutions to general relativity containing closed timelike curves.
questions.whyExplanation: Kurt Gödel proved in 1931 that any consistent formal system rich enough for arithmetic contains true statements unprovable within it, later joining Einstein at the IAS in Princeton.

questions.prompt: Writing frantically through the night of May 29, 1832 before a fatal Paris duel at age 20, this French firebrand founded group theory to prove no general radical formula solves quintic equations.
clues: Twice rejected by the École Polytechnique and jailed as a fiery republican, he mailed his final manuscript to Auguste Chevalier.
His correspondence links polynomial roots to permutation groups, showing degree-5 equations lack a universal quadratic-style formula.
questions.whyExplanation: On the eve of his fatal May 30, 1832 duel at age 20, Évariste Galois summarized the group-and-field correspondence proving the general quintic cannot be solved by radicals.

questions.prompt: In August 2014, this Iranian-born Stanford geometer became the first woman—and first Iranian—to win the Fields Medal for breakthrough insights into Riemann surfaces and their moduli spaces.
clues: A two-time International Mathematical Olympiad gold medalist from Tehran, she earned her PhD at Harvard under Curtis McMullen.
Her 'magic wand theorem' with Alex Eskin transformed how geometers study billiard paths on polygonal tables.
questions.whyExplanation: Maryam Mirzakhani won the 2014 Fields Medal in Seoul as its first female laureate, recognized for deep results on the dynamics and geometry of Riemann surfaces.
